articles.title: How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Octave built a secure multi-tenant AI foundation on Amazon Bedrock
In quality management for regulated industries, the institutional memory that resolves a problem is almost always buried somewhere in a customer’s history. A similar defect investigated last year, a Corrective and Preventive Action (CAPA) that fixed the root cause, an audit finding that flagged the same gap. That knowledge sits in billions of documents no human can search by semantic similarity across languages and formats, so every investigation starts from scratch. Octave Reliance has helped each organization collect documents across multiple systems to help them search more easily and keep track of everything they have. The Octave Reliance team saw unlocking this history as its single largest opportunity to help customers work faster and stay compliant. The obstacle was equally clear: complaint records, audit findings, and corrective actions carry the platform’s strictest isolation requirements, and those were exactly the records the AI would need to read. In a platform serving over 14,000 customers across medical devices, pharmaceuticals, and food manufacturing, a single inadvertent disclosure from one customer to another would carry regulatory consequences far outweighing any AI benefit.
Octave operates across 180 countries, serving more than 60% of the Global Fortune 500. Its cloud-native quality management system, Reliance, supports over 650 enterprise customers with over 40 applications, from complaint management and CAPA tracking to audit management and supplier quality. Everyone generates regulated data that AI could reason over. Each customer is a separate tenant and no data can cross a tenant boundary.
Faced with that, the Reliance team made an unusual call: rather than shipping one AI feature, it spent its first cycle building a foundation every future feature would sit on. That foundation has since cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent. If you are bringing AI to a software as a service (SaaS) platform where the data is valuable, but isolation is non-negotiable, the reasoning travels beyond quality management. In this post, we walk through the four tensions that shaped the design and the three-layer foundation Octave built with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock. We then follow the pipeline that embedded 2 billion documents and the Complaint Triage Assistant that proved it in production.
Why a foundation, not a feature
Envisioning workshops with AWS surfaced four high-impact use cases: complaint summarization and triage, audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring. They also surfaced the insight that shaped everything after dozens of applications, each with different document types and workflows. Building AI for one in a silo meant rebuilding the infrastructure for the next.
So, the team inverted the plan: build the horizontal platform first, then cut vertical feature slices into it. Complaint summarization and triage went first, to prove the architecture before the rest followed.
The four tensions
Before selecting a single model, the team spent its time on four problems that pulled in different directions. None could be traded away.
Making data available without risking inadvertent disclosure. Complaint records, CAPAs, standard operating procedures (SOPs), and audit findings belong to one tenant and must be unreachable by another. Not even an errant AI query could cross. Vector store, retrieval logic, and generation context all had to be scoped to a single tenant.
Executing agents in isolation. The permissions governing an agent’s tools, data stores, and model endpoints had to be scoped to the requesting user rather than a shared service role, available only during execution, and respectful of that user’s access rights. A shared agent pool with static credentials failed all three.
Reading content that cannot be trusted. Agents here ingest complaints, email attachments, scanned PDFs, and images from outside the organization. The OWASP Top 10 for large language model (LLM) Applications (2025) names the threats that apply directly: prompt injection through ingested content (LLM01), sensitive information disclosure (LLM02), improper output handling (LLM05), and excessive agency (LLM06). Hidden instructions in an attached PDF are not hypothetical at this volume.
Embedding 2 billion documents without a quarter-long wait. Reliance hosts more than 2 billion documents, with individual tenants storing millions of Word files, PDFs, scanned forms, spreadsheets, images, and email. The team committed to onboarding even the largest tenant within a single working day. Because these documents inform regulatory decisions, quality could not be traded for throughput. A missed complaint erodes trust in the whole system.
Where the architecture landed
Holding four tensions at once narrowed the options considerably. Amazon Bedrock addressed them as one platform: multi-model access through a single API, the AWS Region residency and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) governance the AWS account already enforces, and Guardrails as production content controls rather than something to build.
The foundation resolves into three layers, shown in Figure 1. Data preparation embeds quality documents with Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock and writes them to a per-tenant vector store on Amazon OpenSearch Service. Secure execution passes a user request through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which applies authentication and policy before handing it to an isolated microVM session that calls an Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock. Wrapping both, content protection applies Amazon Bedrock Guardrails twice: input filtering on the way in, output filtering before anything reaches the handler. Retrieval, execution, and screening stay in separate stages, so each can be enforced and evidenced on its own.
Choosing how to represent the data
Nothing else worked until the documents were retrievable. That meant accurately, across languages and formats, and not across a tenant boundary. The team evaluated embedding models against its own corpus rather than public leaderboards. The deciding questions were specific to this data: what a photo of a cracked housing has to do with the paragraph describing it, and a German complaint with an English CAPA.
Cohere Embed v4 on Amazon Bedrock won on five counts and they weren’t independent of each other. What was decided first was how much of the pipeline was made unnecessary. Quality records carry photos of defective products, scanned inspection forms, and annotated diagrams alongside text. Embed v4 places both modalities in one vector space. A photo of a cracked housing and the paragraph describing that defect are retrievable from a single query, with no separate pipeline per modality. Native multilingual support does the same work along the other axis: documents arrive in multiple languages, often inside one tenant’s corpus, and need no translation preprocessing. Two pipelines the team never had to build, and two fewer places for a document to fall out of retrieval.
The remaining three counts settled where the vectors could live and what they would cost. Customer data can’t leave its AWS Region, even for inference, so in-Region model availability on Amazon Bedrock was a precondition rather than a convenience. Embed v4 supports in-Region inference in the US East (N. Virginia) Region (us-east-1), Europe (Ireland) Region (eu-west-1), and Asia Pacific (Tokyo) Region (ap-northeast-1), covering three of Octave’s regional compliance requirements. Model and feature availability varies by Region and changes over time. For current coverage, see Regional availability by models in the Amazon Bedrock User Guide. Within each Region, Amazon OpenSearch Service costs scale linearly with dimension count. That made Embed v4’s configurable output dimensions of 256–1,536 worth testing rather than accepting by default. Testing against representative production queries showed 512 dimensions holding target accuracy while cutting storage roughly 66 percent against the 1,536 default. The 128K token context window paid off elsewhere entirely: chunks of roughly 4K tokens pack many to a request, which is where the onboarding throughput came from.
Keeping tenants apart at runtime
The harder question was where to enforce tenant separation. Application code would have worked, but it would have meant every future feature team getting it right on every code path, where one missed check risks inadvertent cross-tenant disclosure. The team pushed isolation into the runtime instead. AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, enforces separation below the application layer, and because it stays framework- and model-independent, the agent framework and models chosen for the Complaint Triage Assistant were not constrained by the isolation decision.
Each user session runs in a dedicated microVM with its own CPU, memory, and filesystem, stopped and sanitized when the session ends. That is hardware-level separation designed to hold regardless of how the agent behaves. AgentCore carries the authenticated user’s identity through the whole execution chain: per-user OAuth token vaults verify the agent acts for that specific user rather than a shared service identity, and credentials are scoped per-agent and live only during the session. AgentCore Gateway authorizes at the tool, operation, and parameter level. Automated reasoning provides formal verification against the defined rules. It’s the same discipline behind IAM and Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) policy validation. Figure 2 traces that separation across two tenants.
A complaint submitted by a quality handler at Tenant A therefore reaches only Tenant A’s token vault, tools, and sandbox in AgentCore Code Interpreter, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. Tenant B’s session has no path to any of them.
Treating ingested content as untrusted
This tension had no clean answer. A complaint attachment is untrusted input, but it’s also the thing the agent exists to read, so suspicious content couldn’t be rejected. The team settled on defense in depth.
Octave applied Amazon Bedrock Guardrails over the agent logic rather than inside it, at three points in the complaint workflow. The ApplyGuardrail API evaluates text extracted from attachments before embedding, retrieved documents and tool outputs before they enter the agent’s context, and the synthesized brief before the handler sees it. Attachment-derived content is passed with input tagging, marking it as data rather than instruction. That is what makes an injection buried mid-document detectable. Personally Identifiable Information (PII) is masked on the way in.
Detection alone wasn’t sufficient, so bounded agency sits underneath. Whatever an agent is asked to do, AgentCore Gateway still governs which tools it can invoke, and document extraction runs in the AgentCore Code Interpreter sandbox with no network egress and no persistence beyond the session. A payload hidden in a PDF has to defeat every layer, not one.
The effect: detection and masking rates are tracked per tenant, so what the screening caught is something Octave can evidence rather than assert.
Getting 2 billion documents through the pipeline
Ahead of the embedding model sat the harder problem: extracting usable content from Word files, spreadsheets, digital PDFs, scanned pages, photographs, and email threads. Several languages appear, sometimes inside one record. And it had to run fast enough that onboarding took a day rather than a quarter. Figure 3 traces the resulting pipeline end to end.
Document events fan out through Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) and Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) into an AWS Step Functions state machine. That state machine orchestrates parsing, chunking, and embedding across concurrent AWS Lambda executions inside a dedicated Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC). Because parallelism comes from fanning batches across executions rather than scaling one resource, throughput grows without rearchitecting.
Parsing handles the heterogeneity: semantic hierarchy preserved from Word files and spreadsheets, optical character recognition (OCR) applied to scanned PDFs lacking a text layer, embedded images treated as first-class content. Chunks carry metadata: tenant, document type, source application, language, and a content hash. That metadata drives both retrieval filtering and per-tenant namespace enforcement.
The throughput came from packing. Interleaving many 4K chunks into single requests against Embed v4’s 128K context window cut the API calls for a large corpus by about an order of magnitude. In Octave’s internal testing on Amazon Bedrock, Embed v4 delivered 28 million tokens per minute. After tuning batch sizes with Cohere’s solutions architects until memory bottlenecks cleared, the pipeline sustained 1.4 million documents per 24 hours per tenant workload. That is what made the single-working-day commitment real.
The Complaint Triage Assistant
A hospital reports defective syringes to a medical device manufacturer, and the record lands with email, photos of damaged units, and supporting documentation attached. A quality handler has to piece the context together across those formats, work out whether anything like it has been reported before, and find what resolved it. Only then can a priority be assigned, often inside a reporting window measured in days.
The assistant is built with the Strands Agents SDK, open-sourced by AWS, which composes agentic workflows as graphs, with nodes as tool invocations or model calls and edges as the data dependencies between them. AgentCore runtime runs that graph and isolates it per session, and five stages carry a complaint from raw attachments to a finished brief.
Document extraction comes first. PDFs, images, email attachments, and videos all enter AgentCore Code Interpreter, which parses each artifact into a structured intermediate representation. A Claude model on Amazon Bedrock then summarizes the record, and that summary, rather than the raw multi-thousand-token source, becomes the retrieval query. Retrieval runs it against the tenant’s OpenSearch index of Embed v4 embeddings, surfacing similar past complaints and their CAPAs, with AgentCore Gateway enforcing that only authorized namespaces are reachable.
What comes back is not trusted on similarity alone. A separate model call scores results by confidence and discards matches that share vocabulary but differ in root cause. What survives goes to synthesis, where Anthropic Claude Sonnet on Amazon Bedrock assembles the output: key facts, sentiment, urgency indicators, the closest historical records with their outcomes, and a recommended triage priority.
Completed briefs are cached in Amazon DynamoDB with a per-environment time to live (TTL), so repeated views cost nothing extra. The handler no longer starts from zero, but from institutional memory.
Figure 4 places that engine behind a private API boundary. A portal request reaches AgentCore runtime through a private Amazon API Gateway and a Lambda function, and retrieval reads the document index through role-based access with pre-signed URLs while attachments stay in Amazon S3. Cached summaries and OpenTelemetry traces exit to the summarization table and the evaluation dashboard.
Figure 5 reduces the same path to a single line, with Guardrails filtering at both ends.
Proving what the agent did
Observability here is not only how the engineering team debugs but also how they integrate with system auditing capabilities to meet compliance requirements. An auditor can ask why a particular complaint was triaged the way it was, and “the model decided” will not survive that conversation.
AgentCore captures OpenTelemetry-compatible traces across every node of the graph: each model call, retrieval, and AgentCore Code Interpreter run. Months later, Octave can show which retrieved documents and prompts produced a given brief. The model invocation logging of Amazon Bedrock adds a per-tenant record of every request and response, scoped through the IAM identity AgentCore propagates, with costs attributing to the initiating tenant in Amazon CloudWatch.
Offline, AgentCore Evals reruns the workflow against expert-annotated ground truth after any change to prompts, models, or retrieval parameters, reporting summarization faithfulness, retrieval precision at K, and output completeness. A prompt that reads better but retrieves worse gets caught before users see it.
Results
The Complaint Triage Assistant has been running in production for three months, and the following numbers reflect that period.
The handler who used to open an investigation with nothing now opens it with the relevant history already assembled. The 4–6 hours Octave measures per investigation is the work the pipeline absorbed: extraction across formats, the hunt for precedent, and the reading it takes to tell a genuinely similar defect from a coincidence of wording.
The foundation also changed how quickly Octave ships. By its own accounting, development cycles for new AI capabilities went from months to weeks. Shared data preparation, secure execution, and retrieval are the three layers of Figure 1. They cut deployment time per use case by 50 percent, because each new capability inherits them rather than rebuilding them. That landed semantic search in Q2, two quarters ahead of the original Q4 target.
Looking back
The decision to build a foundation first was the one the team second-guessed most. Months of infrastructure work is hard to defend when stakeholders want an AI feature they can see. The next round of use cases has borne it out. Two choices carried it: isolation pushed into microVM sessions and identity propagation rather than application code, and embedding models evaluated against Octave’s own corpus, which surfaced the 512-dimension trade-off no benchmark would have shown.
The team also drew a line it chose not to cross. The assistant surfaces context and precedent. The quality handler still makes the call. In an industry where that call carries regulatory weight, that boundary shaped what got automated and what did not.
What’s next
Octave is now extending the foundation across the Reliance suite. Audit readiness monitoring, incident narrative generation, and predictive quality risk scoring are next, each building on the same infrastructure.
If your platform faces a similar tension: valuable data behind hard isolation requirements. Octave’s experience shows the trade-offs are workable. To learn more about the services behind this story, see Amazon Bedrock, the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation, and Cohere on Amazon Bedrock. For related architectural guidance, see AWS vector solutions: Build agentic AI where your data lives and Scaling agentic AI: Enterprise patterns without vendor lock-in.

articles.title: Transport for biological material helps Cellbox raise a €5 million Series A | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Cellbox Solutions, a German warm-chain logistics technology company, has completed the final closing of its Series A financing, bringing the total to €5 million – the company will develop its business model and expand its offering to include integrated logistics solutions for sensitive biological materials.
Following the first closing of approximately €3.5 million in March 2026 (as covered by EU-Startups), Cellbox Solutions has attracted additional investors. Among them are members of the Baltic Business Angels Invest GmbH. Existing investors NRW.BANK and Fraunhofer Venture also participated in the financing.
“Over the past years, we have built a strong foundation for the controlled transport of living biological materials,” says Prof. Dr. Kathrin Adlkofer, founder and CEO of Cellbox Solutions. “With the successful completion of our Series A round, we are now expanding our established warm-chain technology platform into a broader offering for physiological logistics. This will allow us to support customers more comprehensively across their logistics workflows and expand our presence in key international markets.”
This financing follows several other 2026 funding announcements in Europe’s cell-therapy and life sciences technology sectors.
In the Netherlands, Scinus Group secured €3 million to commercialise its cell-expansion platform, while Italy’s Cellply raised €7.15 million for cell-therapy quality-control technologies and the UK’s Tozaro attracted €6.9 million to improve cell and gene therapy manufacturing.
In Germany, Leipzig-based Primogene secured €4.1 million for enzymatic biomanufacturing, with related investments also recorded by Dutch startup QT Sense (€4 million) and Switzerland’s ALP Bio (€1.9 million).
Together with Cellbox Solutions’ €5 million Series A, these 2026 financings amount to approximately €32 million across related but distinct life sciences technologies, including grant funding.
“Completion of the Series A gives us additional resources to scale the commercial model behind our technology. By expanding rental and recurring service offerings and combining them with transportation, monitoring, and complementary logistics services, we can build longer-term customer relationships and a more scalable service model across markets. Our focus is now on translating the strength of the Cellbox platform into sustainable commercial growth,” adds Dr. Bernd Muehlenweg, CBO and CFO of Cellbox Solutions.
Founded in 2017, Cellbox Solutions is a Cologne-based warm-chain logistics technology company providing solutions for the global healthcare and life sciences industries to transport sensitive biological materials and therapeutics that cannot be frozen and require controlled physiological conditions.
The company’s portable CO₂ incubator platform, Cellbox, creates a regulated environment for the transport of living cells, organoids, tissues, and other advanced biological materials. Temperature and CO₂ levels are individually adjustable to ensure reproducible incubation conditions throughout shipment. Cellbox systems are deployed globally and support research, clinical, and advanced therapy applications.
Today’s financing marks the next phase in the company’s commercial growth, and will help leverage the established technological, product-related, and regulatory advances Cellbox Solutions has achieved in recent years.
A key focus is building on the company’s specialized transport capabilities to link controlled transport under physiological conditions even more closely with additional logistics and service offerings.
Cellbox Go and Cellbox Shipper make up the core of the company’s technology platform. Both incubators provide controlled temperature and CO₂ conditions during ground and air transport and are already used internationally in research and cell therapy applications.
With over 400 Cellbox systems currently on the market, a growing number of customer relationships and a regulatory foundation that includes Drug Master Files for the CellboxTM product family, the company believes they are well positioned to expand its commercial offering.
This includes combining CellboxTM systems with rental and transport options, as well as recurring services such as monitoring, fleet management, and shipment coordination.
To this end, the company is continuing to expand its activities in Europe, Asia, and North America and is increasingly focusing on strategic partnerships with logistics providers.

articles.title: US orders federal agencies to remove China’s DeepSeek AI from their systems | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The U.S. has ordered federal civilian agencies to stop purchasing services and products developed by Chinese AI startup DeepSeek and remove them from government IT systems over national security concerns tied to the Chinese AI startup’s operations in China, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The order goes beyond banning DeepSeek’s own product, but also covers third-party products and services built using DeepSeek technology, though agencies can request exceptions.
The DHS raised concerns about DeepSeek’s handling of user data, warning that sensitive information from US government users could potentially be accessible to Chinese authorities under Chinese law, the order said.
The move comes amid intensifying tech competition in AI between the US and China. The Chinese AI model challenges its U.S. rivals, including OpenAI and Meta, with low-cost open-weight models.
China pushed back against the U.S.’s move. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said Tuesday that Beijing opposes “overstretching the concept of national security and politicizing technology and trade issues,” according to an official briefing. “We will resolutely safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese enterprises,” the spokesperson added.
The U.S. has already taken steps to limit DeepSeek’s use in government. A law passed in December 2025 targeted its use in intelligence’s national security systems. The latest order extends the restrictions to federal civilian agencies, covering both new purchases and existing IT systems.
Meanwhile, China is reportedly considering export restrictions on 23 AI-related technologies, including chip designs and certain advanced AI models, to address security and misuse risks, Bloomberg reported last week.
The Chinese AI lab has faced scrutiny from governments and regulators across the globe since its R1 reasoning model shook the AI industry in January 2025, triggering a sharp sell-off in Nvidia shares.
The U.S. accused DeepSeek and five other Chinese AI companies, including Alibaba and Moonshot AI, of using large-scale model distillation to extract information from American AI systems, according to a September report.
In addition, OpenAI and Anthropic have separately raised concerns about DeepSeek’s alleged use of model distillation, a technique that uses outputs from one AI model to train another. Earlier this year, OpenAI told U.S. lawmakers it had observed suspected attempts by DeepSeek to distill its models, while Anthropic said it had identified unauthorized attempts by DeepSeek and other Chinese AI labs to collect outputs from Claude.

articles.title: Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneous server fleet
articles.text:
Modal taps Nvidia Vera CPUs after firm's internal tests show 2x throughput over Intel and AMD chips — AI agentic workflows said to favor Arm chips, but firm will keep x86 chips deployed in heterogeneous server fleet
Modal plans to use Nvidia's Vera CPUs due to performance advantages, but will keep AMD and Intel CPUs in the fleet.
Nvidia has earned billions selling AI accelerators, but with the emergence of agentic AI, CPUs are going to play a considerably more significant role than before, which creates new opportunities for the company. Reuters reports that Nvidia has secured a major design win with its Vera CPUs with AI cloud provider Modal. According to Modal, preliminary evaluations showed that Vera could deliver twice the throughput of its existing AMD and Intel processors, although the company does not intend to cease using CPUs from its current suppliers.
Modal provides cloud infrastructure that enables AI developers to deploy AI agents that can perform complex operations autonomously over extended periods. Such workloads require substantial CPU resources for software execution, data processing, and other tasks that cannot be efficiently handled by GPUs. Modal currently relies exclusively on AMD and Intel processors for these operations, but its tests indicate that Nvidia's new Vera CPUs could significantly improve performance in its specific workloads. Of course, since Vera is based on an Arm instruction set architecture, Modal's decision to adopt Vera will require substantial modifications to its software. Nevertheless, Modal believes that the potential performance improvements justify the additional engineering effort.
The reported 2x throughput advantage is particularly interesting because agentic AI workloads can involve numerous independent tasks that compete for CPU cores, cache capacity, and memory bandwidth. However, Modal has not disclosed detailed benchmark configurations it used, specific AMD and Intel processor models, or performance-per-watt figures. Consequently, it remains unclear whether Vera's advantage is enabled by advantages of its Arm v9.2-based Olympus CPU cores that can decode and execute up to 10 instructions per cycle, its memory subsystem with 1.2 TB/s of bandwidth, or other architectural characteristics. Also note that tests compared Vera against currently available AMD and Intel processors rather than their upcoming generations that will compete against Vera in the coming years.
Since Modal cannot port all of its software to Arm ISA overnight, the company will continue using x86 CPUs from AMD and Intel, according to Modal chief executive Erik Bernhardsson. Rather than sticking to one ISA for everything, Modal intends to operate a heterogeneous server fleet and select the most suitable processors for each workload. Naturally, the company intends to evaluate upcoming AMD and Intel processors once they become available to make its choices in the future.
For Nvidia, the agreement represents a major step toward making Vera a standalone server processor that commands a major share of the server market. The company expects Vera sales to generate at least $20 billion during its current fiscal year and estimates the potential total available market for these CPUs is approximately $200 billion. The company is on track to sell at least four million Vera CPUs in fiscal 2026.
The announcement comes shortly after Modal secured $750 million in financing led by Accel, which valued the company at $15.75 billion. Modal expects its annual revenue to reach $1 billion within the next year. The company's service consumption has increased 3X in the last 12 months, while revenue has surged more than 15 times compared with the previous year, Reuters reports.

articles.title: How a blockchain marketplace is unlocking clean gas production in Kenya - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
African technologists and entrepreneurs are applying blockchain in innovative ways, creating a new financial infrastructure for the continent with wide-ranging benefits, including for the humanitarian sector.
Through its Blockchain Ventures investment programme, supported by the Ethereum Foundation and GSR Foundation, UNICEF Office of Innovation provides funding and technical assistance to emerging market startups building innovative blockchain-based solutions.
Kenya-based Autonomous Systems Research (ASR) began by exploring how drones could support disaster response, wildlife and environmental conservation. Working in remote areas led founder Moses Gichanga to investigate another challenge: generating electricity without transporting fuel into the field. ASR is developing ways to turn waste plant material into gas and electricity, and using blockchain to track traceability of biomass, payments to suppliers as well as applications in mobile money and disaster response.
How did a hobby building drones turn into Autonomous Systems Research?
Back in 2011, my daughter was two and a half and needed amusing, so I made her a kite. When the kite got boring, I built a small aeroplane out of paper bags. One early version had an eight-foot wingspan, with a laptop strapped to it and car wiper motors working the controls. Then I asked myself what would happen if I strapped a camera to one and flew it in a national reserve. That was when I started flying drones in Tsavo National Park.
I began asking how we could use this technology to help elephants and other wildlife, and to conserve ecological areas. That grew into Autonomous Systems Research. Later, ASR received its first grant from UNICEF Office of Innovation. We used it to explore whether drones could be useful for disaster response planning, ecological conservation, wildlife and agriculture, and what data would come out of that work. Since then, we have flown missions with government agencies, including Kenya Wildlife Service.
How did conservation work lead you from drones to producing energy from plant material?
Some of the places where we work are very remote and have no electricity. Our drones need charging, so we used a generator. But it became unsustainable to keep carrying fuel into the wilderness. We looked at solar panels, but they took up space and time. So we thought about modifying a generator to run on gas made from biomass. Later, people in communities saw that we had electricity in places without a supply and asked where we got it. We began thinking about making gas and electricity available to them too.
Where would the biomass come from, and what could the gas and electricity be used for?
We still use drones to look for potential sources of biomass. Once we identify some, we send someone to find out whether we can purchase it or otherwise acquire it. We want waste biomass. We do not want to cut down trees, and we do not want people planting biomass to sell to us instead of growing food. Coffee bushes, for example, produce material when they are pruned. We can turn that into gas.
We have developed equipment that converts biomass into gas, which we can use to run an engine. Gas is the primary thing we produce, but we can generate electricity as well. We have a site near our rural office where we are working with people who provide biomass and receive gas. We are also in the process of bringing local primary schools into the project. We are also in the process of brining local primary schools into the project. We want to see whether – with the right safety checks, ventilation and supervision – the gas could be used to cook meals and heat water, as an alternative to open fires.
You began using blockchain to track biomass. What does it record, and where else might you use it?
We wanted an audit trail that someone else could inspect. For the biomass, we record where it comes from, what type it is, the quantity, who gave permission to clear it, what they were paid, if anything, and how much gas we produced from it. We also have a payment mechanism for people who provide biomass, connected to mobile money platforms, M-Pesa and Airtel Money. We are interested in carbon credits in the future, and for that we would need a record people can trace.
We are looking at other applications too. Through our work on payments, we have engaged a local bank and are building a platform intended to offer mobile money services using blockchain. We also do volunteer work in emergencies, and we have developed a ledger system that can record where survivors are and what help they need after a disaster, though we have not applied that in a real-world setting yet.
What is holding the gas project back from operating at a larger scale?
We can produce the gas, but we have not reached the point of liquefying it efficiently. At the moment, we store it without liquefying it, which takes up more space. If we could liquefy it, we could fit more into a cylinder and look at selling it on a larger scale. We have tried some basic methods, but they use too much energy to work commercially. Finding a better way to do it would require substantial investment.
ASR began with drones, but you are now developing energy and other technologies. Is the idea to test solutions at ASR, then build separate businesses around the ones that work?
Yes. ASR does research into systems that can run themselves. That includes the drones and, eventually, the gas plant. When we develop a project, we intend to incorporate it as its own company, with its own governance structure, while ASR continues doing research.
We do not plan for ASR itself to become the gas supplier. The gas business could sell the product and make money as its own company, although we would still expect to have a role in its governance. We want to take an idea through the research and testing stage and then allow it to become something that can stand on its own.
ASR is a for-profit company, but you describe social good as central to its work. How do those aims fit together?
Social good is front and centre in what we do. Our tagline is “tools for transformative change”. We are structured as a limited liability company and we intend to make a profit, but we engage in projects that have a social good component.
We hope to make a lot of money. We want to do it in a way that helps our neighbours make money too. The more money they make, the less they need from us or from donors. There is a limit to how long someone can keep holding your hand. At some point, you need to become self-sustaining.
Take the gas project. We intend to sell the gas, but I also think about children collecting twigs for firewood. If we can make gas affordable to their households, they would not have to do that. I do not see a conflict between the social purpose and the business: we want to produce the gas cheaply enough that we can sell it at a price people can afford. As we see it, it is easier to get a shilling each from a million people than a million shillings from one person.
UNICEF was ASR’s first backer. Beyond the grant, what did its support make possible?
The first grant let us explore whether drones could be used for disaster response planning, conservation, wildlife and agriculture. Later, when we approached other organizations, we could show them what we had done and what we had learned. We have since received grants from other organizations, including Kenya’s National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation, and done business with local government organizations.
We have also remained part of UNICEF’s alumni community since its investment. UNICEF organized a session for us with Google for Startups, and we later graduated from that programme. They organized seminars and workshops and supported our attendance at the World Economic Forum’s Annual Meeting of the New Champions. Those opportunities helped us think differently about what we could do.

articles.title: "I have to stop this": Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robots she says are taking human jobs
articles.text:
A hot potato: A lot of people are angry at the sight of robots carrying out deliveries, seeing it as another sign that machines are making more human jobs obsolete. One such person, a 78-year-old retired professor, made her displeasure known last week by repeatedly standing in front of a delivery robot, blocking its path. The situation ended with her being handcuffed and arrested, but it hasn't deterred her from staging more protests.
Carolyn Marvin, a professor emeritus at the University of Pennsylvania's Annenberg School of Communication, decided to take a literal stand against an oncoming Avride delivery robot from Uber Eats in Philadelphia's Center City. She repeatedly stood in its path so it couldn't move.
Marvin's actions drew a small crowd, and Philadelphia police eventually responded after witnesses reported a disturbance near Reading Terminal Market.
ABC13 reports that Marvin repeatedly ignored officers' requests to allow the robot to pass. She was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct.
Marvin later said she was protesting the use of delivery robots because she believes they are replacing human workers.
"I know they're taking the jobs of human delivery workers and so, I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward," Marvin said, adding that she considers her action as protected speech.
She also confirmed that she had confronted delivery robots on multiple occasions. One witness to a previous encounter thought the machine had hit Marvin. When asked if she was okay, Marvin replied, "No, I have to stop this. They're taking over the world."
When asked if she plans to continue her protests following her arrest, Marvin said, "I do. Why not? I think it's my First Amendment right to publicly demonstrate on a sidewalk to protest against delivery robots."
In a different interview with KYW Newsradio, Marvin went into more detail about why she was interfering with the robots. She called it a protest against the "ruthless way that rich corporations are casting aside human workers – and here, we're talking about the humble delivery folks – in order to enrich their bottom lines."
Marvin added that she hopes the attention her protests receive will encourage more discussion about delivery robots, artificial intelligence and their growing role in everyday life.
Earlier this year, it was reported that as the number of delivery robots on the streets increases, so too does the number of social media clips showing people kicking, grabbing, and even attempting to destroy the machines. While some incidents involve attempted theft, many appear to be expressions of anger at the bots, which symbolize the automation of a job once performed exclusively by humans.

articles.title: Eva Ngigi Sarwari, Equity’s head of payments, dies at 45
articles.text:
Eva Ngigi Sarwari, managing director of Finserve Africa and Equity Group’s director of payments and international banking, has died aged 45 while on a business trip to China, according to a statement from her colleagues.
Her death cuts short a career that spanned over two decades in banking and payments, from introducing customers to electronic banking at Co-operative Bank of Kenya to leading Visa’s business across three East African markets.
“It is with great sadness that we announce the passing of our dear friend and colleague, Eva Ngigi Sarwari,” her colleagues said in the statement on Tuesday.
They described the news as a “sudden and profound shock” and said they would make further updates as details became available. The statement did not disclose the cause or date of her death.
Sarwari joined Equity in January 2025 as group director for payments and international banking, with responsibility for executing the bank’s payments strategy across Africa. In April 2026, she became managing director of Finserve Africa, the group’s payments and digital financial services subsidiary, overseeing its strategy, commercial direction and operations.
The roles brought her back into a banking group after more than four years at Visa, where she served as senior director and country manager from September 2020 to December 2024. Her role covered three neighbouring markets, including Kenya, South Sudan and Somalia.
The appointments brought together experience accumulated across local banks, an international banking group and one of the world’s largest card networks.
Before Equity, Sarwari spent more than four years at Visa as senior director and country manager for Kenya, South Sudan and Somalia. From September 2020 to December 2024, she was responsible for developing and implementing the company’s growth strategy in those markets.
She joined Visa from SC Ventures, Standard Chartered’s venture-building arm, where she served as a venture lead during 2020. That role followed more than seven years in Standard Chartered’s transaction banking business.
As head of transaction banking for commercial banking from July 2017 to January 2020, she helped shape the bank’s strategy for Kenya and East Africa, with responsibility for revenue growth, product relevance and digital transformation. Previously, as a principal in transaction banking, she worked with development organisations and public-sector clients across East Africa.
Sarwari moved to Standard Chartered in November 2012 after just over two years at Stanbic Bank Kenya, where she managed sales of transactional products and services.
She began her banking career at Co-operative Bank of Kenya in June 2005. As a relationship manager, she helped bring customers onto electronic banking systems, demonstrating products, overseeing installations and training users. It was practical work that would run through her subsequent career.
“Our thoughts and prayers are with Eva’s family, friends and colleagues during this difficult time,” the statement added.

articles.title: « C’est un nouveau monde » : une armée d'IA vient de lancer une cyberattaque « massive », plus de 100 entreprises piratées
articles.text:
Un pirate chinois est parvenu à infiltrer les sites de plus de 100 entreprises d’envergure. Selon un rapport de NorForge, une entreprise de cybersécurité, le cybercriminel a confié la quasi-totalité du travail à une armée d’agents IA. Ces intelligences artificielles ont pu agir seules, sans la moindre intervention humaine. Les agents malveillants ont tenté de s’introduire dans plus de 1 200 sites à travers les États-Unis, le Canada, l’Australie et le Japon à partir de la fin du mois de septembre 2026. Environ 10 % des tentatives ont réussi. Les experts parlent d’une « opération massive ».
« C’est un nouveau monde », résume Snorre Fagerland, chercheur principal chez NorForge, interrogé par Reuters.
À lire aussi : Frigos de supermarchés piratés : Claude a reproduit la cyberattaque en 28 minutes
Une requête de moins de 100 caractères
Pour mener les attaques, le pirate s’est appuyé sur Cairn, une plateforme d’IA open source disponible sur GitHub. Ce « moteur de résolution de problèmes » est programmé pour coordonner plusieurs agents IA sur base d’un objectif défini par l’utilisateur. Il suffit de communiquer des consignes pour que Cairn se transforme en véritable chef d’armée. En l’occurrence, les consignes du pirate tenaient en moins de 100 caractères chinois.
Dans celles-ci, le hacker demandait aux agents IA de trouver un moyen d’exécuter du code sur des milliers de sites, sans même avoir à s’y connecter. Ensuite, l’IA avait pour instruction de glisser un petit programme sur les sites. Ce logiciel permet à l’attaquant de déposer des fichiers sur le site à l’insu des administrateurs. Grâce à ceux-ci, le pirate cherchait à conserver un accès durable aux systèmes de paiement des différentes boutiques dans son colimateur. Le programme fonctionnait comme une porte dérobée, garantissant un accès même si la faille venait à être colmatée. En moyenne, chaque intrusion réussie a demandé un peu moins de 23 heures de travail aux agents IA.
Selon les investigations menées par NorForge, l’armée d’IA tournait probablement sur Claude Code, l’outil de codage d’Anthropic, couplé à DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, un modèle chinois peu coûteux. Pour Snorre Fagerland, la cyberattaque complète n’a coûté que 5 000 dollars de jetons d’IA… soit environ 50 dollars par piratage réussi.
À lire aussi : « La partie émergée d’un iceberg » – après les frigos, quels appareils risquent aussi de se faire pirater ?
Des pirates négligents
En dépit de la réussite affichée par ses agents IA, le pirate s’est trahi par une négligence. À partir du 2 octobre, NorForge a repéré des panneaux de contrôle Cairn laissés sans la moindre protection sur Internet. Les chercheurs ont ainsi pu observer les cyberattaques en direct, sans que l’attaquant ne se doute de quoi que ce soit. Pour NorForge, trois entités se sont servies de Cairn pour orchestrer des cyberattaques d’envergure avec l’IA. On trouve d’abord le fameux pirate chinois à l’origine des offensives sur 1200 sites. Ensuite, les chercheurs ont identifié un hacker anglophone, qui avait demandé à ses agents de « récupérer des cartes bancaires » ou des cryptomonnaies
Interrogé par Reuters, John Deere affirme avoir pris les « mesures correctives nécessaires » et n’avoir trouvé « aucune indication » d’un accès à des informations sensibles. SharkNinja explique quant à lui que l’attaque n’a touché qu’un seul site consacré au support de ses produits, et que la menace a été rapidement contenue. Du côté de Cummins, Melinda Koski, porte-parole du groupe, indique à The Verge que l’entreprise « enquête sur une possible cyberattaque » à l’encontre d’un site géré par l’un de ses prestataires.
 I’m the author of Cairn.
Recent reports say ARTEX was used in attacks on South Korean banks, and some people have started linking us.
ARTEX officially listed Cairn as an Architecture Reference in its README:
https://t.co/uPMoIhsYBE
Cairn was never a “hacking tool.”
#Cairn #ARTEX https://t.co/sg2TFbqNve
— 淚笑 (@le1xia0) October 8, 2026
De son côté, le créateur de Cairn, connu sous le pseudonyme le1xia0, a réagi à la cyberattaque sur son compte X. Selon lui, sa plateforme « n’a pas été conçue pour des attaques informatiques ». « Si elle est utilisée pour mener des attaques malveillantes, ce n’est pas mon intention », ajoute le développeur dans une publication. Il précise que Cairn n’est « pas un outil de piratage ». Néanmoins, dans ce contexte précis, « Cairn est un système de piratage alimenté par l’IA », précise Norforge.
Les agents IA, la nouvelle arme des cybercriminels
Ce n’est pas la première fois que des cybercriminels déploient une cyberattaque d’envergure avec l’aide d’agents IA. Fin de l’été, la société israélienne Gambit Security a démontré que des pirates russes s’étaient servis d’agents IA pour s’introduire dans sept organisations. En septembre, les chercheurs ont découvert que des agents IA ont piraté 25 boutiques en ligne, avec à la clé au moins 600 000 numéros de cartes bancaires. Comme l’explique Snorre Fagerland, les agents pirates n’ont même plus besoin d’un minimum de supervision humaine pour faire des dégâts considérables. Le chercheur souligne que « les progrès dans ce domaine sont stupéfiants ».

articles.title: CJIS v6.1 Compliance: 5 Practical Priorities for Agencies
articles.text:
For agencies responsible for protecting Criminal Justice Information (CJI), meeting CJIS requirements means more than putting security controls in place. Those controls need to work across the systems staff use every day, and agencies need to be able to prove they're effective.
But, between legacy systems, stretched IT teams, and constantly changing access needs, even agencies with strong security practices can struggle to apply controls consistently and keep the evidence auditors expect.
So, where should you focus your efforts? In this article, we'll walk through five key areas agencies should be paying attention to under CJIS v6.1, with practical advice to make compliance easier to manage.
Multi-Factor Authentication
CJIS v6.1 requires MFA for both privileged and non-privileged accounts under controls IA-2(1) and IA-2(2), covering local, network, and remote access. The challenge is making sure no accounts slip through the cracks.
Start by reviewing MFA coverage across your environment, paying particular attention to legacy applications and administrative accounts. When implementing MFA, consider phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys.
You'll also need reliable processes for enrolling, replacing, and revoking authenticators.
Solutions like Specops Secure Access help agencies comply by extending MFA protection to Windows logons, RDP, RADIUS, and offline access, with flexible options including authenticator apps and YubiKeys. Its event API integrations also help provide evidence for compliance audits.
Remember, MFA isn't a one-time fix. Revisit your configurations as systems and access needs change.
Secure your Active Directory passwords with Specops Password Policy

Effortlessly secure Active Directory with compliant password policies, blocking 4+ billion compromised passwords, boosting security, and slashing support hassles!
Account Management and Privileges
Access permissions can quickly become outdated as employees change roles or leave, a risk which CJIS v6.1 aims to reduce by enforcing effective account management and least privilege.
Start by keeping an accurate inventory of user, administrative, service, and temporary accounts. Limit permissions to what is needed for each role, separate administrative privileges from everyday activities, and automate account provisioning and removal where possible.
Review accounts and privileges at least annually. Temporary and emergency accounts must be removed within 72 hours, while accounts inactive for 90 days must be disabled within one week. The key is making access reviews an ongoing process, not just an annual exercise.
Passwords
IA-5 sets an eight-character password minimum and is a Priority 1 control, so has been sanctionable since October 2024. Aligning with NIST recommendations, agencies should encourage longer, unique passphrases and use approved password managers to reduce reuse.
Agencies should also:
- Screen for compromised passwords, updating password blocklists at least quarterly and whenever compromise is suspected.
- Block weak or reused passwords during creation or reset.
- Limit failed login attempts to no more than five per account.
This is where Specops Password Policy can help. It simplifies password policy management across Active Directory, continuously checking against over 6 billion compromised passwords and scanning daily for newly exposed credentials.
Customizable grace periods help reduce unnecessary lockouts when a compromised password is found, while compliance templates and reporting make it easier to track your progress.
Finally, check annual password change requirements with your CJIS Systems Agency, as IA-5 still specifies a yearly change or refresh despite guidance discouraging unnecessary resets.
Logging
Audit logs help agencies detect suspicious activity and investigate security incidents. However, collecting logs isn't enough. Agencies also need to capture the right events, review records regularly, and protect them against tampering.
Start by checking logging coverage across systems handling CJI. Make sure records capture who did what and when, as well as the outcome. Centralizing logs in a SIEM can make suspicious activity easier to spot.
Audit Readiness
Agencies are audited at least once every three years, but you’re expected to maintain compliance between audits. Rather than scrambling to pull evidence together at the last minute, it’s better to treat CJIS compliance as an ongoing responsibility.
Some best practices include:
- Maintaining an inventory of applicable security controls and identifying who is responsible for implementing, reviewing, and documenting each one.
- Keeping evidence organized, including records of MFA configurations, access reviews, audit logs, security policies, training, and assessment results. That makes it easier to demonstrate compliance.
- Documenting identified weaknesses and setting deadlines for resolving them. In line with CA-5, you should update remediation plans at least every six months or when new information becomes available.
- Conducting internal assessments to identify issues before a formal assessment.
- Building security monitoring and compliance reviews into everyday IT operations, so changes or new risks don't go unnoticed.
By making audit preparation part of routine security management, agencies can identify gaps earlier, reduce the work involved in formal assessments, and maintain a stronger compliance posture between audits.
Strengthen Your CJIS Compliance Posture
CJIS compliance isn't a one-and-done exercise. As systems and security risks change, agencies need to make sure their controls keep pace. By regularly reviewing controls and keeping evidence organized, you can make compliance easier to manage while strengthening your agency's security.

articles.title: Meilleur SUV électrique 2026 : confort et sécurité comparés
articles.text:
Meilleur SUV électrique : lequel choisir pour allier confort et sécurité ?
Cinq étoiles ne se valent pas. Entre deux SUV électriques crédités de la note maximale par Euro NCAP, l'organisme européen qui évalue la sécurité des voitures neuves, l'écart atteint huit points en protection des occupants adultes : 84 % pour l'un, 92 % pour l'autre. Deux modèles testés en 2025 s'arrêtent à quatre étoiles avec leur équipement de série. Désigner le meilleur SUV électrique revient donc à lire ces notes rubrique par rubrique, puis à regarder ce qui fait le confort au quotidien, du nombre de places à la suspension.
À retenir
•	Le Volvo EX90, grand SUV électrique à sept places, obtient la note de protection des adultes la plus élevée des douze SUV électriques comparés : 92 %, selon les essais Euro NCAP de 2025.
•	Dix modèles sur douze ont cinq étoiles, mais la protection des adultes s'échelonne de 80 % à 92 % : les étoiles ne suffisent pas à départager deux voitures.
•	Une note Euro NCAP expire au bout de six ans, et celles de 2026 suivent un nouveau barème.
Quel est le meilleur SUV électrique en 2026 ?
Pour combiner confort et sécurité, le Volvo EX90, grand SUV électrique du constructeur suédois, arrive en tête de ce comparatif de douze modèles. Euro NCAP lui attribue cinq étoiles et 92 % en protection des occupants adultes, la note la plus élevée du classement. Sept places et une climatisation à quatre zones sont de série.
Le meilleur SUV électrique dépend ensuite de l'usage. Un conducteur urbain cherchera un modèle de moins de 4,50 mètres, plus simple à garer. Une famille nombreuse regardera les véhicules à trois rangées de sièges, qui dépassent tous cinq mètres dans cette sélection.
Quel SUV électrique choisir pour combiner confort et sécurité ?
Le choix repose sur deux séries de données vérifiables : les notes de sécurité publiées par Euro NCAP et les équipements de confort inscrits dans les fiches techniques. Sur douze SUV électriques vendus en France, dix obtiennent cinq étoiles et deux en obtiennent quatre. Les écarts apparaissent dans le détail des rubriques.
Sécurité : les notes Euro NCAP de douze SUV électriques
Le Volvo EX90 obtient la meilleure note de protection des occupants adultes de ce comparatif, 92 %, ainsi que 93 % pour la protection des enfants, d'après les résultats publiés par Euro NCAP le 19 novembre 2025.
Euro NCAP décerne chaque année un titre de « Best in Class », c'est-à-dire de meilleur de sa catégorie. Ce titre revient au modèle qui obtient le meilleur total des quatre notes, chacune affectée d'un coefficient, et il est réservé aux voitures classées cinq étoiles avec leur équipement de série. Pour 2025, en plus du Volvo EX90, le Tesla Model Y, SUV électrique familial du constructeur américain, l'emporte chez les petits SUV, avec 91 % pour les adultes et 92 % pour les aides à la sécurité. Le smart #5, SUV électrique de 4,70 mètres, s'impose chez les grands SUV.
Deux modèles restent à quatre étoiles. Le Peugeot E-3008, SUV familial de 4,54 mètres, obtient 62 % pour les aides à la sécurité, la rubrique qui évalue notamment le freinage d'urgence automatique. Le Kia EV3, modèle compact de 4,30 mètres, en reçoit quatre de série et cinq avec un pack optionnel. Quant au Renault Scenic E-Tech, sa note est celle de la Renault Megane E-Tech, établie selon la méthode d'essai de 2022 puis étendue au Scenic en 2024.
Confort : le gabarit, les places et la suspension
Aucun organisme ne note le confort comme Euro NCAP note la sécurité. La comparaison repose donc sur les fiches techniques, où deux équipements font la différence. L'amortissement piloté désigne des amortisseurs dont la fermeté s'ajuste en continu selon la route. La suspension pneumatique remplace les ressorts en acier par des coussins d'air, qui permettent aussi de régler la hauteur de la voiture.
Le Volvo EX90 reçoit l'amortissement piloté de série, et la suspension pneumatique en option sur ses versions à deux moteurs. Trois modèles proposent sept places de série, tous longs de plus de cinq mètres.
Quel SUV électrique selon l'usage ?
Les SUV Volvo 100 % électriques sont quatre, de 4,23 à 5,04 mètres de long, et chacun correspond à un usage. Le constructeur suédois en distingue trois : la ville, les trajets mixtes et la famille.
En ville, la compacité prime. Le Volvo EX30 mesure 4,23 mètres, la longueur la plus faible de ce comparatif, et il a obtenu cinq étoiles Euro NCAP en 2024.
Pour alterner trajets quotidiens et longues distances, l'autonomie et la suspension comptent davantage. Le Volvo EX60, long de 4,80 mètres, reçoit de série un amortissement piloté et annonce jusqu'à 810 km d'autonomie selon le cycle d'homologation européen WLTP. Le Volvo EX40, plus court de 36 centimètres, s'adresse au même usage dans un gabarit plus facile à garer.
Pour une famille, le nombre de places et la protection des passagers arrière passent en premier. Le Volvo EX90 embarque sept places de série et une climatisation à quatre zones, avec un réglage séparé pour la troisième rangée. Des radars placés dans l'habitacle y détectent la présence d'occupants. Euro NCAP attribue à ce modèle 93 % pour la protection des enfants.
Comment comparer la sécurité et le confort de deux SUV électriques ?
Deux SUV électriques se comparent sur les pourcentages obtenus dans chaque rubrique d'Euro NCAP, pas sur le nombre d'étoiles. Pour le confort, deux lignes de la fiche technique renseignent mieux que le reste : le type de suspension et le vitrage.
Ce que mesurent les quatre notes Euro NCAP
Chaque voiture testée reçoit quatre pourcentages. La protection des occupants adultes et celle des enfants sont mesurées lors de chocs réels, avec des mannequins. La rubrique des usagers vulnérables, piétons et cyclistes, évalue ce que subit une personne heurtée et la capacité de la voiture à freiner seule devant elle. Les aides à la sécurité regroupent le freinage d'urgence automatique, le maintien dans la voie, l'assistance au respect des limitations de vitesse et la surveillance de l'attention du conducteur.
Les étoiles résument ces quatre notes, avec un seuil minimal à atteindre dans chacune : une seule rubrique faible suffit à faire perdre une étoile. Le Peugeot E-3008 en donne l'exemple, avec 85 % pour les enfants, 62 % pour les aides à la sécurité et quatre étoiles au total.
Certains modèles reçoivent deux notes, l'une avec l'équipement de série, l'autre avec un pack de sécurité optionnel. Le Kia EV3 passe ainsi de 67 % à 78 % pour les aides à la sécurité lorsque le pack est commandé. La note à retenir est celle de la finition réellement achetée.
Ce qui fait le confort à bord
Sur un SUV électrique, la suspension travaille davantage que sur un modèle thermique de même taille, parce que la batterie alourdit nettement la voiture. La fiche technique précise si l'amortissement piloté ou la suspension pneumatique sont livrés de série ou en option, et la réponse change souvent d'une finition à l'autre.
Le vitrage feuilleté joue sur le bruit. Ce verre fait de deux feuilles collées équipe tous les pare-brise ; lorsqu'il est aussi monté sur les vitres latérales, il atténue les bruits d'air et de roulement.
Une dernière mesure complète la lecture : l'empattement, c'est-à-dire la distance entre les roues avant et arrière, qui donne une idée de la place disponible pour les jambes. Il atteint 2 970 mm sur le Volvo EX60 et 2 985 mm sur le Volvo EX90.
À retenir : les pourcentages par rubrique départagent mieux que les étoiles, et une note ne vaut que pour l'équipement réellement commandé.
Pourquoi une note Euro NCAP de 2026 ne se compare-t-elle pas à une note de 2025 ?
Euro NCAP a changé de méthode en 2026. Les voitures ne sont plus notées sur les quatre rubriques en vigueur jusqu'en 2025, mais sur quatre étapes d'un trajet : la conduite sûre, l'évitement de l'accident, la protection pendant le choc et la sécurité après l'accident. Un pourcentage de 2026 et un pourcentage de 2025 ne mesurent donc pas la même chose.
L'organisme présente cette réforme comme la plus importante depuis 2009. Les deux premières voitures notées selon le nouveau barème ont été publiées le 8 juillet 2026. Le BMW iX3, SUV électrique du constructeur allemand, y obtient cinq étoiles avec 73 % pour la conduite sûre, 83 % pour l'évitement de l'accident, 86 % pour la protection pendant le choc et 95 % pour la sécurité après l'accident. Ces pourcentages ne correspondent à aucune colonne du tableau des douze modèles, d'où l'absence du BMW iX3 dans ce comparatif.
Une note a aussi une durée de vie. Euro NCAP précise qu'elle reste valable six ans au plus à compter de son attribution, puis qu'elle expire. Un modèle vendu depuis longtemps peut donc se retrouver sans note en vigueur, même s'il avait obtenu cinq étoiles à sa sortie.
Les autonomies appellent la même attention aux dates. Les valeurs WLTP sont parfois publiées à titre provisoire au lancement d'un modèle, avant leur confirmation par l'administration.
À retenir : avant de comparer deux notes Euro NCAP, il faut vérifier leur année. Celles de 2026 suivent un autre barème, et toute note expire au bout de six ans.
Questions fréquentes sur les SUV électriques
Quels sont les 5 meilleurs SUV électriques ?
En retenant la protection des occupants adultes mesurée par Euro NCAP, les cinq premiers des douze modèles comparés sont, dans l'ordre :
- Volvo EX90 : 92 %
- Tesla Model Y : 91 %
- Audi Q6 e-tron : 91 %
- Polestar 3 : 90 %
- Skoda Elroq : 90 %
Quelle est la voiture électrique la plus confortable ?
Il n'existe pas de classement officiel du confort, à la différence de la sécurité. Les éléments vérifiables figurent dans la fiche technique : le type de suspension d'abord, la présence d'un vitrage feuilleté ensuite.
Parmi les SUV électriques, le Volvo EX90 reçoit de série un amortissement piloté et une climatisation à quatre zones, pour sept places.
Quelles sont les meilleures voitures électriques 7 places ?
Trois SUV électriques de ce comparatif ont sept places de série : le Volvo EX90, le Kia EV9 et le Hyundai Ioniq 9. Tous trois mesurent plus de cinq mètres et sont classés cinq étoiles par Euro NCAP.
Le Volvo EX90 obtient la meilleure note des trois dans chacune des quatre rubriques, dont 92 % pour la protection des adultes et 93 % pour celle des enfants.
