articles.title: Forscher entdecken ersten grünen Stern: Ist das Universum doch bunter, als bisher angenommen?
articles.text:
Bunter als gedacht: Warum tote Sterne rosa, blau und sogar grün leuchten können
Forscher:innen haben den ersten grünen Stern entdeckt. Dabei handelt es sich um einen Weißen Zwerg, also einen kleinen, alten Stern. Bisher galt die Temperatur als farbbestimmend: Kühle Sterne erscheinen orange, Sterne wie die Sonne weiß und die heißesten blassblau. Laut einer aktuellen Studie spielen allerdings auch andere Faktoren eine Rolle. Die Ergebnisse wurden in der Fachzeitschrift RAS Techniques and Instruments veröffentlicht.
Universum könnte bunter sein als vermutet
Weiße Zwerge erhielten ihren Namen, weil sie bei ihrer Entdeckung weiß oder blassblau leuchteten. Laut der neuen Studie könnte das aber mit ihrer Entfernung zusammenhängen, weshalb Forscher:innen ihre wahre Farbe von der Erde aus schlicht nicht erkennen konnten. „Niemand hatte sich wirklich damit beschäftigt, was bei Weißen Zwergen sonst noch möglich sein könnte“, sagte Teamleiter Mark Hollands von der University of Warwick gegenüber Space. „Es stellt sich heraus, dass diese unglaublich dichten Sterne Farben erzeugen können, die niemand erwartet hätte, und einige davon haben mich wirklich überrascht.“
Der Schlüssel zur regenbogenartigen Farbpalette der Himmelskörper ist ihre Dichte. Weiße Zwerge entstehen, wenn Sterne mit etwa der Masse der Sonne der Brennstoff ausgeht und ihre Kerne unter der Schwerkraft kollabieren. Die Materie ist danach millionenfach dichter als die Photosphäre der Sonne. Unter diesen Bedingungen wechselwirken Elemente wie Kohlenstoff, Kalzium und Natrium mit dem dichten Heliumplasma und absorbieren Licht über einen breiteren Farbbereich. So verschieben sich die Farben weg vom bekannten Weiß-Blau.
WD J1330+6435 ist der erste grüne Stern
Weiße Zwerge mit hohem Kohlenstoffgehalt schimmern rosa oder violett. Solche, die mit Trümmern verschlungener Asteroiden oder Kometen angereichert sind, wirken laut den Forscher:innen eher gelblich. Kühlere Weiße Zwerge mit gemischten Wasserstoff- und Heliumatmosphären leuchten oft cyanfarben oder blassblau, da Wasserstoffmoleküle mit Heliumatomen kollidieren. Besonders auffällig wird die Färbung allerdings, wenn einer dieser „lebenden Toten” beginnt, sich von Planeten in seiner Umgebung zu ernähren. Manche erscheinen dadurch sogar ein wenig grün.
Ein Beispiel dafür ist WD J1330+6435, der etwa 326 Lichtjahre entfernt ist. Er hat laut den Forscher:innen gesteiniges Material von einem planetarischen Begleiter aufgenommen, wodurch seine Atmosphäre mit Kalzium, Lithium und Natrium angereichert wurde – und dadurch entstand der grüne Farbton. „Die Natriumspuren in der Atmosphäre dieses Weißen Zwergs absorbieren den orangefarbenen Teil des Spektrums und hinterlassen ein gespenstisches grünes Leuchten”, so Holland gegenüber Space. Da bisher noch von keinem anderen Stern glaubwürdig berichtet wurde, dass er grün ist, gilt WD J1330+6435 als der erste bekannte grüne Stern.
Die meisten Weißen Zwerge sind weiß
Trotz dieser Vielfalt bleibt Weiß nach Einschätzung des Teams die häufigste Farbe der Weißen Zwerge. Nur fünf der 151 toten Sterne im Umkreis von etwa 65 Lichtjahren um die Erde zeigen eine außergewöhnliche Färbung. „Einer von dreißig klingt vielleicht nicht nach einem großen Anteil, aber bezogen auf die gesamte Anzahl der Weißen Zwerge im Universum sind das immer noch sehr viele seltsam gefärbte Sterne da draußen“, kommentierte Boris Gänsicke vom Fachbereich Physik der Universität Warwick. „Betrachtet man aber den Median einer repräsentativen Population von Weißen Zwergen, stellt man fest, dass der durchschnittliche Weiße Zwerg tatsächlich weiß ist.“

articles.title: OPINION: Europe needs more than just successful exits | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The acquisition of Berlin-based Talon.One by Dutch payments provider Adyen in July 2026 offers a useful perspective on European technology investing. A company founded in Germany developed technology valuable to a global payments business, and its next chapter is being written within Europe. This is a significant outcome for the founders and investors. However, it also raises a larger question: how can Europe turn individual successes into an ecosystem capable of producing them repeatedly?
The answer is not simply to encourage more European acquisitions. Successful startups need access to the best opportunities available, whether their future lies with a European buyer, an international technology group or the public markets. What matters is that these decisions reflect commercial potential rather than a lack of viable alternatives. For Europe, the challenge is to create the conditions in which successful companies can scale, attract investment and generate lasting economic value.
Exits are a measure of maturity, not the final destination
From a venture capital perspective, exits matter because they return capital to investors and founders, establish reference points for valuations, and help to finance the next generation of start-ups. Therefore, an acquisition is more than just the end of an investment cycle. The wider impact of an acquisition depends on whether experienced founders start again, whether employees launch new businesses, whether investors reinvest, and whether specialist knowledge remains accessible to the local ecosystem.
The Talon.One transaction is particularly interesting in this respect. Adyen paid €750 million for the loyalty and incentives platform, combining complementary European technologies together in a business with international reach. The company’s founders also reinvested some of their proceeds in Adyen shares. This is one possible model for maintaining continuity, although the long-term consequences for jobs, innovation and further investment will only become apparent over time.
Yet a European buyer does not automatically guarantee a better outcome. An acquisition by a US technology group can also give European innovation access to new markets, capital and expertise. The relevant questions concern what happens after the transaction: where future investment takes place, whether technological capabilities continue to develop and how much value flows back into the startup ecosystem. While the identity of the buyer is important, the industrial logic and long-term consequences also deserve equal attention.
Germany’s progress reveals the next challenge
Germany is a useful test case for Europe’s progress. According to the German Startup Monitor 2026, the country added ten unicorns in 2026, indicating that more companies are achieving significant valuations. Yet 62% of respondents considering a stock market listing favour the US. These figures measure different things, but together they capture a tension: Germany is producing ambitious technology companies while many founders still see stronger exit opportunities outside its domestic market.
This preference is not irrational. Founders and their investors have a responsibility to consider factors such as access to capital, market depth, suitable buyers, and prospects for future growth. US markets can offer genuine advantages. Rather than persuading companies to reject opportunities abroad, Europe needs to build more competitive options.
This is important long before a potential exit. Investors assess the availability of future funding and realistic exit routes when deciding whether to back a company. If these options appear limited, promising businesses may struggle to attract the necessary capital to reach their full potential. Therefore, a stronger exit environment can support investment across the entire startup lifecycle.
What a stronger European exit market would require
Three priorities stand out:
- Deeper growth capital: European startups need access to substantial later-stage funding and patient institutional investors, without having to reshape their strategy around capital availability elsewhere. This would also give founders greater flexibility over when and how they pursue an exit.
- More strategic buyers: Acquisitions can provide distribution, customers and resources for expansion. Talon.One and Adyen illustrate the potential of cross-border European combinations. A broader base of established technology companies willing to acquire and develop innovative businesses would create additional exit opportunities.
- Earlier exit planning: Founders should consider which investors could fund the next round, which buyers could offer strategic value, and the potential impact of a transaction on teams, research and future ventures. Investor nationality alone is no substitute for that assessment.
The objective is choice
Europe’s ambition should not be to keep every company, every shareholder or every exit within its borders. International capital and global customers are essential for building competitive businesses. In my experience, a European startup acquired by a US company can still create substantial value for its founders, employees and investors, and a European acquisition can likewise bolster a regional technology group.
The more meaningful test is whether European founders have real alternatives, such as sufficient capital to scale up, credible paths to public markets and a strong base of strategic acquirers and investors who can recycle returns into new ventures.
Successful exits show what European technology can achieve. A mature ecosystem makes those successes less exceptional. This requires a joint effort by founders, investors, established companies and policymakers alike.
Editor’s note: IRIS was an investor in Talon.One.

articles.title: Data centre vs Cloud platform: Is there a difference?
articles.text:
You have probably seen the words “data centre” and “cloud” used interchangeably. They don’t mean the same thing, and the difference matters. It shapes how businesses buy technology, how regulators write rules and where investors see opportunity.
A data centre is a building. It is a secure, purpose-built facility with reliable power, cooling, security and internet connections, so that computers can run around the clock. A cloud platform is a service. It is software that lets customers rent computing power, storage, and networking on demand, switch them on or off themselves, and pay only for what they use.
Think of an airport and an airline. The airport provides the runway, fuel, and terminal; the airline provides the service you actually book. Every cloud platform runs inside a data centre, but most data centres do not offer a cloud platform. Owning an airport does not make you an airline.
Data centre grading and cloud computing standards
Companies that rent space for their own servers in someone else’s facility are buying what the industry calls “colocation”. A facility’s reliability is rated on a four-level scale from the Uptime Institute.
Tier I has no backup equipment, so any fault results in downtime. Tier II adds spares but has a single path for power and cooling.
Tier III has more than one path, so any part can be serviced without switching anything off; it is the level most serious operators aim for. Tier IV survives any single failure.
Be careful, though: “built to Tier III standards” is not the same as certified, so ask which certificate a provider actually holds.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology defines cloud computing by five features: customers can provision resources themselves, access them over the internet, share the provider’s pool of equipment, scale capacity up or down quickly, and pay only for what they use.
A bank that runs virtualised software in a rented cage has a more efficient setup, but it only becomes a cloud when self-service, automation, and metering are added.
Why this matters for Nigeria
Customers spent US$143.4 billion on cloud infrastructure in the second quarter of 2026 alone, with Amazon, Microsoft, and Google capturing about 63 per cent of that spending. None of them runs a full cloud region in Nigeria.
Amazon has a smaller facility called a Local Zone in Lagos, but for Microsoft, Google, and Oracle, the nearest full regions are in South Africa. So when a Nigerian bank says its data is “in the cloud”, that data is often outside the country.
That is why the Central Bank of Nigeria’s order to keep payment data on local infrastructure by 1 January 2027 puts this distinction at the centre of the debate. Moving data home requires local data centres and local cloud platforms that offer the ease, scale, and reliability banks expect. Operators such as MTN, which launched cloud services alongside a new Tier III data centre in Lagos in 2025, are starting to fill that gap.
Power and progress in Nigerian infrastructure
A Tier III data centre is built on the assumption that the public grid will fail. Rack Centre in Lagos runs entirely off-grid on its own 13.5 MW gas-powered system and reports 100 per cent uptime since 2013. Where electricity does matter is cost: generating your own power is expensive, and that shows up in prices. That is a real competitiveness issue, but a different story from “Nigerian data centres keep going down because of NEPA.”
When I chose a data centre for a bank’s workloads in 2012, there was only one commercial option worth serious consideration. Rack Centre in Ikeja opened in 2013 and later became the first facility in Nigeria and West Africa to win Uptime Institute Tier III design certification.
Today, industry counts put Nigeria at around 26 operational data centres, about 28 including those being built, with 210 to 300 MW of capacity expected by 2030. In my experience, the leading operators have not lost a minute of service to a power failure.
A data centre is the foundation; a cloud platform is what you build on it. Nigeria now has a strong, professionally run foundation. The next challenge, made urgent by data localisation and demand for AI, is building cloud platforms on top of it.
Policymakers, journalists, and business leaders should ask not only “Do we have enough data centres?” but “Do we have cloud platforms to make them useful?”
Remi Adejumo is a Cloud and Infrastructure Architect with over 20 years’ experience in cloud computing, data centres, virtualisation, and enterprise IT transformation across the UK, the US, and Africa.

articles.title: Toyota prépare une révolution pour sa voiture la plus vendue au monde : la Corolla passera aussi à l’électrique et sera fabriquée en Chine dès 2028
articles.text:
Toyota prépare une révolution pour sa voiture la plus vendue au monde : la Corolla passera aussi à l’électrique et sera fabriquée en Chine dès 2028
“Je crois qu’on est en train de perdre face à la Chine.” L’aveu d’un ingénieur maison trahit l’urgence chez Toyota. Préfigurée par un concept dessiné en France, capable d’accueillir batterie, hybride ou essence sur une base unique, la treizième Corolla sortira des chaînes d’une coentreprise chinoise dès 2028, alors que le constructeur recule depuis sept mois d’affilée dans l’empire du Milieu.
Douze générations et plus de 50 millions d'exemplaires écoulés depuis 1966 : la Corolla incarne depuis six décennies la fiabilité japonaise à prix raisonnable. Sa descendante verra pourtant le jour en Chine. Selon le quotidien économique Nikkei Asia, Toyota compte en lancer la production dès 2028 chez FAW Toyota, sa coentreprise basée à Tianjin. Détail piquant : le concept qui la préfigure, dévoilé à Tokyo en octobre 2025, a été dessiné en France, chez ED², le studio européen du groupe niché sur la Côte d'Azur.
	
Il semble régner un sentiment de crise considérable dans l'entreprise.
Ces mots ont été recueillis par la télévision publique NHK dans les coulisses du développement de la future Corolla. Un ingénieur du programme y avouait sans détour craindre que Toyota soit en train de perdre la bataille face aux constructeurs chinois.
Corolla électrique, hybride ou essence : une plateforme unique pour toutes les énergies
La nouvelle venue sera la première Corolla bâtie sur la plateforme "multi-pathway" de Toyota, déjà exploitée par certains modèles Lexus. Une même architecture accueillera aussi bien une batterie qu'un hybride rechargeable, un hybride classique ou un moteur thermique. Ces quatre déclinaisons avaient été confirmées dès la présentation du concept. Le constructeur pourra ainsi doser l'électrique selon l'appétit de chaque marché, tout en rognant sur les coûts et les délais de développement.
Aucune fiche technique n'a filtré, ni capacité de batterie ni autonomie. La présentation mondiale est attendue en 2027.
Pourquoi Toyota mise sur la Chine pour réinventer sa compacte
Le pari a tout d'une riposte. En août 2026, les ventes Toyota et Lexus ont plongé de 22,8 % en Chine, septième baisse mensuelle consécutive. En cause, une demande atone pour l'essence et l'hybride, minée par la flambée du carburant et l'offensive des électriques locales. Le groupe remodèle aussi son implantation. Le 8 octobre, FAW, GAC et Toyota ont signé un accord-cadre : GAC rachètera les 50 % détenus par FAW dans FAW Toyota, qui mutualisera ensuite recherche, achats et production avec GAC Toyota.
Et en France ? Rien n'indique que la Corolla chinoise franchira nos frontières. Les versions à hayon et Touring Sports vendues chez nous sortent de l'usine anglaise de Burnaston, et Toyota n'a rien annoncé en sens contraire.

articles.title: This 3D-printed 1980s brick phone brings back the days when mobile phones were just for making calls
articles.text:
In a nutshell: A lot of people cite the 1990s Nokia 3210 as the old-school brick-like mobile phone. But for something that fits the description a lot closer, go back another decade to the 1980's and the first handheld mobile phones: brick phones. Now, a designer has 3D-printed one of these devices, retaining the originals' primary function of making and receiving calls – so there are no modern smartphone distractions.
Cologne-based designer and maker Kevin Noki created the ADHD ONE, the first part of the name being an acronym for Anti Distraction Handset Device.
The device resembles a snazzy update of 1980s brick phones sported by the likes of Wall Street's Gordon Gekko, such as the Motorola DynaTAC 8000X. There's the physical 19-key keypad, small display, and a concerning large antenna.
The phone has a much more modern set of internals. It's powered by a Raspberry Pi Pico and features an FSC-BT1026C Bluetooth module based on Qualcomm's QCC3024 chip. There's also a rechargeable lithium battery, charging controller, and custom-printed circuit board.
Unlike the 1980s originals, the ADHD ONE doesn't have its own cellular connectivity. Instead, it relies on a Bluetooth connection to an iPhone to make and receive calls, so it's not like you can completely replace your distraction-filled smartphone with one of these, but you can at least keep it hidden in a drawer.
Noki designed the phone's enclosure using Autodesk Fusion before 3D-printing the components. He's made the files available on his website for €29.99 ($33.68). The package includes 3D-printable STL files for the main housing, back panels, internal mounting frame, display cover, battery holder, and all 19 keypad buttons.
There are also three speaker grille designs (Classic, Holes, and Stripes), three antenna options (Retro, Slim, and Screw), and an alternative housing without an antenna hole. Other included files cover ready-to-flash firmware in UF2 format, Gerber and drill files for manufacturing the custom PCB, a bill of materials with component sourcing notes, and a quick-start guide to assembling the device.
The package doesn't include the firmware's source code, editable 3D/CAD files, or editable PCB design files. It's also a digital download, so no physical components are supplied. Buyers receive a ZIP file of approximately 20MB immediately after payment. The files are licensed for personal use only, meaning they cannot be redistributed or resold.
Several devices have been released in recent years promising a break from the distractions – such as depression-inducing social media apps – found on smartphones. There were the $299 Light Flip and Light Phone III, the Minimal Phone, and Commodore's Callback 8020, to name a few.

articles.title: The Key to AI Software Security Isn’t Speed, It’s Maturity
articles.text:
Agentic artificial intelligence software development has all the traits of a summer blockbuster, with the prospects of Godzilla-sized productivity gains thrilling business leaders and security implications sending chills down the spines of developers and SOC teams. One difference, though, is that those thrills and chills are going to last longer than a summer, and the fallout could be a lot more serious than some spilled popcorn.
The proliferation of large language models, whether for software development or general use, alongside both sanctioned tools and shadow AI brought in by employees, is expanding the attack surface too quickly for traditional controls to keep up, particularly with the growing use of agentic AI. And the increased risks are coming home to roost, with Gartner predicting that the costs of incidents driven by agentic AI will increase fourfold through 2027.
The impact of agentic AI is a particularly sharp double-edged sword, with SonarSource noting that the frontier LLMs such as Claude and Gemini that write the best, most functional code also produce the most severe security vulnerabilities.
Organizations are aware of the need to gain control over agentic AI’s risk factors, but the protections implemented so far may well be insufficient. Governance is the go-to concept for reigning in AI-driven software development, and with good reason. It’s critical for maintaining control over what AI agents can and can’t do. Along with the improved observability of AI tool use and commits, this can help organizations limit the risk levels of AI while reaping the rewards of improved productivity.
But governance and Governance only go so far when organizations are in other critical ways still working in the dark regarding security controls. Specifically, they may not know where they are on the ascending scale of AI adoption and as a result may not understand what they need at their current stage. Without a clear understanding of the capabilities of their current AI projects, the risks involved and the level of developer skills required to manage AI, they can fall far short in implementing security best practices. They need a governance plan that fully addresses the new reality of software development.
Know the Different Stages of AI Adoption and Maturity
Organizations can navigate the AI implementation puzzle without losing control of risk management, with the context provided by a three-phase, eight-stage AI Adoption Model that mirrors the steps you’ll take along the AI path, from relatively bare-bones AI assistants performing routine tasks to AI agents capable of initiating and finishing tasks completely on their own.
The model is highly detailed in describing each stage, but to summarize it briefly, it consists of eight observable stages defining activity, risk levels and developer skill requirements across the three phases of AI implementation: AI Assisted, AI Native and Agentic.
Phase 1. AI Assisted
The first phase includes stages 1 (Minimal AI Use) and 2 (Supervised Assistance) and covers organizations in the foothills of AI implementation, using AI models that work directly for developers and present low to moderate risk levels. These early stages are an ideal time to establish governance policies. Developers, meanwhile, should receive upskilling on topics ranging from secure coding to code review, and these skills should be verifiable using a tool to establish baselines and track developer performance.
Phase 2: AI Native
Applying to stages 3 (Unsupervised Assistance) and 4 (AI-Primary Development), this is the phase where developers are allowing AI models to work more on their own without close supervision. Productivity can skyrocket with agents taking advantage of information-sharing standards such as Model Context Protocol (MCP), but risk levels run high. A major risk arises when developers trust AI too much, but tools are available to detect over-trust and track MCP activity. Stage 4 begins the transition from AI Native to Agentic. Developers have become code reviewers rather than authors, a significant shift that requires effective education and upskilling.
Phase 3: Agentic
This phase is what every organization is shooting for, but it comes with risk levels ranging from very high and critical to extreme and maximum. The stages steadily climb the ladder of both capability and risk. At Stage 5 (Single Agent), Command Line Interface (CLI) agents, such as Claude Code or Gemini CLI, perform operations from start to finish on their own. At Stage 6 (Multi-agent Parallel), AI can scale quickly as multiple agents work together. Stage 7 (Scaled Agent Management) takes it to the next level, with multiple agents operating at scale, and Stage 8 (Autonomous Orchestration) requires developers to coordinate agents as a unified team. Developer education should cover policy enforcement, the use of application risk scorecards, and the ability to track commits for audit purposes.
As the progression of these stages makes clear, establishing governance and a comprehensive learning program early on is essential because risk levels can quickly get out of hand as AI agents perform more complex, autonomous and unsupervised operations. Failing to establish a governance foundation early can come back to bite you in a big way.
Fortunately, most developers are somewhere between stages 2 through 4 right now, so it’s not too late for organizations to implement the guardrails, oversight and education programs necessary to manage the entirely new world of the Agentic Development Lifecycle (ADLC).
Where to Start, How to Proceed
As with many a new technology, adoption of AI is running well ahead of organizations’ abilities to secure it. The headlong rush into AI, compounded by unskilled employees bringing their own LLMs into the network without understanding how to manage security assessments or perform contextual reviews, has left organizations lacking visibility into who is using AI, how they are using it and the impact it has on production code. They may be flying fast with AI adoption but in many ways are also flying blind without the oversight, guardrails and developer-level observability they need to ensure that AI is being used safely.
Establishing effective AI governance can feel daunting. Organizations can reasonably ask, “Where do we start?” The answer is to understand where they are in the first place. It helps organizations identify the security controls and developer skill levels needed at their current stage of adoption, as well as what will be required at the next one.
No matter where an organization is in AI adoption, the next level of both capability and risk will arrive faster than expected.

articles.title: 'We love a good challenge': Logitech head tells us why the AI age could revolutionize collaboration as we know it, as it reveals its biggest product overhaul in years
articles.text:
'We love a good challenge': Logitech head tells us why the AI age could revolutionize collaboration as we know it, as it reveals its biggest product overhaul in years
Simplification can be key to better communication, Logitech believes
As more and more companies press their workers into coming back into the office, even if only for a few days in increasingly popular hybrid working models, the need for effective and reliable communication technology has never been greater.
A common sight in offices and homes across the world, Logitech is ideally placed to monitor trends in what workers at every level require - and at its recent Logi Work 2026 event, it took the opportunity to show off how its latest suite of releases can revolutionize the collaboration experience for all.
To find out more, I spoke to Henry Levak, VP and general manager, Logitech, to see what it sees as the future of meeting rooms, offices, and even the humble home working desk.
Broad portfolio paying off
“We want people to think of us as that simple and flexible partner - the word 'proprietary' and being locked in is luckily something we're moving away from,” Levak tells me.
“The reality is that you will have a world of different configurations,” he notes, highlighting how many of Logitech’s customers are asking workers to come back into the office, meaning the company needs to broaden its offerings even further.
“That's been a huge catalyst for our success,” he notes, “we have an incredibly broad portfolio that covers people working from home, to people working in the boardroom, and everything in between.”
At the event, Levak had spoken about the upcoming launch of Logitech’s new portfolio, which the company had described as its biggest enterprise-focused launch in years.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
The new lineup, which includes the Rally Bar 2, Rally System 2 Pro and Sound Shape technology, will revolutionize the way businesses of all sizes collaborate and communicate, with not only more powerful, but more customizable technology being the watchword.
For example, the new Rally Bar 2, the successor to the popular sound bar now seen in boardrooms and meeting spaces across the globe, not only features a Qualcomm Dragonwing chip to allow for better AI processing, but offers a 115 degree POV and much easier wall mounting due to its smaller form factor
The Rally System 2 Pro provides a “modular yet streamlined” offering which looks to simplify complex installs which can be difficult to maintain and manage - making larger rooms better spaces to have these vital meetings in.
In spite of its new range of releases, Logitech had spoken about its goal to “simplify everything” - so I ask Levak how the company can pursue that goal while still offering a range of products attractive to all different kinds of customers.
“It's a big pain point,” he says, “one of the things you can almost always predict is that simplifying will be a request...people want things to be dramatically simpler - but they also want consistency and experience.”
“What they don't want, is that if you walk into a room, like a smaller space with some sort of AI features and capability - and then you walk into a larger room, and for some reason that space doesn't have that feature.”
“The technology should just disappear and blend away into the background, and everyone should just focus on collaboration and creation, not necessarily the technology - and the only way to achieve that is if you have consistent technology.”
Simplify, simplify
Going forward, this will mean that even in a large room or meeting space, customers will only require a small simple device such as a video bar set up, Levak says, removing unnecessary friction and allowing everyone to work effectively.
“The way you simplify it is by dramatically reducing the number of components,” he points out, “what we're doing is something that dramatically simplifies all of that, from installation, provisioning, setup and deployment - it's a reduction in terms of complexity of what's out there today.”
“In terms of what it can bring, it's the first time modern AI is available in much larger rooms - now you have a full ecosystem of components that will deliver that experience.”
Looking forward, Levak is keen to point out the role AI can play in spaces as incongruous as meeting rooms.
With AI agents playing an increasingly important role for many workers, the need for context has never been greater. Such information needs to be collected by a range of sensors, and Logitech feels that products such as microphones and cameras could play a key role in expanding this - as long as effective privacy controls are used - making its equipment the physical layer of a company’s AI ecosystem.
“You can see the power when (an AI agent) has context about you, and the same thing will apply at work,” Levak says, “at a higher level, we’re deploying these sensors in every space, so that the context you need in order to build out a more thoughtful agent for you.”
“We're making sure the products are built for what's coming next,” he concludes, “both from the simplicity and elegance perspective, but also from features and capability.”

articles.title: Spotify launches paid podcast memberships with perks beyond bonus content | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Spotify on Tuesday launched paid memberships, a new way for podcasters to make money from their biggest fans beyond paywalled bonus episodes. Creators can decide which perks to offer listeners, which could be bonus audio or video, fewer ads, early access to shows, or some combination of these.
The streaming service first previewed the idea at its Investor Day in May, where it also introduced AI capabilities that let listeners ask questions about what they’re listening to or watching and debuted new tools for managing creator sponsorships.
As the company explained at the time, memberships would help to “create a natural path to go deeper, unlocking new and exclusive experiences for fans and new revenue opportunities for creators.”
The feature is now rolling out to 34 markets globally, including the U.S.
The launch is the latest example of Spotify’s effort to make its platform more attractive to podcast creators, particularly as it moves further into the video space to compete with YouTube. Though podcasters have long been able to monetize through ads, the new memberships could entice more fans to support creators by offering more than just an occasional bonus episode.
Creators keep 90% of the membership revenue and can package their benefits across multiple tiers and pricing options to appeal to fans at different levels of commitment. To qualify, podcasters must host their shows on Spotify for Creators or Megaphone, have at least 100 consumption hours, 100 listeners or viewers, and at least three published episodes.
Fans will see memberships promoted on the show’s Spotify page, where they can subscribe, pay, and immediately access the exclusive content. (The company tells us that memberships will be purchased on the web, not through in-app purchases).
A handful of shows will offer memberships at launch, including “The Adam Friedland Show,” “Making Sense with Sam Harris,” “Shawn Ryan Show,” “The Sculpt Society,” “Two Hot Takes,” as well as YMH Studios, which is bringing memberships to 12 shows across its network.
Memberships join other Spotify monetization tools, including advertising and the Spotify Partner Program, as well as features that help creators grow their audience, like promotions, free trials, and analytics. Soon, Spotify says creators will be able to offer fans membership badges and welcome clips, too.

articles.title: Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
articles.text:
Windows 98 SE users get a Thunderbolt 4 driver, thanks to AI assistance — vibe-coded xHCI98 driver works in Microsoft OSes up to Windows 7
If you've ever wanted to run Windows 98 SE on your mid-2010s or newer PC with fast USB hub support, here's your chance.
Windows 98 SE devotees can now enjoy (experimental) support for USB4 and Thunderbolt 3/4. Developer and maker Yeo Kheng Meng, who also enjoys retrocomputing, recently released the vibe-coded xHCI98 v3.0.0.0, enabling the practical use of generic USB 3.x, USB4, and Thunderbolt 3/4 host controllers on systems running Windows 98 SE, ME, 2000, XP, Vista, and 7. An extensive blog post by the dev provides further reading about the driver, compatibility, its creation, and usage.
Demo video “shows many different USB devices being hotplugged to a modern 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 with only xHCI controller.”
Some of you will be wondering why a project to bring USB4 (Thunderbolt 3 and 4) to PCs running Windows 98 SE exists. Retro computing fan Meng explains on his GitHub that this project should appeal directly to users of PCs from the mid-2010s that have xHCI-only (USB 3.x) chipsets and no legacy EHCI controller. However, older OSes don’t have xHCI drivers, and that’s where xHCI98 steps in. “Without xHCI support, even keyboards, mice, and flash drives need the BIOS's legacy support, cannot be hotplugged, and devices such as Ethernet and audio do not work at all,” explains Meng, revealing his motivation. “This project fills that gap.”
Impressively, xHCI98 drives a lot more than USB storage. It replaces Windows’ own USB port and hub drivers to facilitate the connection and use of USB 1.1 and 2.0 and SuperSpeed (USB 3.x) devices and hubs, UAS (USB Attached SCSI) storage through a second driver (xhciuas.sys), and Thunderbolt 3 and USB4 docks and NVMe enclosures through a third driver (xhcicm.sys).
Meng has developed and tested xHCI98 mostly on Intel hardware, as that is what he owns. Candidly, he admits “this is a solo human's project with AI assistance, so bugs are not unexpected,” even if you do have the same hardware as the dev - a 2020 ThinkPad P14s Gen 1 (Comet Lake xHCI, no EHCI). It stands up pretty well during the plug/unplug video demo above, though the test rig used is not quite the USB cart of death.
As a solo developer, Meng isn't shy to admit he leaned heavily on AI assistance to prepare the xHCI98 release. His vibe coding adventure was supported by Claude Fable 5.1 for planning, Claude Opus 5.5 for coding, and Codex GPT 6 Astra as an adversarial reviewer.
In addition to a few bug warnings, there are some other things to know about using this driver with the various older versions of Windows it supports, standby and hibernation, and more. The dev helpfully sketches out a process for checking your hardware, outlines various install methods, discusses updating, and talks about tuning the driver for those who will be jumping in at the deep end with this project.

articles.title: Arturia’s MiniFreak 49 makes its Freak synths more professional
articles.text:
Arturia is adding to its Freak line of proudly weird digital synths with the MiniFreak 49. Under the hood, it’s almost identical to the current MiniFreak, but it adds a number of more professional features and some interface improvements.
Arturia’s MiniFreak 49 makes its Freak synths more professional
The MiniFreak 49 adds full-sized semi-weighted keys and proper pitch and mod wheels to the Freak lineup.
The most noticeable change is that, rather than the MiniFreak’s 37 minikeys or the MicroFreak’s 25 “key” touchplate, the MiniFreak 49 has (as you may have guessed) 49 full-sized, semi-weighted keys. Though it’s somewhat disappointing that they feature only mono aftertouch instead of polyphonic aftertouch. It also trades the touchstrips of the other Freak instruments for proper aluminum pitch and mod wheels.
The MiniFreak 49 also has a larger LCD than its siblings and dedicated controls for its two sound engines, so you don’t have to switch between them. Like the MiniFreak, it offers over 30 digital oscillator types, each with analog filters. It also adds audio-rate filter FM for even freakier sounds and has 256MB of storage for user samples and wavetables, which were just added to the original MiniFreak in a firmware update last month.
Lastly, there’s a new XYZ touchpad that not only replaces the mod matrix’s intuitive but slow knob-based interface, but also adds performance features and speeds up preset browsing. You can swipe through presets, control macros, manipulate the filter, and more.
MiniFreak 49 is available now with an MSRP of $849, though the street price is likely to be lower.

articles.title: The new economics of enterprise AI
articles.text:
Sponsored
The new economics of enterprise AI
As enterprise AI shifts from isolated experiments to becoming foundational infrastructure, companies need to focus on efficiency, not just consumption.
Provided byHPE
Imagine your company just discovered electricity. At first only a few machines run on it, and nobody worries about efficiency — consumption is low and the value is obvious. But once electricity becomes infrastructure, every process depends on it, and the question changes from "can we use it?" to "how efficiently are we using it?"
Enterprise AI is going through the same shift. What began as isolated chatbot and copilot experiments is becoming a foundational layer of the business, with models, agents, and data increasingly interconnected in production workloads. The important question stops being what a token or GPU-hour costs. It becomes how efficiently the AI environment converts paid capacity into useful business outcomes.
That's the metric worth tracking: effective cost per useful outcome — the total platform, model, operations, and capacity cost required to complete work the business can actually use, whether a resolved request or a completed workflow.
Three ways to run AI
Utilization is central to the economics. Directing more work to paid-for capacity lowers effective unit cost; idle GPUs, fragmented workloads, and oversized models all raise the cost of every useful result. Enterprises generally choose among three models:
A bespoke stack — procuring infrastructure and controls in-house. This approach is flexible, but it creates a continuing burden, since teams must revalidate the environment as models and policies change.
On-demand consumption — hyperscalers reduce the assembly burden and suit low or uncertain demand, but charges rise with every prompt or agent action.
An integrated private AI platform — owned or dedicated capacity paired with a validated stack. The advantage isn't free inference; it's control over efficiency levers like scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management.
The right model depends on the workload. APIs can be rational for experimentation or variable demand. As workloads become sustained and business-critical, enterprises need to weigh not just what they consume, but how efficiently they operate the system.
Ownership is an operating discipline
Buying a Formula 1 race car and parking it in your garage means owning one of the most sophisticated vehicles ever built — but ownership alone doesn't make you competitive; you still need drivers, mechanics, and track time to justify it. AI infrastructure works the same way.
One of the biggest misconceptions in enterprise AI is that owning infrastructure automatically improves economics. Owning GPUs creates the opportunity for better economics, but only if the organization has sufficient demand and operational discipline to keep resources productive.
The infrastructure that returns the best ROI isn't a reference architecture or a bespoke build-out — it's a fully integrated, qualified stack that lets teams route tasks to the least costly model that meets quality requirements and reuse context through techniques such as KV-cache management, reducing wasted capacity while maintaining responsiveness.
Without these practices, committed infrastructure can become stranded capital. With them, rising demand improves economics as fixed costs are amortized across more useful work — increasingly important in agentic systems, where economics are shaped less by any single prompt than by the efficiency of the complete environment.
From deployment to value
HPE Private Cloud AI is a production-ready foundation combining infrastructure, software, models, tools, governance, and services, reducing the integration burden of operating private AI at scale. Its architecture lets teams manage scheduling, model selection, GPU partitioning, and cache management as operational levers, aligning capacity and service levels with each workload's requirements. It also includes a 90-day engagement with forward-deployed engineers who help customer teams deploy initial use cases and establish repeatable operating practices.
In independent testing commissioned by HPE, an integrated platform serving multiple workloads at high utilization delivered a lower effective cost per token than repeatedly renting equivalent capacity. Actual results will vary based on workload mix and utilization.
Measure what matters
Token consumption remains useful, but it isn't a complete measure of AI economics. A fuller enterprise view tracks cost per business-relevant outcome, accelerator utilization, and model choice relative to task complexity.
Enterprises already operating private AI should ask how mature their utilization is, and how workload volume will change over the next 12 to 18 months. Those earlier in the journey should build these practices in from the first deployment, so strategy anticipates growth before demand becomes a bottleneck.
For low-volume, unpredictable demand, an API or hyperscaler may remain sensible. But as AI becomes a continuous production capability, enterprises have a growing incentive to control utilization, amortize fixed costs, and manage the environment as a long-term operating asset. The strategic question isn't whether enterprises will pay for AI — it's whether they will understand, and ultimately own, the economics behind it.

articles.title: Ahold Delhaize Restoring Services Disrupted by Cyberattack
articles.text:
Dutch-Belgian grocery giant Ahold Delhaize has restored some of the services impacted by last week’s cyberattack and expects more to come back online within days.
On October 12, the company took its systems offline in response to “a security issue” within its network, which impacted its online services, including orders and deliveries across Europe and the US.
Without providing details on the incident, Ahold Delhaize confirmed last week that its local brands were affected, but said stores have remained open.
On Monday, the company confirmed that a cyberattack disrupted its services, which are now coming back online. Many of its European websites and applications are now restored, and Albert Heijn, its Dutch brand, is expected to resume home deliveries by Friday.
E-commerce services at Ahold Delhaize’s US brands are expected to be restored within days, but the company has not provided a specific timeframe.
“All stores across all brands have remained open throughout the incident, while we have continued the phased restoration of our systems and services to support the distribution of groceries to our brands’ customers as quickly as possible,” the grocery giant said.
While it refrained from sharing information on the type of cyberattack it fell victim to, Ahold Delhaize said it has no evidence that customer, associate, or partner data was stolen in the incident.
The company says it notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) and relevant authorities shortly after discovering the attack and filed a formal police report this week.
“Taking systems offline to help protect them was a precautionary measure that affected most of our brands across Europe and the United States. Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused – especially to our customers,” Ahold Delhaize president and CEO Frans Muller said.

articles.title: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS
When AI agents access databases, APIs, and sensitive business operations, establishing cryptographic identity through X.509 public key infrastructure (PKI) becomes a critical requirement. The core challenge is proving which agent made a request, preventing forgery between agents, and confirming that each agent acts only on behalf of an authorized user. Traditional approaches such as sharing API keys between components or passing OAuth tokens through agent chains fall short of the zero-trust requirements that enterprise deployments demand.
Multi-agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations. However, MCP has no built-in authentication standard. It is transport-agnostic by design. This creates a critical gap: Without proper identity mechanisms, any component could impersonate an agent, replay intercepted credentials, or invoke tools without authorization.
In this post, we show you how to address this gap using Keyfactor EJBCA combined with AWS services. EJBCA is a PKI platform that supports high-availability deployment, REST API automation, and Online Certificate Status Protocol (OCSP) validation. The reference architecture uses four complementary security mechanisms. First, signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every agent call. Second, user-signed delegation assertions authorize agents without sharing credentials. Third, RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any single token disclosure. Fourth, real-time OCSP revocation checking propagates credential changes immediately across all agents.
The solution uses Amazon Bedrock for LLM inference through the AWS Strands Agents SDK. While this reference architecture uses a database as the protected resource, the same authentication pattern applies to any MCP-compatible tool server. Complete source code for all examples is available in the accompanying GitHub repository.
About Keyfactor EJBCA
Keyfactor provides a widely adopted machine identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide, according to Keyfactor. These organizations span financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, and government. Keyfactor helps organizations establish and maintain cryptographic trust through certificate lifecycle management, PKI operations, and machine identity governance.
EJBCA Enterprise is Keyfactor’s Certificate Authority (CA) and PKI platform, designed for high-availability deployment and REST API automation. Available as an enterprise product, EJBCA provides X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list (CRL) distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management through both a web console and REST API. EJBCA supports deployment on-premises, in containers, or on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2).
The partnership between AWS and Keyfactor brings together AWS managed services (Amazon Bedrock, AWS Secrets Manager, Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS)) with PKI infrastructure that supports certificate lifecycle management, automated enrollment, and real-time revocation. This combination addresses a gap in the AI agent ecosystem. While AWS provides the compute, storage, and AI inference layers, Keyfactor provides the cryptographic identity layer that binds agents to verifiable, revocable, short-lived credentials. This joint reference architecture, developed collaboratively by the AWS and Keyfactor engineering teams, demonstrates how to integrate these technologies. You can adapt the patterns shown here to your own multi-agent deployments.
Solution overview
The architecture implements three authentication layers, each addressing a different trust boundary in the agent communication chain. These three layers use the four security mechanisms introduced earlier: signed envelopes for proof-of-possession, delegation assertions for credential-free authorization, audience-scoped tokens for exposure limitation, and OCSP for real-time revocation. The mechanisms combine across layers as shown in the following table.
| Layer | Trust boundary | Mechanism | Validates | 
| 1. User Auth | User to System | OAuth + X.509 cert + delegation minting | User identity, credential binding | 
| 2. Agent-to-Agent | Agent to Agent | Signed envelopes (PoP + nonce + timestamp) | Caller identity, request freshness, no replay | 
| 3. MCP Auth | Agent to Tool Server | Scoped token + envelope + delegation | All identities, authorization chain, OCSP | 
Figure 1 shows the three authentication layers and how credentials flow between the user, agents, and the MCP tool server. The diagram illustrates the separation between user credentials (which stay in the login flow), agent credentials (scoped per agent), and the delegation chain that connects them.
Figure 2 illustrates the detailed traffic flow during a typical user session. It shows the sequence of authentication steps from login through certificate issuance, agent delegation, tool invocation, and session cleanup.
AWS services used
The following AWS services form the foundation of the reference architecture.
| Service | Purpose | 
| Amazon Bedrock | LLM inference through Strands Agents SDK | 
| Amazon RDS for MySQL | Application database accessed through MCP tools | 
| Amazon Simple Email Service (Amazon SES) | Email delivery for the Email Agent | 
| AWS Secrets Manager | Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata | 
| Amazon EC2 | Hosts Keycloak IDP and EJBCA PKI server | 
Solution walkthrough
The following steps walk through each component of the architecture, from initial user login through to session cleanup. Each step builds on the previous one, establishing a chain of trust that connects the human user to the final tool execution.
Prerequisites
- An active AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock, Amazon RDS for MySQL, Amazon SES, and AWS Secrets Manager.
- Keycloak 26.2 or later (required for RFC 8693 standard token exchange. Previous versions use a legacy exchange that is incompatible).
- Keyfactor EJBCA Enterprise with REST API V1 and an OCSP responder configured.
- EJBCA API administrator certificate (api-admin.p12) for REST API authentication.
- Python 3.9+ development environment.
- Familiarity with X.509 certificates, OCSP, OAuth 2.0, RSA digital signatures, and PKCS#12 key stores.
Step 1: User login, certificate issuance, and delegation minting
The login flow establishes the user’s identity through three mechanisms and then delegates authority to the AI agents without sharing the user’s credentials. This separation is critical: Agents receive proof of authorization without ever holding the user’s private key or full-session OAuth token.
First, the application authenticates the user against Keycloak using an OAuth 2.0 password grant, receiving a full-session access token and refresh token. Immediately after, the application performs an RFC 8693 token exchange to obtain a downscoped token. This token’s audience is restricted to the MCP server. Only this limited token is handed to agents. If it’s inadvertently exposed, it can’t access any other service in the organization.
Second, the application generates an RSA 2048+ key pair locally and submits a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll REST API endpoint. EJBCA signs the CSR and returns the certificate. The application bundles the certificate and private key into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager. The private key never leaves the application boundary. It is not sent to EJBCA, not shared with agents, and not stored on the filesystem. Three agent certificates are issued using the same CSR-based flow, one per agent role.
Third, the user’s private key signs a delegation assertion. This is a JSON document listing the SHA-256 fingerprints of all three agent certificates, along with the user’s subject name, issuance time, and expiry. This delegation proves that the user authorized these specific agents to act on their behalf. Agents carry this delegation instead of the user’s certificate.
Step 2: Agent-to-agent signed envelopes
When the orchestrator agent routes a request to a sub-agent (such as the MySQL agent or Email agent), it does not simply pass its certificate for identification. Instead, it signs the entire request payload, including the tool name, arguments, a timestamp, and a cryptographically random nonce, using its private key with RSA-PSS-SHA256. The resulting signed envelope provides proof-of-possession. The receiving agent can verify that the caller actually holds the private key corresponding to the presented certificate.
The receiving agent performs six validation checks on the envelope before processing the request:
- Signature verification: Proves the sender possesses the private key (proof-of-possession).
- Timestamp freshness: The envelope must be within ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (default 60 seconds) of the current time.
- Nonce uniqueness: The ReplayCache rejects any previously seen nonce, preventing request replay.
- CA chain validation: The sender’s certificate must chain to the trusted CA (UserCA.pem).
- Role authorization: The certificate CN’s role suffix must be in ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES for this agent.
- OCSP revocation check: A real-time check against EJBCA confirms the certificate has not been revoked.
If the orchestrator needs to re-send the same prompt (for example, after a transient failure), it must create a new envelope with a fresh nonce. Old envelopes can’t be replayed, even by the legitimate sender.
Step 3: MCP server authentication
The MCP server (FastMCP) is the final trust boundary before any database operation runs. It performs four validation checks on every tool invocation, implementing defense-in-depth. Even if one credential is subject to unauthorized access, the remaining checks prevent unauthorized operations.
The authentication sequence:
- Token introspection: A POST to the Keycloak /token/introspect endpoint verifies the token is active and its audience contains “mcp-server”. A full-session token without the correct audience is rejected.
- Envelope verification: The agent’s signed envelope is validated for signature correctness, timestamp freshness, nonce uniqueness, CA chain trust, role match (mysql-agent), and OCSP non-revocation.
- Delegation verification: The user’s delegation assertion is validated. The signature proves the user’s key holder authorized this delegation, the calling agent’s certificate fingerprint appears in the authorized list, and the user’s certificate is checked through OCSP.
- Identity cross-check: The token username, the delegation subject, and the agent certificate CN prefix must all match. This confirms a single consistent identity chain from user through to tool execution.
Step 4: Replay prevention
Every signed envelope carries a unique nonce, a 128-bit cryptographically random hex string generated with Python’s secrets module. The ReplayCache is a thread-safe in-memory store that remembers every nonce until its freshness window expires (2x ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS). If the same nonce appears in a second request, the envelope is immediately rejected, even if its signature is valid and the timestamp is fresh.
The timestamp validation complements the nonce check. An envelope’s timestamp must be within ENVELOPE_MAX_AGE_SECONDS (default 60 seconds) of the server’s current time. Together, these mechanisms address four unauthorized access scenarios:
- Recorded replay: An unauthorized user captures a valid envelope and resubmits it later. The nonce was already seen.
- Delayed delivery: An envelope intercepted in transit arrives after the freshness window. The timestamp check fails.
- Stale request reuse: An old envelope cached by a proxy is resubmitted. Both nonce and timestamp checks fail.
- Precomputed forgery: An unauthorized user cannot predict future nonces to pre-sign envelopes.
Step 5: Client-side key generation
A critical security property of this architecture is that private keys are generated locally and never transmitted to any external system. The application generates RSA 2048+ key pairs using the Python cryptography library. It constructs a CSR containing only the public key and subject information, and sends only the CSR to EJBCA through the pkcs10enroll endpoint.
EJBCA validates the CSR, applies the certificate profile (7-day validity, key usage constraints), signs it with the CA key, and returns the issued certificate. The application then bundles the locally held private key with the returned certificate into a PKCS12 container and stores it in AWS Secrets Manager.
This design provides several security properties:
- The user’s private key is used only at login to sign the delegation assertion. It’s never shared with agents.
- Each agent’s private key is used only by that agent to sign envelopes. It’s never shared between agents.
- EJBCA never sees or stores private keys. It operates purely as a certificate authority.
- If Secrets Manager is subject to unauthorized access, the PKCS12 password (stored separately) adds an additional layer.
- Key material can be rotated independently by re-enrolling with a new CSR at next login.
Step 6: Complete logout and credential revocation
Logout triggers a revocation cascade that immediately invalidates all outstanding credentials. The sequence results in no remaining valid credentials after completion:
- Revoke user certificate in EJBCA: This immediately invalidates all outstanding delegations, because delegation verification checks the user’s certificate through OCSP in real time.
- Revoke all three agent certificates: This invalidates all outstanding signed envelopes, since envelope verification includes OCSP.
- Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager: Using ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery for immediate removal with no recovery window.
- Terminate Keycloak session: Invalidates the downscoped token through the session termination endpoint.
The revocation cascade is the key security property. Revoking a single user certificate at the PKI layer promptly revokes all downstream agent authority without needing to individually revoke tokens, delete sessions, or contact each agent. OCSP provides the propagation mechanism, and because every request checks OCSP, the effect is immediate.
Security considerations
The design choices in this architecture address several security properties that are important for production multi-agent deployments.
Private key isolation. The user’s private key exists only during the login flow and is used solely to sign the delegation. Agent keys are scoped per-agent and never shared. No key material crosses trust boundaries.
Delegation compared to credential sharing. Agents prove their authority through a cryptographic chain (delegation to agent fingerprint to envelope signature) without ever holding user credentials. If an agent key is exposed, only that agent’s key is revealed, not the user’s.
Audience-scoped tokens. RFC 8693 token exchange produces a token accepted only by the MCP server. An inadvertently disclosed downscoped token cannot authenticate against Keycloak admin APIs, other services, or even a different MCP server instance.
Replay prevention. The combination of per-request nonces and a 60-second freshness window confirms that every request is single-use and time-bound. The ReplayCache is thread-safe and self-cleaning.
Fail-closed design. Every validation failure results in immediate denial. OCSP unreachable: deny. Invalid signature: deny. Expired timestamp: deny. Replayed nonce: deny. Wrong audience: deny. There’s no graceful degradation for security checks.
Revocation cascade. Revoking one user certificate promptly invalidates all delegations, all agent authority, and all outstanding envelopes. This is propagated through real-time OCSP without requiring individual credential cleanup.
Forward-only trust chain. The ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES map enforces that only orchestrator-agent can call mysql-agent and email-agent. Sub-agents cannot call each other, can’t call upward to the orchestrator, and cannot impersonate the user.
AI governance considerations
The PKI architecture provides built-in behavior boundaries for the AI agents in this system. Production deployments should use Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to enforce content filtering, topic avoidance, and grounding checks on agent responses, alongside the PKI-based access controls described in this post.
- Tool boundaries: The AI agent operates under strict tool constraints. It can only invoke pre-defined MCP tools (execute_sql, describe_table, list_tables). The agent can’t execute arbitrary code or access resources outside its certificate scope.
- Human oversight: All agent actions are logged and auditable. AWS CloudTrail captures AWS API calls, and the MCP server logs every validated tool invocation with the full identity chain (user, agent, timestamp, and operation).
- Data handling: User queries and results stay within the authenticated session boundary. The audience-scoped token confines data access to the specific MCP server instance.
- Certificate-based behavior boundaries: Agents can only invoke tools they hold valid certificates for. An agent without a mysql-agent certificate cannot access the database, regardless of what the LLM might generate as instructions.
Extending the architecture
You can extend this architecture to support additional agent types, horizontal scaling, and multi-tenant isolation. The following paragraphs describe the most common extension points.
- To add new agent types, you only need to add an entry in ALLOWED_CALLER_ROLES. Certificates are automatically issued at login, and the delegation assertion dynamically includes the new agent’s fingerprint. No infrastructure changes are required.
- For horizontal scaling, you can deploy EJBCA’s OCSP responder in high-availability mode behind a load balancer. AWS Secrets Manager supports high request rates suitable for this workload. The ReplayCache can be backed by Amazon ElastiCache for distributed deployments.
- To harden the architecture for production, you can use hardware security module (HSM)-backed EJBCA signing keys through AWS CloudHSM or an on-premises HSM. OCSP response stapling reduces validation latency, and Certificate Transparency logs provide a full audit trail of issued certificates.
- For multi-tenant deployments, you can create per-tenant Certificate Authorities or per-tenant delegation authorities for cryptographic tenant isolation. Combined with per-tenant AWS accounts, this delivers strong isolation between tenants.
- You can also complement PKI-based agent identity with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Use PKI for agent-to-agent authentication and IAM for AWS service authorization. The two systems work independently, providing defense in depth.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, remove the resources created during this walkthrough:
- Delete the Amazon RDS for MySQL instance (or the AWS CloudFormation stack if you used the scripted setup).
- Delete all secrets from AWS Secrets Manager, including user certificates and agent certificates under the mcp/ prefix.
- Remove the verified sender email address from Amazon SES.
- Terminate the Amazon EC2 instances running Keycloak and EJBCA (if deployed for this demonstration).
- Revoke and delete all test certificates in EJBCA by using the EJBCA admin console or REST API.
- Remove the Keycloak realm (mcp-realm) and associated clients.
- If you used the scripted setup, run ./scripts/cleanup.sh (Linux) or ./scripts/cleanup.bat (Windows) to automate these steps.
Conclusion
In this post, we demonstrated a reference architecture for securing AI agent communications using X.509 PKI with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS services. The architecture addresses the fundamental identity gap in multi-agent AI systems through four complementary mechanisms:
- Signed request envelopes provide cryptographic proof-of-possession on every inter-agent call, making it significantly harder for an unauthorized party to forge an agent’s identity or replay its requests.
- User-signed delegation assertions decouple authorization from credential sharing. Agents prove they are authorized to act on the user’s behalf without holding the user’s private key or full-session token.
- RFC 8693 audience-scoped tokens limit the scope of exposure from any token disclosure to a single service boundary.
- Real-time OCSP revocation checking confirms that credential revocation takes immediate effect across the entire system. Revoking one user certificate promptly ends all downstream agent authority.
This architecture is framework-agnostic. While we demonstrated it with the AWS Strands Agents SDK and FastMCP, the same PKI patterns apply to LangChain, CrewAI, AutoGen, or any other multi-agent framework that uses tool protocols. As AI agents proliferate and gain access to increasingly sensitive operations, agent identity infrastructure moves from optional to essential.

articles.title: Trade Republic geht unter die Versicherer: Das steckt dahinter
articles.text:
Trade Republic geht unter die Versicherer: Das steckt dahinter
Gerade erst ist Trade Republic mit einem kostenlosen Angebot in den Wettbewerb um das kommende Altersvorsorgedepot eingestiegen, da zeigt sich: Das Fintech hat für den staatlich geförderten Riester-Nachfolger wohl noch weitere Pläne.
Wie der Branchendienst “Versicherungsmonitor” als erster berichtete, hat der Berliner Neobroker unter dem Namen „Justinian Versicherungs AG“ einen eigenen Lebensversicherer gegründet. Damit wäre Trade Republic künftig auch in der Lage, eine Variante des Altersvorsorgedepots anzubieten, die eine Garantie-Komponente enthält.
Kampf um die besten Konditionen
Derzeit tobt ein Preiskampf um die Konditionen für die neue private Rentenvorsorge. Das Altersvorsorgedepot ist als Nachfolger der Riester-Rente geplant und soll Anfang 2027 starten. Der Staat steuert dann bis zu 540 Euro jährlich bei, wenn Sparer über Fonds, ETFs oder Anleihen fürs Alter vorsorgen.
Anbieter eines geförderten Altersvorsorgedepots müssen ein sogenanntes Standarddepot bereitstellen, bei dem die Effektivkosten maximal ein Prozent betragen dürfen. Das Geld wird dabei nach gesetzlichen Vorgaben auf einen Aktien- und einen Anleihen-Fonds verteilt.
Daneben bieten viele Broker auch eine günstige Variante für Selbstentscheider, bei der Kunden die Anlagen selbst aus einem Bündel von Aktien-, Anleihen- und Rohstoff-ETFs, Fonds oder ELTIFs auswählen können.
Einen gesetzlichen Kostendeckel gibt es hierfür nicht, aber aktuell werben viele Anbieter auch bei dieser Variante mit günstigen Einstiegsprodukten, in der Hoffnung, die neuen Kunden dann langfristig an sich zu binden. Insbesondere Neobroker unterbieten sich gerade mit dem Versprechen, beide Varianten weit unter dem vorgesehenen 1-Prozent-Deckel für das Standarddepot anbieten zu wollen.
Erst in der vergangenen Woche kündigte Trade Republic an, das Altersvorsorgedepot sogar komplett kostenlos anzubieten. Dazu verzichtet der Neobroker ähnlich wie Konkurrenten auf Depot- und Ausführungskosten. Darüber hinaus werden bei ausgewählten ETFs aber auch keine laufenden Verwaltungsgebühren fällig, die normalerweise bei bis zu 0,2 Prozent liegen. Bei diesen ausgewählten Fonds werden die Gebühren sogar reinvestiert, ähnlich wie es Trade Republic bei den Kinderdepots macht.
Was der Einstieg ins Versicherungsgeschäft bedeutet
Die Gründung eines eigenen Versicherers deutet darauf hin, dass Trade Republic bald ein Altersvorsorgedepot mit Beitragsgarantie anbieten könnte. Solchen Produkten zahlen Kunden im Rentenalter mindestens 80 oder 100 Prozent des investierten Geldes aus, selbst wenn es gerade einen Börsencrash gab. Diese Sicherheit geht jedoch zulasten der Rendite, da ein großer Teil des Geldes in sichere, niedrig verzinste Anlagen fließt, um die Garantie zu finanzieren.
Vor allem Kunden, die bisher einen Riester-Vertrag bespart haben, könnten auf ein Depot mit Beitragsgarantie umsteigen, da sie diese Absicherung bereits gewohnt sind. Auch ältere Sparer, die kurz vor der Rente stehen, oder sicherheitsorientierte Anleger, die Börsenturbulenzen schlecht aushalten, könnten so ein Produkt bevorzugen.
Für Trade Republic eröffnet sich damit ein neuer Kundenkreis, der bisher von klassischen Versicherern bedient wurde. Zu welchen Konditionen der Neobroker diese Variante des Altersvorsorgedepots anbieten wird, ist jedoch noch nicht bekannt.

articles.title: Disrupt Africa, Touch Inspiration launch accelerator to help non-technical founders build and launch apps - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Disrupt Africa has partnered with Kenya-based digital product and technology company Touch Inspiration to launch Disrupt Launchpad, an app development accelerator that helps non-technical founders turn their ideas into working applications and bring them to market.
Founded in 2014, Disrupt Africa is the leading news platform dedicated to the African tech startup ecosystem, and a producer of research publications and podcasts.
Touch Inspiration was founded in 2017 and helps entrepreneurs and businesses turn their ideas into working digital products. The company specialises in developing web and mobile applications, AI-powered solutions and business platforms, taking products from defined requirements through development and launch.
The two organisations have joined forces to launch Disrupt Launchpad, a programme designed for entrepreneurs who have a clear app idea but lack the technical skills, team or resources to bring it to life. Through Touch Inspiration, founders can get their apps professionally built and launched at startup-friendly rates, while Disrupt Africa helps put those products in front of a wider audience of potential users, customers and investors.
“We meet so many people who are inspired to create something, but don’t know how to bring it to life. What makes this partnership with Disrupt Africa so exciting is that we get to help those people build their apps and, just as importantly, get them in front of the people who will actually use them. It’s one thing to have a great idea, but seeing it come to life and reach the market is where the real value is realised,” said Robert M., founder of Touch Inspiration.
“The whole point of Disrupt Africa has always been to make entrepreneurship accessible to everyone, and with this partnership with Robert M. and the amazing team at Touch Inspiration we’re going right in at the start. Funding is important, networking is key, but being able to build your great idea in the first place is absolutely essential,” said Tom Jackson, co-founder of Disrupt Africa. “This programme will help you build, and launch, and put you in a strong position to turn it into a success.”
Aspiring entrepreneurs and existing startups with clear app ideas are invited to apply through Disrupt Launchpad. The programme offers startup-friendly development rates, while selected ventures may even qualify for an equity-based partnership, reducing the upfront cost of getting their applications built.

articles.title: Windows Server 2025 gets support for quick machine recovery
articles.text:
Microsoft announced that IT administrators can now use quick machine recovery on Windows Server 2025 after installing the October 2026 security update.
Quick machine recovery (QMR) lets IT admins fix critical boot failures with targeted Windows Update fixes without physical access to affected systems.
When enabled, it boots into the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) and launches the QMR Tool if Windows 11 fails to start because of a configuration change or a new driver. It then sends crash data to Microsoft, which can remotely fix issues by adjusting settings or removing problematic drivers or updates.
"With the October 2026 security update, quick machine recovery extends to Windows Server 2025," the company said in a message center update.
"Quick machine recovery is designed to help restore devices experiencing widespread boot issues by using the Windows Recovery Environment (WinRE) to search Windows Update for applicable remediations."
On Windows Server 2025, cloud remediation is disabled by default, but admins can enable it via Group Policy under Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Quick Machine Recovery to retrieve and apply cloud-sourced remediation.
For local configuration, admins must sign in to the target server with administrator permissions and use the Local Group Policy Editor. In domain configurations, they can use Group Policy Management on a Windows Server or an administration computer, but they also need permissions to edit the GPO and link it to the intended organizational unit (OU).
To disable QMR through Group Policy, admins have to explicitly turn off 'Enable Cloud Remediation' to prevent cloud-sourced remediation and disable 'Enable Auto Remediation' to block automatic application of local remediation packages.
This can be done by going through the following steps:
- Open the local policy or domain GPO that manages the target Windows Server 2025 computers.
- Go to Computer Configuration > Administrative Templates > System > Quick Machine Recovery.
- Open Enable Cloud Remediation, select Disabled, and select Apply, then OK.
- Open Enable Auto Remediation, select Disabled, and select Apply, then OK.
- (Optional) Verify the effective configuration.
Microsoft introduced quick machine recovery in November 2024 as part of its Windows Resiliency Initiative at Ignite 2024, in response to a July 2024 outage caused by a buggy CrowdStrike Falcon update that rendered millions of Windows devices unbootable.
It began testing in late March 2025, rolling it out to Windows Insiders in the Beta Channel. In November, it also began testing a faster version that now runs a single scan to fix systems with boot problems, rather than looping through solutions.
