articles.title: The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
articles.text:
The Download: the claim shaking up AI and the internet’s agent problem
Plus: The US Army is trying to get AI agents to hack its enemies.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
“We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.
Cammarata claims that LLMs might be far easier to understand, and thus to monitor and control, than people previously thought. If true, it’s a huge deal. But not everyone is convinced.
I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. We discussed what he thinks researchers are getting wrong, what his work actually shows, and why skeptics aren’t ready to celebrate just yet.
Read the exclusive interview to find out what Cammarata’s claims could mean for AI.
—Will Douglas Heaven
Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
Until recently, you could split internet users into just two categories: bots and people. But personal AI agents are slowly but surely disrupting that divide by taking on online tasks, from booking flights to reserving hotel rooms. Meta’s Muse alone was downloaded 5 million times in its first month.
The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents.
If that demand keeps rising, the internet could be redesigned for agents rather than people. Find out what that could mean for the rest of us.
—James O'Donnell
This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Moment Energy and its work to repurpose used EV batteries
Moment Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.
Demand for energy storage is surging, with capacity expected to grow eightfold in the next decade. To meet that demand, Moment Energy wants to shortcut a supply chain that now flows largely through China by domestically repurposing EV batteries into new grid-connected storage systems.
Ongoing trade battles between the US and China have been a shot in the arm for the company. And soon, it will be able to categorize its repurposed batteries as domestic products in both Canada and the US, where it’s building its next plant.
Learn more about how Moment stands to gain from the current climate.
—Emma Foehringer Merchant
Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from carbon dioxide batteries to helium-cooled nuclear reactors.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

Documents outline a plan to let software find and disable targets. (Intercept)
+ But experts warn they could damage unintended systems. (Gizmodo)

+ “Humans in the loop” in AI warfare is an illusion. (MIT Technology Review)

A filing cites royal-family contacts and a military-funded flight. (BBC)
+ The FBI says he had a folder called “Saudi Gov Docs.” (Ars Technica)
+ A judge denied him bail despite a Saudi consulate offer to pay. (CNBC)

Products built using DeepSeek’s models are also banned. (CNBC)
+ The US has sanctioned China’s Y Combinator over AI theft. (Bloomberg $)
+ What’s next for Chinese open-source AI? (MIT Technology Review) 
4 Europe is trying to build its own version of Starlink 
Four major carriers are exploring a joint bid for spectrum. (Verge)
+ A stratospheric airship has tested a cell tower in the sky. (Ars Technica) 
+ Stratospheric internet could take off this year. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Trump officials asked a federal cyber agency to hack voting machines
CISA employees turned down the request. (ProPublica)
+ AI persuasion is entering elections. (MIT Technology Review) 
6 US fossil fuel projects are gaining ground again
The White House is backing gas as data center demand rises. (Verge)
+ A climate report row could give polluters a reprieve. (New Scientist $)
7 El Niño is causing sea levels to rise rapidly 
Coastal flooding could worsen from Alaska to Chile. (New Scientist $)

New research shows they produce more lasting breakthroughs. (Nature)

Drivers don’t want to sacrifice convenience or familiarity. (Atlantic $)

Hotspots are banning them to protect peace and privacy. (Guardian)
Quote of the day
“They all truly hate each other, and they’re all trying to make as much money as they can as fast as they can.”
—JB Pritzker, governor of Illinois, tells The Verge that the fierce competition between AI companies is complicating efforts to regulate the industry.
One more thing
Is fake grass a bad idea? The AstroTurf wars are far from over.
In 2001, Americans installed just over 7 million square meters of synthetic turf. By 2024, that number was 79 million square meters—enough to carpet all of Manhattan and then some. The increase worries folks who study microplastics and environmental pollution.
While the plastic-making industry insists that synthetic fields are safe if properly installed, lots of researchers think that isn’t so. Find out why AstroTurf has ignited heated debates.

articles.title: Motorola desafía a Xiaomi: su próximo móvil tendrá una batería gigante y precio rompedor
articles.text:
Motorola prepara el lanzamiento de un nuevo móvil de gama media con gran autonomía. A unos meses de presentar el Moto G47, el fabricante tiene todo listo para desvelar el Moto G47 Power, la variante que llega con una batería de mayor capacidad. Tal y como ha ocurrido con las generaciones anteriores, Motorola tomará como base el G47, por lo que este terminal comparte muchas de sus características.
Una filtración reciente ha revelado todas las especificaciones, incluido el precio. De acuerdo con GSMArena, el Moto G47 Power llegará con una batería de 7.000 mAh que es prácticamente idéntica a la que vimos en el G37 Power. Esta garantiza hasta dos días completos de uso sin necesidad de conectarlo y admite carga rápida TurboPower de 30 W por cable.
Por fuera, el Moto G47 Power ofrece una pantalla LCD de 6,67 pulgadas con resolución de 1604 x 720 píxeles y tasa de refresco de 120 Hz y recubrimiento Gorilla Glass 7i. Bajo el capó encontraremos un procesador MediaTek Dimensity 6300 de ocho núcleos junto con una configuración de 4 GB de RAM y 128 GB de almacenamiento interno. La filtración no menciona otras variantes, aunque podríamos esperar una de 8 GB + 128 GB, si es que la escasez de memoria lo permite.
En el apartado fotográfico tampoco habrá muchos cambios, ya que el Moto G47 Power usaría la misma configuración que su hermano menor. El módulo trasero incluye una cámara principal de 108 megapíxeles con zoom de 3 aumentos sin pérdida de calidad y una lente macro dedicada para fotografía de cerca. Este modelo no incluye gran angular y la cámara frontal solo alcanza los 8 MP, que son suficientes para las selfies y las videollamadas.
Moto G47 Power vs Moto G47: ¿qué cambia?
La diferencia fundamental entre ambos modelos está en la autonomía. El Moto G47 Power eleva la capacidad de la batería hasta los 7.000 mAh, mientras que el Moto G47 se queda en los 5.200 mAh. Otro ajuste importante lo vemos en la carga rápida, que pasa de 20 W a 30 W por cable. El resto de especificaciones se mantiene idéntico, incluidas las cámaras y el procesador.
Si lo comparamos con el G37 Power que se presentó en abril de este año, la única diferencia es el tiempo adicional de soporte que obtendrás. A juzgar por las filtraciones, el Moto G47 Power sería prácticamente idéntico, por lo que podrías comprar esta variante y ahorrarte unos cuantos euros.
De acuerdo con el último rumor, el Moto G47 Power tendría un precio de salida cercano a los 270 euros para la versión de 4 GB + 128 GB. El móvil se venderá en dos acabados: uno negro y otro verde turquesa con el acabado fino de Pantone que caracteriza a la marca. Por el momento no hay detalles sobre su disponibilidad, aunque está confirmado que lo veremos en España, puesto que Motorola publicó su documentación sobre la Etiqueta Energética Europea hace unos días.

articles.title: 👨🏿🚀TechCabal Daily – Nedbank checks into Nairobi - TechCabal
articles.text:
Good morning. ☀️ ️️️
If procrastinating on buying your Moonshot ticket were an Olympic sport, some of you would be bringing home medals. 🥇 We’re now eight days out, and have decided to reward even the latecomers: all Moonshot tickets are 30% off until October 24.
On October 28–29, the National Theatre in Lagos, Nigeria, will convene the founders, investors, operators, and builders shaping Africa’s tech ecosystem.
Read smart insights about Francophone Africa’s tech ecosystem—weekly.
M&A
Nedbank clears the final hurdle to take control of NCBA
Nine months after putting R13.9 billion ($855.5 million) on the table, Nedbank is finally at the end of its NCBA takeover.
The South African lender’s offer to acquire 66% of NCBA Group, one of East Africa’s largest banking groups, is now unconditional after clearing the remaining regulatory approvals.
Settlement begins this week, with the transfer of shares to Nedbank expected from early November. NCBA will become a Nedbank subsidiary, but keep its name, Nairobi headquarters, management, and Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) listing, according to its Monday filings.
Catch up: Nedbank first announced the deal in January. In February, Kenya’s capital markets regulator allowed it to buy 66% without making an offer for the entire company. The tender opened in May, and by July, shareholders had offered 79.9% of NCBA’s shares, more than Nedbank wanted. Those offers had to be scaled back to 66%.
Shareholders who sell will receive 80% of their payment in newly issued Nedbank shares and 20% in cash. The remaining 34% of NCBA will stay in public hands.
Between the lines: Nedbank is buying more than a Kenyan bank. NCBA already operates across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania and Rwanda, with digital businesses in Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire. Its digital business accounted for 32% of group profit in 2025, and it disbursed KES 1.4 trillion ($10.8 billion) in digital loans.
The deal also shows how Nedbank’s Africa strategy has changed. In 2025, it sold its 21% stake in Ecobank and shifted towards markets where it can control the banking operation rather than remain a minority investor. NCBA gives it that control, plus customers, licences, and infrastructure across East Africa, without building them country by country.
What to watch: Nedbank has previously talked about using NCBA as a springboard into Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Now it has the platform to try.
Happy customer service week.
Your success and ours are the same story. Happy Customer Service Week. This year’s theme is The Extra Mile, and it’s the only way we know how to do this. Visit: fincra.com.
Fintech
Why Onafriq shut down its Nigerian agent banking business
In hindsight, it is not hard to see the play Onafriq, the pan-African payments company, was making when it expanded into Nigeria by acquiring Baxi in 2021.
Nigeria still relied heavily on cash, and Baxi already had more than 90,000 agents. Onafriq could enter with a ready-made distribution network instead of spending years building one.
The timing looked good, too. OPay and Moniepoint had begun building large agent networks in 2019, while PalmPay entered agent banking later. In 2021, Baxi was already one of Nigeria’s biggest independent agent networks, giving Onafriq an early lead over some newer competitors.
But the lead did not hold. By the end of 2024, PalmPay reportedly had more than 700,000 agents, while Moniepoint had over 800,000 point-of-sale (PoS) terminals. But as of 2025, Baxi had just over 460,000 agents, paling in comparison. In October, it finally decided to shut down the business, months after trying to sell Baxi.
Between the lines: Agent banking became a scale game. Rivals poured money into terminals, agent recruitment, and incentives, making it easier to close the distribution gap. At the same time, agents could work with several providers, making a large network less defensible than it first appeared.
The economics also changed. More terminals entered the market much faster than transaction volumes grew, so providers competed over the same payments.
Meanwhile, account-to-account (A2A) transfers—direct bank payments—gave customers another way to move money without visiting an agent.
Onafriq’s attempt to sell Baxi before shutting it down shows that the problem was bigger than one bad year. The company had already decided the agent business no longer fit where it wanted to put capital.
Zoom out: Onafriq bought Baxi partly because physical distribution was scarce. Five years later, the market had plenty. Being early gave Baxi a head start, but it did not stop competitors from catching up and, eventually, passing it.
Ten years of telling African tech stories.
Class of 2016, stand up! Meet the storytellers behind a decade of storytelling for African tech. 230+ startups, VCs, and more. From first cheques to unicorns. Have a story to tell? Let’s make it count. #TheWimbarts
Ecommerce
South African union want Shein and Temu banned to protect local jobs
Behind the low-cost tops you see on Shein and Temu is a dispute over how foreign shopping platforms compete with local businesses, and what that means for the people who make and sell clothes in South Africa.
What happened? The Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), the country’s largest trade union federation, wants South Africa to ban Shein and Temu. It backed a proposal from the Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers’ Union (SACTWU), which says the platforms hurt local jobs by undercutting domestic retailers and manufacturers.
Explain like I’m new here: Shein entered South Africa in 2020, while Temu followed in 2024. Both sell directly to consumers online, offering a wide range of clothing and other goods at prices that traditional retailers can find hard to match. A 2025 study by the Localisation Support Fund (LSF), a South African organisation focused on strengthening local production, estimated that Shein and Temu generated R7.3 billion ($444 million) in South African sales in 2024, equivalent to roughly 3.6% of the country’s retail market.
Can South Africa ban them? South Africa has already taken steps to narrow the tax advantage to benefit some low-value imports. Previously, goods worth less than R500 ($30.41) were cheaper to bring into the country. In 2024, the South African Revenue Service (SARS), the country’s taxman, introduced value-added tax (VAT) on low-value imports and subsequently ended their special customs-duty treatment.
However, COSATU’s proposal goes further than changing tax rules. If both platforms are banned, some consumers could pay more without automatically creating new jobs in local factories. South Africa still has to work out how to protect local jobs while allowing competition and preserving affordable choices for shoppers. Closing tax loopholes is one part of that effort; making local manufacturers more competitive is another.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
Telecoms
Cameroon wants to put more Internet on its electricity poles
Building a fibre-optic network requires a place to lay the fibre, permission to use the land, and a lot of money. But what if the poles that already carry electricity could also help carry the Internet? Cameroon is exploring that option.
What happened? On October 16, Camtel, Cameroon’s state-owned telecoms operator, and Socadel, the country’s electricity provider, signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to explore sharing infrastructure for fibre deployment.
How would it work? Camtel has the fibre network and telecoms expertise, and Socadel has electricity infrastructure, such as utility poles and rights-of-way. Instead of Camtel building entirely new infrastructure to carry fibre cables, it could attach overhead cables to suitable electricity poles and use existing routes to reach more locations. The two companies will now study whether they can combine those assets for faster Internet access.
Cameroon has tried this before: In 2023, the government transferred about 812 kilometres (km) of overhead fibre that Eneo, Socadel’s predecessor, had installed on electricity poles along Cameroon’s southern interconnected grid to Camtel.
That network served major cities including Douala and Yaoundé, its capital, and added to Camtel’s fibre infrastructure, which stood at about 12,000km. The latest agreement focuses on closer infrastructure sharing, including the possibility of incorporating fibre into future electricity infrastructure projects.
What happens next? The companies have not yet announced a nationwide rollout or a specific number of new kilometres. Their immediate job is to determine where the arrangement makes sense and identify pilot sites. If the model works, Camtel could expand fibre routes without building every supporting telecom structure from scratch, reducing deployment costs.

articles.title: “Des mesures sensées” : Anthropic veut qu’une IA ne soit stoppée que si elle risque de tuer plus de 50 personnes
articles.text:
“Des mesures sensées” : Anthropic veut qu’une IA ne soit stoppée que si elle risque de tuer plus de 50 personnes
"Des mesures sensées"
Dans un projet de loi confidentiel révélé par Politico, le créateur de Claude propose que Washington ne puisse suspendre une IA qu'en cas de danger imminent pour plus de 50 vies ou d'un milliard de dollars de dégâts. Un seul juge aurait le dernier mot.
Des émissaires d'Anthropic, la société qui développe Claude, font discrètement circuler au Capitole un projet de loi destiné à encadrer les modèles d'IA les plus avancés. Politico a éventé l'affaire le vendredi 16 octobre, sur la foi de trois sources proches des discussions et d'une copie du document. Aucun parlementaire n'a encore déposé le texte. L'entreprise en revendique pourtant la paternité, un mois après l'appel de son patron, Dario Amodei, à ralentir délibérément la course aux modèles.
	
Ce texte reprend les propositions de l'Advanced AI Framework d'Anthropic, que nous défendons auprès des élus fédéraux et des États depuis juin. Ce sont des mesures sensées que le Congrès devrait adopter.
Arme biologique, cyberattaque, perte de contrôle : les trois seuls motifs d'arrêt
Le gouvernement pourrait bloquer la sortie ou l'usage d'un modèle face à un risque "prévisible et imminent" de plus de 50 morts ou blessés graves, ou de plus d'un milliard de dollars de dommages. Encore faudrait-il que le danger découle d'une arme biologique, d'une cyberattaque ou d'une IA échappant au contrôle de son concepteur. Un scénario devenu concret en juillet, lorsqu'une IA d'OpenAI a piraté Hugging Face sans intervention humaine.
La surveillance reviendrait à des évaluateurs indépendants enregistrés auprès du département du Commerce, rémunérables par les laboratoires tant que le paiement ne dépend pas du verdict. Une menace repérée devrait être signalée au Commerce sous 72 heures. Le ministère saisirait alors un juge fédéral du district de Columbia, seul habilité à ordonner la suspension. Toute autre administration fédérale se verrait interdire de geler le développement, le déploiement ou même l'usage interne d'un modèle.
	
Il devrait exister, au bout du compte, un moyen de bloquer ou de dissuader le déploiement de modèles présentant des risques catastrophiques importants. La meilleure façon d’y parvenir reste largement à débattre, tout en évitant un pouvoir réglementaire trop étendu ou trop lourd.
Un seuil venu de Californie, des États mis sur la touche
Ce barème a déjà force de loi en Californie, gravé dans la SB 53 promulguée en septembre 2025 avec la bénédiction d'Anthropic. Les représentants Jay Obernolte (républicain) et Lori Trahan (démocrate) l'ont aussi repris dans leur projet de loi bipartisan dévoilé le 4 juin.
La préemption promet davantage de remous. Le texte écarterait certaines lois des États sur la publication des risques, l'évaluation par des tiers et le signalement d'incidents critiques. Terrain miné au Congrès, où les démocrates refusent de voir détricoter les règles de la Californie, de l'Illinois ou de New York, et où plus de 1 300 salariés des grands laboratoires réclamaient fin juillet les outils pour freiner l'IA.
L'Europe a tracé une autre route. Depuis le 2 août 2026, la Commission peut réclamer le retrait d'un modèle à risque systémique ou infliger une amende jusqu'à 3 % du chiffre d'affaires mondial, sans qu'aucun nombre de victimes figure dans le règlement.

articles.title: How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Eon built multi-cloud investigation with an MCP Gateway on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This is a guest post co-written with Roei Zavida from Eon.
Independent software vendors (ISVs) building AI-powered products need to connect agents and humans to dozens of operational tools across clouds, each with different authentication models, network boundaries, and access policies. When those tools span AWS, GCP, and Azure simultaneously, the integration surface multiplies.
This post describes how Eon used Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Eon used it to replace per-tool credentials and local Model Context Protocol (MCP) processes with a single authenticated gateway. The result gives developers and autonomous agents unified access to investigation tooling across three clouds. New engineers now reach all their investigation tools in about two minutes instead of the two days it previously took to configure credentials and local MCP servers.
About Eon
Eon provides the Autonomous Data Foundation for the AI era. The platform discovers and classifies cloud resources across AWS, Azure, and GCP. It provides continuous deduplicated backup that reduces storage costs by up to 50 percent in Eon’s internal measurements. It also detects ransomware and rogue-agent damage and delivers live grounded context for AI agents. All of this runs from a single read-only AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, storing data in Apache Parquet and Apache Iceberg formats. Founded by former AWS engineers, Eon runs its software as a service (SaaS) infrastructure on AWS.
The challenge
Eon’s internal engineering team investigates production incidents across multiple clouds and dozens of operational systems. A crashed Kubernetes pod requires checking container logs, Grafana metrics, the deployment’s GitHub pull request (PR), and cloud-provider health status within the same session.
Eon needed to address several key requirements:
- Credential consolidation — Each new tool added another integration to configure, secure, and rotate, which got harder to keep consistent as the toolset grew.
- Eliminate local MCP processes — Each developer ran several MCP servers locally, which was hard to standardize and keep current.
- Identity separation — Engineers accessed each system with role-based permissions, but there was no single place to decide which tools each person or agent could call.
- Cross-account access without networking overhead — Hosting MCP servers across multiple AWS accounts required virtual private cloud (VPC) peering or AWS PrivateLink per account, multiplying operational cost and setup time.
- Developer onboarding — New engineers spent roughly 2 days configuring credentials and local MCP servers before investigating their first incident.
- Agent access — Eon’s autonomous site reliability engineering (SRE) agent (running Claude on Amazon Bedrock) needed the same tool access as humans, but with different permissions.
Growing engineering headcount combined with a fast-expanding set of AI tools and MCPs made maintaining credentials and local MCP servers increasingly costly. This pushed Eon toward a centralized solution.
Approaches considered
Before building on AgentCore, Eon evaluated alternatives:
Option 1: Centralized proxy with custom auth
Every harness had its own proxy configuration with all the targets. A single reverse proxy aggregating all tools, with a custom authentication layer. This handled credential consolidation but only supported remote MCP and required building and maintaining tool protocol translation, session management, and authorization logic from scratch. The implementation and maintenance burden was significant.
Option 2: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is a managed gateway with built-in identity federation, Cedar-based authorization policies, and Runtime hosting that converts local MCP servers to remote HTTP endpoints. This addressed all requirements without custom infrastructure.
Eon chose Option 2 because it provided identity separation, cross-account connectivity, and policy enforcement as managed capabilities rather than code they would need to build and maintain. These were the only two options on the table.
Solution overview
Eon deployed the full Amazon Bedrock AgentCore stack: AgentCore Gateway, Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, AgentCore Runtime, and AgentCore Identity, all capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The following diagram shows how client requests flow through the authentication layer to a single gateway. The gateway routes authorized tool calls to targets hosted on AgentCore Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts.
The architecture has five layers:
Clients
Developers using Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenAI Codex connect to a single MCP URL. An autonomous SRE agent running Claude on Amazon Bedrock connects to the same gateway with a different identity.
Identity plane
Corporate single sign-on (SSO) federates through Amazon Cognito, which mints the JSON Web Token (JWT) and hands it to the gateway. Amazon API Gateway sits in front as the OAuth entry point for humans, proxying the MCP session. Agents authenticate with Cognito client_credentials grants directly against the gateway.
One gateway, least-privilege access
A single AgentCore MCP Gateway serves as the company-wide front door. Cedar policies in ENFORCE mode control which principals can invoke which tools. Read operations are available to selected groups, not every authenticated user. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only.
Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Cedar policies map each principal to permitted tools. Write operations are limited to low-impact collaboration actions, such as commenting on a PR or ticket, and production tools are read-only. The gateway evaluates every tools/call request against Cedar before forwarding to the target.
Targets
Dozens of target MCP servers exposing hundreds of tools on the one gateway, served by AgentCore Runtimes distributed across multiple AWS accounts. Each Runtime converts local stdio-based MCP servers into Streamable HTTP endpoints accessible through the gateway.
A developer opens their integrated development environment (IDE), configures one MCP URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and the gateway aggregates hundreds of tools into a single tools/list response. No local setup and no per-tool tokens.
Identity and access separation
The core security decision was enforcing read and write boundaries through Cedar policy at the gateway level.
Single gateway, policy-enforced separation:
The gateway accepts both JWT tokens (humans through corporate SSO and Cognito) and client_credentials tokens (agents). Cedar policies determine what each principal can do. Humans in approved groups get read access. Write operations require explicit Cedar permits granted only to specific agent identities.
Cedar reinforces per-tool granularity:
Cedar policies are managed as code through GitHub PRs with review comments, giving the team version control and audit trail on every permission change.
Within the gateway, Cedar policies scope tool access by SSO group, and groups map to job role. Engineers have access to development and testing environments by default. Production access follows Eon’s security and compliance controls: it is read-only, granted just-in-time through an approval process, and audited. A new team member’s group is scoped the same way, by role rather than by which service they happen to own. Because every agent action is checked against Cedar in ENFORCE mode and scoped to a least-privilege tool set, the autonomous agent operates within safe, bounded limits. It can only invoke the specific tools its identity is explicitly permitted to call.
        “Before, our internal agent couldn’t reach the same investigation tools developers used. After, it uses the same Gateway with its own identity and a tighter tool set.”
— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon
Cross-account connectivity
Eon runs Runtimes across multiple AWS accounts, organized by environment or service boundary. AgentCore Gateway reaches each Runtime through IAM cross-account role assumption. The Runtime in Account B trusts the AgentCore Gateway execution role in Account A through a standard IAM trust policy.
What this eliminated:
- VPC peering configuration and route table management across multiple AWS accounts.
- PrivateLink endpoint costs per account.
- Security group coordination between accounts.
- Days of setup per new account (replaced by one IAM trust policy, deployable in minutes).
Target attachment patterns:
Depending on each tool’s authentication and hosting model, Eon uses two primary attachment patterns. The following table summarizes when to use each pattern and gives an example.
| Pattern | When to use | Example | 
| Runtime + IAM | Tool needs a cloud hop through IAM credentials | Grafana queries, Kubernetes API calls | 
| Runtime wrapping remote MCP | Tool surface needs filtering or credential translation | Linear | 
Most targets use Runtime + IAM. Eon only wraps a remote MCP to shrink its catalog or slot in a credential the gateway cannot otherwise supply.
Investigation session flow
The following flow traces a developer investigating a production incident:
- Authentication. The developer opens Claude Code (or Cursor/Codex) and connects to the gateway MCP URL. The IDE initiates OAuth through corporate SSO. Cognito issues a JWT carrying the developer’s identity and group memberships.
- Tool discovery. The gateway aggregates `tools/list` from dozens of connected targets and returns a unified manifest of hundreds of tools to the IDE. The developer sees all available investigation tools in one list.
- Tool invocation. The developer asks: “Show me the error rate spike for the payments service in the last hour.” The IDE’s agent selects the Grafana query tool and sends a `tools/call` request.
- Policy evaluation. The gateway evaluates the request against Cedar. The developer’s group membership grants access to the Grafana tool. The request passes.
- Runtime execution. The gateway forwards the request to the Runtime hosting the Grafana MCP server (running in a separate AWS account). The Runtime authenticates to Grafana using a service credential stored in the AgentCore Identity vault, executes the query, and returns results.
- Cross-tool correlation. The agent follows up by checking the Kubernetes deployment status and the related GitHub PR, each routed to different Runtimes. The developer sees correlated results without switching tools or re-authenticating.
Lessons learned at scale
Deploying to 100+ developers and approximately 10,000 sessions surfaced production challenges:
Managing Cedar policy size
Every tool schema that the gateway pre-indexes contributes to Cedar policy size. With dozens of targets exposing extensive tool manifests, Eon’s policy grew toward the size quota. The fix: DYNAMIC listing mode for high-tool-count targets. In DYNAMIC mode, the gateway forwards tools/list calls to the MCP server at request time instead of pre-indexing schemas, adding zero bytes to the policy.
The trade-off is that semantic tool search is unavailable for DYNAMIC targets. Eon runs a hybrid configuration: DEFAULT mode for targets requiring per-user OAuth (smaller tool counts, need pre-indexed schemas for the consent flow) and DYNAMIC mode for large-catalog targets.
OAuth session binding for standard MCP clients
Claude Code, Cursor, and Codex expect the OAuth state parameter for cross-site request forgery (CSRF) protection. AgentCore uses session-URI binding. Eon built an Amazon API Gateway shim that translates between the two protocols so standard MCP clients can complete the OAuth flow without modification.
Filtering tool surfaces
Some MCP servers expose hundreds of tools. Individual developers need only a subset for their service. Eon built a Runtime wrapper that filters the tool manifest at the Runtime layer, reducing noise in tools/list responses and preventing accidental invocation of irrelevant operations. This approach also keeps those targets on DEFAULT mode, preserving semantic search and embedded features that DYNAMIC mode sacrifices.
Results
| Metric | Before AgentCore | After AgentCore | 
| Credential sets per developer | One per system/MCP server (GitHub, Grafana, cloud accounts, etc.) | 0 (one SSO login) | 
| Local MCP processes per machine | 10 | 0 | 
| Developer onboarding time | 2 days | 2 minutes | 
| Cross-account networking configs | VPC peering per account | 0 (IAM-only) | 
| Tool authorization | Configured per tool | One Cedar policy for humans and agents | 
| Developers on the platform | — | 100+ | 
| Tools accessible from one URL | — | Hundreds (across dozens of targets) | 
| Sessions processed | — | ~10,000 | 
The single-gateway architecture has run in production for Eon’s internal engineering team for several months. The clearest outcome is developer onboarding. Setting up access to the full tool set dropped from roughly two days of configuring credentials and local MCP servers to about two minutes. A new engineer connects one gateway URL, authenticates through corporate SSO, and immediately sees the tools their role allows.
The internal agent accounts for most of the time saved, because it gains access to more context through the gateway, improving investigation accuracy. Engineers save the time previously spent on AI tool setup, because they only need to connect to the gateway URL.
Eon is exploring how the same patterns can support AI capabilities in its own product.
        “AgentCore gave us one authenticated MCP Gateway instead of per-tool tokens and local MCP processes. Developers and our internal agent now reach Kubernetes, Grafana, GitHub, and our cloud accounts from a single URL.”
— Roei Zavida, Senior DevOps Engineer, Eon
Conclusion
This post described how Eon replaced per-tool credentials and local MCP processes with a single Amazon Bedrock AgentCore MCP Gateway. The result is Cedar-based identity separation, cross-account connectivity without VPC peering, and unified tool access for more than 100 developers and autonomous agents across three clouds. The single-gateway architecture, Cedar least-privilege enforcement, and hybrid DEFAULT and DYNAMIC policy mode are reusable patterns for ISVs connecting agents and developers to tools across multiple clouds.
To learn more about building on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, review these resources:
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway documentation.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime documentation.
- Getting Started with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Workshop.

Breville is, of course, responsible for some of the best coffee machines in Australia, and as a result, it can make choosing the ideal model for your household a little bit trickier. To help guide you to cafe-quality coffee at home, I’ve picked out some of my favourite models below. All of them have received an initial discount, and I’ve listed the final price after our 10% discount code has been applied.
The Barista Express Impress is one of the true standout models in Breville's repertoire. Key to its success is the Impress tamping lever, which ensures you apply the same tamping force to your ground beans each time for optimal results. It also benefits from smart dosing, which will automatically correct the grind size if the machine detects the previous espresso was under- or over-extracted.
The Barista Touch is a great choice for anyone who wants to see the drink they're hoping to make. A large colour touchscreen dominates the front panel, with a drinks menu to swipe through. Making adjustments to your coffee is a breeze, and combined with a compact integrated grinder, tamping functionality, auto-dosing, and auto milk frothing, and even Thermo Jet technology for quick heat-up times, it's practically foolproof.
The Oracle Jet is no doubt an investment, but one that's well worth it if you take your coffee seriously. It too gets a large colour touchscreen, making it easy to select and see whatever drink you want. It will grind and tamp for you (and give intelligent feedback), and can steam milk (including non-dairy) automatically too. Plus, it heats up and is ready to use in seconds.
If it's a more simple coffee maker you're after, then the Bambino Plus deserves your attention. It make look basic, but it's rather intelligent, and can take care of most of the coffee making process for you. Grind some beans into the porta filter (you will need a separate grinder), insert it into the group head and use the one-touch controls to brew. It also has a hands-free milk texturing system for expertly frothed milk, while ThermoJet technology means the machine is ready to use in seconds. There's very little you need to do other than simply enjoy the results.
The Barista Express is about as iconic as they come. It has everything one needs for cafe-quality coffee at home, including built-in grinding, dosage control and a hand tamp. You can also customise the water volume and temperature for the perfect espresso. While it's available in various colours, the three different shades of black work out to be the most affordable once our coupon code is applied.
The Oracle is one of Breville’s older machines, but it still more than holds its own against newer alternatives. It boasts automatic grinding, dosing, tamping and milk texturing, while its dual boiler means you can extract espresso and foam milk at the same time.

articles.title: The Gospel according to Peter (Thiel)
articles.text:
It’s a time of apocalyptic worldviews in Silicon Valley. The latest AI doom cycle is driven by effective altruism (EA), a philosophy that has lurked around the fringes for years but recently burst into the mainstream because its adherents are embedded across the AI industry, from Anthropic to newly appointed AI safety watchdog METR. EA is a utilitarian approach to charity premised on doing the most good for the most people over the longest time, and EA advocates see halting an AI-induced doomsday as critical to saving as many humans as possible.
The Gospel according to Peter (Thiel)
We have Peter Thiel’s secret lectures about the Antichrist.
But EA has an important and equally apocalyptic rival in the crosscutting cosmologies of the tech titans — a strain of Christianity best represented by Peter Thiel, who believes EA will bring about the Antichrist. It’s an issue on which the billionaire techno-capitalist is a self-styled expert, and, somehow, Thiel has become America’s most provocative and visible Christian theologian.
Thiel’s current fixation on the End of the World as We Know It is in theological language called eschatology, the study of the “last things.” His specific bête noire is the Antichrist, the villain of these end times scenarios. Thiel’s riffs on the Antichrist began a little over three years ago, first in a 2023 talk at the Catholic University of America but then, starting in 2025, only in closed-door, invitation-only, multipart lectures out of San Francisco. While that secrecy is frustrating for those of us interested in how uber-rich and politically powerful tech titans see the future of our world, it’s also rather savvy — no surprise from the guy who started hugely successful ventures like PayPal and Palantir. “It’s a pretty good marketing shtick if you want everybody to hear about something, not to let anybody in the room,” Thiel reportedly told one San Francisco audience last fall.
In March, he traveled to Rome for another private, four-part series on the Antichrist. Taking his shtick to the doorstep of the Vatican was guaranteed to generate publicity, and it did.
Months ago, recordings of Thiel’s lectures were leaked to The Verge. We have listened to and read transcripts of all four of these lectures, which provide a window into Thiel’s dizzying religious and sociocultural philosophy. He comes off as an intellectual magpie who somehow combines disparate elements into grave warnings against the AI and general “safetyism” that he claims precedes the Antichrist.
“Peace and safety” — the slogan of the Antichrist, according to Thiel — trouble him throughout the lectures. In the first, he wonders if we’re headed toward World War III or Cold War II, and afterward, potentially, an unjust peace, the corollary to an unjust war:
Somehow, it’s very strange how the first Cold War from ’49 to ’89 ended. But it ended with roughly what I think of as a just peace. Where somehow you didn’t have a nuclear war. And somehow our side, which I think was more the good side, basically won. And you ended up not with a perfect peace, but more or less a just peace. And so if we have World War III, it will be an unjust war. If we have Cold War II, maybe it can end in a just peace or an unjust peace.
Reflecting on this material and thinking about it, it’s obviously not written in stone and there’s a lot of different ways this stuff can go. But I keep thinking that, if you had to put odds on it, aren’t the odds that we’re trending towards the fourth quadrant this time? The fourth possibility is that Cold War II will end an unjust peace. And it’s because the Antichrist talks about Armageddon nonstop. We’re all scared to death that we’re sleepwalking into Armageddon. And then because we know World War III will be an unjust war, that pushes us very hard towards peace at any price.
What I worry about in that sort of situation is you don’t think too hard about the details of the peace and it becomes much more likely that you get an unjust peace. This is, by the way, the slogan of the Antichrist: 1 Thessalonians 5:3. It’s “peace and safety,” the unjust peace. And then what Christ says in Matthew 24:6, the full verse: “And you shall hear of wars and rumours of wars, see that ye be not troubled.” If you’re too troubled, will we always end up with very unjust peace? Or something like this.
We are publishing an analysis of these lectures now because Thiel published a version of these same ideas in the conservative religious journal First Things in July. You can read along for yourself. Titled “The Pope and the Antichrist,” the essay fills in the huge gaps in Thiel’s thinking and allows us to better understand his ideas, such as they are.
The bottom line is that after sifting through all of the arcane references and esoteric exegesis, it turns out that Thiel — a Protestant who likes to describe himself as a “heterodox Christian” — offers a fairly standard-issue American evangelical worldview, and a rather fundamentalist one at that.
He’s less a coherent religious thinker than a repackager of recognizable ideas — dressing them up in the rhetoric of a tech nerd turned theological hobbyist — which he uses to promote his own ideology. He reads everything from the Bible to pre-papal writings of a future pope to Robert Hugh Benson’s 1907 novel Lord of the World to semi-obscure Scottish poetry with an eye toward his own, sometimes shockingly literal interpretation of the Antichrist’s arrival (ideally, he should make his mark, as it were, more quickly than Jesus, who died at 33 and a few months — although Thiel allows in his third lecture that perhaps “in our gerontocracy, 66 is the new 33”). While his mashup of religious concepts and authoritative assertions on dubious interpretations make him sound like an undergrad who just took his first philosophy class and then a few too many hits on the bong, the goal of his eschatology is the same as every apocalyptic visionary: to divide the world between the saved and the damned. And Thiel is, clearly, one of the righteous.
It’s notable here that Thiel is coming from the heart of what is arguably America’s latest, and most unexpected, religious revival — one concentrated among the Silicon Valley elite, like the ACTS 17 Collective, which is a reference to St. Paul’s preaching to the Greek pagans in the Acts of the Apostles and an acronym for “Acknowledging Christ in Technology and Society.” But that movement presents an upbeat message of self-improvement through Jesus, the kind that the clean-and-fit Bay Area crowd tends to embrace. Thiel’s worldview is quite unusual for Silicon Valley, and perhaps especially unexpected for a gay German billionaire; he’s right at home in the US tradition of apocalypticism.
The key to Thiel’s theological vision comes at the very opening of his most recent First Things essay, and it is his fixation on, and fear of, the Antichrist. The Antichrist has traditionally been associated with, as Thiel himself put it elsewhere, “an evil king or tyrant or anti-messiah who appears in the end times.” That is true, though Thiel says that the Antichrist interests him “mostly because nobody else is talking about it.” That would be news to anybody with even a passing familiarity with American Christianity.
In fact, the Antichrist and eschatology are arguably the central religious impulse running through American Christianity, and that focus distinguishes the US from most other churches and cultures around the globe. In America, biblical teachings tend to jump from the Ten Commandments at the beginning of the Old Testament to the Book of Revelation at the end of the New Testament. The Gospels, the Beatitudes, all that provides the key teachings of Jesus Christ is a footnote.
The enthusiasm for the end of the world has been fueled in large part by the series of sweeping revivals, or “Great Awakenings,” that have marked American religious history from the Colonial era up through the 1800s and, some would say, on into the 20th century. These revivals focused not only on personal conversion but on dark warnings about the “end times” as foretold in the New Testament, when Christ would return to gather believers up to Heaven and those who remained would be stuck facing various tribulations on their own.
For American Christians especially, the quest to save souls from eternal damnation was increasingly driven by the fear that the Second Coming was imminent, so you’d better repent now. New apocalyptic movements and sects and cults continued to flourish, from those early tent revivals through the more slickly branded televangelists and, later, the enormously popular Left Behind series of novels in the 1990s. Forecasters variously took snippets in the Book of Daniel and other prophets in the Hebrew Bible and joined them with the often phantasmagoric array of visions from the Book of Revelation, and eventually what had been a confusing jumble of end times scenarios solidified into a widely accepted timeline: increasing natural and human-made disasters, the Second Coming of Jesus, aka the Rapture of true believers, followed by the rise of the Antichrist and seven years of the Great Tribulation on Earth, ending with a final battle between good and evil and a thousand years of peace.
Peter Thiel on
Bill Gates
“One of my friends was telling me that I should not pass up on the opportunity to tell those people in San Francisco that Bill Gates is the Antichrist. I will concede that he is certainly a Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde-type character. The public Mr. Rogers, the neighborhood character — but I saw the Mr. Hyde version about a year ago, where it was just a nonstop Tourette’s, yelling swear words, almost incomprehensible what was going on. Certainly, of course, there are a lot of people who are wannabe Antichrists. They sort of want peace and safety. [He] definitely wants a Nobel Peace Prize. He would give his soul for that, no question about it.”
Eliezer Yudkowsky
“There is another book — I haven’t been able to get a copy of it because it’s coming out tomorrow, but we sort of downloaded it — that fits this thesis even better. It’s from the East Bay rationalist Eliezer Yudkowsky. I’m embarrassed about all the ways I was once affiliated with these various people and how deranged and crazy they’ve all gone. It started with these Baconian aspirations of transformative technology: We’re going to build it, it’s going to change the world. And then it’s somehow ended in some sort of blackpilled thing that’s probably more depressed and more Luddite than Greta.”
Greta Thunberg
“I think one of the ways these things always get reported is I denounce Greta as an Antichrist. And I want to be very clear, Greta is not, I mean, she’s maybe sort of a type or a shadow of an Antichrist of the sort that would be tempting, but I don’t want to flatter her too much.”
Marc Andreessen
“It’s not Andreessen, by the way. I think Andreessen is not the Antichrist. Because, you know, the Antichrist is popular.”
Phew. Now enter Peter Thiel. He is in effect the latest in a long line of apocalypticists, though his own spin is that anxieties over strange new technologies like AI will prompt demands for greater regulation and that would be a grave, almost apocalyptic, mistake. Given the latest warnings from AI leaders themselves that the new technology could risk human extinction within a decade, Thiel’s concerns run counter to what you’d expect from an apocalypticist.
Thiel’s theological justification for criticizing this instinct toward what he derides as “safetyism” rests on a verse in St. Paul’s first letter to the Thessalonians in which the apostle warns that many will promote “peace and safety” to lull people into a false sense of security and then POOF, Jesus returns and the Antichrist appears and unbelievers are doomed.
Thiel identifies promoters of this kind of peace and safety with a “restraining” force that will be a sign of the coming of the Antichrist and which will eventually pave the way for the Antichrist. He has pointed to Anthony Fauci as one example of such a “restrainer.” And now the apostles of effective altruism, with their concern for protecting as many people as possible, are in Thiel’s sights. Thiel uses the original Greek term for “the restrainer,” katechon, because of course he does. Deploying arcane terms is part of the mystery that gives apocalypticism its allure, and prophets their power.
So who is actually the Antichrist? Thiel at one point dismissed such speculations as “down-market” behavior, but he himself cannot resist weighing in. Viewing the Roman pontiff as the Antichrist or a collaborator with the Antichrist is a standard trope of end times theology, and in his First Things essay Thiel follows that tradition by suggesting that the late Pope Francis could have been the Antichrist. In previously leaked snippets of Thiel’s talks he has accused the current American pope, Leo XIV, of being a “Chinese communist agent” or, more recently, Beijing’s “useful idiot,” because he wants to regulate AI — all very Antichrist-adjacent behavior.
Thiel has a somewhat unusual relationship to the Catholic Church. True to the more anti-papist strains of his tradition, he worries that Pope Leo XIV is a “woke American pope” who will join with American liberals to create a tyrannical “Caesaro-Papist fusion.”
At the same time, the German-born Thiel’s record-breaking financial support propelled JD Vance, a relatively recent Catholic convert, to the US Senate and now a heartbeat away from the presidency. Thiel has also made a little-known Catholic literary theorist from France, René Girard, a spiritual guide for America’s political right — though only by completely inverting Girard’s famous teaching about the scapegoat mechanism by which a society eases internal divisions by blaming a single person or subgroup of people for their problems.
Thiel’s latest essay is also unusual, or inventive, in that rather than denouncing the papacy as the Whore of Babylon — a traditional fundamentalist Protestant trope drawn from a stark image in Revelation 17 — he tries to co-opt one pope, the late Benedict XVI, into his very American and Protestant worldview and against the papacy and the Catholic Church itself.
“I did not come to Rome to try to be more Catholic than the pope, but I did hope, even as a Protestant, to be more Catholic than the average Catholic,” Thiel says. His aim is to use Benedict — who resigned as pope in 2013 and died in seclusion in the Vatican in 2022 — as the one Catholic leader who understood the imminent threat of the Antichrist and the end times, the one Catholic who got it right.
Granted, Benedict is the one pope who provides Thiel with the kind of opening, however tiny, that Thiel could run with. Benedict was “a decided Augustinian,” as he wrote during his earlier days as Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger, and he shared St. Augustine’s rather pessimistic view of humankind. Thiel spends much time on the young Ratzinger’s dissertation on St. Bonaventure’s theology of history — a recondite topic in which the 13th-century Italian Franciscan rebutted the odd apocalyptic writings of Joachim of Fiore, an Italian abbot who lived a century before St. Bonaventure.
Thiel somehow reads Ratzinger’s endorsement of Bonaventure over Joachim of Fiore as a sign that Ratzinger saw the apocalypse coming rather than what Ratzinger actually wrote and meant. In his third lecture Thiel extrapolates wildly on this theme from a quote within a footnote, saying:
The TL;DR: My belief is that Benedict literally thought that the historic falling away from the church during his papacy was a sign of the end times.
Is there evidence for this? There’s all sorts of subtle hints. Writing the 1959 professorial dissertation on Bonaventure, he uses all this colorful language on the Antichrist, the Whore of Babylon. What does one make of this? In a footnote, it’s sort of the most cryptic, esoteric way to write it. Not in his own words but quoting another professor, Ratzinger wrote — obviously before he’s Pope — quoting this other professor: “In the case of Bonaventure, we see how difficult it is to succeed in placing the proper limits on apocalyptic images. Apocalyptic images are like a torrent of water that overflows the banks and it’s difficult to keep in bounds. And regardless of all efforts to mollify the imagery, the apocalyptic tone predominates. Even a Mozart cannot make a trumpet forget to sound like a trumpet.” So it’s sort of like you are saying, if you think about this stuff, you can never, ever talk about it. If you talk about it even one peep, it will dominate everything and you can’t say anything else.
The proof that future Pope Benedict was as focused on the literal end times as Thiel? That he would never talk about it, of course.
What Ratzinger actually wanted was to avoid the idea that humanity could bring peace and justice to this world through our own efforts — a preview of his decadeslong campaign against what he saw as Marxist-influenced liberation theology, not on behalf of the Antichrist. Yet Thiel continues to pick out various comments on eschatology — “breadcrumbs,” Thiel calls them — from Ratzinger’s lectures and writings as the decades progressed and Ratzinger’s own theological vision admittedly grew darker and more conservative. He interprets Benedict’s resignation from the papacy — unprecedented in modern times — as one of Benedict’s “winks and hints” that the Antichrist is coming.
This ventriloquizing is as bizarre as it is morbid, but Thiel is convinced that when it comes to talking about the Antichrist “these apocalyptic paroxysms make Benedict sound like a fire-and-brimstone Southern Baptist.”
That comment shows Thiel’s basic problem, which is that he wants to view Roman Catholicism through an Evangelical Protestant lens that sees the end times as a global apocalypse where the “saved” will be rescued — and confirmed in their righteousness. Ratzinger, and later as Pope Benedict, was a thoroughgoing Catholic churchman who was less concerned about the end of time than he was “anxious about the end of a historical era of the Catholic Church,” as the Italian theologian Marcello Neri put it. Ratzinger saw Catholic liberals who would dilute church doctrine and dogma as the apocalyptic threat, and it’s a threat to the Catholic Church, not the planet. History will go on, Ratzinger believed. It’s the church’s fate that’s less certain, thanks to infiltration by modernist currents. Thiel is making a category error that undermines his entire argument. It’s typical Thiel.
At the end of the day, and of his essay, Thiel’s grandiose language and project is shown to be a rather ordinary ideological one. “Thiel is above all a political theologian operating at the very heart of the Silicon Valley ecosystem,” the Italian Franciscan Paolo Benanti wrote in a sharp riposte to Thiel’s Rome talks. As Benanti explains, this ideology includes the “pathological radicalization” of a handful of Western values — “competition, technology, the individual” — resulting in outcomes “radically divergent from the common democratic project.” Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor elaborate on that theme in their new book, End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World.
If liberals want to “immanentize the eschaton,” as William F. Buckley once put it, by focusing on doing good in this life instead of being anxious about the world to come, conservatives tend to focus on personal salvation ahead of the apocalypse. That end times theology is a perfect match for them because it tends toward a libertarian ethos like Thiel’s; Jesus is coming back soon, let’s not get bogged down in overregulating or overthinking. “We moralize way too much,” as Thiel said in a podcast last month with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner. “If you’re evil, you’re at least competent. And if you’re evil, you’re not bad, and therefore you’re actually maybe kind of good because you’re at least getting something done.” Instead, Thiel suggests, let’s make hay — meaning, bushels of money — while the sun shines. Climate anxiety? Your worries about the future show a lack of faith! That’s why, in addition to the previous pope and the effective altruism movement, Thiel has also been reported as suggesting climate change activist Greta Thunberg might be the Antichrist.
Or maybe, he suggests in one lecture, it’s the system that’s the real Antichrist — specifically the financial regulatory system.
The Book of Revelation tells us, sort of, the Antichrist will abolish financial freedom. Revelation 13:16–17: “He causes all, both great and small, rich and poor, free and bond, to receive a mark in their right hand or in their foreheads, that no man might buy or sell save that he had the mark, or the name of the beast, or the number of his name.”
There’s this whole constellation of things, where over the last 25 years — this uneventful, Groundhog Day 21st century since 2000 — under cover of relative peace and safety, an incredible machinery of tax treaties, financial surveillance, and sanctions architecture has been constructed. And all these tech fortunes are downstream of this vast system. You have the illusion of power and autonomy, but you have this sense it could be taken away at any moment. It’s become quite difficult to hide one’s money.
He admits that “this Antichrist-like system, this machinery” moves at a different speed than a human Antichrist (who, again, should probably be 33.5 or younger), but insists it was set up “not overnight but relatively quickly, and there’s a feeling it could be activated at the flip of a switch.” If that all seems like a definition of the Antichrist that only a billionaire could love, he assures his listeners it’s more than that.
And then, of course, it’s not just a financial system. It’s also, in some sense, an ideological system. The Antichrist won’t stop just at money. Money is not enough to stop the Antichrist and follows that he wants something more from you.
It’s also, per Thiel, the International Criminal Court and the way it has spooked Vladimir Putin, Benjamin Netanyahu, and erstwhile members of the George W. Bush administration, and it’s Germany’s strict laws around Nazi symbolism and libel online, and it’s Australian age verification laws, which all cobble together into a vision of the end of days that so transfixes him. It’s not exactly fire and brimstone, but to Thiel, it is.
For all of Peter Thiel’s prominence and brilliance — Vance called him “the smartest man I’ve ever met” — his spiritual preoccupations are ultimately quite mainstream. Vance recently spent part of a long podcast with a popular Evangelical influencer talking about the End Times and the Antichrist. It blew the mind of most Catholics, but as Vance’s friend conservative Christian commentator Rod Dreher said, this is “a very, very common belief.”
These beliefs are also very representative of an increasingly DIY religious culture in America that is disconnected from traditional practices and flesh-and-blood congregations. When it comes to religion, seemingly everyone now does their own research and generates their own social media ministry.
The difference is that Thiel is an uber-wealthy influencer with political power. The theological thrifting by which he has sewn together his own apocalyptic vision would at one level be seen as quirky but innocent if not for the fact that he is using that vision to set himself up as a godlike judge between the saved and the damned — one might almost say a kind of Antichrist. That’s what eschatology has always done, but few apocalyptic preachers have wielded the kind of power Peter Thiel does, and he doesn’t seem to view many of us outside his circle as worthy of salvation.
Additional reporting by Tina Nguyen

articles.title: Oura adds new fitness metrics to show how workouts impact your body | TechCrunch
articles.text:
As competition in the smart ring market escalates, Oura is introducing two new features to give people more insight into their workouts and how they impact their bodies. The company announced on Tuesday it’s rolling out Cardio Effort and VO₂ max metrics to expand workout tracking beyond exercise duration and heart rate zones.
While Oura has largely dominated the smart ring market for years, rivals like RingConn and Ultrahuman are emerging to dethrone it, putting pressure on the company to keep innovating. By launching more advanced workout metrics, Oura is looking to differentiate itself from competitors.
With Cardio Effort, users will be able to see how much a workout taxes their cardiovascular system. This measurement is aggregated over the week relative to each user’s individual baseline to provide more insights. Oura explained that this metric shifts users’ focus from “How many minutes did I move?” to “Am I maintaining my fitness, building it, or overdoing it?”
Since Cardio Effort accounts for both intensity and duration, a shorter, more intense workout can yield a similar score to a longer, less intense one, the company says.
Oura notes that the metric has two components: Workout Cardio Effort and Weekly Cardio Effort. The first metric evaluates the impact of an individual workout, while the latter aggregates effort into a weekly total, categorized as “Light,” “Fair,” “Maintaining,” “Building,” or “Reaching.”
Oura measures elevated heart rate relative to each member’s long-term resting heart rate, avoiding the variability associated with maximum-heart-rate estimates. Weekly effort levels are then determined using personalized ranges based on recent activity patterns.
Cardio Effort is rolling out to Oura Ring Gen3 and later models.
As for VO₂ max, the metric shows how workouts contribute to long-term fitness. It measures how effectively the heart, lungs, and muscles work together to deliver and use oxygen during exercise. Previously, measuring VO₂ max typically required a lab test or a six-minute walking test. Oura can now estimate it passively using GPS-enabled workouts.
After completing five qualifying activities, users receive an initial VO2 Max estimate. Within the My Health Heart Hub, they can view their current VO2 Max estimate in ml/kg/min, their fitness category (Low, Fair, High, or Peak), how their estimate has changed over time, and when it was last updated. Users also receive insights highlighting meaningful changes in their VO2 Max or indicating when their estimate remains consistent.
VO₂ Max is launching in Oura Labs, the company’s hub for experimental features, for members with Gen3 and newer Oura Ring devices.
Oura says these two new features are designed to work together to show users how hard they’re working and how that effort is adding up over time.

articles.title: Chinese crime ring steals more than $5 million in gift cards from Staples customer service — more than 15,000 gift cards acquired through internal Nexus system, nearly $500,000 spent before being deactivated
articles.text:
Chinese crime ring steals more than $5 million in gift cards from Staples customer service — more than 15,000 gift cards acquired through internal Nexus system, nearly $500,000 spent before being deactivated
Over $5 million worth of gift cards for retailers like Target and Sephora were stolen when thieves gained access to a system called Nexus.
Millions of dollars worth of gift cards were stolen and then used to buy high-value tech gear at retailers like Target, Sephora, and Lowe's after a Chinese crime ring gained access to an internal Staples system and then used it to issue more than 15,000 cards to itself. While the hack hasn't been made public to date, a 404 Media report notes that it actually took place back in 2023.
The outlet reviewed court records that show that Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) was told about the hack in October of that year. The hack came to light after it led to a search warrant that was unsealed last week. And while the document doesn't specifically name Staples as the victim of the hack, 404 Media has confirmed that it was the company affected based on other information. Such information includes the fact that the victim company is headquartered in Massachusetts, that it uses Blackhawk Networks to fulfill gift card orders, and that the company uses an internal customer support system called Nexus. The report notes that a reference to Nexus can be found on a former Staples executive's LinkedIn profile.
While Staples was under the impression that Nexus could not be accessed from beyond its own network, hackers found that not to be the case. They then "performed multiple heap dump requests," a process that captures all of the data held in an app's memory. That information gave the hackers the tools they needed to hijack logged-in sessions of Staples customer service employees. From there, they were able to issue gift cards at will.
Once the gift cards had been issued, the crime group sent runners to physical retail stores to spend them before they were identified and canceled. Target found that 35 gift cards were used at a New Hampshire store, with high-value products from Apple, Bose, and Beats all bought. All 35 cards were used within a period of just a single hour, although not all of them were obtained via this hack.
In total, Target told investigators that 3,850 gift cards worth over $140,000 were used across 85 different stores in just two days. Sephora was hit for $58,600 worth of sales, while Lowe's saw $226,000 spent across online and in-store purchases. In total, 4,630 stolen gift cards were used with a value of around $425,000.
This hack was just the tip of the iceberg, too. Last April, a Department of Justice announcement confirmed that three Chinese nationals had been sentenced for their part in a gift card fraud conspiracy. Including the Staples hack, the crime group stole more than $100 million worth of gift cards.
Chinese organized crime groups often pop up on the radar of U.S.-based law enforcement. Earlier this year, a Chinese phishing service that was used to generate scam websites using AI was dismantled. The service was linked to almost $2 billion in losses.

articles.title: Over $963,000 worth of graded Pokémon and sports cards were stolen from FedEx
articles.text:
Last week over 200 packages of graded trading cards being shipped back to their owners were stolen from a FedEx truck parked outside the headquarters of Professional Sports Authenticator (PSA) in Santa Ana, California, according to a report by The Athletic. PSA is one of the largest third-party sports and hobby card grading companies in the world and it reported to the Santa Ana Police Department that the majority of the stolen packages had an approximate value of over $963,000, but that amount could further increase as PSA continues the process of confirming exactly which cards included in the shipment were taken.
Over $963,000 worth of graded Pokémon and sports cards were stolen from FedEx
Over 200 packages of collectible cards were taken from the delivery truck outside of PSA’s headquarters.
In a statement shared to its website, Collectors Holdings, the parent company of PSA, acknowledged the theft and that it’s working closely with local law enforcement and FedEx as the investigation continues. In response to the incident the company says it has “notified marketplace partners so they can be on the lookout for rare and serialized items” to help prevent the stolen cards from being resold. All cards graded by PSA are assigned a unique certification number that the company has since deactivated for all the cards that have so far been identified as stolen.
Collectors Holdings also says it has contacted affected customers to arrange compensation based on the fair market value of their missing collectibles, but “up to the maximum insured value for each item selected by the customer prior to grading,” according to the report.
In a video posted over the weekend, YouTuber Sky-B Cards identified themselves as one of the victims of the theft and shared the response they were sent by PSA. They had paid $8,468 to have 104 collectible sports cards graded by the company, many of which are irreplaceable, and had opted to insure the order for up to $156,000. It is not yet known what compensation they have received. Other collectors affected by the incident have started to reach out to another YouTuber, Boston Card Hunter, who is working to compile a shared list of serialized cards that were stolen including detailed descriptions of each one in hopes it can help other collectors identify them.

articles.title: AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
articles.text:
Sponsored
AI adoption by industry shows what other sectors can learn
Tech and finance are setting the pace on AI adoption. TripleTen research shows which skills will reach healthcare, education, and retail next.
Provided byTripleTen
The current narrative around artificial intelligence in the workplace is largely driven by Silicon Valley. But treating the tech sector as an island misses the actual trends in technology adoption–tech is just the first industry in line.
As generative AI and automation tools mature, the shifts currently reshaping software engineering and product management will inevitably filter into healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing. The variation in adoption rates today isn't a sign that non-tech industries are falling behind, but rather a reflection of the different speeds at which industries absorb new workflows. For leaders and their teams outside of tech, this differential pace provides a practical blueprint for how AI adoption unfolds, and where the opportunities lie.
The AI adoption spectrum by industry
Recent survey data from TripleTen highlights just how stark the current adoption curve is across different sectors of the economy (see Figure 1).
Figure 1: The AI adoption curve remains steep across industries, but non-tech industry adoption rates are increasing.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
While tech leads the way, finance emerges as a clear second: 48% of finance workers have been asked to use AI chatbots, and 32% have been asked to automate parts of their workflow. This demonstrates how rapidly knowledge work integrates AI once clear use cases emerge.
By contrast, sectors like healthcare (18% asked to use chatbots) and education (25%) reflect lower initial exposure. Because these broad industry categories encompass a mix of specialized hands-on professionals, clinical or instructional personnel, and back-office administrative staff, universal adoption was never going to happen overnight. Integrating automated tools into compliance-heavy or human-facing operations requires a more deliberate pace, which is reflected by the lower numbers.
The AI skills workers are being asked to learn
Across all surveyed industries, 79% of workers report being asked to learn at least one skill they didn't previously have. Looking at the specific competencies demanded in tech today offers a preview of the skill sets likely to shift into other sectors (see Figure 2).
Figure 2: Workforces across industries are learning new skills.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
Although some of these sound like niche skills confined to tech, many of them will translate to frontline work across sectors—from hospital systems managing patient logistics to school districts processing administrative reporting.
One skill gets less attention than it should. Only 30% of managers and owners call judging whether AI output is right or wrong an absolute must, which puts it sixth on a list of seven. As AI tools reach more industries, this is the skill that catches mistakes before they cause problems. It is also where work experience helps most: To spot a wrong answer, you need to know what the right one looks like.
How early AI adoption helps your career
Early AI adoption offers clear professional leverage: TripleTen’s survey data shows that when managers learned a new skill or automation process from an employee, 88% of those employee-led AI innovations became standard company practice.
In early-adopting industries, employees who identify repetitive administrative tasks and use AI tools to streamline them have a voice in shaping organizational policy. As healthcare networks, educational institutions, and retail operations begin broader rollouts of AI-enabled software, workers who understand how to validate outputs, prompt models, and automate routine tasks will hold a strong advantage. Being the person who can streamline administrative overhead promises better chances for retention, promotions, and wage growth.
Ana Riabova, the AI strategy and enablement lead at TripleTen, says, “Everyone talks about saving time, but the real win with early adoption is expanding what you can actually do. People who get ahead are using it to handle things they used to have to hand off. It doesn't matter how senior or junior you are. You keep your core skills, but suddenly you aren't boxed in by them anymore.”
The AI resource gap: Who pays for training and how workers learn
If non-tech industries absorb these tools more gradually, the challenge for workers lies in getting access to quality learning resources. Workers’ out-of-pocket investment in training varies significantly by industry:
- Tech: $1,758 average (13% spent $0)
- Finance: $1,664 average (24% spent $0)
- Healthcare: $990 average (45% spent $0)
- Education: $883 average (42% spent $0)
Nearly half of healthcare and education workers spent nothing out of pocket on professional development last year. Furthermore, tech workers actively leverage a larger variety of learning channels (see Figure 3).
Figure 3: Professional development efforts mirror the AI adoption curve.
Source: TripleTen, 2026
Tech workers are nearly twice as likely as all workers to use AI chatbots as learning tools (48% vs. 27%), and more than twice as likely as workers outside tech (21%), effectively using AI to accelerate their acquisition of other skills.
However, ask workers whom they trust most to teach them a new job skill, and they choose someone currently doing that job (31%). Fewer pick an official certification program (19%), an AI tool (16%), or a university professor (6%).
Conclusion
The difference in AI adoption rates across industries is not a story of who is succeeding and who is failing. Rather, it’s a timeline of how technology diffuses through an economy. Tech and finance are testing the mechanics of AI integration today. For workers in healthcare, education, retail, and manufacturing, the current phase provides a valuable window to observe which skills generate real productivity gains—allowing them to build those competencies before they become standard industry expectations.
