articles.title: Ahold Delhaize: Cyberattack affects services across US and Europe
articles.text:
Ahold Delhaize, one of the world's largest food retail chains, confirmed that last week's cyberattack disrupted services at stores across Europe and the United States.
Right before the cyberattack was disclosed, customers couldn't use websites, apps, and customer service platforms at Albert Heijn, Etos, and Gall & Gall stores in the Netherlands, and Delhaize in Belgium, while employees at the Stop & Shop American regional supermarket chain reported having trouble accessing their schedules and pay stubs.
When BleepingComputer asked right after the incident whether it also affected both corporate and store systems and whether any devices were encrypted during the attack, an Ahold Delhaize spokesperson redirected us to the company's statement.
In a Monday update, Ahold Delhaize said the cybersecurity incident announced last week forced it to take some systems offline, including its brands' websites and apps, causing service issues, although stores remained open to serve customers.
While most store websites and apps in Central and Southeastern Europe (CSE) are now online, the company says it's still working to restore some systems and services for European and US brands that remain down.
"Albert Heijn's website and app are back online, with home deliveries expected to resume from Friday, October 23. The Etos and Gall & Gall websites are also available for customers. E-commerce services at our Ahold Delhaize USA brands are expected to come back in the coming days. In Belgium, e-commerce is now fully operational," Ahold Delhaize said.
"As part of our response, we notified the Dutch National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) within 24 hours of discovering the malicious activity and have continued to provide timely updates to the NCSC, law enforcement and other relevant regulatory authorities. Today, Ahold Delhaize has filed a formal police report with the Dutch police.
The retail giant did not share further details that could interfere with response efforts or compromise security measures protecting its systems, but noted that an ongoing investigation has not yet found evidence that sensitive customer, associate, or partner data was stolen in the incident.
"Although this incident was caused by the malicious actions of others, we apologize for the inconvenience this has caused - especially to our customers," said Frans Muller, President and CEO of Ahold Delhaize.
This is the second major cyberattack to affect Ahold Delhaize's systems in recent years, after the personal, financial, and health information of over 2.2 million individuals was stolen in a November 2024 attack that impacted the company's U.S. systems and was claimed by the ransomware group INC Ransom.
The multinational retailer employs more than 384,000 people and operates 9,551 stores serving 77 million customers each week across the United States, Europe, and Indonesia.

articles.title: Yelp can now call on your behalf to check wait times at a restaurant | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Over the last few weeks, personal assistants like Instinct, Fo, and Muse have enabled users to call businesses for customer support and appointment booking. Following this trend, Yelp is adding the ability for its app users to get a voice agent to call a restaurant to check wait times.
The new feature, Check for Me, will show up on restaurant pages in the app, where users can enter their party size and phone number. The AI agent then calls on behalf of the user to check wait times and texts them the results to decide if they want to go to that particular restaurant.
Last year, Yelp debuted its voice solution for restaurants and service providers. With this new feature, the discovery platform is fulfilling the consumer side of the equation, though there is a possibility that a user’s agent will talk to the restaurant’s agent, and agent-to-agent communication might break down the conversation.
The company is also updating its Yelp AI assistant that helps users discover restaurants and services. With the new OpenTable integration, users can easily book a restaurant without leaving the app.
Yelp is adding better personalization to its assistant by having it remember preferences that you might have mentioned in previous chats. Plus, you can access your chat history from the past 30 days in the app, with full history available soon.
Users can ask the chatbot to set custom reminders, such as sending suggestions for weekend activities every Friday. The company is also letting users build their own lists, starting with two “Been Here” and “Want to
Go” lists. You can filter your lists by location, category, and cuisine, reorder, add notes to items, and share them with others. 
Next month, the company will start showing weekly personalized recommendations based on your saved items and rankings. Yelp is also working on converting collections to lists and giving the lists tab a new look, rolling out later in the year, along with a maps view.
To cap off all these changes, Yelp has been thinking about enhancing customer support and business processes through AI. In the new update, the company is releasing a new paid product called Smart Lead Reply, which can reply to customers and engage with them to qualify a lead. Business owners, who will be charged $30 per month for these services, can specify how an agent should handle a conversation with a customer. Other companies like Meta have also been courting small businesses with AI offerings to handle inbound customer inquiries.

articles.title: Elon Musk et Anthropic s'engagent à redistribuer les richesses générées par l’IA
articles.text:
« Il est courant que les entreprises technologiques offrent des rémunérations progressives à leurs dirigeants. Nous, au contraire, orientons ces capitaux vers le bien public » : Anthropic a annoncé la création de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, une entité dédiée à la redistribution d’une partie des bénéfices générés par l’intelligence artificielle. Elon Musk a réagi à cette annonce en présentant sa vision des choses et en faisant une promesse à tous les enfants américains.
Anthropic crée un fonds pour redistribuer les bénéfices générés par l’IA
Anthropic a annoncé le lancement de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Pour être plus précis, il s’agit d’une LLC (Limited Liability Company), c’est-à-dire une entité juridique américaine entièrement détenue par Anthropic. Son principe est relativement simple : redistribuer une partie des bénéfices de l’entreprise à des personnes dans le besoin ou à des entités d’intérêt public. Anthropic explique : « nous pourrions envisager des dons importants à des organisations à but non lucratif traditionnelles ou des distributions directes à des populations spécifiques », tout en précisant ensuite que « L’impact sur le marché du travail en est un exemple ».
L’intelligence artificielle risquant d’entraîner d’importantes pertes d’emploi dans certains secteurs, Anthropic voudrait donc aider financièrement les personnes concernées. Il ne s’agit pas ici d’un revenu universel, mais de fonds attribués dans le cadre de situations spécifiques. Anthropic précise au passage que cette entité ne sera « en aucun cas utilisée à des fins de lobbying ou de financement politique, que ce soit aux États-Unis ou à l’étranger ». Avec cette annonce, près de 20 % des actions d’Anthropic seront consacrées à l’intérêt général. Sous réserve de l’approbation des actionnaires, 5 % des actions seront attribués au nouveau fonds, dont la part pourrait encore augmenter en fonction de la valorisation de l’entreprise.
Elon Musk promet de donner une action de SpaceX à chaque enfant américain
Pour Elon Musk, il n’est pas question de financer des ONG, dont certaines, selon lui, défendent des intérêts politiques ou financiers. En réponse au post X d’Anthropic annonçant la création de l’Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, Elon Musk a donné sa vision de la répartition des bénéfices générés par les grands fournisseurs d’IA et fait une promesse pour le moins surprenante.
Le dirigeant de SpaceX recommande ainsi aux grands fournisseurs d’IA « de donner les actions directement au public », sans passer par des ONG ou toute autre entité se présentant comme d’intérêt général. Il effectue ensuite une annonce en grande pompe : « L’année prochaine, je donnerai une de mes actions SpaceX à chaque enfant en Amérique. Ce sera la première d’une longue série ». Comme le souligne l’Associated Press, cette promesse représenterait un don d’une valeur estimée à 10,66 milliards de dollars, sur la base du cours de clôture de l’action SpaceX et du nombre d’enfants vivant aux États-Unis.
Elon Musk et Anthropic affichent donc une vision résolument philanthrope de la redistribution des richesses générées par l’IA, tout en divergeant sur un point : les modalités de cette redistribution, directe ou indirecte, à la population. Il reste maintenant à voir comment ces belles promesses pourraient être appliquées dans les faits.

articles.title: Artemis 2: Zu welchem Zeitpunkt der Kommandant des Raumschiffs „schreckliche“ Angst verspürte
articles.text:
Artemis 2: Zu welchem Zeitpunkt der Kommandant des Raumschiffs „schreckliche“ Angst verspürte
Die Artemis-2-Mission zum Mond hat für großes Aufsehen gesorgt, von einem Aufbruch in eine neue Ära war die Rede, oft fiel das Wort „historisch“. Die Nasa übertrug die Mission per Livestream, wodurch die Öffentlichkeit die Besatzung virtuell begleiten konnte.
Doch sie hatte auch Schattenseiten – und zwar für die direkt Beteiligten. Der Kommandant der Mission, Reid Wiseman, hatte Angst, die Besatzung könnte nicht mehr zur Erde zurückkehren. Auf dem Starmus-Festival auf Teneriffa (Spanien) erzählte der 50-jährige Astronaut von seinen Ängsten – und konnte sogar einen genauen Moment benennen, als diese am größten waren: als die Crew die Rückseite des Mondes umrundete.
Artemis-2-Kommandant: „Ich hatte schreckliche Angst“
Das Kontrollzentrum in Houston hatte der Crew mitgeteilt, dass die maximale Entfernung von der Erde 219.667 Seemeilen (knapp 407.000 Kilometer) betragen würde. „Ich beobachtete die Anzeige, und als sie 219.667 erreichte, dachte ich: ‚Großartig, das ist der am weitesten von der Erde entfernte Punkt; der nächste Wert wird 219.666 sein – wir sind auf dem Rückweg.‘“ Doch daraus wurde erst einmal nichts, denn rund drei Minuten später stand auf der Anzeige 219.668. Der Wert stieg weiter an. Wisemans Gedanken dazu: „Moment mal, das ist aber seltsam.“
Als die Anzeige auf 219.669 kletterte, „überkam mich echte Angst, denn ich befürchtete, wir seien zu weit geflogen. Ich dachte, wir würden nie wieder nach Hause kommen“, erzählte Wiseman. „Ich hatte schreckliche Angst.“ Als der Wert schließlich zu sinken begann, brach die Besatzung in Jubel aus. „Da wusste ich, dass eine gute Chance bestand, dass wir es schaffen würden“, sagte der Astronaut.
Die Weltraumreise hat Wiseman zutiefst geprägt
Die Artemis-2-Mission war der erste bemannte Flug zum Mond seit Apollo 17 im Jahr 1972. Sie startete am 1. April vom Kennedy Space Center in Florida, erreichte nach sechs Tagen die Mondumlaufbahn und kehrte anschließend zur Erde zurück.
Im Gespräch mit der britischen Tageszeitung The Telegraph berichtete Wiseman, dass die große Entfernung von unserem Planeten bei ihm eine spezielle Art des Heimwehs ausgelöst hat, eine Art „Erde-Weh“. Die Weltraumreise hat ihn zutiefst geprägt: „Man blickt auf eine Erde, die so winzig ist, dass sie unter den eigenen Daumen passt. Um sie herum herrscht absolute Schwärze, und dieser winzige Punkt da unten ist unser Zuhause.“
Kommandant Wiseman dachte an seine Kinder
Sein stärkstes Gefühl war: „Ich möchte meine Kinder wiedersehen, meine Freunde in die Arme schließen, auf grünem Gras sitzen, frischen Salat essen – einfach das Leben auf diesem Planeten wieder spüren. Es war kein Heimweh im herkömmlichen Sinne, sondern ein Sehnen nach der Erde selbst.“
Als sich die drei Hauptfallschirme der Orion-Kapsel kurz vor der Rückkehr auf die Erde öffneten, ergriffen die Besatzungsmitglieder:innen die Hände der anderen und jubelten, denn da wurde ihnen laut Wiseman zum ersten Mal klar: „Wir werden das Ganze tatsächlich überleben.“

articles.title: Apple restringe las reservas del iPhone Duo para combatir la reventa
articles.text:
Apple parece haber tomado medida para combatir la reventa del iPhone Duo. En las últimas horas, la firma de Cupertino ha implementado un límite a la cantidad de unidades de su móvil plegable que un mismo cliente puede reservar. Esto, luego de que las fechas de entrega se demoraran hasta enero de 2027 apenas minutos después del inicio de la preventa.
Según se observa en las versiones online de la Apple Store, las reservas del iPhone Duo se han limitado a un máximo de 2 unidades por cliente. Si intentas cargar una cantidad mayor, la tienda muestra un mensaje informando de la restricción y obligando a respetar el tope para poder continuar con el procedimiento de compra.
El nuevo límite de dos iPhone Duo por comprador impacta sobre todas las variantes del smartphone. Esto da a entender que el objetivo de Apple es limitar el impacto que los scalpers tienen sobre la disponibilidad de su primer smartphone plegable, si bien ya estuvieron haciendo estragos durante la primera jornada de reservas.
La preventa del iPhone Duo se puso en marcha el pasado viernes 16, con un alto nivel de demanda. Esto, combinado con la poca cantidad de unidades del móvil que se han producido hasta la fecha, resultó en una combinación fatal para la mayoría de los compradores que apostaban a recibirlo el primer día.
Las unidades disponibles para entregar el viernes 23 de octubre se agotaron en apenas minutos, de modo que un gran número de compradores debió conformarse con fechas esparcidas entre noviembre y diciembre próximo, y también en enero de 2027. La situación no fue puntual de un mercado, sino que afectó a todas las versiones de la Apple Store.
Apple restringe las reservas del iPhone Duo: solo 2 por comprador
Más allá de la demanda genuina del público, el lanzamiento del iPhone Duo ha padecido el accionar de los scalpers. Esto no solo ha derivado en la aparición de unidades del plegable en eBay, revendiéndose a precios infladísimos (y ridículos), sino que también expuso operaciones para obtener el móvil usando sistemas total o parcialmente automatizados.
Es cierto que el uso de bots para comprar productos de escasa disponibilidad ni bien se habilita su venta, no es algo nuevo. Sin embargo, con el iPhone Duo generó todavía más ruido por la expectación generada entre el público y porque el responsable de una de las maniobras de scalping no tuvo mejor idea que salir a presumirlo en X (Twitter).
Que Apple ahora limite las reservas del iPhone Duo es una señal de que se están tomando medidas para evitar que la situación se repita. Claro que el daño inicial de los revendedores ya está hecho y nunca se va a dar respuesta definitiva a este tipo de problemas. Por lo pronto, el plegable de la manzana mantiene su fecha de entrega más temprana para el 22 de enero del próximo año.
Lo que todavía es un misterio es si el iPhone Duo se podrá comprar sin reserva previa y de forma presencial en las Apple Store físicas. Los de Cupertino no han brindado detalles sobre cómo piensan lidiar con este asunto cuando se formen largas colas en sus tiendas alrededor del mundo.

articles.title: Revolut outage disrupts online banking operations worldwide
articles.text:
Fintech company Revolut is working to resolve a massive outage that disrupted most of its services worldwide earlier today.
Since the incident began, thousands of users on the Downdetector outage tracking platform have reported issues with the Revolut app, mobile banking services, and transferring funds between accounts.
In a statement today, the company said the outage has affected its services since Tuesday morning and added that customers' data and funds are safe.
"We are currently experiencing a service disruption affecting multiple services. We can confirm that all our customers' money and data are safe," Revolut said.
"We've been working to fix the issue since it was identified this morning and apologise to anyone affected and for any inconvenience caused."
On its official status page, the company says the outage affects 28 services, including sign-ins, card payments, transfers, currency exchange, stock trading, and live support chat, which are now flagged as partially unavailable.
According to Reuters, the Revolut outage is reportedly linked to ongoing service disruptions affecting Google Cloud's London-based europe-west2 data center after a "power event."
A Revolut spokesperson was not immediately available when BleepingComputer reached out earlier about the root cause of today's outage.
Last month, Revolut also disclosed a data breach after it shared personally identifiable information (PII) from an undisclosed number of customers with a threat actor who was impersonating a government agency.
Four years ago, Revolut disclosed another data breach after threat actors stole the personal, contact, and financial information of more than 50,000 customers in September 2022.
Revolut provides banking, money management, and investment services to more than 80 million customers across 160+ countries and regions, including 800,000 business customers.
Update October 20, 13:52 EDT: Revolut has linked today's outage to the Google Cloud incident and said that all services have now been restored.
"Due to a recent Google Cloud outage, customers may have experienced temporary service disruption on the Revolut app today," the company said.
"The issue has now been fixed, and services are now restored. All our customers’ money and data is safe, and has remained safe throughout this incident. We apologise for any inconvenience caused."

articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Agentic AI applications need governed access to live enterprise data. That data can live in operational systems, analytical warehouses, SaaS applications, other clouds, or on premises. In the previous post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. A Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore queried that layer. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This post uses the same customer 360 pattern, but swaps in a different semantic layer implementation and extends the source mix.
Two things change here. First, the semantic layer is the Denodo Platform: an AI data layer that provides active context and live, zero-copy access to distributed enterprise data. The agent talks to it in VQL, Denodo’s SQL dialect. Second, the source mix includes an on-premises PostgreSQL database alongside Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift, so the federation problem is no longer bounded by an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC).
The rest of the pattern carries over. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock plans and writes queries. The Denodo MCP Server exposes governed views to the agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent, terminates inbound authentication, and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to Denodo. Everything the model reasons over lives inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt: the joins, the metric definitions, and the row and column filters that apply to the caller.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to federate Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and an on-premises PostgreSQL database in Denodo into a single customer 360 view an agent can query.
- How to expose that semantic view to an AgentCore-hosted agent through the Denodo MCP Server, and how to register the MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target.
- How the end user’s identity flows from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity On-Behalf-Of token exchange to Denodo.
- How Global Security Policies apply row and column filters at query time.
- The two deployment options for Denodo on AWS: Agora, the fully managed cloud service, and self-managed installation on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS).
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the previous post: what it is, what it’s for, and why the model plans query without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the previous post covers the ground.
The example: Customer 360 with a source outside AWS
We stay with the same customer 360 pattern from the previous post. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit used in the previous article models an ecommerce retailer with two motivating use cases: understanding churn and identifying customers for auto-enrollment in a rewards program. The schema doesn’t change in this post. What changes is where one table lives: rewards_account sits on an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster rather than in Amazon Aurora with the rest of the customer profile data.
That placement isn’t a special case. Enterprise data sources might be outside AWS: on premises, in a SaaS tool like a CRM, or in another cloud. The semantic layer must reach whichever applies. We use on-premises PostgreSQL for the walkthrough that represents data from a third-party application. The Extending to other sources section covers what changes when the source is a SaaS tool, a CRM, or a mainframe. It also covers the other hundreds of data sources that Denodo supports by default.
Amazon Aurora (PostgreSQL-compatible): Customer profile
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
Amazon Redshift: Order history
| Table | Key columns | 
| order | id (PK), cid, pid, order_date, quantity, price, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
On-premises PostgreSQL: Rewards program
| Table | Key columns | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
The shared identifier is cid, a plain integer that appears as the primary key in the Aurora customer table. It appears as a non-foreign-key column in the Amazon Redshift order table and the on-premises rewards_account. Within Aurora itself, the customer.location column is an integer foreign key to address.id, which is how the profile joins to the address record. There is no foreign key that spans two engines, and no ETL job to build one. Answers that join customers to their purchases and their rewards enrollment must reconcile cid at query time.
A representative question this setup answers: “Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?” This is the auto-enrollment scenario from the Stardog kit, and it needs profile data from Aurora, lifetime spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from the on-premises cluster to answer.
Denodo plans the federated query at execution time, deciding what to push into Aurora, what to push into Amazon Redshift, what to fetch from the on-premises cluster, and how to combine the results. No data moves between sources, and the semantic layer stays declared once for every consumer to reuse.
Denodo terms used in this post
Denodo implements the semantic layer as a data virtualization platform. Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) is the query engine at the core: it’s where the semantic-layer objects live, where VQL executes, and where access policies evaluate. Design Studio is the browser-based authoring surface for VDP. Every object modeled in this post is defined there.
Three object types come up repeatedly.
- A base view is a mapping between a physical table, API, or file in a source system and a logical view in VDP. One Aurora table maps to one base view.
- A derived view is a VQL query over one or more base or other derived views. The customer_360 view in this post is a derived view.
- A metric view defines a business measure once (for example, lifetime_customer_value) and lets other derived views reference it. Metric views separate the definition of a measure from any specific query that uses it.
VQL is Denodo’s SQL dialect. It’s ANSI-aligned SQL plus a set of Denodo-specific constructs, notably DDL constructs to represent data sources and syntax for semantic metric views. In an agentic scenario, the specific syntax of VQL is provided by a skill that will be used by the LLM when using Denodo tools to facilitate correct use of Denodo’s syntax.
A Global Security Policy (GSP) is a runtime access-control rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag. GSPs are how row filters and column masks get enforced at query time, evaluated per caller.
For a fuller reference, see the Denodo Platform documentation.
Reference architecture
The runtime has two flows. Inbound: A client sends the user’s request to the agent through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process. The agent invokes a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 in this walkthrough) to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound: AgentCore Gateway also acts as the outbound proxy for the agent’s tool calls. The Denodo MCP Server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls the agent makes for enterprise data route through Gateway to the MCP Server. Before the request reaches Denodo, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange, converting the human user’s inbound token into a scoped access token that represents the same user with Denodo as the audience. The Denodo MCP Server accepts the exchanged token as a bearer credential and forwards the VQL request to Denodo Virtual DataPort (VDP) over JDBC. VDP validates the token independently, resolves the caller to a Denodo role, applies access policies, and plans the federated query against Amazon Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL cluster.
Only the VQL request travels down to VDP and the result set travels back up. No source data moves between engines. Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster respond to native SQL rewritten by VDP’s federated optimizer. The following sections cover the identity propagation and policy enforcement in detail. Additional sections cover the MCP Server registration and agent deployment steps.
Build the semantic layer
The semantic model in Denodo is not a single artifact. It’s a collection of base views, derived views, metric views, and tags in VDP that together present business-meaningful data to consumers. Building the semantic model in this post means creating each of those pieces.
We build in three passes: base views over each source table, a derived view (customer_360) that joins the base views on cid at the customer level, and a metric view (lifetime_customer_value) that defines a reusable spend aggregation queries can join in when they need it.
In practice, this modeling is done visually in Denodo Design Studio. You drag Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises PostgreSQL source onto a canvas, draw joins between them, and rename or re-type fields (for example, mapping cust_ref to customer_id) through a form rather than hand-written DDL. Attaching the security policies covered later in this post also happens inside the same UI.
Metric views live beside the derived views that reference them, defined once and reused. If two teams build two different customer-level views over the same base data, both surface the same metric definitions.
Base views
Each source table becomes a base view in VDP. For the Aurora customer table, that means introducing Aurora using the specific connector in Design Studio, pointing at the schema, and letting VDP introspect the columns. Design Studio handles the introspection. The resulting base view is a one-to-one mapping between the physical columns and their VDP counterparts, and it doesn’t transform the source data.
Two additional configurations happen during creation:
- Column tags for governance. ssn on the base view over customer gets the tag pii_sensitive. card_num on the base view over credit_card gets the same tag. These tags are what the Global Security Policy defined in the Governed access section binds to.
- Primary keys and join fields. cid is marked as the primary key on aurora_customer and as the join field on redshift_order and postgres_rewards_account. Design Studio infers primary keys from source metadata when it’s available. Otherwise, you set them once in the base view definition.
Repeat for the source tables introduced earlier. Six base views result: aurora_customer, aurora_address, and aurora_credit_card over Amazon Aurora; redshift_order and redshift_product over Amazon Redshift; and postgres_rewards_account over on-premises PostgreSQL.
Design Studio also supports natural-language authoring through Denodo Assistant. A developer can describe a view in plain English (for example, “join customer profile from Aurora with order totals from Amazon Redshift on cid”) and get back a candidate VQL definition to review and refine in the same canvas before saving. Refinement is iterative: follow-up prompts adjust filters, joins, or field mappings before the definition is finalized. The governance and typing rules described in this section still apply to objects created this way.
Derived view: The customer 360
customer_360 is the customer-level view across the three sources, with one row per customer. Order details and aggregations live separately, in the metric view we define next.
Two properties of this definition matter for the rest of the architecture. First, the joins live in Denodo Platform rather than in a pipeline. There is no ETL job maintaining a materialized customer_360 table. VDP resolves the joins at execution time: Aurora returns the profile plus card, the on-premises cluster returns the rewards enrollment record, and VDP combines them on cid. Second, the derived view carries every column, including ssn and card_num.
For governance and AI, we also add metadata: column tags for personally identifiable information (PII) fields, and descriptions that document the view and each field. Denodo’s Assistant can use an LLM to suggest these. Later sections show why this metadata matters.
Metric view: Lifetime customer value
Metric views define reusable business measures with a specific SOURCES/DIMENSIONS/METRICS structure. See the Defining a Metric View reference in the VQL guide for the full syntax. lifetime_customer_value doesn’t live inside customer_360. It lives beside it, as its own object:
Other views and external reporting tools can reference lifetime_customer_value the same way it references other views. When a business rule changes (say, lifetime_spend should exclude canceled orders), the update happens once in the metric definition. Every consumer picks up the change at the next query, without touching the derived view or the downstream application. Different teams can stand up their own derived views to convey the way their line of business sees the world. The base data stays shared while the semantic interpretation stays independent, so neither team’s edits disturb the other.
How VDP executes the federated query
When the agent runs the auto-enrollment question from The example (“Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?”), the corresponding VQL uses the metric view to compute the result set and evaluate the desired metric:
Although this query only references the metric view, VDP’s cost-based optimizer plans the federated execution across the three engines where the corresponding data is originating. The resulting plan looks approximately like this:
- Push down to Amazon Aurora: Denodo pushes a join of customer, address, and credit_card to Aurora, returning customer profile fields including first_name, last_name, state, and cid.
- Push down to on-premises PostgreSQL: Denodo pushes a projection of rewards_account returning cid and create_date.
- Push down to Amazon Redshift: Denodo pushes the spend aggregation to Amazon Redshift as SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid.
- Combine inside Denodo: Denodo left-joins the Aurora profile result with the PostgreSQL rewards result on cid, then right-outer-joins that result with the Amazon Redshift aggregated spend on cid. Denodo filters rows where rewards_since IS NULL, evaluates the metric as the outer grouped aggregation (sum(sum) AS lifetime_spend) grouped by first_name, last_name, and state, orders by lifetime_spend descending, and returns up to 20 rows.
The plan reflects the strengths of each source. Amazon Redshift does the aggregation, Aurora does the customer-profile join because all three profile tables live there, and the on-premises cluster returns a small set of rewards records. VDP handles the final cross-engine join and the top-N filter, working with three compact intermediate result sets that carry one row per customer rather than one row per order. A hand-written pipeline usually approximates this same shape and then must keep it in sync forever.
VDP also handles type reconciliation where it’s cheapest. If the same identifier is stored as an integer in one source and a string in another, VDP pushes the cast into the source that can still filter on the resulting predicate, rather than pulling data across engines and reconciling types afterward.
Beyond query push-down and on-demand federation, VDP also offers caching, aggregate-aware acceleration, and point-to-point replication. These techniques complement push-down capabilities in use cases where pre-calculating complex transformations may be necessary, while preserving access control rules and data lineage.
Publish for discovery
A semantic view that only exists as a queryable endpoint leaves a discoverability gap. The next team that needs a “customer lifetime value” measure has no way to know lifetime_customer_value already exists, what it’s built on, or who else depends on it. Publishing customer_360 and lifetime_customer_value to the Denodo Data Marketplace turns them into reusable, governed enterprise data products and closes that gap: both objects appear with their VQL definitions, ownership, business descriptions, custom properties, and lineage back to the base views. Consumers search by business meaning rather than by knowing the schema. The Denodo Data Marketplace also provides other features focused on self-service for non-technical users, including data preparation wizards, endorsements and deprecations notes from the administrators, and the capability to make requests and ask questions to data product owners.
Denodo extends this with the 360 graph, a relationship view around a business concept. This graph attaches the reports, dashboards, notebooks, or agent tools that already use customer_360, along with glossaries that define the meaning of the data in the table or conditions of use, for instance. Consumers can inspect the surrounding context of the dataset before writing a query.
A note on interoperability
The semantic model in Denodo is defined in VQL, but Denodo natively exposes any view over multiple open protocols. The same customer_360 view can be reached as SQL through JDBC, ODBC, or ADBC, as GraphQL through the Denodo GraphQL Service, as OData 2.0 or 4.0 through the Denodo OData Service, or as MCP tools through the Denodo MCP Server. Choosing MCP for this walkthrough is a fit for AgentCore. The same view is available to a Power BI dashboard, a Tableau workbook, or a Java application without additional modeling.
Denodo also joined Apache Ossie (incubating), formerly Open Semantic Interchange (OSI), in March 2026, a vendor-neutral open-source specification for semantic metadata. Apache Ossie is at an early stage, but the intent is portability of semantic definitions across applications that adopt it. That said, Denodo already offers integration through Denodo Connects to share metadata with other data catalogs such as SageMaker Catalog, Collibra, Purview, and others.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Broad reach across data sources is one of the core characteristics of an enterprise-wide semantic layer, but that same reach creates a real risk when runtime access control is missing. If per-user filtering lives in the agent’s code, it’s one prompt injection away from being bypassed. If it lives in the LLM, it doesn’t really live anywhere. If it is enforced only in individual source systems, policies can be inconsistent and may not account for business meaning created across sources. Aurora doesn’t know what “top spender” means in the semantic layer, and neither does an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster behind a bastion host. And very often, especially in hybrid scenarios that blend on-premises and cloud systems, Identity Providers across all of them are not even an option.
The approach in this architecture is to enforce access at the semantic layer, using the identity of the human user who initiated the request, propagated end-to-end from the IdP through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore to Denodo Virtual DataPort.
The identity propagation chain
Figure 6 zooms into the identity portion of the reference architecture in Figure 1, expanding the outbound path from the app to Denodo VDP into an eight-hop sequence. The following numbered steps correspond one-to-one to the numbered arrows in the figure.
- The user authenticates to the app against the enterprise IdP. The IdP returns a JWT carrying the user’s identity and attribute claims — role, region, department, and whatever else the IdP is configured to emit.
- The app calls the agent through AgentCore Gateway with the user’s JWT as the bearer token.
- Gateway routes the request to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent process.
- When the agent invokes an outbound tool call, AgentCore Identity performs an On-Behalf-Of token exchange and returns a new access token whose sub claim is the human user and whose aud claim is Denodo.
- The agent presents the new access token to the Denodo MCP Server as Authorization: Bearer <access_token> on the MCP request.
- Denodo VDP validates the JWT against the configured JWKS URL, checks the issuer and audience, extracts the scope claim, and maps the caller to a Denodo role.
- VDP evaluates Global Security Policies at query time and returns a filtered result set to the agent.
- VDP queries the data sources to satisfy the request and combines the results before returning them.
Gateway JWT validation at step 2 is optional because VDP re-validates the token in step 6. With Gateway validation on, malformed tokens fail earlier in the request path.
The token exchange at step 4 uses either the RFC 8693 token-exchange grant or the RFC 7523 JWT-bearer grant, based on the credential provider configuration. The credential itself does not enter agent code. AgentCore Identity injects it at call time.
The caller-identity passthrough option at step 8 is enabled per data source and requires Denodo and the source to share the same IdP. When it applies, the caller’s identity is forwarded end-to-end, giving full auditing at the source.
Applying access policies in Denodo
Customer 360 data is regulated. For example, some users (HR, fraud analysts) may need to see PII like a Social Security number (SSN) and full credit card number. But most users (marketing, analytics) must not.
Denodo’s mechanism for this is Global Security Policies with attribute- and role-based access control. A Global Security Policy is a rule that applies to views or columns carrying a specific tag, evaluated against the caller’s role and session attributes at query time. The underlying view is not restructured.
To illustrate this, we’ve tagged two columns (ssn and card_num) as PII on the base views over Aurora. We create a Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns.
- Audience: The caller’s role is not hr_user.
- Elements: Applies to columns with the pii_sensitive tag.
- Action: Mask with asterisks (****).
We then define two Denodo roles.
- hr_user: Has Execute on customer_360. Sees every column.
- marketing_user: Has Execute on customer_360. Will see ssn and card_num as **** because the policy applies.
When marketing_user runs the VQL query:
VDP evaluates the Global Security Policy before planning the query. It sees that ssn carries the pii_sensitive tag and the caller’s role is not hr_user, so it rewrites the projection to return *** for ssn.
For row-level filtering (a US-East analyst who should only see east-coast customers, for example) the same mechanism scales. The policy condition can even depend on session attributes mapped from the JWT token, or pulled dynamically from an external table.
A note on Responsible AI
Denodo’s Global Security Policies filter PII at the semantic layer, so the model never sees ssn or card_num for callers who shouldn’t. Even then, agent responses can echo customer identifiers, locations, or spending patterns in natural language. Treat agent outputs with the same handling and retention policy you apply to the underlying regulated data: scope logging and transcript storage, apply Amazon Bedrock Guardrails for content and sensitive-topic controls, and limit who can read the responses. For broader guidance, see Responsible AI in Amazon Bedrock.
Audit and observability across layers
Each layer of the request path logs independently. AgentCore runtime emits invocation records to Amazon CloudWatch. AgentCore Gateway logs inbound MCP requests, including the caller’s JWT sub claim. The Denodo MCP Server records tool calls to its own log. Denodo VDP’s audit log captures the full VQL request, the mapped Denodo role, the resolved federated plan, and policy evaluation outcomes.
These logs can also be incorporated into Amazon CloudWatch. When per-source audit tied to the human user is required (for HIPAA or SOX compliance, for example), configure pass-through session credentials on the base views for those sources so Denodo forwards the caller’s identity to the source system where the source supports it, instead of relying on service accounts.
Expose the layer through the Denodo MCP Server
The Denodo MCP Server is an add-on component that sits between MCP clients and VDP: download the distribution, extract it, edit config/application.properties, and start it. The server listens for streamable HTTP MCP requests at http://<mcp-host>:8080/<database>/mcp and forwards them to VDP over JDBC.
Three configuration values matter for this walkthrough.
- mcp.security.oauth2.enabled=true: accepts OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens on inbound MCP requests. Paired with VDP’s OAuth authenticator configuration, the token forwards to VDP for validation and role resolution (see also the Governed access section).
- vdp.datasource.jdbcUrl=jdbc:vdb://<vdp-host>:9999/: the JDBC URL where VDP is reached. The specific database targeted per request comes from the MCP endpoint path.
- mcp.visibility.tags=mcp controls which views are visible from the MCP Server. If defined, only views tagged with at least one of these tags will be visible.
The server implements the MCP OAuth 2.0 authorization flow, including RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and RFC 7591 Dynamic Client Registration.
A note on IdP compatibility
The Denodo MCP Server documents support for the automatic Dynamic Client Registration flow with Okta, Ping Identity, and Keycloak. For other identity providers, the MCP Server also accepts manual client configuration where the OAuth token is obtained out of band and forwarded as a static Authorization header on the MCP request, as described in the Denodo MCP Server User Manual.
Front the server with an Application Load Balancer
If the Denodo MCP Server runs on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS in the same VPC as VDP, expose it through an Application Load Balancer with an HTTPS listener and a certificate from AWS Certificate Manager. This gives AgentCore Gateway a stable HTTPS endpoint and offloads TLS termination from the MCP Server process. Target group: HTTP, port 8080. The health check path should accept both 200 and 404 as healthy responses, since the root path returns 404 and /health returns 200 when the server is up and connected to VDP.
Register as an AgentCore Gateway target
The full step-by-step walkthrough, including AgentCore Gateway creation, IAM service role configuration, and Gateway target validation, is in Denodo’s Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server integration guide.
Add Denodo VQL skill in the harness
The Denodo VQL skill acts as a system prompt extension for the LLM within the agent framework (such as Strands or Bedrock AgentCore). When registered in the agent harness, it instructs the model on VQL syntax rules and how to help prevent SQL errors.
Deploy and run the agent
The Denodo AgentCore documentation reference has the full agent code in the Denodo KB. The pattern is short: a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock, an MCP client pointed at the Denodo MCP Server, and an AgentCore runtime entrypoint that wires them together.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we run three query categories through the agent, plus one governance rerun that demonstrates the same-query-two-users property from the Governed access section. We can use Denodo’s Data Marketplace assistant, which relies on equivalent tools behind the scenes, to get a quick validation on our scenario.
Query 1, Aurora-only
“List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.”
The agent generates and runs:
VDP’s optimizer determines that only Aurora-side data is needed for the projection and filter, and pushes a single query down to Amazon Aurora. Based on a probe query, the agent can translate the filter from Wisconsin to the predicate state = 'WI'. Amazon Redshift and the on-premises cluster are not touched.
Query 2, Redshift-only
“What are our top 10 products by units sold?”
The agent generates:
Query 3, three-way federation
“Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime value haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?”
The agent generates:
VDP plans across the three engines as described in the Build the semantic layer section: profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, enrollment records from the on-premises cluster, and the final join and top-N inside VDP. The top result in the POC data was Marcus Chen from Milwaukee, WI, with $47,832 in lifetime spend, a customer with high spend and no rewards enrollment, exactly the auto-enrollment target from the example question in The example. Note that the LLM didn’t need to come up with the definition of lifetime_spend, since the formula is part of the semantic model as defined in the metric view.
Governance rerun
We run Query 1 with ssn added to the projection, as two different callers:
As hr_user, the result includes the ssn values. As marketing_user, the result returns the same rows with ssn with asterisks as a masked value. No changes to the query text, the agent code, the MCP Server, VDP, or Aurora between the two runs. The Global Security Policy mask_pii_columns from the Governed access section evaluates against the caller’s role at query time, and VDP rewrites the projection accordingly. The same behavior applies to card_num.
Extending to other sources
Adding a source outside AWS to customer_360, whether that’s Salesforce for CRM records, ServiceNow for customer service data, or SAP for ERP tables, is the same modeling exercise as Aurora, Amazon Redshift, and the on-premises cluster. Create a base view, join it into the derived view on cid, and tag sensitive columns. The metric views, the Global Security Policy, and the agent’s VQL don’t change. What changes is the wrapper VDP uses to reach the source. For example:
- Salesforce connects through the Denodo Salesforce connector with OAuth 2.0 authentication and VQL-to-SOQL translation over the REST or Bulk API.
- ServiceNow, Microsoft Dynamics 365, and other SaaS tools use Denodo’s SaaS wizard templates, pre-configured for common APIs.
- SAP ERP connects through BAPI sources using the SAP Java Connector. VDP calls SAP RFCs and shapes the response into rows.
The agent doesn’t know which of these sits underneath. It queries customer_360 in VQL. Denodo’s wrapper handles the source-native translation, and Denodo’s Global Security Policy applies uniformly whether the row comes from a JDBC engine, a REST API, or an RFC call.
One deployment-time decision varies by source: whether to pass the caller’s identity through to the source or connect as a service account. Pass-through gives end-to-end audit at the source when the source supports it (Kerberos to SAP or OAuth to Salesforce, for example). Service-account connections are simpler, and the source’s audit shows the query as coming from Denodo.
Deployment: Denodo Agora versus self-managed
Denodo on AWS runs in one of two shapes. Both use the same Virtual DataPort, same VQL, same Global Security Policies, same MCP Server. The choice is operational.
Agora: Fully managed
Denodo Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service, available on the AWS Marketplace. Agora runs on a split-plane architecture. The Control Plane (Solution Manager, Design Studio, Scheduler admin, Monitoring/Diagnostics) runs in Denodo’s cloud accounts, and the Execution Plane (VDP, Scheduler, Data Catalog) runs inside the customer’s AWS account. The compute that touches the data lives in the customer’s VPC. The management surface is operated by Denodo.
Choose Agora when you don’t want to operate the application and the update cadence Denodo publishes works for your organization.
Self-managed on Amazon EC2 or Amazon EKS
Self-managed deployments install Denodo Platform entirely in the customer’s AWS account. Denodo publishes VM images on AWS Marketplace and ships container images with Helm charts for Amazon EKS. You handle the cluster, upgrades, and backups.
Choose self-managed when compliance requires a specific deployment posture, when you want to control the version cadence, or when the reference architecture calls for a Denodo cluster inside a specific VPC.
Reaching sources outside AWS
Both deployment shapes place VDP in the customer’s AWS account. Reaching an on-premises source is the same problem in both cases: a network path from the VPC that hosts VDP to the on-premises cluster, provisioned through whichever hybrid connectivity option the organization already uses. For SaaS sources like Salesforce or ServiceNow, no additional setup is needed, since the Execution Plane has outbound internet access by default, which is sufficient for OAuth 2.0 authentication and REST API calls.
Conclusion and where to start
Reliable agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that presents business-meaningful data over live source systems, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, Denodo Platform, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.
The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the underlying databases. Base views, derived views, metric views, tags, and Global Security Policies live in VDP. When a source schema drifts, when a new source comes online, or when a governance rule changes, the update happens in the semantic layer and every consumer picks it up at the next query. The additional metadata the semantic layer carries (documentation, descriptions, metric formulas, and the 360 graph) gives the model more grounded business context to reason over, rather than raw schema alone.
Where to start
Try Agora on AWS and follow the instructions to deploy. Agora is Denodo’s fully managed cloud service for deploying an AI data layer on AWS, providing live, governed access to distributed enterprise data.
Most teams get this working by starting narrow and expanding.
- Pick one agentic workflow that spans two or three distinct source systems that takes longer than it should to answer today.
- Write three to five specific questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer must support on day one.
- Connect data sources and create base views over the source tables the workflow touches. Tag PII columns during creation.
- Build the derived views and metric views the questions require.
- Implement Global Security Policy to help protect PII, protected health information (PHI), payment card industry (PCI), or other sensitive information.
- Register the Denodo MCP Server as an AgentCore Gateway target and wire a Strands agent to it using the pattern in the earlier section. Deploy with agentcore deploy.
Further reading
- Integrating Amazon Bedrock AgentCore with Denodo via MCP Server: Denodo Community reference implementation.
- Denodo MCP Server User Manual.
- Denodo VQL Guide, including Defining a Metric View.
- Denodo Global Security Policies.
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore developer guide.

articles.title: Test de Final Fantasy Resonance : le retour aux sources qui touche en plein cœur
articles.text:
La série Final Fantasy est passée de la 2D à des personnages en 3D dans des décors précalculés en 2D, puis à la 3D intégrale. La suite logique ? Des personnages en 2D dans des décors en 3D. La boucle est bouclée, et la licence atteint peut-être sa forme ultime avec cet épisode Final Fantasy Resonance, en HD-2D, qui sort le 22 octobre 2026 sur PC, PS5, Xbox Series S, Xbox Series X, Nintendo Switch et Nintendo Switch 2.
Si la proposition peut paraître désuète, quelques mois avant la sortie de Final Fantasy VII Revelation, dernier volet du remake en trois parties, attendu le 8 avril 2027, elle n’en reste pas moins fascinante. Au-delà de ses graphismes, Resonance touche une corde sensible : celle qui vibre chez les fans de longue date de Final Fantasy, celles et ceux qui étaient là à l’époque de la NES, ou qui ont fait leurs premières armes avec les épisodes de la PS1.
Mais, au-delà de son aspect nostalgique, est-ce que ce nouvel épisode, qui reprend dans les grandes lignes l’épisode mobile Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, lancé en 2015 et aujourd’hui fermé, vaut que l’on y investisse plusieurs dizaines d’heures de jeu, alors que la fin d’année est très, très chargée ? Réponse dans notre test.
Points forts
- Une direction artistique HD-2D exceptionnelle
- Un système de combat prenant et dynamique
- Un retour aux sources réussi
Points faibles
- Une récupération des Visions trop simpliste
- Quelques poncifs qui font lever les yeux au ciel
- Un Final Fantasy qui ne plaira pas à tout le monde
La HD-2D la plus aboutie de Square Enix
J’ai une théorie : tous les jeux en HD-2D de Square Enix, d’Octopath Traveler aux remakes de Dragon Quest III puis I & II, ont été autant d’essais de la part de l’éditeur pour peaufiner ce rendu graphique. Square Enix a confié le développement de Resonance au studio japonais Lancarse, associé à la Team Asano, l’équipe interne justement à l’origine d’Octopath Traveler et du style HD-2D. En effet, quand on voit Final Fantasy Resonance, c’est une évidence : jamais la HD-2D n’a été aussi bien exploitée dans un jeu.
Je ne parle pas seulement de beauté graphique. Dragon Quest I & II mettait déjà la barre haut, et, récemment, The Adventures of Elliot: The Millennium Tales avait également fait fort dans sa proposition. Non, ici, en plus d’être beau, le jeu se permet ce que les autres titres en HD-2D de Square Enix n’osaient pas : bouger la caméra dans les décors.
Ce n’est rien dit comme ça, mais le principal défaut de la HD-2D était que la caméra restait finalement figée, en mode diorama, sur l’action, cinématiques comprises. Resonance reprend pourtant les ingrédients qui font le charme de cette approche graphique : des personnages en pixel art d’une finesse remarquable, qui semblent tout droit sortis d’un jeu rétro, évoluent dans des décors en 3D mis en valeur par des éclairages, des effets de profondeur et une profusion de détails. Mais là où la HD-2D donnait jusqu’ici l’impression d’admirer de petites scènes miniatures, Resonance fait voler en éclats cette sensation de diorama en donnant une liberté inédite à la caméra.
Ainsi, la mise en scène gagne en dynamisme, ce qui permet d’intensifier chaque scène, chaque émotion, en plus d’offrir des cinématiques de toute beauté. Dans les villes comme au cœur des combats, la caméra ne tient jamais en place. Elle balaie les décors à l’horizontale, glisse sous une arche, pivote autour des bâtiments ou accompagne les déplacements en gravissant des marches. Les cinématiques ne sont pas en reste, multipliant travellings et panoramiques avec une fluidité et une élégance remarquables. Quant aux combats, ils profitent eux aussi de cette mise en scène dynamique, avec des mouvements amples et certaines attaques qui n’ont rien à envier aux Final Fantasy modernes.
Les combats ont d’ailleurs fait l’objet d’un soin tout particulier dans leur mise en scène, entre les effets de certaines magies dévastatrices qui remplissent tout l’écran dans un déluge de particules, les Visions, particulièrement belles, et les chimères, toujours aussi impressionnantes, quel que soit l’épisode de la saga. Non, vraiment, si le remake de Final Fantasy VII est le plus impressionnant techniquement parlant, Resonance pourrait bien être l’un des plus beaux par sa direction artistique et son audace visuelle.
Une histoire qui va droit au but
Final Fantasy Resonance se déroule dans le royaume de Grandshelt, dont l’équilibre repose sur plusieurs Cristaux liés aux différents éléments. Mais lorsque de mystérieux guerriers menacent de les détruire, Rain, commandant d’une escadrille d’aéronefs, Lasswell, son second et ami d’enfance, et Fina, une mystérieuse jeune femme, se lancent à leur poursuite pour empêcher la destruction du royaume.
Le récit de Resonance s’appuie d’ailleurs sur les Cristaux, qui donnent également leur nom à l’un des thèmes principaux de toute la série : le thème du Prélude, aussi appelé Crystal Theme, l’un des thèmes les plus emblématiques de la Final Fantasy. Une note d’intention évidente de la part de Square Enix, faire de cet épisode un hommage à 40 ans de Final Fantasy.
Passée une introduction qui nous plonge directement dans l’ambiance et soulève d’emblée de nombreuses questions sur les enjeux et les personnages, Final Fantasy Resonance présente ses protagonistes et son univers avec une efficacité qui rappelle immédiatement les premiers épisodes de la saga. Le royaume de Grandshelt, ses Cristaux, ses aéronefs et la menace qui pèse sur le monde : tous les ingrédients du RPG japonais classique sont réunis, avec le charme des anciens épisodes.
Si, sur le papier, Square Enix veut faire un Final Fantasy hommage, manette en main, c’est une capsule temporelle que l’on découvre. L’exploration de temples, la carte en 3D, les musiques qui rappellent d’anciens épisodes, les villes et les PNJ, les menus, tout cela évoque évidemment l’ère Super Nintendo, Final Fantasy VI en tête, mais aussi les épisodes de l’ère PS1 et leur simplicité apparente.
Resonance renoue surtout avec une écriture qui laisse de la place à l’aventure, sans esbroufe. À l’heure où certains RPG multiplient les dialogues interminables et les séquences explicatives, le jeu revendique une approche plus classique, presque intimiste, sans pour autant renoncer à la mise en scène. La structure narrative, héritée de la première saison de Brave Exvius, que cette version réorganise en profondeur, peut sembler limitée par moments. Elle se déroule heureusement avec une grande fluidité au fil de l’aventure.
On en vient à s’attacher à ses personnages, alliés comme ennemis, et à vouloir progresser dans l’aventure par pur intérêt pour son récit, chose qui, personnellement, ne m’était pas arrivée depuis Final Fantasy X. Square Enix laisse de côté, le temps d’un épisode, les délires scénaristiques à la Tetsuya Nomura, le célèbre character designer et directeur créatif derrière Final Fantasy VII et Kingdom Hearts, pour offrir un épisode du cœur, et ça fait un bien fou.
Un mot sur les quêtes annexes, qui encouragent à explorer les environs et permettent de développer les personnages. Elles s’intègrent très bien au rythme de l’aventure et étoffent l’univers et les relations entre les protagonistes, en plus de rapporter de précieux objets, utiles notamment pour vos Visions.
Le retour du tour par tour, mais bien plus dynamique
Les Visions justement, parlons-en. Ces Visions sont des héros et héroïnes d’autres Final Fantasy qui viennent vous prêter main-forte. À travers elles, Resonance fait aussi office d’épisode musée, de quoi faire plaisir aux fans de longue date. On pourrait se demander ce que Cloud ou d’autres héros de la saga viennent faire dans Resonance, mais Square Enix trouve une justification plutôt bien fichue. Ces fantômes d’autres mondes sont un petit bonbon sucré que l’on savoure avec plaisir, et leur présence se limite aux combats.
Comme dans tout bon Final Fantasy, les combats sont au cœur de l’expérience. Ici, on a affaire à du tour par tour, mais sans jauge ATB, cette barre qui se remplit jusqu’à la prochaine attaque. Resonance affiche à la place la chronologie du combat, avec les prochains tours des alliés et des ennemis. À vous de gérer les actions de vos personnages, en attaque comme en défense, en gardant plusieurs coups d’avance.
À son tour par tour, Square Enix ajoute une composante diablement efficace : la jauge de Choc. Le principe consiste à exploiter les faiblesses des adversaires pour les mettre en état de choc et ainsi les priver d’actions. S’ensuit alors un véritable déchaînement de violence, durant lequel vous pouvez enchaîner les attaques dévastatrices avant de déclencher une puissante capacité de Résonance grâce à vos Visions.
Pour le reste, on est dans le classique : l’expérience gagnée au combat fait monter vos personnages en niveau, l’argent sert à acheter armes et armures, et les points de compétence débloquent de nouvelles capacités sur les Visions équipées. Une fois une Vision maîtrisée à 100 %, vous pouvez vous en séparer tout en conservant certaines de ses compétences.
Globalement, n’importe quel néophyte pourra progresser dans l’aventure sans rencontrer de réelle difficulté. Il faudra toutefois faire monter votre équipe en niveau pour affronter des ennemis plus coriaces, tenter de capturer des chimères ou venir à bout de certains boss un peu trop punitifs si vous manquez de préparation. Square Enix pense aussi à celles et ceux qui voudraient simplement parcourir l’aventure grâce à un mode Histoire, qui rend le jeu bien plus facile. Une fonction permettant de tripler la vitesse des combats est également présente, parce que les ados d’hier qui passaient leur temps sur FF7 ont maintenant un travail et moins de temps libre.
Un contenu généreux et des surprises
Il arrive bien sûr un moment où vous mettrez le sauvetage du monde de côté pour aller vous amuser à droite et à gauche. La carte du monde à parcourir n’est pas très grande, mais entre les villes, les passages cachés, les îles mystérieuses et les lieux facultatifs, il y a de quoi multiplier la durée de l’aventure par deux. Vous pourrez vous déplacer à dos de chocobo et voyager rapidement vers des endroits déjà visités, ce qui évite, encore une fois, de perdre trop de temps pour aller d’un point A à un point B.
Si le jeu peut se terminer en 35 heures environ avec le mode facile activé, comptez plutôt 70 heures pour en voir le bout à 100 %, avec quelques surprises à la clé. Certains ennemis nécessitent un niveau élevé, et les affronter en mode facile serait dommage, tant les combats sont stratégiques et amusants. Certaines quêtes annexes vous demanderont également un peu de matière grise pour être accomplies.
Concernant les Visions, elles ne se récupèrent pas par un système de tirage aléatoire comme dans le jeu mobile Brave Exvius, mais s’obtiennent dans des sanctuaires qui misent très fort sur la nostalgie et divulgâchent allègrement les Final Fantasy dont elles sont issues. La manière d’obtenir une Vision est d’ailleurs le seul véritable défaut de cet épisode : il vous suffit de les ramasser dans les sanctuaires dédiés, comme vous ramasseriez une potion tombée par terre, tout simplement. On aurait aimé que ces retrouvailles avec les héros emblématiques de la saga soient un peu plus mises en valeur, plutôt que de se résumer à une simple collecte à la Pokémon.
Malgré ses qualités indéniables, pas sûr que cet épisode parvienne à convaincre les joueuses et les joueurs qui ont découvert la série avec ses épisodes les plus récents. Si, de mon côté, je retrouve un plaisir fou et ai l’impression de replonger dans une époque bénie, où le JRPG était à son apogée, les nouveaux venus pourraient se sentir démunis face à un épisode plus léger, qui mise avant tout sur le classicisme et la nostalgie. Une approche qui fait mouche auprès des nostalgiques, mais qui risque de paraître un peu trop sage à celles et ceux qui attendent de la saga qu’elle continue à se réinventer. Pour se faire une idée, une démo gratuite, qui couvre tout le premier chapitre, est disponible depuis le 3 septembre, et la sauvegarde se transfère vers le jeu complet.
Le verdict
Final Fantasy Resonance
Voir la fiche
On a aimé
- Une direction artistique HD-2D exceptionnelle
- Un système de combat prenant et dynamique
- Un retour aux sources réussi
On a moins aimé
- Une récupération des Visions trop simpliste
- Quelques poncifs qui font lever les yeux au ciel
- Un Final Fantasy qui ne plaira pas à tout le monde

articles.title: Espoo's Coherence Quantum raises €2.78 million to build infrastructure for larger quantum computers | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Coherence Quantum, an Espoo-based quantum hardware company developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for future quantum computers, has raised €2.78 million in Seed funding to develop a new approach to the cryogenic infrastructure surrounding solid-state quantum processors.
The round was led by Helsinki-based early-stage investor Lifeline Ventures, with participation from technology entrepreneur Mårten Mickos.
Petteri Koponen of Lifeline Ventures said, “The quantum industry has proved that increasingly capable processors can be built. The next challenge is building the infrastructure that allows them to scale. Coherence Quantum is going after a fundamental part of that problem.
“They have an exceptional technical team with a clear view of where the industry is heading and the ambition to build far more than a single component. If quantum computers are going to scale, the architecture around the qubits has to scale with them, and we’re backing them to become a key part of how larger quantum computers are built.”
Coherence Quantum was founded in 2026 by Aashish Sah (CEO), Suman Kundu (CTO), and Erkki Soininen (CPO), and originated from research at Aalto University’s Quantum Computing and Devices group. The company is also supported by founding advisor Mikko Möttönen, a professor of quantum technology at Aalto University.
Sah is a quantum physicist specialising in superconducting qubits and their interaction with the electromagnetic environment. Kundu is an experimental quantum physicist who played a key role in building and setting up Aalto University’s 20-qubit Q20 quantum computer. Soininen holds a PhD in Physics and previously held a product leadership role at the cryogenics company Bluefors.
Coherence Quantum is developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform for solid-state quantum computers, including superconducting and spin-qubit systems. 
According to the company, its goal is to help quantum systems scale, enabling more qubits while maintaining the low-noise, high-coherence environment needed for reliable operation.
But it says that scaling quantum computers by adding more qubits creates another scaling problem: everything needed to control them must scale as well. “As quantum processors grow, more control and readout signals need to reach the quantum processing unit (QPU). Conventional approaches require more wiring and signal-conditioning hardware inside a system with very limited space and cooling power. At the same time, the qubit environment has to remain protected from thermal noise and other disturbances that can affect performance,” the Finnish startup explained.
Coherence Quantum claims to be developing an integrated cryogenic signalling and control platform to address this scaling challenge. It notes that its first technologies focus on cryogenic signal conditioning, helping protect the environment around the qubit. From there, the company is developing higher-density signal interfaces and working towards bringing more control functionality inside the cryostat and closer to the quantum processing unit.
Sah said, “Quantum computers won’t scale by adding qubits alone. The infrastructure around them has to scale too. We’re starting with signal conditioning and building towards higher-density interfaces and, ultimately, more integrated cryogenic control. Our aim is to give quantum-computer builders an architecture that can support larger systems without wiring, cooling requirements, and complexity growing at the same rate.”
The company is building dedicated R&D, testing and manufacturing capabilities in Espoo, Finland, close to Aalto University and Finland’s growing quantum technology ecosystem. It plans to use the fresh capital to establish its lab in Espoo, build its first product prototypes and manufacturing process, continue R&D, and grow the team.
Starting with cryogenic signal-conditioning technologies, Coherence Quantum is working towards higher-density interfaces and increasingly integrated control inside the fridge. Its long-term ambition is to help establish a standardised blueprint for the cryogenic signalling and control stack, bringing its own technologies together with complementary technologies from across the quantum ecosystem.

articles.title: Android lie désormais votre numéro à tous vos comptes Google : comment l’en empêcher
articles.text:
Android a discrètement commencé à relier votre numéro de téléphone à tous les comptes Google connectés à votre smartphone. Mais il est encore possible de l'en empêcher.
Le numéro de téléphone est devenu une information clé pour Google. La firme, que Donald Trump dit avoir à sa botte, a, en mai dernier, ramené à 5 Go le stockage gratuit pour les nouveaux comptes qui refusaient de fournir le numéro de leur smartphone. Un nouveau réglage de Google Play Services pourrait bien faire grincer des dents les utilisateurs. On vous explique.
Google rattache de force votre numéro de téléphone à tous vos comptes
C’est un utilisateur de Reddit qui a tiré la sonnette d’alarme : « Les services Google Play se « vérifient eux-mêmes » et lient votre numéro de téléphone à TOUS les comptes connectés sans autorisation explicite. Juste un petit avertissement pour quiconque valorise la confidentialité de base sur Android. ». Dans les faits, cela voudrait dire qu’Android relierait votre compte perso, votre compte pro et vos adresses secondaires à un seul et même numéro sans vous demander votre avis.
Les contenus ne se mélangent pas pour autant, mais cela suffit à prouver que tous ces profils ont le même propriétaire. Si vous avez choisi de créer plusieurs adresses pour cloisonner vos usages, cela complique sérieusement la tâche, d’autant que la documentation officielle de Google indique que ce nouveau réglage est activé par défaut.
« Nous validons le numéro de téléphone et l’ajoutons à tous les comptes Google connectés à l’appareil. Cela s’applique aux comptes et numéros de téléphone actuels et futurs (…) Lorsque la validation du numéro de téléphone est activée, vous autorisez Google et votre opérateur à vérifier régulièrement vos numéros de téléphone », peut-on également y lire.
Est-il possible de reprendre la main ?
Il existe, heureusement, un moyen d’éviter que tous vos comptes soient reliés à un seul et même numéro de téléphone. Voici la marche à suivre, partagée par Google :
- Rendez-vous dans les réglages de votre téléphone ;
- Cliquez sur « Services et Préférence Google », à côté de votre photo de profil puis sur l’onglet « Tous les services » ;
- Sélectionnez « Validation du numéro » dans la section « Confidentialité et sécurité » ;
- Désactivez l’option « Valider automatiquement le ou les numéros de téléphone ».
Notez toutefois que cette manipulation ne fonctionne que pour les futurs rattachements : pour les numéros qui sont déjà reliés, il faudra vous rendre sur la page « Informations personnelles » de votre compte Google, puis aller sur « Informations de contact » > « Téléphone » et effacer manuellement le numéro sur chaque profil. Une véritable corvée qui ne fonctionnerait, de plus, pas à tous les coups : certains utilisateurs ont remarqué que l’option de vérification du numéro de téléphone avait tendance à se réactiver toute seule.
Vous l’avez compris, Google est de plus en plus gourmand en données personnelles et son appétit ne semble pas près de faiblir.

articles.title: Ibai le alquila a Netflix su noche más vista: La Velada del Año será exclusiva de la plataforma hasta 2029
articles.text:
Netflix emitirá en directo y en exclusiva las ediciones de 2027, 2028 y 2029 de La Velada del Año, según un comunicado de la propia plataforma. La séptima edición será la primera que no se retransmita en el canal de Twitch de Ibai Llanos, su casa desde 2021. Kick le ofreció el triple, según ha contado el propio streamer, pero lo cierto es que nos quedamos sin saber ningún detalle económico jugoso de esta nueva vida para el evento que arrancó en 2021 en una sala de conciertos de Barcelona.
Nueve millones de pantallas. La Velada tiene un formato con el crecimiento ya garantizado, aúnque ahora esté en una plataforma con un alcance más cerrado que Netflix. La audiencia media pasó de cerca de un millón de espectadores en 2021 a más de seis millones en 2026, y la quinta edición, la de 2025, llegó a un pico de 9,3 millones de espectadores simultáneos. Las ediciones de 2022 y 2023 batieron el récord de espectadores de un solo canal en Twitch. Y el crecimiento ha sido sostenido (salvo el retroceso de la última). Para la quinta, el evento ya tenía una categoría propia dentro de Twitch.
Los dineros. Velaris-Kena Productions, la sociedad propia desde la que Ibai organiza la Velada, ingresó 11,7 millones de euros en 2025 y cerró el ejercicio con 1,7 millones de beneficio neto. Por calibrar el peso del evento en las finanzas de Ibai, en 2024 esa misma sociedad apenas había facturado 208.000 euros, porque la Velada todavía se gestionaba desde otra firma.
Durante años, Ibai y Kosmos, la empresa de Gerard Piqué, compartieron al 50% Goatch Global, que llegó a facturar más de ocho millones de euros en 2022 y en 2023. Fue esa sociedad la que registró la marca La Velada del Año; la titularidad pasó a Ibai en octubre de 2024. Para la quinta edición, Ibai ya había dejado fuera a Piqué. La presencia de Ibai en la Kings League, la liga que impulsa Kosmos, en calidad de presidente del Porcinos FC, es su único vínculo empresarial restante con Piqué.
Los comentarios de Ibai. Tras el anuncio, Ibai grabó un vídeo para aclarar los términos. "Yo no he vendido La Velada del Año", dijo. Ibai conserva el 100% de la propiedad y lo que ha cedido son los derechos de retransmisión, algo que comparó con la exclusividad que mantuvo con Twitch durante cinco años. El streamer también ha avanzado que la presentación, los pesajes y las entrevistas seguirán en sus canales de Twitch y YouTube, que Netflix pondrá dinero en la producción y en la promoción de combates y artistas.
Lo de Kick. Ibai ha contado que Kick había puesto sobre la mesa el triple de dinero que Netflix, allá por diciembre de 2024. Según relató entonces en directo, la plataforma le ofrecía más del doble de lo que cobraba de Twitch por menos horas de emisión, y decidió quedarse donde estaba. Eso sí, en el mismo directo anunció que bajaría de unas 1.300 o 1.400 horas anuales en Twitch a unas 500 y que se volcaría en YouTube. La sexta Velada, en 2026, ya se emitió también en YouTube y TikTok, así que es obvio que el streamer siempre ha tenido clara la importancia de no casarse con nadie a base de exclusividades.
Hasta ahora. Y aún así, con matices, porque Netflix no es una excepción: Ibai alquila la emisión por temporadas mientras retiene la marca y la conversación previa en sus propios canales.
A Netflix le gusta el boxeo. Netflix acumula casi dos años de grandes noches de boxeo en directo. El combate entre Jake Paul y Mike Tyson de noviembre de 2024 alcanzó un pico de 65 millones de streams simultáneos y una audiencia media de 108 millones de espectadores, pese a los problemas técnicos de la retransmisión. En septiembre de 2025, el Canelo-Crawford sumó 41,4 millones de espectadores con un pico de más de 24 millones de streams. Desde enero de 2025, además, Raw de la WWE tiene directo cada semana.
Las cifras. El cambio de casa va a suponer, muy posiblemente, un impulso notable para el espectáculo, ya que alcanzará una audiencia más global. Además, el contrato incluye la opción de un año extra de contrato si los resultados lo justifican. Si se activa, la Velada llegaría a 2030 en Netflix, el mismo año en que la plataforma emitirá el Mundial en España, convirtiéndose así la plataforma en un actor más que relevante en el campo de emisión en directo de deportes a nivel global.

articles.title: Spectrum costs squeeze African telecom investment and growth
articles.text:
Africa’s mobile networks have expanded significantly over the past decade, bringing coverage to more people. But wider coverage has not translated into widespread internet use or network quality on par with other regions.
A new report by the GSMA, Spectrum Policy in Africa: Enabling Investment and Empowering Consumers Through Effective Spectrum Pricing, identifies the high cost of accessing radio spectrum—the invisible radio frequencies that carry mobile calls and internet data—as a central bottleneck. African mobile operators pay significantly more for relatively less spectrum, leaving them with limited capacity to expand or improve service quality.
According to GSMA Intelligence, spectrum costs consume 0.82% of mobile operators’ revenue per 100 MHz in Africa, compared with 0.66% in the rest of the world. Meanwhile, African operators hold an average of about 570 MHz of spectrum below 7 GHz, 24% less than the global peer average of approximately 750 MHz.
The imbalance extends beyond price and availability to licence duration. Only nine African countries routinely grant spectrum licences lasting 20 years or more, while licences of 20 years or indefinite duration are standard across Europe, North America and developed Asian markets.
Lowering spectrum fees could free up vital capital for network expansion, but lower fees alone do not guarantee better connectivity. The crucial test for African regulators is whether more affordable access can be tied to measurable improvements in network quality and internet adoption, particularly in underserved communities where initial financial returns remain low.
