articles.title: Ex-OpenAI Worker Accused of Bugging Conference Room Planned to Fly to Saudi Arabia, Prosecutors Say
articles.text:
A former OpenAI engineer charged with secretly installing a recording device in a conference room to glean company details had been “mere days” away from absconding to Saudi Arabia before his arrest last week, federal prosecutors revealed in new court filings.
Abdulrahman Alfozan’s wife and young son also left the country the day after the 35-year-old Saudi national’s arrest, traveling on a one-way ticket booked and paid for by a Saudi military official, prosecutors said in a memo Sunday seeking his continued detention.
“Ultimately, the defendant has little incentive to remain in the United States to see this case through,” federal prosecutors wrote. “He has ample resources —including his significant compensation from a decade of high-tech employment in the Bay Area and at least two bank accounts in Saudi Arabia — and what appears to be considerable support from a foreign government.”
A federal judge in San Francisco sided with prosecutors Monday, denying a request by Alfozan’s lawyers to release him to home confinement. His next court date is Nov.
Alfozan’s lawyer William Pernik argued in court that his client had strong ties to the U.S. and was “weeks away from achieving every immigrant’s dream” — U.S. citizenship.
Alfozan had a naturalization interview with federal officials scheduled next month and has been a lawful permanent resident since 2020, his lawyers said in their legal filings. He has also lived in the U.S. for 15 years and attended MIT and the University of California, Berkeley, they said.
Pernik said Alfozan is willing to put up “almost the entirety” of his assets — about $1 million currently in a U.S. investment account — to cover his bond.
“Everything this man has he’s willing to surrender,” he said, adding that Alfozan’s wife is also willing to return to the U.S. as she still holds a visitor visa that expires in 2033.
Judge Alex Tse appeared doubtful, questioning whether Saudi Arabia’s government would simply reimburse Alfozan if he fled and forfeited his bond.
After the hearing, Pernik said he was disappointed with the ruling but declined further comment.
Pernik had argued in court filings that Alfozan purchased one-way tickets for his family to Saudi Arabia more than two weeks before prosecutors allege the recording devices were installed. They said the couple planned to spend Alfozan’s roughly two-month paternity leave in Saudi Arabia following the birth of their U.S.-citizen son.
But prosecutors said Saudi officials purchased new plane tickets for Alfozan’s wife and son after his arrest, allowing them to leave the U.S. sooner than the Oct. 12 flight Alfozan had originally booked.
Prosecutors have not said what Alfozan might have wanted to do with the recordings, but say he was in “frequent communication” with a member of the Saudi royal family. They said the royal family member repeatedly tried to recruit Alfozan to an artificial intelligence venture being launched in Saudi Arabia.
Alfozan had told the unnamed person he wouldn’t leave OpenAI until his stock was vested, even as he explored other career opportunities in the Middle Eastern kingdom, prosecutors wrote. He had worked at the ChatGPT maker since July 2025 but was fired after his arrest.
Prosecutors say Alfozan concealed an audio recording device in toilet paper and plugged it into a USB port on the back of a television in an executive conference room he wasn’t authorized to access. They say security cameras captured him entering the room and checking behind the television after installing the device. It remained there for several days before being found Sept. 30.
Prosecutors say the conference room was typically used for meetings involving company leaders, government officials and other executives and “discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, as well as nonpublic information.”
OpenAI has said the recording device Alfozan used was sophisticated, designed to evade detection and featured advanced encryption and audio-monitoring capabilities. They also said they had evidence Alfozan planned to place other listening devices elsewhere in the office.
Alfozan has been charged with using or endeavoring to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications. If convicted, he faces a five-year prison sentence.

articles.title: Otter.ai raises $320 million from General Catalyst's growth fund for its meeting tool | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Meeting note-taking tool Otter.ai announced on Tuesday that it has raised $320 million from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund (CVF), which provides capital to startups without diluting equity and gets returns on the results of marketing spend.
Otter.ai said that it will use these funds for enterprise growth, go-to-market strategy, international expansion, and product innovation.
The startup, which has been around for nearly a decade, has raised $50 million in total funding with its last round in 2021, according to PitchBook data.
Last year, Otter hit a revenue milestone after crossing $100 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR). The company said it’s now approaching new milestones, but didn’t provide updated figures.
The company said that 40 million users have used its product to date, up from 25 million last year. However, given the crowded space among meeting note-taking products, a pertinent challenge for Otter would be to have its customers stick around. Unfortunately, the startup didn’t provide any numbers around its monthly active users or churn.
“Voice is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in enterprise AI, and Otter is at the forefront of it – a conviction that’s only deepened watching Otter’s growth,” said Pranav Singhvi, Partner and Co-founder of CVF, General Catalyst. “When Otter enables enterprises to capture critical voice data and turns it into actionable business insights, teams move faster, decisions get sharper, and productivity compounds across the organization, and that’s why it’s a strong partner for CVF.”
There is a lot of competition in the market with well-funded meeting notetakers like Fireflies.ai, Granola, and Read AI; new entrants like Calendly, Wispr, and Superhuman, which acquired Fathom; and other notetakers like Circleback, Talat, and Quill.
Most of these notetakers want to connect to enterprise systems and, based on data captured in meetings, automate workflows. Otter is also heading in that direction. In the last few years, it introduced a meeting assistant, a search function that works across apps, and integration with other AI tools.
Otter’s newly appointed CMO, Alex Gay, who comes from Superhuman, told TechCrunch at a sit-down at the HumanX conference last month that the company sees a big opportunity in turning transcripts into an actionable roadmap for people who are in back-to-back meetings.
“When we start thinking about what is actually the bigger problem that people are facing right now, we saw this large pain point in meeting-heavy roles, where people are back-to-back in conversations. These meetings are the work for them. That’s either customer conversations or, from a sales standpoint. That’s where strategies are discussed. But meetings are terribly inefficient because when you come into a meeting, you spend the first twenty minutes recapping what was said before to catch everybody up,” he said.
The company is now experimenting with providing insights before, after, and during meetings. It has been testing a feature to send a pre-brief to users with details and background information, with context from previous conversations across surfaces. Plus, it is also trying out a Live Assist feature to let users ask questions to the AI assistant during the meeting to get knowledge.

articles.title: 'It's a beast, but not at everything' — RTX Spark-powered Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra lives up to expectations, but you need to be a big fan of local AI
articles.text:
'It's a beast, but not at everything' — RTX Spark-powered Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra lives up to expectations, but you need to be a big fan of local AI
Is the Surface Laptop Ultra price tag justified? This depends on what you need
Nvidia's RTX Spark laptops hit the shelves last week, led by Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra, and the chip supports up to 128GB of memory.
This laptop starts at $2,599.99, but does its performance justify the price tag?
I took a look at some of the earliest in-depth reviews of the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra to ascertain what this device offers and whether it is worth every penny.
What reviews say
The prowess of the RTX Spark laptop was acknowledged, but all the reviews agreed on one thing: it’s not foolproof and has some downsides.
“It's a beast, but not at everything,” said Zac Bowden of Windows Central, while Tom's Guide went further, calling it “not a MacBook Pro killer but something much weirder and wildly powerful.”
The praise is concentrated in one area: local AI models. Every outlet that tested them put the Surface ahead of Apple's M5 Max and AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395, the most powerful mobile chips for laptops.
Its gaming performance, however, did not exactly get much praise – while some said it is just okay, others think it’s a weak spot.
Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed!
Price
Cost is the sticking point for RTX Spark. Microsoft's Surface Laptop Ultra starts at $2,599.99 for the 18-core model with 24GB of memory and 512GB of storage.
The 20-core, 128GB, 1TB configuration tops out at $5,899.99, and the lead times on this model already stretch to late December.
The jump is steepest where the platform is strongest. The 64GB to 96GB of GPU-accessible memory that lets 35B-parameter models run well only comes with the 128GB build, and a 32GB or 48GB Surface won't fit the same models.
Tom’s Hardware warns that “sky-high DRAM and NAND price hikes” will be a headwind for the platform in the near term. That is a lot to spend, and you need a local AI workload to justify it.
The biggest challenge is the “eye-watering price tags,” since that money still buys “a lot” of cloud tokens from OpenAI and Anthropic, as Tom's Hardware puts it.
As Windows Central notes, comparable devices offer just enough and cost less.
CPU
Multi-core speed is the strength, and single-core speed is the weakness.
The 20-core N1X pairs 10 performance cores with 10 efficiency cores, targeting heavy multi-threaded work.
In single-core tests, it was found to “edge” the Dell Pro Precision 5 16S, scoring 558.5 against 534.8 in Cinebench 2026.
But across the wider suite, single-thread results, StorageReview says it “sit 15 to 30 percent behind the x64 field,” which is “just okay.”
Moving to multi-core, the Surface is an absolute "beast", finishing “34 percent ahead of the Razer Blade 16.”
Compared with Apple, however, it “simply doesn’t compete with Apple’s latest Max chips,” consistently trailing the M4 Max and M3 Ultra.
Under a heavy all-core CPU workload (an OpenBLAS double-precision solve), this device lost power repeatedly, though most buyers will never run anything like it.
On real-world work, it “won nearly every multi-threaded CPU test,” compiling LLVM in 206 seconds against 327 for the next-fastest system.
But there are weak spots: its Arm64 SVT-AV1 encoding managed about “a fifth” of what the x64 systems produced, and memory latency of 251 ns was the “worst in the group.”
That’s not to say it’s slow. Day-to-day use “feels fine,” and even emulated apps feel native. But for single-threaded, browser-bound work, “the x64 field is likely the better buy.”

|---|---|---|
| Outlet | Benchmark | Score | 
| Windows Central | Cinebench 2026 (Multi-Core) | 6,885 | 
| StorageReview | Cinebench 2026 (Multi-Core) | 6,963 | 
| Windows Central | Cinebench 2026 (Single-Core) | 558 | 
| StorageReview | Cinebench 2026 (Single-Core) | 558.5 | 
| Windows Central | Geekbench 7.1 (Multi-Core) | 23,571 | 
GPU
The 6,144-core Blackwell GPU is the real engine of the chip, with 5th-generation Tensor Cores built for AI workloads and up to 96GB of memory to draw on.
In local AI tests, it was “the fastest overall” at agentic tasks, finishing about 25% quicker than the M5 Max MacBook Pro.
In Stable Diffusion 1.5 INT8, it scored 11,294 and “substantially outperformed” the RTX 5080, 5070 Ti and 5060.
However, for models that fit in 24GB, the Razer Blade 16’s RTX 5090 generates tokens “2.3x faster,” and video rendering trails even the RTX 5060.
Gaming is a secondary strength. Performance is “similar to an RTX 4070 or 5060,” and Cyberpunk 2077 held 60fps at 1440p with frame generation.
But shared memory bandwidth and input latency are limited. Its shared memory bandwidth hit 300GB/s, below the 384GB/s on a mobile RTX 5060.
Gears of War: E-Day averaged 77.7 fps with 1% lows of 39.9 fps and 83.5 ms of latency. Control Resonant reached 109.2 fps, but only with 3X frame generation.
If AI is not your thing and you need low latency and top performance, “a separate gaming laptop with a dedicated RTX 50-series GPU will still provide a superior experience.”
AI
Nothing else in a laptop gives a GPU this much room to work with. The RTX Spark pairs its Blackwell GPU with up to 128GB of unified memory, and 64GB of it, adjustable up to 96GB, can go straight to the GPU.
That is “more than any NVIDIA laptop GPU before it,” and it is what lets 35B-parameter models run at up to 89 tokens per second. Models up to 120B parameters can fit entirely on the GPU.
In agentic tests it was “the fastest overall,” finishing about 25% quicker than the M5 Max MacBook Pro and in roughly half the time of the Ryzen AI Max+ 395.
Quantized models are where it truly leads, with Stable Diffusion 1.5 INT8 scoring 11,294 and “substantially outperforming” the RTX 5080, 5070 Ti and 5060.
It also makes local agents practical. Hermes Agent organized a cluttered downloads folder and built a website without sending any data to the cloud, so “you are no longer constrained by usage limits.”
That’s not to say it beats everything. For models that fit in 24GB, the Razer Blade 16’s RTX 5090 generates tokens “2.3x faster.”
Still, for those running models locally all day, it is “king”.
This, then, is a machine for the local AI believer, built for privacy, offline use and tinkering.
Who should buy it
Nvidia has built a compelling workstation for certain AI workloads, although conventional laptop buyers have several reasons to remain cautious.
Developers and analysts running 20B to 35B models locally are the clear audience.
Gamers, browser-heavy users, and anyone whose models fit in 24GB are better served by a laptop with a dedicated GPU.
Verdict
The good
· Strong multi-threaded CPU
· Up to 96GB of GPU memory runs 35B models at up to 89 tokens per second
· Fastest in agentic AI tests
The bad
· Expensive, from $2,599.99 to $5,899.99
· Weak single-thread speed and high memory latency
· Gaming is only decent, with high input latency
The verdict
Grab it if local models above 24GB are your daily work. Opt for a dedicated-GPU laptop for everything else. Avoid it if gaming is your focus.

articles.title: Spotify pulled 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from its recommendations
articles.text:
Spotify says it has removed more than 50 million songs considered AI-generated slop or spam from user recommendations over the past year. That’s according to an announcement on Tuesday that says Spotify has also made changes to its recommendation system to highlight more music made by human artists.
Spotify pulled 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from its recommendations
Spotify has also made changes to its music recommendation system to highlight songs from human artists.
“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” Spotify says. “Since we made these changes, we’ve seen a marked decrease in listener concerns about this content showing up in recommendations.”
Though Spotify has stopped short of mandating labels on all AI tracks, it launched an “AI Persona” badge for artists that use an AI identity and don’t represent a real person. It also won’t recommend music from AI personas. Other music streaming platforms are taking a tougher stance on AI music, with YouTube Music putting labels on AI songs, Deezer giving users an option to filter out AI slop, and Bandcamp banning AI music entirely.
Spotify says it uses a combination of listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and third-party AI detection tools to determine whether a track may be AI-generated slop. Last year, the company said it took down more than 75 million songs identified as spam. It’s also partnering with Universal Music Group and the independent music publisher Believe to launch a tool for creating AI music remixes.

articles.title: How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
articles.text:
How to study a swiftly melting climate disaster
I helicoptered into the Alaskan wilderness with scientists on the frontlines of permafrost research.
Andrew Haverdink, a tall grad student in a rain bib and rubber boots, wrenched a double-handed drill from the frozen soil that underlies much of Alaska’s Denali National Park and then unclipped the hollow barrel from the end of the bit.
He knelt in front of a blue tarp, lined the barrel up with a plastic tray, and pushed a rod through the opposite end. A perfect solid, cylindrical core of ancient soil emerged—dark, rich permafrost at least a foot long.
On that late morning in early July, Haverdink was among a team of Northern Arizona University students and staff gathering samples and data from a research plot, divided by surveyor’s tape unspooled atop tussocks, alders, and fireweed.
In late June of 2013, a lightning strike sparked a fire in this stretch of mostly treeless tundra, in the northern backcountry of the park. Whipped by the Chinooks, intense downslope winds created as moist ocean air surmounts and then descends the Alaska Range, the fire ripped across nearly 35,000 acres. It burned through much of the vegetation and deep into the topsoil, stripping away the insulating layer that preserves the frozen permafrost, a massive storehouse of carbon that underlies 85% of Alaska.
During their first survey, in 2016, the researchers found that in places where the fire burned hottest and deepest, the thawed soil above the permafrost (known as the active layer) extended between a foot and nearly two feet deeper than in plots outside the burn scar—an indication of deep thawing.
Crucially, the fire also crossed two sets of survey grids that the National Park Service established in 2001, including the one where the researchers stood that morning. That pre-fire snapshot offered the Northern Arizona group a rare opportunity to study how the blaze has altered the vegetation, carbon, and permafrost across time, says Xanthe Walker, one of the principal investigators on the project, who was watching over Haverdink’s work that morning.
These direct observations from high-latitude fires are helping scientists to better understand the impacts of wildfire and permafrost loss on climate change, she says.
“There’s a lot of uncertainty,” Walker says. “These are huge biomes with massive fires that no one’s ever been to or ever looked at.”
They’re among a growing group of researchers striving to untangle what happens in the aftermath of fires in the Arctic-boreal region as they occur more often, burn hotter than before, and expose the landscape and frozen permafrost to a warming climate.
The work is providing critical clues into the complex mechanisms driving cascading climate feedback effects: As warming temperatures fuel more frequent and severe fires, more permafrost thaws, releasing greenhouse-gas emissions that threaten to fuel more warming, fires, and permafrost loss.
Understanding just how powerful these effects are, how they compound, and to what degree other transformations of the landscape may mitigate them is essential to gain a clearer picture of our climate future.
Notably, past modeling suggested that the carbon dioxide uptake from expanding trees and plants may largely offset the release of carbon from warming soils and melting permafrost, at least over long periods and under moderate levels of warming. But the improving observations and analyses have revealed worrisome signs about the impacts of rising Arctic-boreal emissions in the immediate decades ahead, as the world struggles to keep global warming within relatively safe boundaries.
The permafrost problem
Permafrost makes up 15% of the land surface of the Northern Hemisphere and holds about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, roughly twice the amount in the atmosphere. Most of it formed during the last ice age, but it’s been thawing at an accelerating rate during the last half-century, amid rising temperatures and worsening fires. As it melts, microbes begin to break down that organic matter, releasing it into the air in the form of carbon dioxide and methane. Both are powerful greenhouse gases that fuel climate change.
The impacts of permafrost loss, however, aren’t as straightforward as they may initially seem. Notably, there has been a long-running scientific debate over what would have the strongest effect on the exchange of greenhouse gases over the next few centuries: the loss of carbon in soil and permafrost or the carbon uptake from so-called “Arctic greening,” which describes the spread of carbon-absorbing plants across the landscape as temperatures rise.
Thawing permafrost itself can contribute to the latter phenomenon as the unfrozen soil layer deepens and makes more nitrogen, phosphorus, and other nutrients accessible to plants. Carbon-sucking trees and shrubs with deeper root systems can take hold and thrive in places where they wouldn’t have been able to in the past.
But as more Arctic-boreal fires ignite and more permafrost melts, researchers have been able to closely study what exactly happens in the aftermath, using on-site surveys like those conducted by the Northern Arizona University team, satellite observations, lidar flights, a widening network of greenhouse-gas-measuring towers, and other tools.
The findings have alarmed many researchers.
In particular, permafrost seems particularly prone to abrupt thawing rather than the gradual version that major climate models have simulated. A 2020 paper found that this could release far more carbon than previously understood, doubling the emissions from thawing permafrost and offsetting the carbon uptake from future plant growth.
In addition, even if carbon levels eventually net out through Arctic greening, the emissions from high-latitude fires and permafrost loss appear to be accelerating warming right now.
Susan Natali, an Arctic climate scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, and her colleagues have published several papers in recent years concluding that the combined emissions from these feedback effects will push the planet past 2 °C faster than currently predicted. She and other researchers also found that about 40% of the Arctic-boreal zone has already flipped from a carbon sink into a carbon source, when the emissions from permafrost melting, fires and other forces are taken into account.
“The more we learn about processes like abrupt thaw, deeper-burning fires, and cold-season emissions, and the more we see disturbances increasing, the more likely it is that the sink will weaken and source areas will expand,” Natali said in an email.
But there’s still considerable uncertainty about the differences between the ways fires and thawing permafrost might alter landscapes, under different circumstances in different biomes.
“This is just a challenge of the science, because it's really hard to measure such a huge area, which is not one system,” she says. “It’s many, many, many, many different types of ecosystems.”
Results may vary
The Northern Arizona University researchers have been at the forefront of efforts to study the aftermath of intensifying fires across different parts of Alaska. Over the last two decades, Michelle Mack, a professor of ecosystem ecology who was previously Walker’s postdoctoral advisor, has overseen repeat survey work on fire sites across forests and tundras, from the relatively warm southern interior to the frigid North Slope.
Her husband and frequent collaborator, Ted Schuur, is also a professor at the university and oversees several permafrost monitoring and experimental research sites at the Eight Mile Lake study area, just north of Denali National Park.
If there’s a single takeaway from the body of science that the Northern Arizona scientists have produced, it’s this: It’s complicated. The local climate and ecosystem, the severity of the fires that have occurred, the type of permafrost, and numerous other factors can substantially shift the uptake or loss of carbon, the amount of permafrost that’s thawed, the extent to which it may recover, and the future flammability of the landscape.
In one early study, the researchers and their collaborators surveyed dozens of stands dominated by black spruce trees in the aftermath of a series of large boreal fires in 2004, between the Brooks Range and the Alaska Range. One of the notable findings: Severe burns that left little behind of the decaying organic matter in the topsoil induced a shift toward faster-growing and less flammable deciduous trees. The sites where deciduous trees dominated stored about five times as much soil carbon as stands that returned to black spruce, Mack, Walker, and their coauthors noted in a 2021 Science paper.
That means the subsequent uptake of carbon on those stands “more than compensated” for the amount released in the initial fire, Walker says.
But the 2007 Anaktuvuk River tundra fire, which remains the largest fire on record in Alaska’s North Slope, offers a starkly different case study. In the initial analysis there, Mack, Schuur, and their coauthors found that the fire released more than 2 million tons of carbon to the atmosphere, basically negating the amount that tundra ecosystems around the world removed from the air that year.
Subsequent studies found that more than a third of the scorched landscape sank, slid, and crumpled as the ice wedges below collapsed, the telltale signs of abrupt permafrost melting. Nearly two decades later, much of that thawed, decaying organic matter continues to release carbon dioxide and methane in the most severely burned patches of the fire scar, says Adrian Rocha, an associate professor at the University of Notre Dame.
It will take decades to centuries to recover all the carbon lost there, if ever happens at all, according to Rocha, who continues to monitor the site using Eddy covariance flux towers, which measure the exchange of greenhouse gases between Earth and atmosphere.
Mack says these on-the-ground measurements are critical to understanding what sorts of ecosystems recover, which shift into new states, whether they release a lot of carbon or a little, and when and where plant growth can offset that.
That said, the stakes of thawing permafrost are clear.
“If we step back as ecosystem ecologists, we know that there’s a lot more carbon stored below ground in permafrost than there is above ground in vegetation,” she says. “If permafrost carbon is released, it could swamp all of these other interesting details.”
In the lab
The Northern Arizona University research team shipped a pallet of soil samples back from Denali. The material included plugs of moss and decaying plant matter known as “brownies,” as well as permafrost cores and samples of the unfrozen soil layer. In the months since, they’ve cut, dried, weighed, combusted and analyzed various samples and inputted their field and lab findings into databases.
Walker says they’re exploring a variety of research questions, including how much that top organic layer has recovered since the initial post-fire survey and how much carbon has been lost and recovered since the fire.
The analysis is still underway, but in the most severely burned sites, it appears that the thawed layer of soil above the permafrost remain deeper some 13 years.
“Thaw still reaches further into the soil each summer than it probably did before the fire, which exposes more soil to decomposition,” Walker explained in an email.
They’re now hoping to use lab analyses to determine how much of that carbon is being lost.
Stepping into the climate future
On my last afternoon in Healy, Alaska, I followed Schuur along a narrow walkway of wooden boards suspended above a tundra field just north of Denali, hoping to get a glimpse into our climate future.
In 2008, he and his research team devised a way to subject permafrost to the temperature levels expected two or three decades from now by setting up snow fences around dozens of designated research plots. That allowed extra snow to build up—which, counterintuitively, acts like a blanket, adding thermal insulation during the winter that kept the test plots warmer than the controls.
Over the course of the 13-year experiment, the soil carbon levels in those 10-by-10-meter plots declined by 23%, Schuur and his coauthors found. The land collapsed in many of the sites, forming craters several feet deep.
As I stepped heel-to-toe along the planks into the middle of one plot, I descended about four feet, experiencing subsidence in three dimensions. Looking up at the edge from the walkway, I felt as if I were diaphragm deep in an empty pool.
Schuur, though, had another thing to show me. As we crested a ridge between plots, he pointed down to a shallower—though no less obvious—pool on the other side. It was a control site that had melted and collapsed on its own, without any assistance from simulated warming or fires.
“Every plot is just going off in its own trajectory,” he said. “This stuff is happening because the whole place is warming … and all these changes just go faster if you first burn the surface.”
Schuur expects that the permafrost underlying the whole field will thaw deeply by the end of 2040.
“There won’t be any surface permafrost based on our current warming,” he says.
Unless the world radically cuts emissions and gets fires under control, this same phenomenon will creep up the state, decade by decade, until even the permafrost under Alaska’s North Slope sinks to similar depths and gives up the carbon it has held for millennia.

articles.title: TikTok employees said they knew about child safety issues, but execs failed to act
articles.text:
TikTok was repeatedly warned by its own staffers about risks its platform posed to child safety, according to court records obtained by NPR. The publication reports that employees were frustrated over TikTok executives failing to appropriately act on concerns they raised, including minors bypassing age-restricted content, and appearing in “transactional sexual content” the company could financially benefit from.
TikTok employees said they knew about child safety issues, but execs failed to act
‘I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn’t think the harms are severe enough.’
The previously unreported depositions of TikTok staffers were filed in federal court in March, and connected to a multi-district litigation initiated in 2022 that brings together hundreds of lawsuits alleging that TikTok, Meta, Snap, and Google knew that they social media platforms are harmful to children, and failed to disclose those risks.
One deposition from Reagen Maher, who held senior safety and investigations positions between 2021 and 2024, described flagging the prevalence of “transactional sexual content” to then-TikTok CEO V Pappas, regarding minors stripping on TikTok’s Live feature in exchange for “gifts” that can be converted into real currency. Forbes reported on the issue in 2022, and Maher said the company was already aware of the sexual exploitation concerns before the article was published.
”I have been fighting about fixing this for months with people who didn’t think the harms are severe enough,” Maher said in an excerpt from an internal chat with a colleague. “Put simply, senior leaders know about this issue. There are some ongoing projects to fix parts of it, and frankly, I’m hoping [that] this article puts a fire behind other potential solutions.”
Another deposition from TikTok’s former head of safety Eric Han says he was concerned about harmful algorithm “rabbit holes” in 2020, describing them as having a “real contagion effect” regarding “suicidal ideation and behavior” in an internal TikTok report. Despite flagging that “minor safety is an urgent issue that we must address effectively,” Han said that TikTok failed to warn parents of the potential dangers of their child using the platform.

articles.title: Spotify se sube al modelo Patreon con sus nuevas membresías para podcasts
articles.text:
Spotify acaba de incorporar una nueva vía de monetización para podcasts, de la mano de membresías. En adelante, los usuarios podrán comprar suscripciones de pago para apoyar a sus creadores de contenido favoritos, recibiendo contenidos exclusivos y otros beneficios a cambio.
A través de las membresías, los realizadores de podcasts contarán con una nueva opción para generar dinero a través de Spotify. De esta manera, ya no dependerán de la publicidad como fuente de ingresos y podrán fortalecer la conexión con su público y forjar una comunidad más estrecha.
Los requisitos de Spotify para ofrecer membresías a través de los podcasts son bastante accesibles. La plataforma exige que las producciones estén alojadas en Megaphone o Spotify for Creators, y que tengan al menos 3 episodios publicados, 100 oyentes/espectadores y 100 horas de consumo en Spotify en los 30 días previos.
Otro detalle interesante es que los creadores podrán quedarse con el 90 % de los ingresos que sus podcasts generen a través de las nuevas membresías de Spotify. Sin dudas, una opción muy atractiva para ampliar la monetización del material y fidelizar todavía más a su audiencia.
Los podcasts de Spotify adoptan el modelo Patreon a través de membresías
A través de las membresías de Spotify, los creadores de podcasts podrán ofrecer contenidos exclusivos y otros beneficios a quienes les apoyan económicamente. La plataforma de streaming se ha inspirado en el modelo de Patreon, aunque no es la primera en hacerlo. Otros servicios de distribución de contenidos llevan tiempo brindando soluciones similares, como YouTube.
Es importante mencionar que para comprar la membresía de un podcast no será necesario pagar por Spotify Premium. Esta nueva función estará disponible tanto para los usuarios de pago como para quienes tienen una cuenta gratuita en el servicio.
Respecto de los beneficios que se pueden brindar a través de las membresías, Spotify indica que los podcasts podrán dar acceso temprano a nuevos episodios, entregas exclusivas o menos anuncios, por citar algunos ejemplos. También será posible implementar distintos niveles de apoyo, con precios y perks diferentes para cada uno. La nueva vía de monetización incluso admite pruebas gratis por 7 días.
Quienes compren las membresías para los podcasts de Spotify recibirán insignias que se podrán mostrar junto a su perfil al momento de comentar publicaciones. Una iniciativa interesante y que ya se está poniendo en marcha con títulos seleccionados (y bastante populares) como The Shawn Ryan Show, Two Hot Takes y The Adam Friedland Show.
Eso sí, las nuevas membresías no llegarán a todos los países de inmediato. Spotify está ofreciendo esta herramienta para podcasts en 34 mercados, entre los que se encuentra España. Por lo pronto, Latinoamérica no aparece entre los territorios contemplados. Seguramente se expandirá a más lugares con el correr del tiempo, aunque no hay precisiones en tal sentido.

articles.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
articles.text:
A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
At the world’s biggest chipmaking complex, Samsung is building the fabs it needs for the AI memory boom.
Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring.
It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers.
They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes.
In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment.
Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street.
Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips.
Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

articles.title: EU-Startups identifies 20 startups among 77 projects selected for €3.4 billion net-zero funding | EU-Startups
articles.text:
According to research by EU-Startups, 20 of the 77 European net-zero technology projects selected for €3.4 billion in EU Innovation Fund support involve startups, scaleups and younger technology ventures, highlighting the role of emerging companies in Europe’s industrial decarbonisation efforts.
Announced on 19 October 2026, the European Commission’s latest selection covers projects across 23 countries in the European Economic Area, spanning clean energy, industrial manufacturing, carbon removal, sustainable fuels and critical raw materials.
While established industrial groups account for much of the programme, EU-Startups’ analysis of the selected projects and their coordinating companies identifies 20 projects associated with younger technology businesses, representing approximately 26% of the total selection.
These 20 businesses span all five funding categories, from large industrial developments to smaller-scale demonstrations and manufacturing facilities.
Big industrial ambitions, startup origins
Among the 12 large-scale projects selected, two companies previously covered by EU-Startups stand out: Germany’s Vaeridion and France’s GravitHy.
Munich-based Vaeridion
- Founded in 2021, is developing the Microliner, a fully battery-electric regional aircraft designed to carry nine passengers. Its CAROLUS project aims to advance the aircraft towards certification, industrial production and commercial operation in Germany, with a targeted range of approximately 400 kilometres.
- In December 2024, EU-Startups reported on Vaeridion’s €14 million Series A funding round in order to support aircraft development and progress towards certification. Total funding sits at €17 million.
France’s GravitHy
- Founded in 2022, aims to decarbonise the steel industry by producing low-carbon iron using hydrogen instead of conventional coal-based processes. Its Fos-sur-Mer project plans to establish a facility capable of producing two million tonnes of hot briquetted iron annually, which steelmakers can use as an input for lower-emission steel production.
- In March 2025, EU-Startups covered GravitHy’s €60 million financing round. The capital was earmarked for engineering, permitting, recruitment and preparations for the company’s flagship industrial facility.
The remaining startup identified as large scale projects is Spain’s Greenertis.
From waste to circular chemistry
The medium-scale category includes five startup-associated projects, four of which involve companies previously covered by EU-Startups.
Netherlands-based ChainCraft
- Founded in 2010 as a spinout from Wageningen University, develops fermentation technology that transforms organic waste into valuable fatty acids. These chemicals can replace fossil-derived or palm oil-based ingredients used in products ranging from animal feed and lubricants to coatings and industrial chemicals.
- The company was previously included in EU-Startups’ overview of biotechnology companies in the Netherlands, which highlighted its proprietary fermentation processes and the range of applications for its medium-chain fatty acids. Total funding sits at €18.5 million.
Germany’s traceless materials
- Founded in Hamburg in 2020 by Dr Anne Lamp and Johanna Baare, develops natural polymer-based materials from agricultural residues as alternatives to conventional plastics. Total funding sits at €39 million.
- In September 2023, EU-Startups reported on the company’s €36.6 million financing round to support the construction of its first industrial production facility in Hamburg, which opened in 2026.
Spain’s H2SITE
- Founded in 2021 as a spinout from TECNALIA and Eindhoven University of Technology. The company develops membrane reactor technology that enables hydrogen to be separated from different gas streams and hydrogen carriers, including ammonia.
- EU-Startups previously covered H2SITE’s €36 million Series B round in January 2025. The company planned to use the investment to expand its hydrogen production and separation technologies into additional markets. Total funding sits at €57.9 million.
Sweden’s Cemvision
- Established in Stockholm in 2020, is pursuing a different industrial challenge: reducing the emissions associated with cement manufacturing.
- In March 2024, EU-Startups reported on Cemvision’s €10 million seed financing. The company was already working towards commercial adoption of its technology, having secured an initial customer contract.
The remaining startup in the medium-scale category is Sweden’s GreenIron.
Small projects, tangible applications
Among the 20 small-scale projects selected, EU-Startups identified four startups.
Dublin-based XFuel
- Develops technology for converting waste streams into lower-carbon fuels suitable for existing transport infrastructure. Its approach focuses on producing drop-in alternatives that can be used without requiring major modifications to engines or fuel distribution systems.
- In January 2026, EU-Startups included XFuel in its weekly funding roundup, following a €16.76 million financing announcement to support its development of sustainable fuels for road, marine and aviation applications. Total funding sits €30 million ($33.8 million).
The three other startup-associated small-scale projects are France’s Enosis, Lithuania’s Refinis and France’s Epyr.
Pilot projects put emerging technologies to work
Five of the 16 pilot projects selected involve startups identified by EU-Startups, including several companies that have previously attracted venture capital investment.
Brussels-based Sirona Technologies
- Founded in 2023 by Thoralf Gutierrez and Gauthier Limpens, develops modular direct-air-capture technology designed to remove carbon dioxide directly from the atmosphere.
- Its Project Furu, located in Øygarden, Norway, has been selected for a grant of up to €9.1 million, subject to the finalisation of the funding agreement. In June 2024, EU-Startups reported on Sirona’s €6 million seed funding round to support the development and deployment of its direct-air-capture systems.
Germany’s Reverion
- Founded in 2022 as a spinout from the Technical University of Munich, is developing reversible power plants capable of converting gases such as biogas and hydrogen into electricity, while also enabling electricity to be stored through gas production.
- The company has featured several times in EU-Startups’ reporting, most recently in September 2026, when it announced a €154.2 million Series B financing round. The financing is intended to expand the company’s production capabilities and bring its reversible energy systems to additional industrial customers. Total funding sits at €228 million ($256 million).
Berlin-based C1 Green Chemicals
- Founded in 2022, is developing new chemical production processes using advanced catalysis. Its initial commercial focus is renewable methanol, which can replace fossil-derived methanol in industrial manufacturing and serve as an alternative fuel for shipping.
- In March 2025, EU-Startups covered C1 Green Chemicals’ €20 million financing package, comprising €15 million in investment and €5 million in approved research grants. The financing was intended to support the development of a demonstration plant and accelerate commercialisation. Total funding sits at €25 million.
Completing the startup-associated pilot projects is Germany’s ICODOS and France’s Flying Whales.
Manufacturing Europe’s CleanTech future
The CleanTech manufacturing category includes three startups – all companies previously featured by EU-Startups.
Sweden’s Orbital Systems
- Founded in Malmö in 2012 by Mehrdad Mahdjoubi following collaboration involving NASA and Lund University, initially gained attention for its water-recycling shower technology.
- Orbital Systems was featured by EU-Startups in March 2019 as one of ten European CleanTech startups developing solutions for a more sustainable future. Total funding sits at €61 million ($69 million).
France’s HoloSolis
- Established in 2022, is developing a large-scale solar photovoltaic manufacturing facility in Sarreguemines-Hambach, France.
- In November 2025, EU-Startups reported that HoloSolis had secured more than €220 million in public and private financing. The company expects the facility to support European solar manufacturing and create jobs in the region. Total funding sits €220 million.
Germany’s Additive Drives
- Founded in Dresden in 2020 by Philipp Arnold, Axel Helm and Dr Jakob Jung, develops high-efficiency electric motors using a combination of additive manufacturing and conventional production technologies.
- In February 2026, EU-Startups covered Additive Drives’ €25 million financing to accelerate industrial scaling and international expansion.
The Innovation Fund
The broader Innovation Fund selection reflects the European Commission’s efforts to support technologies at different stages of commercial readiness. The programme includes 12 large-scale, 17 medium-scale, 20 small-scale, 12 CleanTech manufacturing and 16 pilot projects.
According to the Commission, the 77 selected projects could collectively avoid approximately 290 million tonnes of CO₂-equivalent emissions during their first ten years of operation. The programme is financed through revenues from the EU Emissions Trading System, which reinvests carbon market proceeds into low-carbon technologies.
The December 2025 call attracted 358 applications requesting €17.5 billion in funding, considerably exceeding the initially available budget of €2.9 billion.
However, selection does not yet constitute a final grant award. The 77 project promoters have been invited to prepare grant agreements with the European Climate, Infrastructure and Environment Executive Agency (CINEA), with final funding amounts and contractual arrangements expected to be confirmed in the first quarter of 2027.
Although the precise share of the €3.4 billion that will ultimately support startup-associated projects remains unclear, our findings highlight the involvement of emerging technology companies in Europe’s industrial transition.

articles.title: Google DeepMind says four AI agents beat Minecraft in 27 hours by writing 2,783 programs of their own — AI team died 605 times on Easy difficulty and ran up an estimated $520 in tokens
articles.text:
Google DeepMind says four AI agents beat Minecraft in 27 hours by writing 2,783 programs of their own — AI team died 605 times on Easy difficulty and ran up an estimated $520 in tokens
About half the run was spent fighting the dragon, solved by stacking dirt to reach its crystals.
The game of Minecraft is no match for a team of four Gemini 4 Argon agents, as they were able to defeat it in 27 hours with 2,783 self-written programs, a paper from Google DeepMind reveals. The agents did die 605 times, even on Easy, and about half the run was spent fighting the Ender Dragon, the final boss of the game. The run finally came to completion when the End was solved by stacking dirt to reach the boss’s crystals, at an estimated cost of around $520 in tokens.
The experimental run was designed from the get-go with one goal: kill the Ender Dragon. The playthrough involved a random, shared survival world on Easy with four agents — a fifth agent existed only for reporting — from Gemini 4 Argon, Google’s latest frontier model. Each agent had its own player through the open-source Mineflayer JavaScript library for Minecraft bots, but they were able to coordinate through in-game chat and shared notes. Every program used in the run was written by the agents themselves, and the emphasis is on coding and teamwork rather than game-playing.
The authors say this is the “first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents,” at least “to our knowledge,” qualified by the use of Mineflayer “without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans.” Mineflayer tells the agents where blocks and creatures are, with a pathfinding plugin to plan routes. There was “no human input during the run” and “no one assigned roles or wrote game logic.” The run, starting with the first program and ending with the dragon's death, took 27 hours and 14 minutes.
Although the agents were not given roles, within about 10 minutes a division of labor was proposed in chat by bot janesick. Bot Auratian offered an alternative plan while Bot Gyldenia acknowledged it. The roles ended up being: Gyldenia for food, beds, and flint; Bulicame for diamonds; Janesick for iron and tools; Auratian for the Nether portal. Moments of losses, such as a Ghast fireball destroying dropped items, led the team to diagnose the cause and write rules to prevent it in the future.
Finding the stronghold involved janesick, who threw two Eyes of Ender from different spots and sampled each eye’s flight once every 50 ms, triangulating the location. Carrying the eyes involved its own dire moment when Auratian drowned during the task, but the spot was noted, and the eyes were rescued.
The eventual fight with the dragon led to 69 deaths, and the ten crystals kept regenerating the boss until Auratian discovered they could use dirt pillars to reach the crystals. Four hours and 40 minutes later, all ten crystals were downed, and the dragon was dead 39 minutes after that.
The agents operated by writing short JavaScript programs, almost 2,800 in total, with 42 helper functions kept alive between programs, while a Mineflayer bot ran them in the shared world. Text was returned with status data, not pictures. This is a shared approach to the non-screenshot GPT-6 Astra clear of the Orc starting zone in World of Warcraft earlier this month. AI agents playing games is an ongoing trend, with Pokémon Red probably being the most popular, a game defeated in multiple ways, including with a Jev decision model layer.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
Minecraft has also been a popular target, and the authors admit this, highlighting two earlier community dragon kills: a planner with an action-selection model on a fixed speedrun seed in Peaceful mode, and a single Claude Opus 5 agent that used 37 ready-made, high-level tools on Normal, versus Mineflayer alone for the Gemini team. AI Bengineering’s Claude run, relying mostly on Opus 5 at high effort, took 3 hours and 56 minutes from start — “no human input after the prompt” — to kill with 388 tool calls and only one death. The cost in that case, at API-equivalent rates, was about $93.
Google’s Minecraft run, using Gemini 4 Argon’s 50% introductory pricing, which runs from initial API access that followed the model announcement through Nov. 30, cost more than half a grand; at normal pricing, that’s more than a grand. A GPT-6 Astra Portal run last month, which took about 24 hours, came in at $571 in tokens.
Google’s run took about 1.35 billion input tokens with 91% served from cache. About 24,000 model calls involved around 16 million output tokens, a quarter of them thinking. In total, if we’re also including the observer agent, the session would be estimated at $810, or $1,620 after the promotion, at list prices.
Each player is driven by a “general-purpose Gemini 4 Argon coding agent,” which is a fancy way of saying that it’s not specialized for Minecraft. Gemini 4 Argon itself is a frontier model for “real-world software engineering, enterprise knowledge work like legal and finance, and cybersecurity defense,” according to a company blog. With Minecraft, 22% of the agents’ programs ended in an error, with more than 600 deaths.
Although the model was used for a game here, the run was designed to show that Argon is capable of “complex, long-horizon workflows” for complex real-world tasks and agent coordination. Such long projects can involve decompiling a game back into source code, as we covered recently with a Modern Warfare 2 rebuild that now has 83% of its functions matching the original byte for byte.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

articles.title: Fausses cagnottes : attention aux arnaques qui profitent des pillages du 17 octobre
articles.text:
Les pillages survenus ce week-end à travers la France ont laissé un certain nombre de commerçants complètement dévastés. Marchandises volées, investissements partis en fumée, vitrines cassées, agressions physiques : les conséquences sont lourdes pour les commerçants touchés, qui doivent désormais faire face aux dégâts, aussi bien matériels que psychologiques. Face à cette situation, les cagnottes de soutien se sont multipliées. Certaines ont été mises en place par les commerçants eux-mêmes, tandis que d’autres sont mises en ligne à l’initiative de personnes désirant aider. Malheureusement, certains lancent aussi de fausses cagnottes, autrement dit, des arnaques.
Des escrocs profitent de la détresse des commerçants
Un gérant d’un magasin Micromania situé à Nice a été victime de pilleurs. Il a été agressé physiquement, tandis que son magasin a été pillé et ses vitrines cassées. Face aux images de l’agression et du pillage, mais aussi du courage dont l’homme a fait preuve, plusieurs personnes ont lancé des cagnottes afin de lui venir en aide. Cependant, le gérant a alerté sur la prolifération de fausses cagnottes en ligne.
Il explique dans une story Instagram : « Mon équipe et moi, on est très touchés par le soutien, merci pour ce que vous faites. Maintenant, je vois des cagnottes en ligne, je ne suis au courant de rien, personne ne m’a contacté, elles ne sont pas de mon fait. Prenez soin de vous. Évitez ce genre d’arnaque, ne vous faites pas avoir. Pour le moment, rien n’est fait. Si vous voulez de mes nouvelles, peut-être que j’en donnerai ici ».
Le problème est que nous n’avons aucune garantie que l’argent versé sur une cagnotte en ligne non officielle sera bel et bien reversé à un commerçant en difficulté. Un escroc peut profiter de l’empathie des personnes pour tout simplement détourner les fonds collectés. À noter que le gérant du magasin Micromania a depuis sa dernière story Instagram validé une cagnotte officielle (et sûre) disponible ici.
Comment éviter les fausses cagnottes en ligne ?
Si vous désirez aider un commerçant impacté par les pillages de ce week-end, le premier réflexe à adopter est d’aller sur l’un de ses moyens de communication officiels (page Instagram, site web, compte Facebook, etc.). Si un commerçant n’en propose aucun, vérifiez l’identité du bénéficiaire et l’origine de la collecte. Pour rappel, le fait qu’une collecte soit hébergée sur une plateforme connue (Leetchi, GoFundMe, etc.) ne constitue en aucun cas une garantie absolue de fiabilité.
Méfiez-vous également des collectes dont le créateur reste anonyme, dont l’utilisation des fonds est floue ou qui ne fournissent aucun élément permettant de vérifier le lien avec le commerçant concerné.

articles.title: Star Wars Battlefront 3 en route chez Bungie (Halo) ?
articles.text:
Neuf ans après le fiasco des lootbox de Battlefront II, qui avait poussé Disney à intervenir en coulisses auprès d’EA, l’engouement du public pour le jeu n’a paradoxalement jamais faibli. D’après EGM, les dirigeants de Lucasfilm déploient « activement des droïdes sondes » pour trouver un studio partenaire capable de relancer la série sans rejouer le fiasco de 2017. DICE et Bungie seraient dans le collimateur.
Le retour de DICE pour Star Wars Battlefront 3 ?
Le nom de DICE n’a rien d’une surprise : le studio suédois a développé les deux Battlefront d’EA, en 2015 et 2017, et maîtrise le moteur Frostbite comme les grandes batailles multijoueur. Celui de Bungie est beaucoup plus inattendu. Racheté par Sony en 2022, le studio connaît déjà Lucasfilm : les deux entreprises ont travaillé ensemble sur Destiny 2: Renegades, une extension inspirée de Star Wars, avec sabres laser et blasters, sortie le 2 décembre 2025. EGM ne dit pas si cette collaboration a pesé dans la balance.
Pour Lucasfilm, chaque option a ses atouts et ses risques. L’option DICE représente la facilité technique et la sécurité des ressources graphiques déjà existantes, à condition que le studio ait retenu les leçons du passé et ne soit pas totalement essoré par le développement de ses propres franchises.
L’option Bungie, ce sont des des sensations de tir reconnues et une longue expérience des jeux services, des jeux en ligne entretenus pendant des années, mais avec le risque de transformer Battlefront en jeu de tir très monétisé.
Rien n’est signé, et le jeu n’est pas encore en production
Pour l’heure, aucun contrat n’a été paraphé et la production n’a pas formellement démarré. Selon l’insider Jeff Grubb, la démarche de Lucasfilm en est encore au stade des repérages et des discussions préliminaires. L’intérêt de deux studios de cette taille montre que la marque Battlefront reste attractive, neuf ans après le dernier épisode.
Ni Lucasfilm, ni EA, ni Bungie n’ont réagi, et aucune plateforme ni fenêtre de sortie n’a filtré.

articles.title: Votre vieille Radeon et votre Xbox s’offrent une seconde jeunesse : AMD déploie le FSR 4.1 avec des mois d’avance — Frandroid
articles.text:
AMD a publié ce mardi 20 octobre le pilote Adrenalin 26.10.1, qui active le FSR 4.1 sur les Radeon RX 6000, des cartes graphiques sorties en 2020. La marque l’annonce dans un billet et une vidéo qui couvrent aussi les PC portables, les consoles portables et les Xbox. Jusqu’ici, seules les RX 9000 et, depuis juin, les Radeon RX 7000 y avaient droit. Avec une RX 6600 ou une RX 6800, on obtient donc une image plus propre dans les jeux compatibles, sans changer de carte.
Le FSR (FidelityFX Super Resolution) fait calculer au jeu une image dans une définition plus basse, puis la remonte à celle de l’écran. Le gain d’images par seconde vient de là. Depuis la version 4, AMD confie cette reconstruction à un modèle d’apprentissage automatique entraîné à retrouver les détails, alors que le FSR 3.1 utilisait un algorithme classique. L’image obtenue est plus nette, avec moins de scintillement sur les bords des objets.
Pourquoi ce délai pour les RX 6000 ? Le modèle a été pensé pour les RX 9000, qui calculent nativement en FP8, un format de nombres sur 8 bits. Les cartes plus anciennes passent par une variante en INT8, un format différent, ce qui demande un travail d’adaptation. En mai, AMD visait encore « début 2027 » pour ces cartes. L’entreprise dit avoir retravaillé le modèle et optimisé son code pour leur architecture, RDNA 2. Le pilote couvre toute la gamme, de la RX 6900 à la RX 6400.
Un modèle allégé pour les PC portables et les consoles portables
Le même pilote ajoute les processeurs Ryzen AI Max 300 et 400 et Ryzen AI 9 300 et 400, dont la partie graphique est intégrée à la puce (on parle d’APU). Pour les puces graphiques les moins puissantes, AMD a conçu un second modèle, qui fait moins de la moitié de la taille de l’original. Il vise les Ryzen AI 9 des PC portables et les Ryzen Z2 Extreme et Z2 A des consoles portables.
AMD dit avoir validé ce modèle sur des centaines de configurations et promet d’autres APU plus tard. Il y a moins de deux semaines, Jack Huynh, vice-président chargé du calcul et du graphisme chez AMD, promettait cette arrivée sur les APU avant la fin de l’année.
Attention si vous jouez sur une console portable sous Windows : le pilote d’AMD ne suffit pas. Ces machines attendent une mise à jour de leur fabricant. Asus a déjà confirmé le FSR 4.1 pour sa ROG Xbox Ally, sa tablette ROG Flow Z13 et son PC portable TUF A14.
Sur PC, attendez-vous par contre à perdre quelques images par seconde par rapport au FSR 3.1, comme sur les RX 7000. Avec une version bricolée par la communauté, des tests relayés par Tom’s Hardware en mai mesuraient une perte de 10 à 20 % sur RX 6000 face au FSR 3. Ces mesures portaient sur un code non officiel, antérieur au pilote de ce mardi.
Sur Xbox Series, il faudra attendre les studios
Dans la vidéo d’AMD, Microsoft annonce aussi le FSR 4.1 « bientôt » sur Xbox Series X et Series S. Ces consoles utilisent la même architecture graphique RDNA 2 que les RX 6000. Aucune date ni liste de jeux n’a été donnée. Pour l’instant, le kit de développement Xbox ne propose que les FSR 1 et 2.
Microsoft présente le FSR 4.1 comme un outil de plus pour les développeurs. Chaque studio devra donc l’intégrer à ses jeux. Microsoft cite déjà la génération suivante, le FSR Diamond, pour Project Helix, sa prochaine Xbox.
Sur PC, le pilote Adrenalin 26.10.1 est disponible depuis ce mardi. Sur la ROG Xbox Ally, AMD annonce le FSR 4.1 dès cette semaine, via la mise à jour d’Asus.
Les bons plans n’attendent pas : abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp Frandroid Bons Plans ! (zéro spam, promis, juste de super bons plans).
