articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Strategy Mosaic and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
This post is co-written with Zhili Cheng, Principal Product Manager, George Earle, Director, AI Engineering, and Kyler K, Sales Engineer of Strategy.
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift and ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with Strategy Mosaic as the semantic layer.
Stardog’s semantic layer is ontology-based: concepts and relationships modeled as RDF, with IRIs as the unit of federation and SPARQL as the query language. Denodo’s is data virtualization: base and derived views composed in VQL. Mosaic’s is dimensional: attributes, hierarchies, facts, and metrics composed through Strategy’s metric expression syntax, with linked models as the unit of federation. That model serves four native protocols from one definition: Model Context Protocol (MCP) for AI agents, JDBC/ODBC over Trino for SQL clients, XMLA for Power BI and Excel, and REST for custom applications. Behind those protocols is a long list of certified data sources. Supported systems include cloud warehouses such as Snowflake and Databricks. Operational databases include Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), Oracle, and SQL Server. Analytical engines include Amazon Athena, Trino, and SAP HANA, and software as a service (SaaS) sources include Salesforce. The linked-model pattern extends beyond the Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora pair this walkthrough uses. In this walkthrough, a Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, reaches Mosaic through the MCP endpoint. The joins, metric definitions, and per-caller row and column filters live inside Mosaic, not in the agent prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series. If any of it is new, the Stardog post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to model a C360 domain in Strategy Mosaic across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora using two linked models, with no ETL.
- How Mosaic’s metric syntax (base, advanced with named filter objects, level qualifiers, and compound) captures the business definitions the agent must reason over.
- How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP server, and how user identity propagates so per-user Row-Level Security (RLS) and Object-Level Security (OLS) hold end-to-end.
- How to choose between live pushdown and in-memory execution for agent traffic.
- How to publish the same governed definitions to Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, and custom apps, and how to export them in Apache Ossie format for tools outside Mosaic.
The source of truth for the walkthrough is Strategy One (March 2026), the release when Mosaic access through the MCP server became available by default.
Strategy Mosaic terms used in this post
A short reference before we get to the model.
- Mosaic Schema and Mosaic Models. Two modeling paths within one universal semantic layer. Mosaic Schema is the centrally governed enterprise model. Mosaic Models is the self-service, AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio. Models can map to Schema attributes and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS. This walkthrough uses Mosaic Models.
- Model. The top-level artifact within either modeling path. Publishes attributes, metrics, hierarchies, and security rules over physical tables. The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, one over Amazon Redshift and one over Aurora, linked together.
- Attribute. A business entity such as Customer. Carries multiple forms: an ID form for joining and a display form for reading. Mosaic uses forms to resolve names like “Carolyn Inworth” to the underlying cid.
- Hierarchy. A parent-child relationship between attributes. Category rolls up through parent to Department. Address rolls up to City to State.
- Fact and metric. A fact is a numeric column. A metric aggregates it. Purchase Amount = price * quantity is a base metric. Metrics can also be advanced (an aggregation qualified by a named condition) or compound (a formula over other metrics).
- Filter object. A named condition referenced from metrics in angle brackets. [Large Orders] is a filter whose qualification is Purchase Amount > 500. A metric references <[Large Orders]> without inlining the predicate.
- Level qualifier. Metric expression syntax that pins aggregation grain. {~+, !Customer+} sets the grain to Customer regardless of how the query is sliced.
- Model linking. Composition across models on shared attributes (Customer, Time). Mosaic pushes aggregates to each source and joins intermediate results on the linking attributes.
- Certified model. Only certified models are reachable through the MCP server.
- Live or in-memory. Two per-model execution modes: live pushdown to the source, or answers from a Mosaic-resident cube. Details later in this post.
The example: Customer 360 across Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora
The C360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. The schema is adapted from Stardog’s C360 Knowledge Kit, so a reader following the series sees the same entities, keys, and anchor question answered by a different semantic layer. A retail organization has customer records, addresses, credit cards, and rewards enrollment sitting on the operational side, and orders, products, and product categories sitting in the warehouse. Business users want answers that span both without knowing which system holds which fact.
Where this post differs is how Mosaic reaches the two sources. Mosaic does not federate rows across engines at query time. It plans one query per source, pushes native SQL down, and joins the intermediate result sets in the Mosaic engine on the shared attributes declared through model linking. The C360 walkthrough models the analytical side as a Purchase model over Amazon Redshift and the operational side as a Customer model over Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible edition.
The schema across the two databases:
Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible (operational)
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
Amazon Redshift (analytical)
| Table | Key columns | 
| purchase | id (PK), cid, pid, date, quantity, price, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
| category | id (PK), dept_name, parent | 
| vendor | id (PK), vendor_name, industry | 
The shared ID is cid, an integer that appears as the primary key in customer on Aurora and as a plain column in purchase on Amazon Redshift. There is no SQL constraint linking them, and there can’t be, because they live in different engines. Every question that joins a customer to their orders must reconcile that integer somewhere. Mosaic absorbs it through model linking rather than a materialized cross-engine join.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post. It needs customer profile from Aurora, aggregated spend from Amazon Redshift, and enrollment status from Aurora, ranked and filtered on definitions that live in the semantic layer.
Reference architecture
Figure 1 shows the end-to-end runtime. The inbound authentication path runs from the client through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, and the runtime. The outbound query path runs from the Strands agent through the Mosaic MCP endpoint to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora.
The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP). It then routes the request to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent. The agent invokes Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, its MCP tool connects directly to the Mosaic MCP endpoint at https://<env-domain>/collaboration/mcp/mosaic over HTTPS. The agent presents an OAuth 2.0 access token in the Authorization: Bearer header. Mosaic validates the token against its bundled OAuth authorization server and resolves the caller to a Strategy user. It then applies the Use MCP Server privilege and certified-model gate, evaluates row-level and column-level security for that user, and plans the query across the linked Purchase and Customer models. Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora respond to source-native SQL that the Mosaic engine emits per source.
Two properties matter for the rest of the walkthrough. Cross-source joins happen because a modeler declared a link, not because two sources happen to be reachable. The agent can only traverse links that exist in the model. The token that reaches Mosaic represents the human user, not a service account, so RLS and OLS evaluate against the caller’s identity end-to-end. AWS Secrets Manager holds the caller’s refresh token between calls, and the Governed access section walks the full identity chain.
Build the semantic layer
The walkthrough uses two Mosaic Models, the self-service AI-assisted modeling path in Mosaic Studio, linked on shared attributes. Mosaic Studio is the authoring suite, and the screenshots in this post come from its Design Center modeling workspace. Three passes: datasets and joins on each side, attributes and hierarchies, then metrics that carry the business logic. A team with an existing centrally governed Mosaic Schema can map the model’s attributes to it and inherit dimensions, object ACLs, and RLS from the enterprise schema without a parallel security review. Do this early if your data architects already maintain a governed schema.
Two linked models
Each Mosaic model connects to one live source. Model linking composes them.
- Purchase: Live against Amazon Redshift. Facts on the purchase table (price * quantity), dimensions on product, category, vendor, and the purchase date.
- Customer: Live against Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-compatible. Dimensions on customer, address, credit_card, rewards_account.
Inside each model, the physical joins are declared once against the source schema. The Purchase model resolves purchase.pid = product.id, product.dept = category.id, and product.brand = vendor.id, plus a self-reference on category.parent = category.id for the department rollup. The Customer model resolves customer.location = address.id, customer.cid = credit_card.cid, and customer.cid = rewards_account.cid. These are the relationships Mosaic uses to plan the source-native SQL it pushes down. Nothing physical crosses between Purchase and Customer.
The two models link on Customer and Time. When a question needs both (for example top spenders in Wisconsin pulls state from address and spend from purchase), Mosaic pushes the appropriate aggregation to each source and combines the results on the linking attributes. No ETL, no third copy.
Domain ownership follows the model boundary. The CRM team owns Customer, and the data system team owns Purchase. Neither hands over its source. They agree on the linking attributes, and security propagates from the underlying models automatically. There’s no materialized cross-engine join and no shared physical schema between Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora. The join is the linking-attribute agreement.
Attributes and hierarchies
Attributes carry multiple forms. Customer uses cid as the ID form and first_name + last_name as the display form, so an agent can ask about “Carolyn Inworth” and Mosaic resolves it to the right key on both sides of the link. Figure 2 shows the Customer attribute authored in Mosaic Studio, with cid as the ID form and Full Name, First Name, and Last Name as display forms.
Two hierarchies matter for C360:
- The Category hierarchy rolls up through parent to Department. The category.parent self-reference means a department-level question aggregates consistently.
- Address rolls up through City to State in the same pattern. That makes State = 'WI' a single attribute qualification rather than a join the agent must construct.
Figure 3 shows the geography hierarchy authored in Design Center, chaining State through City and ZIP Code down to Customer.
The agent asks for State = 'WI', not for address.state. Physical column names don’t leave the model. Every consumer of the semantic layer sees the attribute form and its display forms, and the hierarchy carries the rollup automatically.
Metrics: Base, advanced, compound, time-intelligence
A base metric applies a group function to a fact. Purchase Amount is Sum(price * quantity) on the purchase table.
Figure 4 shows the Purchase Amount base metric authored in Mosaic Studio: the formula Price * Quantity, with a description field that tells the agent what the metric means in business terms.
The interesting C360 concepts are advanced metrics: an aggregation qualified by a named condition. In Strategy, conditions are references to filter objects in angle brackets, not inline predicates. Filter objects are model objects with their own name, description, and permissions, so they are reusable and auditable across metrics that share a definition.
Define the filters once:
| Filter object | Qualification | 
| [Large Orders] | Purchase Amount > 500 | 
| [Sports Category] | Category = "Sports" | 
| [Rewards Members] | Rewards Account is not null | 
| [Card Present] | Purchase Card is not null | 
| [Big Spender] | Customer Lifetime Spend > 10000 | 
Each filter object carries a name, description, qualification, and access permissions. The shape a modeler authors or exports for [Large Orders] looks like this:
Then reference the filters in metric expressions. Each of these is an advanced metric: a base aggregation qualified by a named filter.
Figure 5 shows the Design Center view of an advanced metric with a filter condition applied. It uses the same authoring pattern as the preceding Large Order Spend.
Customer Lifetime Spend also needs a level qualifier, because lifetime means the whole history regardless of how the current question is sliced:
The ! before Customer sets grouping to none, so the metric returns each customer’s full total on every row rather than collapsing to one row per customer. See Strategy Metric Level Symbols for the full syntax.
Notice that [Big Spender] in the filter table qualifies on a metric expression rather than an attribute predicate. Filter objects can gate on either. Share of wallet is a compound metric, built from other metrics:
Levels and conditions carry through from the components unchanged. Share of wallet is a ratio, so it doesn’t add or average. The share across an AWS Region isn’t the average of each customer’s share, and the metric description tells the agent that. See Strategy Conditional Metrics.
Beyond base, advanced, and compound, Mosaic ships governed time-intelligence metrics as first-class expressions. Previous Year, Previous Quarter, Year-to-Date, and Quarter-to-Date are declared once on the model and preserved through slice, so a question like how does Sports spend this year compare with last year becomes an attribute pick and two metric references rather than a hand-written SQL date filter. Custom calendars attach at the model level, so the same year-over-year expression works for a fiscal year that ends in September and a calendar year that ends in December. See Governed Time-Intelligence Metrics in Mosaic.
Edit the filter object once and the Power BI dashboard, the SQL extract, and the agent all move together. That is what a named, governed model artifact gets you that an inline SQL predicate cannot.
How Mosaic plans and executes queries
The Mosaic engine parses each MCP query call as Trino-dialect SQL, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying Purchase and Customer models, applies the RLS or OLS that the caller is subject to, and plans physical SQL per source. The dialect matches what Strategy publishes for the MCP query tool, so the SQL the agent emits is portable across MCP clients connecting to the same certified model.
For the auto-enrollment question, planning unfolds like this:
- Push down to Amazon Aurora: a join of customer and rewards_account on cid, projecting profile and rewards_account.create_date, filtered where enrollment is null. Returns one row per unenrolled customer.
- Push down to Amazon Redshift: SUM(price * quantity) grouped by cid. Returns one row per customer with total spend.
- Combine inside Mosaic: join the two intermediate result sets on cid (the linking attribute), rank by lifetime spend, and return the top 20.
Aurora runs a transactional profile join. Amazon Redshift runs the fact aggregation. Mosaic handles the cross-engine join on a small intermediate set (one row per customer, not one row per order). A hand-written pipeline approximates the same shape and then must be kept in sync forever.
One SQL detail matters. Metrics are governed values, but Trino treats them as selected columns, so when a query uses GROUP BY, metrics need an aggregation wrapper such as SUM(metric_name). The metric’s definition, conditions, and join paths are still resolved by Mosaic. The outer aggregation is the caller’s. A non-additive ratio like share of wallet therefore needs to say so in its description.
Live pushdown or in-memory
Every Mosaic model runs in one of two modes.
| Mode | Behavior | Best fit | 
| Live | Pushdown to Redshift or Aurora at query time | Consistently-current data. Source security applies directly | 
| In-memory | Answered from a Mosaic-resident cube | Bounded recent windows. Predictable latency. No per-query warehouse compute | 
Both modes enforce the same security rules. RLS and OLS are set once on the model and evaluated regardless of where the answer comes from. The choice is a performance and cost question.
Agent traffic is repetitive and bursty. An agent decomposing top spenders in Wisconsin into several exploratory follow-ups fires many small queries over the same recent slice. Serving that from memory turns variable per-query warehouse spend into fixed Mosaic capacity, and it’s usually faster. For interactive agent workloads over a bounded window, in-memory is often both quicker and cheaper. Configure Mosaic-side entitlements before switching a model to in-memory, and validate them in the same test pass you use to validate the numbers.
One definition, four interfaces
The metrics, attributes, hierarchies, and security rules built in the previous section reach every consumer through native protocols. No connector translation, no metric re-implementation, no drift.
| Protocol | Typical consumer | What it uses Mosaic for | 
| MCP | AI agents (Strands, Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Gemini) | Semantic discovery + governed query | 
| SQL / JDBC / ODBC (Trino) | Tableau, SQL clients, Python notebooks | Flexibility and ad-hoc analysis | 
| DAX / XMLA | Power BI, Excel PivotTables | Semantic fidelity for BI | 
| REST | Custom applications, data science | Programmatic access | 
The same certified Mosaic model that the Strands agent in this walkthrough consumes also serves a business analyst working in Amazon Quick, which registers Mosaic MCP as an OAuth-authenticated connector. No second integration is required.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Mosaic enforces access in the semantic layer, before a query reaches Amazon Redshift or Aurora. HR and fraud roles see personally identifiable information (PII) fields like ssn and card_num. Marketing and analytics roles do not. Enforcement is identical whether the caller is a Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One set of RLS and OLS objects, one certified-model gate, one privilege check. Attributes and metrics marked as sensitive also feed Mosaic Sentinel Risk Management, which alerts on queries that touch flagged objects and detects behavioral anomalies as a defense-in-depth layer next to OLS.
Figure 6 shows the identity propagation chain across two lanes: the front-door OAuth handshake that runs once per user, and the per-request path that runs on every agent tool call. Each lane carries the user’s identity end-to-end so Mosaic can enforce RLS and OLS on the caller rather than a service account.
The chain follows two lanes.
Front-door OAuth handshake (once per user). The human user authenticates against the enterprise IdP. The application starts an OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code flow against Strategy Library at /collaboration/authorize with scope offline_access. Strategy Library, federated to the same IdP through SAML or OIDC, returns a refresh and access token pair at /collaboration/token. The app persists the refresh token to AWS Secrets Manager, keyed by the user’s IdP sub claim.
Per-request path (every agent tool call). AgentCore Gateway validates the IdP JWT and routes to AgentCore runtime, which hosts the Strands agent invoking Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock. The agent’s MCP tool retrieves the user’s refresh token from Secrets Manager, exchanges it for a fresh access token, and presents Authorization: Bearer <access_token> to /collaboration/mcp/mosaic. Mosaic resolves the token to a Strategy user, enforces the Use MCP Server privilege, certified-model gate, and RLS and OLS, then plans and executes against Purchase and Customer. A marketing analyst doesn’t see ssn or card_num. A fraud analyst does.
Nothing in the chain re-scopes to a service account. Governance evaluates on the caller’s identity from IdP to Mosaic engine.
Expose the layer through the Mosaic MCP server
Strategy Library exposes two MCP endpoints:
| Endpoint | Path | What it does | 
| Agents MCP | /collaboration/mcp/agent | Routes a question to a certified Strategy agent, which answers using its own data and instructions | 
| Mosaic MCP | /collaboration/mcp/mosaic | Queries Mosaic models and AI-enabled cubes directly, no Strategy agent required | 
Both work independently. This walkthrough uses Mosaic MCP. Putting the semantic layer directly in front of the Strands agent skips an inference hop.
The tool chain
Four tools, chained from project to model to semantics to query.
| Tool | What it does | Parameters | 
| get_projects | Lists Strategy projects the caller can access | none | 
| get_models | Lists certified Mosaic models and datasets in a project | project | 
| get_semantics | Returns a model’s full definition: attributes and metrics with data types, descriptions, and metric formulas | model | 
| query | Runs a read-only Trino SQL query. Writes and DDL rejected with MOSAIC_SQL_WRITE_REJECTED | sql | 
The agent chains these calls automatically. get_projects and get_models narrow to the right model by description before the agent reads a column name. get_semantics returns the governed definitions the agent then uses to compose SQL against real object names: Sports Share of Wallet as a compound metric, Customer Lifetime Spend scoped to Customer, the Category hierarchy, and the formula for every metric.
Two Mosaic-specific SQL conventions matter. Column identifiers follow a <form>__<name> pattern and must be wrapped in double quotes ("customer__customer name"). Time attributes are exposed both as base columns and as pre-bucketed interval columns ((day interval), (month interval)), and the docs explicitly say to use the interval columns for time-grouped aggregations rather than date_trunc.
Metadata is what makes it accurate
get_semantics returns definitions, but the agent still must choose the right metric. Without descriptions, Total Spend and Customer Lifetime Spend look interchangeable, and they aren’t. Four properties do most of the work: object descriptions (what the metric means and when not to use it, including aggregation behavior for non-additive metrics), semantic definitions (how compound metrics compose), relationships (which attributes are valid slices), and governance context (so the agent can say what it can’t see rather than presenting a filtered number as complete). The model description is the first thing get_models returns and it’s how the agent picks the right model. Mosaic can import metadata from upstream catalogs, so column descriptions already maintained flow in rather than being retyped.
Deploy the agent
Strands is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the Mosaic MCP endpoint as a tool source. The AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and forwards the human user’s JWT.
The system prompt matters. Give the agent explicit instructions to follow the three-step call pattern before writing SQL: get_projects, then get_models, then get_semantics on the target model. Tell it to reference only attribute and metric names that get_semantics returned. Include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (Customer Lifetime Spend is the customer’s total across their history regardless of the current slice. Sports Share of Wallet is a ratio. And so on). This is the prompt engineering that pays the most in accuracy.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The get_semantics payload runs to a few thousand tokens and doesn’t change within a model version, so caching drops the input-token cost per call on repeated invocations. Agent traffic against a stable semantic layer is exactly the repetitive, bursty pattern that benefits most.
Two effects compound on the MCP path. First, get_semantics returns compressed business context (metric definitions, hierarchies, attribute forms) instead of raw schema DDL, so the model reasons over a smaller, higher-signal payload. Strategy’s published benchmark measures the input-token and per-query cost impact of serving semantic context versus raw schema. Second, Bedrock prompt caching keeps that already-compressed payload warm across calls. For repetitive agent traffic, both effects apply per call: the model reasons over compressed context, and repeat calls hit the cache.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three query categories through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them as a different role.
Query 1, Aurora-only. List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a query against the Customer model that projects the display forms of Customer and City and filters state to WI:
Mosaic pushes a single query to Aurora and returns the rows. Amazon Redshift is not touched.
Query 2, Amazon Redshift only. What are our top 10 products by units sold?
The entire query pushes to Amazon Redshift. Aurora is not touched.
Query 3, cross-model. Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?
Mosaic plans across both models. Profile and enrollment status come from Aurora, spend aggregation from Amazon Redshift, joined on the Customer linking attribute inside the Mosaic engine, then filtered and top-N’d. The agent did not need to define Customer Lifetime Spend. It referenced the metric by name and Mosaic resolved the formula, level qualifier, and linking paths.
Governance rerun. We ran Query 1 with ssn added to the projection as two callers. As a fraud analyst, get_semantics returned the SSN attribute and the query returned the values. As a marketing analyst, get_semantics returned a Customer attribute without ssn at all, so the agent had no attribute to project. Same request, same query text, two correct answers from one definition.
Cross-interface confirmation. We opened the same certified Customer model in Excel through the Mosaic XMLA endpoint and dragged State and Customer Lifetime Spend onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals matched the agent’s numbers exactly.
Early in the run, the agent averaged share of wallet across customers, the classic non-additive mistake. Adding one line to the metric description (“ratio metric. Do not average across customers, recompute from components”) stopped it. That’s the case for writing metric descriptions in the first sprint rather than the last.
Extending across data sources
The same linking mechanism extends to a third source: clickstream events in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) queried through Amazon Athena, tables in Apache Iceberg on Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon S3, or a SaaS source such as a CRM. Model the source in Mosaic, link it on Customer and Time, and browse-to-buy questions compose into the same customer view without a third pipeline. Adding a source doesn’t change the metric definitions that already exist. The agent can only travel paths a modeler declared. AWS Lake Formation governs access to the underlying lake tables. Mosaic’s RLS and OLS apply on top.
The same live-source pattern applies to every system in Strategy’s supported data source catalog, covering on-premises databases such as PostgreSQL and MySQL alongside the warehouses and engines already named in this post.
Interoperability with Apache Ossie
Some tools will not take a dependency on a single semantic layer. Apache Ossie (incubating) is the open specification for that gap, launched as the Open Semantic Interchange on September 23, 2025 and now in the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie (incubating). It defines a vendor-neutral format for metrics, dimensions, relationships, and business concepts so definitions move between tools without being retyped. Strategy participates alongside Snowflake, Dremio, dbt Labs, Salesforce, and others.
Mosaic exports and imports Ossie artifacts. Metric and dimension definitions modeled over Amazon Redshift publish as Ossie YAML consumable by Ossie-aware tools without a Mosaic connector. Definitions authored elsewhere (a metric maintained in dbt, a dimension standardized in a catalog) flow into Mosaic instead of being re-implemented. The artifacts are plain text, so they live in Git and promote through environments like other code.
Apache Ossie is early. Use it where portability matters most and fidelity matters least, for example formulas, dimensions, descriptions, and ownership metadata, while keeping governance policy, execution strategy, and security configuration native to Mosaic.
Deployment: Strategy Cloud
Mosaic runs as a managed service on Strategy Cloud. Strategy operates the application. Connections to Amazon Redshift and Amazon Aurora go over the network from Strategy Cloud egress. You allow-list the Strategy Cloud CIDRs on the source security groups.
Observability
Two observability planes cover the path from question to answer.
Sentinel and Platform Analytics cover the query side. Sentinel captures near real-time query duration, slow queries, and usage by user, tool, and model.
AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, covers the agent side: planning steps, tool calls, latency per turn. Sentinel and Platform Analytics show what happened once the request reached Mosaic. AgentCore Observability shows what the agent was doing before it got there.
Conclusion
Reliable agentic analytics combines strong reasoning, trusted business context, and secure execution. Amazon Bedrock provides the model, Strategy Mosaic provides the governed semantic layer over live data, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the agent and terminates authentication. The agent talks to the semantic layer, not to Amazon Redshift or Aurora directly. Schemas evolve, the semantic model absorbs the change, and the same definitions serve Power BI, Tableau, notebooks, the Strands agent, and Amazon Quick. Through Apache Ossie, they also reach tools that do not connect to Mosaic.
Where to start
- Pick one metric currently argued about (NRR, contribution margin, active customer are common candidates). One metric with more than one definition in circulation.
- Write three to five business questions about it. These become your acceptance tests.
- Model your primary source in Mosaic and get the metric returning a defensible number.
- Link additional sources incrementally, one at a time, on the attributes that already exist in the model.
- Author descriptions on every metric and attribute the agent will see. This is where accuracy moves most.
- Connect the Strands agent over Mosaic MCP and run your acceptance questions.
- Observe real query patterns for a couple of weeks, then move what’s hot to in-memory.
- Export stable definitions to Apache Ossie and put them under version control.

articles.title: Le marché des vidéoprojecteurs a beaucoup changé en 2026, notre sélection aussi
articles.text:
Plus lumineux, mieux équipés et surtout beaucoup plus souples à installer, les vidéoprojecteurs ont franchi un cap en 2026. Après plusieurs mois de tests, nous avons donc largement revu notre sélection des modèles que nous recommandons aujourd’hui.
Il y a encore quelques années, choisir un vidéoprojecteur revenait souvent à arbitrer entre un modèle home cinéma relativement contraignant à installer et un appareil « lifestyle », plus simple à utiliser mais aussi plus limité sur l’image ou l’optique. Cette frontière est devenue beaucoup moins nette.
Ces évolutions nous ont justement conduits à revoir en profondeur notre comparatif des meilleurs vidéoprojecteurs de 2026, avec sept modèles testés par Clubic et retenus pour des usages bien distincts.
La frontière home cinéma / lifestyle s’efface
Le triple laser RGB s’est largement installé sur les modèles premium, les systèmes de mise au point et de cadrage automatiques ont progressé, tandis que le zoom optique et le lens shift apparaissent désormais sur des appareils qui conservent Google TV et une approche très grand public. Le XGIMI Horizon 20 Max en est probablement l’exemple le plus parlant : lors de notre test, il nous avait justement convaincus par sa capacité à se rapprocher d’une véritable expérience home cinéma sans abandonner la simplicité qui a fait le succès de la marque.
Plus de lumière, mais surtout de nouveaux efforts sur le contraste et l’installation
La course aux lumens continue évidemment. Le Titan Noir Max pousse par exemple l’exercice jusqu’à 7 000 lumens ISO annoncés. Mais ce qui nous avait surtout intéressés lors de son test était ailleurs : XGIMI utilise deux iris et son traitement DBLE pour essayer d’améliorer simultanément la profondeur des noirs et la dynamique de l’image. C’est notamment ce travail qui lui a permis de décrocher notre note maximale de 10/10.
On retrouve la même volonté sur les vidéoprojecteurs à ultra-courte focale. L’AWOL Vision Aetherion Max associe ainsi son triple laser à un iris mécanique et au traitement EBL pour renforcer le contraste, tout en conservant la philosophie du « Laser TV », avec une très grande image produite à quelques dizaines de centimètres de l’écran.
L’installation évolue elle aussi. Le JMGO N3 Ultimate combine balancelle motorisée, zoom optique et lens shift, tandis que le Horizon 20 Max dispose lui aussi d’un vrai décalage optique. Ce sont des fonctions importantes : elles permettent de repositionner l’image sans dépendre uniquement du trapèze numérique et des traitements susceptibles de réduire la définition réellement exploitée.
L’idée est désormais de privilégier des profils bien distincts plutôt que d’empiler des références trop proches. Le Nebula X1, notre Clubic Award 2025, côtoie ainsi le Titan Noir Max, l’Aetherion Max ou le N3 Ultimate, tandis que le BenQ W4100i conserve sa place avec une approche plus traditionnelle, centrée sur la fidélité de l’image et la souplesse optique.
La sélection pourrait encore bouger dans les prochaines semaines
Une mise à jour de ce type reste forcément une photographie du marché à un instant donné. Et celui-ci continue d’avancer rapidement.
Le JMGO Iris Ultra Max, que nous avions découvert à l’IFA en septembre, en est un bon exemple. La marque annonce une chaîne 4K à 120 Hz, jusqu’à 6 500 lumens ISO, un double iris et un contraste natif de 10 000:1, le tout avec un zoom optique, du lens shift et une rotule motorisée. Lors de notre première prise en main, ce n’était d’ailleurs pas tant le 120 Hz qui nous avait marqués que sa capacité à conserver une image lisible avec davantage de lumière dans la pièce et le travail effectué sur les scènes sombres.
| Source lumineuse | Laser | 
| Entrées vidéo | HDMI (x2) | 
| Technologie de projection | DLP | 
| Résolution native | 4K UHD via pixel shifting | 
| Luminosité | 6 500 lumens ISO | 
| Norme HDR | HDR10, HDR10+, Hybrid Log Gamma (HLG) | 
| Bruit annoncé | 26dB | 
Cette fois, nous avons désormais l’Iris Ultra Max à la rédaction pour un test complet. Il faudra donc voir si les promesses observées à Berlin se confirment dans nos conditions de mesure et, surtout, s’il parvient à se faire une place dans une sélection devenue particulièrement disputée.
Car c’est probablement ce qui résume le mieux 2026 : le vidéoprojecteur premium n’est plus seulement jugé sur sa capacité à produire une image gigantesque. Contraste, optique, facilité d’installation, HDR, jeu vidéo et usage quotidien pèsent désormais tout autant dans la balance. Et c’est précisément pour suivre cette évolution que notre comparatif continuera, lui aussi, à bouger.

articles.title: Comitê da Meta aponta falhas na moderação durante eleições no Brasil
articles.text:
O Comitê de Supervisão da Meta criticou falhas recorrentes na moderação de conteúdos políticos durante eleições. Em comunicado divulgado nesta terça-feira (20), o órgão citou restrições que afetaram a campanha de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva no Brasil e a suspensão temporária de uma conta política nos Estados Unidos.
A entidade cobrou mais transparência e consistência nas decisões da empresa, que podem restringir manifestações políticas legítimas ou deixar de proteger a integridade eleitoral.
Denúncias no Brasil
A campanha de Lula acusou a Meta de interferência eleitoral após restrições que teriam afetado conteúdos no Instagram e no WhatsApp. O partido do presidente também denunciou um possível tratamento desigual pela inteligência artificial do WhatsApp, que, segundo a acusação, recusaria gerar conteúdo eleitoral favorável a Lula, mas não a Flávio Bolsonaro.
Na segunda-feira, a Justiça Eleitoral deu à empresa prazo de 24 horas para demonstrar que adota medidas para garantir tratamento igualitário às duas campanhas. A cobrança ocorreu a menos de uma semana do segundo turno presidencial.
A Meta negou favorecer qualquer candidato, mas reconheceu que anúncios da campanha de Lula foram desativados por engano. A empresa atribuiu os problemas a incidentes técnicos que, segundo ela, não se limitaram ao Brasil.
O Comitê de Supervisão vê dois tipos de falha nesse cenário: a aplicação excessiva das regras, que pode restringir o discurso político, e a aplicação insuficiente, que compromete a proteção do processo eleitoral.
Ao comentar o caso, o órgão afirmou que a empresa precisa corrigir sua atuação. O comitê declarou: “Está claro que a Meta precisa fazer mais para garantir que suas práticas de moderação durante as eleições sejam transparentes e consistentes”.
Conta suspensa nos Estados Unidos
A preocupação também envolve o caso No Kings. Nos Estados Unidos, a Meta desativou temporariamente a conta da coalizão de associações que incentiva a participação dos cidadãos nas eleições de meio de mandato, previstas para o início de novembro.
A empresa pediu desculpas pela suspensão. Andy Stone, porta-voz da Meta, afirmou na rede social X que a desativação foi resultado de uma ação automatizada realizada por engano.
O comitê questionou por que o problema não foi resolvido mais rapidamente e por que a conta não estava incluída no programa de verificação cruzada da Meta. O mecanismo permite que entidades cívicas consideradas importantes tenham suas publicações analisadas por uma pessoa antes de decisões que possam prejudicar sua participação em eventos políticos relevantes.
Cobrança por indicadores públicos
A discussão não é nova. Após problemas na moderação durante as eleições presidenciais brasileiras de 2022, o comitê recomendou que a Meta estabelecesse critérios mensuráveis para avaliar a eficácia de suas ações eleitorais.
Segundo o órgão, a empresa divulga números gerais, como a quantidade de anúncios armazenados e de contas removidas, mas ainda não apresenta indicadores públicos suficientes para demonstrar se suas medidas funcionam.
Entre os pontos que o comitê considera importantes para melhorar esse acompanhamento estão:
- Métricas que permitam comparar resultados e identificar falhas na moderação.
- Critérios claros para avaliar o impacto das decisões sobre a participação política.
- Sistemas automatizados capazes de interpretar diferenças de idioma, nuances e contexto político.
Em 2025, a Meta prometeu ampliar a liberdade de expressão e reduzir erros durante eleições e debates políticos. Para o Comitê de Supervisão, os casos recentes mostram que a empresa ainda precisa avançar para cumprir esse compromisso.
Valdir Antonelli é jornalista com especialização em marketing digital e consumo.

articles.title: Microsoft Targets Rogue AI Agents With Dynamic Permissions, Risk Scoring
articles.text:
Microsoft on Monday announced new controls to monitor and restrict potentially rogue AI agents in enterprise environments, arguing that organizations should treat these agents as insiders rather than trusted software.
The capabilities extend Project Perception, the agentic security system Microsoft launched in July. Perception was initially pitched as a defense against AI-driven attacks from outside, but it is now being applied to the agents companies run internally.
Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, said companies tend to trust the agents they deploy by default. She warned that frontier models are trained to get results and aren’t built around organizational norms or judgment. “These agents are frequently overprivileged, have access to data, tools and systems and can take actions and make decisions in critical processes,” Gallot wrote.
Nadim Abdo, Microsoft’s corporate vice president of identity and network access, clarified the insider label. “This does not mean agents are inherently malicious. It means they are capable tools that can be granted access to important systems by users. They can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised,” he explained.
One of the new features, Dynamic Permissions, gives agents no permissions, or the bare minimum, at the outset. Access is then granted per task and expires or shrinks as the task changes or ends, while high-impact actions require human review.
Dynamic Agent Risk gives each agent a risk score that is continuously updated, drawing on the agent’s activity as well as identity, data, endpoint, cloud, network and runtime signals. The score factors in the agent’s security configuration, the resources within its reach, how much damage it could do if something goes wrong, and whether it is straying from what the user or organization intended.
Dynamic Conditional Access, which brings Entra Conditional Access to agents, acts on those risk changes. Rather than simply allowing or blocking an agent, it can scale back its permissions, let it read but not write, limit the data and network resources it can reach, or require a person to approve consequential actions. If the risk climbs high enough, the agent’s runtime can be isolated or its execution halted.
To make this work at scale, Microsoft is introducing Playbooks and a team of Guardian Agents in Project Perception. Humans establish the rules and approval limits, Playbooks specify what the security response should achieve, and Guardian Agents execute it, looking into why an agent’s risk shifted and suggesting or enforcing containment.
Microsoft is also expanding discovery to 35 more types of local agents, bringing the supported total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and GitHub Copilot.

articles.title: Blackwall quadruples valuation to $2.2B as websites wrangle an increasingly crowded internet | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Estonia-based Blackwall, which builds web traffic security tools for hosting providers, said on Tuesday that it has raised $100 million at a $2.2 billion valuation. It builds products that helps websites grapple with the skyrocketing volume of bot traffic, especially AI agents.
The Series C was led by AVP, with participation from existing investors Dawn Capital, MMC Ventures and Tera Ventures. Blackwall’s executive chairman, Roi Carthy, told TechCrunch this funding round increased the company’s valuation by 4 times since its previous fundraise in 2025.
Over the past few years, web infrastructure companies like Cloudflare, Akamai, Imperva and Blackwall have found themselves in an increasingly valuable but difficult space: They’re on the frontlines, dealing with DDoS attacks, indiscriminate scraping, botnet farms, malicious requests, and these days, even swarms of AI agents going rogue. But it’s also a chance to make a killing by helping hosting providers and websites deal with all the potentially unwanted traffic.
Blackwall, however, isn’t interested in competing with the bigwigs in its space. Instead of selling its platform directly to websites, the company uses a “channel” approach, working with web hosting, managed service and cloud providers to understand their needs, and then handing over a bundle of tools which they can customize. Those providers can then offer Blackwall’s security tools to their own clients under their own branding and retain control of that relationship.
There’s money in it for both sides. Co-founder and CEO Nikita Rozenberg told TechCrunch that hosting companies can mix and match security components to build their own solution according to what they want to provide to their end customers, set the prices, and share a cut of the revenue with Blackwall. The company initially gives its customers a free tier showing the traffic and threats hitting their network, but charges for any protection or tools to address the threats.
In addition to providing services like threat intelligence, certificate management, DDoS protection and traffic routing, Blackwall examines its customers’ web traffic to differentiate actual visitors and legit AI agents from malicious bots, intruders, and disruptive traffic. Rozenberg said the company uses techniques like digital fingerprinting to identify the software sending a request — for example, Microsoft Office or Codex — to filter out bots. In addition, the company uses its own AI models at customers’ endpoints to analyze the intent and behavior of the requests coming in to differentiate agents sent by a person for a real request versus a malicious bot.
In the coming years, Rozenberg sees a big opportunity emerging as AI agents begin interacting and transacting with websites on behalf of their users. This should eventually require systems to manage which agents get access, and on what terms, and how they are authorized to make payments.
Blackwall isn’t alone in eyeing that opportunity. Cloudflare’s AI Crawl Control lets website owners allow or block individual AI crawlers, and there’s also an option to charge them for access. But Rozenberg argues that Blackwall’s advantage lies in letting hosting providers offer such traffic management services themselves instead of handing the customer relationship to another security provider.
Blackwall plans to use the funding to expand its operations across North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, and develop more security tooling for hosting, cloud and managed service providers.

articles.title: Repeat tech entrepreneur Ryan St. Germaine joins Raven as partner | BetaKit
articles.text:
Vancouver’s Raven Indigenous Capital Partners has bolstered its investment team as it prepares to raise its next fund.
The news: Ryan St. Germaine has joined the impact-driven venture capital (VC) firm as a general partner (GP). He and Raven announced the news on LinkedIn last week, when he officially assumed the role. Raven, which claims to be North America’s only Indigenous-led and owned VC firm, backs Indigenous-led tech businesses across the continent, from seed to Series A rounds. Its portfolio includes AdvancedAg, Animikii, CruxOCM, and PLATO Testing, among others.
From the source: “We talk about wanting more Indigenous folks in venture, and if we want to do that, we’ve got to take bets on the people that we believe can get it done,” St. Germaine told BetaKit in an interview. “I think people recognize my abilities. I’ve founded and led and exited companies on the other side, and it’s not that different.”
The context: In VC, moving straight to GP is rare, as most people gradually work their way up the ranks. But St. Germaine and Raven are confident that he has the chops to excel in this position. The Métis serial technology entrepreneur behind BCjobs.ca, Jobcast, and Indigenous Tech Circle had sat on Raven’s investment committee for its $100-million CAD second fund and served as an entrepreneur-in-residence since early 2024, where the firm said he has played “an important part” in its work.
St. Germaine joins existing Raven GPs Althea Wishloff and Sean McCormick under managing partner Stephen Nairne. He said there are no other immediate changes to Raven’s leadership. Raven plans to begin raising its next fund in late 2025 or early 2026. For now, he’s supporting existing Raven companies from Fund II and its $25-million predecessor. The firm is also deploying a $32-million Indigenous Outcomes Fund that’s geared toward supporting climate and health initiatives that improve outcomes for Indigenous communities.
Final thought: The new Raven GP said Indigenous companies don’t receive enough early-stage risk capital. St. Germaine is excited by the chance to help create “more equitable outcomes” for the community. He is also looking forward to working more closely with the startups he previously pitched on participating in Indigenous Tech Circle, where he plans to transition out of the CEO role but stay involved on the board.
Feature image courtesy Raven Indigenous Capital Partners.

articles.title: Adobe Lightroom mobile can now open closed eyes in photos with a simple tap
articles.text:
Adobe announced yesterday that the mobile version of Lightroom, available for iOS, iPadOS, and Android, can now open closed eyes in photos using generative AI with just a single tap. When the app detects a person, or a group of people, have their eyes closed in a photo it will automatically present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action that appears as an icon over the image providing easy access to the new feature.
Adobe Lightroom mobile can now open closed eyes in photos with a simple tap
When the mobile app detects closed eyes in a photo it will present users with a new Open Eyes Quick Action tool.
Being able to easily save an otherwise great photo by opening a subject’s eyes has been a feature in Adobe’s Photoshop Elements for nearly a decade, but as DPReview points out, Elements sources the replacement from another photo of the subject with mixed results depending on variations between the two images. Open Eyes in Lightroom mobile instead relies on generative AI so the replacement eyes match the lighting and pose, and the app will use other images of the same person in your Lightroom library as reference so the open eyes will accurately match the color, size, and shape of their own.
You can perform a similar fix in other Adobe apps like Photoshop using its own generative AI tools, but it’s not a one-tap fix, and it’s not free. Those using the free version of the Lightroom mobile app can try the Open Eyes feature twice before they’re given a prompt to subscribe to an Adobe Creative Cloud plan that includes more credits for its various AI-powered tools, according to DPReview.

articles.title: Revolut sufre una caída masiva y no se puede ni usar la app ni pagar... o acceder a tu dinero
articles.text:
Revolut ha confirmado una caída masiva de sus sistemas que está impidiendo a los usuarios poder acceder a la app (y por tanto a sus cuentas) o poder pagar. Desde esta mañana, múltiples usuarios han reportado que no podían pagar con las tarjetas de Revolut, ni tampoco a través de sistemas de pago de terceros.
Ahora la compañía ha confirmado que ha sufrido una caída generalizada de sus sistemas que afecta a varios de sus servicios, aunque están trabajando en ello. Se desconoce cuándo volverán a estar operativos o qué nivel de disrupción está experimentando la compañía, así como las causas de la misma:
Actualmente estamos experimentando una interrupción en el servicio que afecta a varias funcionalidades, lo que podría hacer que algunos servicios no estén disponibles. Nuestro equipo de ingeniería está trabajando activamente para restablecer el servicio por completo a la mayor brevedad posible. Agradecemos su paciencia y pedimos disculpas por cualquier inconveniente que esto haya podido causar.
Actualmente, la web de servicio de la compañía confirma que 31 de sus instancias están afectadas o no disponibles, incluyendo los sistemas de registro, inicio de sesión, transferencias o pagos con tarjeta, sin que haya trascendido cuándo volverán a estar disponibles.
Si eres usuario de Revolut, te recomendamos estar atento al estado del sistema de la compañía y, mientras tanto, usar otros servicios bancarios alternativos.

articles.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
articles.text:
These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
Beef is a climate burden. Can “blended meat” finally succeed in getting us to cut back?
In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs.
Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef.
The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.”
Through his consulting company, K–12 Food Solutions, Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The proprietary blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the most intractable challenges of the climate crisis, at least on the individual level: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef.
Livestock production accounts for somewhere between 10% and 20% of all greenhouse-gas emissions related to human activity, and nearly two-thirds of that comes from ruminants like cows raised for meat and dairy products. Beef herds create four times the emissions of dairy herds per kilo of food produced. And for US households, food makes up as much as 30% of emissions.
Unlike other polluting sectors, such as electricity and transportation, cattle farming has little potential for a big fix. Ruminants produce about 30% of the methane associated with human activity, and this gas has 28 times more global-warming potential than carbon dioxide. What’s more, it would be virtually impossible to raise them in a perfectly climate-neutral manner. “We don’t have a technical solution to change the stomach of a ruminant,” says Fredrik Hedenus, a professor in sustainability and systems analysis at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. Technologies to dampen the impact of their burps have been in the works for a while but have yet to scale. They also fix only part of the problem with red meat: Cows need a lot of land for pasture and for feed, which has made livestock a top driver of deforestation in the Amazon and elsewhere around the world.
Even if the world stopped burning all fossil fuels tomorrow, emissions from agriculture would push the planet past 2 °C over preindustrial temperatures by 2070, Hedenus says. According to his research, more efficient livestock farming methods would still leave agriculture eating up over half of humanity’s carbon budget by that time. Only with the addition of dietary changes does his model show a winning scenario.
He’s far from alone in his conclusions: A 2024 survey of more than 200 climate scientists, conducted at Harvard, found that the vast majority believe reducing emissions from livestock is important to meeting climate goals. People have to eat less beef. “Essentially, you need a culture shift,” Hedenus says.
Yet the culture has proved intractable. Not only do people like the taste of meat, but across most of the world, meat-eating tends to be associated with status. As societies have grown wealthier, it has increased. A United Nations report showed that global meat production quadrupled between 1961 and 2022, while vegetarianism has held steady at about 4% of the population in the US since 1999.
What could move the needle is a carbon-light and delicious meat replacement. But from a food-tech standpoint, all we have to show is a menu of mostly failed solutions. Lab-grown meat has generated endless headlines since the 2000s but has yet to become commercially available (and affordable) at scale. And while breakthroughs in taste and texture inched plant-based meats from companies like Impossible Foods and Beyond Meat toward mass adoption, the hype—and the appetite—has somewhat fizzled.
So instead of asking people to change their preferences, startups like Joyn are trying a different tack. They’re creating what are broadly referred to as blended meat products, which combine plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat.
Paul Shapiro, cofounder of the startup BMC Ingredients, which markets a plant protein related to mushrooms, says the math is easy to understand: If we imagine that Impossible Whoppers at Burger King account for about 2% of sales, that’s only a 2% reduction in meat. But if a conventional Whopper were 20% plants, that would be a 20% cut right off the bat.
Those aren’t quite the numbers climate models are calling for, but some estimates say they could lead to outsized gains relative to the status quo: A 2022 study in Nature found that replacing 20% of beef globally could halve the annual rate of deforestation. And unlike the other solutions tried thus far, this particular Hail Mary is one a lot of omnivores seem open to giving a try.
The idea of blending meat and vegetables together is, of course, nothing new. Food cultures from around the world boast an array of dishes that combine small amounts of meat with plants. Today, home cooks still add veggies and legumes to dishes to stretch tight grocery budgets or to sneak extra greenery into their children’s supper.
But in the mid to late 2010s, however, the focus was largely on companies that appeared to have cracked the code for ditching meat entirely. When Impossible debuted its namesake burger in 2016, it impressed with an ingredient called heme, an iron-rich molecule in the protein soy leghemoglobin that allowed all-plant burgers to “bleed” like beef.
Impossible and its biggest competitor, Beyond, swaggered through the media and the markets. In 2019, Impossible’s founder told the New Yorker he intended to wipe out all animal agriculture by 2035. Beyond’s 2019 IPO was the most successful since the 2008 financial crisis. A flood of imitators followed.
But within a few years, tastes shifted. In 2023, Impossible employees’ stock values tumbled 89% from a 2021 high. That same year, Beyond laid off 20% of its staff, and a bruising Businessweek feature labeled the entire sector a fad. Sales have been slipping for years, with a 10% year-over-year drop in 2025, according to the Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on alternative proteins.
 Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef.
Several factors were likely at play. Megan Krogius, a spokesperson for Impossible Foods, says the dip is a “correction not a crisis” after “an outsized pop in demand” between 2020 and 2022. She also says that a flurry of plant-based products muddied the category’s reputation. Indeed, some disruptors (and their imitators) have struggled to compete on the sensory level. Nectar, an organization that conducts research on meat alternatives, has found that taste and texture are among the major factors that keep people from adopting plant-based meats. “Our consumers identify products as having bad aftertaste and off flavors five to six times more than in animal counterparts,” says Caroline Cotto, the group’s director.
At the same time, discourse around processed foods tarnished plant-based meat’s halo. In 2019, the Center for Consumer Freedom, a since-dissolved lobbying group backed by the meat industry, launched an ad campaign against plant-based alternatives, demonizing them as “ultra-processed imitations.”
While Impossible’s Krogius warns against conflating processed food with junk food (she points, for example, to a study in The Lancet finding mock meat to be nutritionally preferable to red meat), some of the bad press stuck. Now, the term “ultra-processed” has become something of a political cudgel—one wielded by the meat-loving MAHA movement and the US secretary of health and human services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In 2025, he flipped the food pyramid and stacked a steak on top.
Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef, and consumption rose by 4.3% over the previous year, according to an industry report. Rising prices could be slowing this down a bit, but cost can dampen only so much demand.
Blended meat, which has meat’s own juiciness and texture, rose alongside the plant-based superstars, but it did not get New Yorker profiles or headlining IPOs. At the height of mock-meat hype, companies like Tyson and Perdue launched blended products, and firms working on lab-grown meat explored cutting their products with plants.
The big advantage of blended meat is that large numbers of consumers—what some call “flexitarians”—are curious about it, and when they try it, they like it. A blind taste test co-funded by the USDA in 2022 showed that diners preferred blended burgers to fully plant-based ones. And a report from the major food processor ADM found that large proportions of every generation of Americans were interested in trying blended meats, including 75% of millennials. “This is a solution that we can do today, that consumers will accept today,” says Tim Dale, a director at Food Systems Innovations, the nonprofit group that oversees Nectar.
At this point, even Impossible has acknowledged the potential. In a wide-ranging interview with the Wall Street Journal in 2025, the company’s former CEO Peter McGuinness admitted the brand’s struggle to win over consumers, and suggested a hybrid burger could bridge the divide.
Plenty of newcomers are entering the fray. “Shiitake-infused beef burgers” from Australia-based Fable Foods are in restaurants and moving “incredibly well” at the high-end grocery store Central Market in Austin, Texas, says CEO Michael Fox. The Both Burger from Los Angeles–based 50/50 Foods is available in a smattering of California stores and eateries. And Spare Food in New York signed a deal with Premier, one of the nation’s biggest spenders in the health-care sector, for its blend of surplus produce and ground beef.
One major insight for all these upstarts is that consumers react best when marketing focuses on pleasure, not environmental virtues or health benefits. Though many companies actually create a burger or meatball with a better nutritional profile (fiber!) and fewer of meat’s downsides, like saturated fat, that doesn’t get people to buy it. They like that it tastes good. Beef and mushrooms, for example, contain complementary flavor compounds, including the glutamates that yield deep umami, which is why they’re so often paired in dishes like beef Wellington and stroganoff.
Food-production companies are a big target. BMC Ingredients, which collaborated with Perdue on a line of blended nuggets, markets a plant-based protein that can be mixed with meat to up its nutrition and flavor. BMC grows mycelium—the root-like structures of fungi. It underpins popular meat alternatives like Quorn and also features alongside mushrooms in Joyn’s 50/Cut. Shapiro likens his factory to a brewery, but instead of yeast fermenting barley, a fungus called Neurospora crassa digests starch to produce a protein with a dense network of fibers that makes for a meat-like chew. “We grow four hours before we get a harvest,” Shapiro says. “It’s among the most efficient ways to produce protein on Earth.”
Joyn also sees its path forward outside the grocery store. Food eaten away from home accounts for more than half of what US consumers spend on grub, according to the USDA. Padraic Doherty, who joined Joyn from the meat distributor D’Artagnan and holds the title of chief growth officer, says its main areas of focus are K–12 and college cafeterias and other major food service providers, like stadiums. These organizations, he says, often have sustainability goals and also are pressured to find both nutritious and affordable options. The 50/Cut Joyn sells to cafeterias is between 5% and 15% cheaper than beef.
But can cafeteria mushroom burgers prompt a larger cultural shift?
The folks touting the idea of going halfway see it as a bridge. BMC’s Shapiro thinks the movement toward meat-light eating reflects the reality of how these changes happen. Nectar’s Cotto compares blended meat to a hybrid car. “Moving people toward blended products [is] a way to drive demand for some of the fully plant-based ingredients that don’t scale right now to bring the price down,” she says. “So it’s both a short- and a long-term approach.”
Not everyone is so sure market forces will be enough, though. Nil Zacharias, a longtime entrepreneur in food sustainability who offers plant-based options to New York City delis through his company Plantega, isn’t sold on the notion. “Too many people in the space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat and costs the same, people will eat it,” he says. “I think the plant-based backlash to ultraprocessed foods shows you that’s not necessarily how things are going to go.” He believes blended meat’s main impact will be on institutional dining, in places like schools and health-care facilities.
 “People in this space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat, people will eat it.”
Nil Zacharias, founder and CEO, Plantega
Meat hybrids could, however, taste just familiar enough to open consumers’ minds to alternatives. Some research has found that thinking about mock meats prompts people to reconsider the whole system. In the 2010s, Clemens Driessen, a cultural geographer who teaches at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands, worked on a project that asked people in pubs, supermarkets, and other public spaces what they thought of lab-grown meat. “There’s a first response, which is ‘Oh, that sounds horrible,’” Driessen says. Then people tended to reflect that the meat they consume is also heavily industrialized. “A whole train of thought emerges out of proposing something very new,” he says.
If the category succeeds, climate advocates will need to make peace with imperfection. A life-cycle analysis Joyn commissioned on the 50/Cut burger confirms that the product has half the greenhouse-gas footprint of a beef patty, which—if you go by company claims—means it has about five times the impact of a burger from Impossible or Beyond. Hedenus, the climate scientist, says that even if blended products don’t reduce impact as much as plant-based ones, he’s all for trying any solution that works. “It is very difficult to change how we eat, so I think most good suggestions should be explored,” he says.
Meanwhile, the products are finding their way to more plates. They’re in cafeterias, high-end grocery stores, and small burger chains. They’re in the catalogues of major distributors like Sysco. The Both Burger has even been at Disneyland.
The 50/Cut meatball is on the menu this school year in seven states. At Cane Bay High it’ll take the form of a sub. The school is buying 200 cases at a time, with 150 meatballs in a case. Jason Ciaccia, the systems specialist for child nutrition in the school district, says he won’t be using the word “mushroom” to describe it. “If they hear ‘mushroom,’ they’re going to skip over it,” he says.
He is, however, considering his branding. He’s asked AI to help him come up with something fun. He thinks “Marvelous Meatball Sub” has a nice ring.
Meghan McCarron is a food and culture journalist based in Los Angeles.

articles.title: Inma y Jesús, españoles trabajando en Noruega: “Hemos ahorrado 10.000 € en tres meses; en España, con suerte, ahorrábamos 400 € al mes”
articles.text:
Inma y Jesús se van a trabajar durante algún tiempo a Noruega para ahorrar dinero y poder seguir viajando por Asia. “Hemos ahorrado 10.000 euros en tres meses; en España, con suerte, ahorrábamos 400 euros al mes”, comentan sobre su experiencia. En España antes ejercían como trabajadores sociales.
Antes de marcharse, los dos probaron a cortar gastos para poder ahorrar cada mes algo más. “Pensábamos que el problema era que gastábamos mucho”, afirman. Dejar de salir con amigos y de comprar ropa les parecía una forma rápida de acumular ahorros, pero apenas consiguieron un incremento con el que quedar satisfechos.
El proceso para encontrar trabajo llevó varios meses hasta que lograron dar con una oportunidad en el extranjero para trabajar en Noruega durante la temporada de verano. Llegaron a dedicar “cinco o seis horas diarias” a buscar empleo. Además de ello, el trabajo que consiguieron es temporal.
Ahorrar para seguir viajando
El cálculo a partir de las cifras que da la pareja es sencillo. Si ahorraran 400 euros al mes, les llevaría 25 meses ahorrar 10.000 euros. Suponiendo, claro está, que consiguieran mantenerse ahorrando esa cantidad todos los meses, ya que era lo que podían guardar en España en el mejor de los casos.
La pareja tampoco hace hincapié solo en el dinero, precisamente porque le gusta viajar y quiere poder elegir adónde va y cuándo. El alojamiento en Noruega es de pago, aunque la empresa para la que trabajan les proporciona una vivienda en un lugar remoto. Los dos aprovechan para explorar el entorno. Según Inma, esto les permite gastar menos en ocio.
El vídeo recoge una experiencia personal que puede ser muy diferente para otras personas. El mensaje advierte de que otros podrían ahorrar más o menos que ellos. Para valorar una oferta concreta, hay que tener en cuenta el sueldo neto y el coste del alojamiento.
 @elviajedejein Esta es una experiencia personal y no significa que todo el mundo en Noruega pueda ahorrar eso! Jajaja Quizás puedas ahorrar más o menos! En nuestro caso ha sido una decisión maravillosa que nos está permitiendo acercarnos más a la vida que de verdad queremos ❤️ #trabajarennoruega #noruega #españolesennoruega
♬ sonido original - Inma & Jesús
Buscar trabajo en Noruega
En primer lugar, hay que buscar ofertas de trabajo en Noruega. La búsqueda en plataformas como EURES, la red europea de servicios de empleo, nosotros ya te la hemos contado.
Por supuesto, las condiciones de cada oferta pueden ser diferentes, pero una forma de acotar la búsqueda es filtrarlas por el idioma de trabajo. Según el servicio público de empleo noruego Nav, al utilizar su buscador de empleo Arbeidsplassen, hay que elegir “Engelsk” dentro de “Arbeidsspråk” para mostrar los puestos que indican el inglés como idioma de trabajo. Esto es importante debido a las condiciones específicas de los puestos en lo que respecta al idioma.
Antes de solicitar un puesto, hay que fijarse bien en los requisitos de los puestos en los que uno esté interesado, ya que cada puesto puede indicar su propio nivel de dominio del idioma.
Cuando se llega a trabajar en Noruega, hay que revisar los términos del contrato, que debe proporcionar el empleador. Según la Inspección de Trabajo noruega, todos los trabajadores deben tener un contrato escrito. Para periodos laborales de más de un mes, debe estar firmado y listo lo antes posible o, a más tardar, siete días después del inicio del trabajo. Para periodos de un mes o menos, o si una empresa de trabajo temporal cede al trabajador a otra, debe estar listo el mismo día en que comienza el trabajo.
El salario mínimo y los impuestos
Como regla general, en Noruega no hay un salario mínimo garantizado por ley para todos los sectores. La Inspección de Trabajo noruega publica salarios mínimos para determinadas actividades, y es responsabilidad del empleador respetar los que correspondan.
Si la oferta de trabajo no se ajusta a un mínimo obligatorio, debe corregirse. Si una persona encuentra una oferta de trabajo concreta, tal vez incluso con el mismo salario que otra, eso no significa necesariamente que vaya a ahorrar la misma cantidad de dinero si trabaja allí. El importe del sueldo neto no podrá calcularse solo con el salario bruto anunciado, sin tener en cuenta la tributación aplicable.
En Noruega existe un sistema específico de tributación salarial para los extranjeros que gestiona la Administración tributaria. Se llama PAYE, es voluntario y aplica un tipo general del 25 %, con requisitos y excepciones. El trabajador puede optar por las reglas generales de tributación, tal y como explica la Administración tributaria sobre PAYE.
La Administración tributaria menciona que la mayor parte de los trabajadores extranjeros que llegan se incorporan al sistema PAYE al solicitar su tarjeta de retención fiscal. Esta tarjeta es un documento electrónico obligatorio para quienes trabajan en Noruega, no solo para los que están en PAYE, y, si no se dispone de ella, los empleadores deben retener el 50 % del salario.
Según la Administración tributaria, esta retención es un anticipo y puede no coincidir con la cantidad total de impuestos que se deberán. Aunque el asunto pueda resultar complicado, esa retención reduce el dinero disponible mientras se tramita la tarjeta, algo que afecta al ahorro con el que se pueda contar durante una estancia corta.

articles.title: Apple annonce un événement le 28 octobre : voici les nouveautés attendues
articles.text:
Apple donne rendez-vous à la presse le 28 octobre à Los Angeles pour une nouvelle présentation placée sous le slogan « Pro and tell ». Plusieurs produits seraient au programme, dont un MacBook Pro à écran tactile OLED et un iPad mini remanié.
Apple n’aura pas attendu longtemps avant de reprendre la parole. Après les annonces du 13 octobre à New York, la marque a fixé un nouveau rendez-vous au mercredi 28 octobre, à 18 heures, heure française. Son invitation tient en trois mots : « Pro and tell ». Elle ne précise pas les produits concernés, mais Mark Gurman de Bloomberg a déjà évoqué plusieurs nouveautés susceptibles d’être présentées.
Un MacBook Pro tactile avec écran OLED en préparation
Apple préparerait tout d’abord une nouvelle génération de MacBook Pro de 14 et 16 pouces. D’après Mark Gurman, ces modèles adopteraient pour la première fois un écran OLED tactile. La Dynamic Island ferait également son apparition sur les ordinateurs portables de la marque, qui seraient nettement plus légers que les modèles actuels. Les dernières rumeurs évoquaient par ailleurs une commercialisation le 6 novembre.
Ces MacBook Pro seraient équipés des puces M5 Pro et M5 Max, toujours selon Mark Gurman. Apple n’ayant pas encore dévoilé le programme de son événement, il faudra toutefois attendre le 28 octobre pour savoir si ces nouveaux modèles seront bien de la partie.
Un autre MacBook Pro de 14 pouces serait aussi en préparation, avec un positionnement plus abordable et une puce M6. Contrairement aux modèles OLED attendus, il conserverait le design actuel. Enfin, un nouvel iMac serait également attendu avec une puce M6. En revanche, aucun changement de design n’a jusqu’ici été évoqué pour cette version. Espérons qu’Apple nous réserve quelques surprises de ce côté-là.
L’iPad mini pourrait lui aussi passer à l’OLED
Le MacBook Pro ne serait pas la seule nouveauté de cette présentation. Le géant de Cupertino préparerait également un iPad mini revu de fond en comble, avec un écran OLED, un système de haut-parleurs amélioré et une caméra frontale déplacée. De quoi, on l’espère, donner un nouveau souffle à la petite tablette, si ces changements se confirment, bien que son prix risque d'en refroidir plus d'un.
Apple n’aura donc laissé qu’une quinzaine de jours entre ses deux rendez-vous d’octobre. Après l’écran connecté HomeView, le HomePod mini 2 et la nouvelle Apple TV 4K présentés à New York le 13 octobre dernier, place cette fois aux Mac et à l’iPad mini. Le 28 octobre, Apple pourrait bien avoir quelques belles surprises dans sa manche.
Source : 9to5Mac

articles.title: Test du VZMore AX9 MAX : le mini-PC allemand venu de Chine — Frandroid
