articles.title: Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with AtScale and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
In the first post in this series, we built a semantic layer on AWS using Stardog’s knowledge graph over Amazon Aurora and Amazon Redshift. We ran a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore against that layer. The second post kept the same customer 360 (C360) pattern and swapped in Denodo’s data virtualization platform, extending the source mix to include an on-premises PostgreSQL cluster. This post uses the same C360 pattern again, with AtScale as the semantic layer.
AtScale takes a different shape from the first two. The semantic model is dimensional (dimensions, hierarchies, and measures) rather than a graph of triples or a set of views. AtScale authors the model in the Semantic Modeling Language, an open, YAML-based specification versioned in Git, and exposes it simultaneously, from a single deployed model, over three protocols: SQL, XML for Analysis (XMLA), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The Strands agent and the business intelligence (BI) tools the enterprise already uses get the same computed answer from the same definitions.
The rest of the pattern carries over from the earlier posts. A foundation model on Amazon Bedrock (Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 for the walkthrough) plans and writes queries. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore hosts the Strands agent and manages the outbound credential the agent presents to AtScale. The joins, metric definitions, and row and column filters that apply to the caller live inside the semantic layer rather than the prompt.
We assume you’re familiar with the semantic-layer architecture from the first post in the series: what a semantic layer is, what it’s for, and why the model plans queries without owning the joins. If any of that is new, the first post covers the ground.
By the end of this post, you will know:
- How to model a C360 domain in the Semantic Modeling Language (SML): datasets, dimensions and hierarchies, facts, measures, calculated measures, and perspectives, versioned in Git.
- How AtScale plans a dimensional query against Amazon Redshift, and how AtScale’s autonomous aggregate management accelerates the query patterns an agent generates.
- How to expose the model to an AgentCore-hosted Strands agent through the AtScale MCP server, and how to register that MCP server with AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
- How the human user’s identity propagates from the enterprise identity provider through AgentCore Identity, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to AtScale, and how AtScale enforces role-based access control (RBAC), row security, and perspectives at query time.
- How to deploy AtScale on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) using the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository.
The source of truth for the walkthrough is the AtScale C2026.7 release. Where a specific tool name or endpoint applies, we cite the AtScale documentation.
The example: Customer 360 on Amazon Redshift
The customer 360 pattern from the first two posts stays in place. A retail enterprise has customer records, orders, products, and rewards enrollments spread across systems, and business users want to ask cross-cutting questions without knowing which system holds which fact. The Stardog C360 Knowledge Kit we adapted for the first post in the series models this scenario with Customer, Order, Product, and Address entities joined on an integer cid that appears as a primary key in the customer table and as a plain column in the purchase table.
Where this post differs from the first two is where the data physically sits. Stardog and Denodo federate at query time across two engines. AtScale plans a dimensional query as native warehouse SQL and pushes it to one engine per query, so cross-engine data is consolidated upstream. For this walkthrough, all analytical C360 data lives in Amazon Redshift Serverless. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL remains the operational system of record, and a replication path (AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL to Amazon Redshift) keeps the analytical copy current. The agent queries a single AtScale model that maps to the Amazon Redshift tables.
The schema in Amazon Redshift:
| Table | Key columns | 
| customer | cid (PK), first_name, last_name, email, ssn, phone, location | 
| address | id (PK), city, state, zip, street_name | 
| credit_card | id (PK), cid, card_num, card_type | 
| rewards_account | id (PK), cid, account_id, create_date | 
| purchase | id (PK), pid, purchase_date, quantity, price, cid, card | 
| product | id (PK), name, brand, price, dept | 
| category | id (PK), dept_name, parent | 
| vendor | id (PK), vendor_name, industry | 
Nine columns of interest across eight tables. cid links customer records to purchases. pid links purchases to products. dept links products to categories. Everything analytical is in Amazon Redshift, so joins push down to native SQL rather than being resolved in the semantic layer or in an extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline.
A representative question that exercises the whole model: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? This is the auto-enrollment question from the Denodo post, carried over so a reader following the series can see the same request answered by a different semantic layer. It touches customer profile, address, purchase history, and enrollment status: one row per customer across four logical entities.
AtScale terms used in this post
AtScale implements the semantic layer as a dimensional model over a warehouse. The AtScale documentation and the SML specification use a specific set of primitives that come up throughout this post. A short reference is useful before we get to the walkthrough.
- Semantic Modeling Language (SML) – An open, YAML-based specification for describing semantic models. Every SML object (model, dataset, dimension, hierarchy, metric, calculation, perspective, row security) is a YAML file. The specification lives at github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML.
- Model – The top-level artifact. A model references datasets, dimensions, facts, and metrics, and exposes them through the AtScale query engine.
- Dimension and hierarchy – A dimension groups related attributes (customer, product, date). A hierarchy inside a dimension organizes those attributes into levels (product → category → department, or year → quarter → month → day).
- Fact and measure – A fact is a dataset that holds measurable events joined to dimensions on key columns. A measure is a quantity aggregated from a fact column, for example SUM(price * quantity) for revenue.
- Calculation – A derived measure expressed as a formula against other measures.
- Perspective – A publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group. Perspectives are how AtScale controls which dimensions and measures a caller can see.
- Row security – A model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes.
- Autonomous aggregate management – AtScale watches query patterns across consumers and materializes summary tables in the warehouse when a pattern is expensive enough to justify one. Subsequent queries that match the pattern route to the aggregate transparently.
- Design Center – The AtScale authoring surface. A modeler edits SML through a visual canvas or a text editor. Either way the artifact on disk is SML YAML in Git.
- AtScale MCP server – The in-product MCP endpoint at <atscale-host>/mcp that exposes the semantic model to any MCP client.
Where more detail is useful, the AtScale documentation and the SML specification are the authoritative references.
Reference architecture
The runtime splits into an inbound path and an outbound path, following the same shape as the Stardog and Denodo posts.
Inbound. A client sends the user’s question to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway. Gateway validates the JSON Web Token (JWT) that identifies the human user against the enterprise identity provider (IdP), then routes the request to AgentCore runtime (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), which hosts the agent process. The agent invokes Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to interpret the prompt and plan the query.
Outbound. When the agent decides to query the semantic model, it invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server. AgentCore Gateway serves as the outbound proxy: the AtScale MCP server is registered as an MCP target on Gateway, so tool calls route through Gateway and AgentCore Identity injects the credential at that hop. AtScale’s MCP endpoint accepts either a bearer token (for development and single-identity scenarios) or an OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak instance (the production path). The AtScale engine validates the token, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query against the deployed C360 model.
The query request travels down through the AtScale engine, and the results travel back up. There’s no ETL job that pre-materializes cross-database joins. The analytical copy in Amazon Redshift is the source of truth for the semantic model, kept fresh from Aurora by the upstream replication path.
The architecture is deliberately opinionated on identity. Gateway and Identity hold the tokens at the runtime edges. The agent doesn’t see them and only orchestrates the conversation and the tool calls.
Build the semantic layer
AtScale’s semantic model is a collection of SML objects (datasets, dimensions, facts, measures, calculations, perspectives, row security) versioned in Git. A working model has a shape a data engineer will recognize from a star schema, but every object is expressed as YAML rather than data definition language (DDL), and every object is a separate file. Building the C360 model happens in three passes: datasets over the Amazon Redshift tables, dimensions and hierarchies with the joins between them, and measures and calculations that express the business logic.
Datasets. Each Amazon Redshift table becomes an SML dataset. A dataset declares the physical connection, the schema, the table, and the columns AtScale will surface. Datasets can be authored visually in Design Center or edited directly as YAML. Either surface writes the same SML file to Git.
Dimensions and hierarchies. The C360 model has seven dimensions. dim_customer holds customer profile attributes and joins to dim_address through the location key and to dim_rewards through cid. dim_product holds product attributes and organizes them into a hierarchy through dim_category. dim_date supports date-based analysis. dim_vendor groups products by supplier. dim_rewards holds one row per enrolled customer with account_id and create_date, and snowflakes off dim_customer so that never-enrolled customers surface as null in the enrollment attributes.
AtScale’s hierarchy primitive is the concise expression of the product-to-category relationship. A query against the model can navigate product → category → parent category without a recursive SQL common table expression, and the large language model (LLM) sees a single dimensional path rather than a join graph.
A representative SML fragment for the product hierarchy:
Facts and measures. The fact table for C360 is fact_purchase, mapped to the Amazon Redshift purchase table. It joins to dim_customer on cid, to dim_product on pid, and to dim_date on purchase_date. Measures come off the fact: total_revenue as SUM(price * quantity), order_count as COUNT(id), and units_sold as SUM(quantity).
Calculated measures. Business logic that lives in the model rather than in the query. customer_lifetime_value is total_revenue evaluated at customer grain, the same formula applied to a coarser slice of the fact. Segments like big_spender and spend_tier are calculated measures with conditional expressions:
The expression is evaluated at query time. A column would hold one answer at one grain. The expression recomputes for whatever slice the query asks about, by customer, by customer and year, or by region. When the definition changes (the threshold moves from $10,000 to $15,000), the update happens in one YAML file, gets reviewed as a pull request, and deploys through the AtScale CI hook. Each consumer picks up the new definition on the next query, whether that is the agent, Excel over XMLA, or Tableau over Multidimensional Expressions (MDX).
The artifact on the right of Figure 3 is not a description of the model. It is the model. Design Center’s visual canvas and the YAML editor are two views of the same file, and the Git diff is the authoritative record of every change. The files conform to the open-source SML specification, so the repository can be read without the engine.
After it’s deployed, the model is simultaneously reachable over SQL (for JDBC-based BI tools and notebooks), XMLA (for Excel and Power BI), and MCP (for the agent). The total_revenue calculation returns the same number to Claude Sonnet 4.6 as it does to an Excel PivotTable pointed at the same XMLA endpoint. We confirm this match in Verification.
How AtScale plans and pushes down queries
When the agent asks a question against the semantic model, AtScale’s AI Computation Engine (ACE) does the planning. The steps a query goes through are the same for a dimensional SQL request from the MCP run_query tool and for an XMLA request from Excel. Only the parser at the front differs.
Take the auto-enrollment question: Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet? The agent, prompted with the model context returned by describe_model, composes a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model. ACE parses that query into a logical plan, resolves the dimensional references to the underlying fact_purchase, dim_customer, dim_address, and dim_rewards datasets, applies any row security the caller is subject to, and then plans the physical query against Amazon Redshift.
Two things happen at the physical-planning stage that separate AtScale from a hand-written pipeline. First, the join is pushed to Amazon Redshift as a native SQL join rather than materialized in the semantic layer. The Amazon Redshift optimizer sees a single SQL statement with a filter and an aggregate, and executes it accordingly. Second, AtScale’s aggregate manager checks its registry for a pre-built aggregate that matches the query pattern. If a summary table exists that groups purchases by customer at the right grain, AtScale rewrites the query to hit the aggregate instead of scanning fact_purchase. The query returns in a fraction of the time it would take against the raw fact table, without the agent or the modeler doing any manual work to route it.
The aggregate manager is what makes an agent-driven workload economically feasible. LLM-driven analysis fires more queries than a human analyst would, and open-ended prompts like Tell me something interesting about our sales can spawn a dozen. AtScale watches the query pattern, materializes aggregates in the warehouse itself (not a separate cache), and routes matching queries transparently. Aggregate creation is demand-defined against observed traffic across consumers, not only the agent.
The audit record for the query captures both the dimensional SQL the LLM wrote and the warehouse-native SQL AtScale rewrote it into, along with whether an aggregate served the query. That record is available to an operator through the AtScale Queries page in Design Center, and it’s what the following governance section builds on.
A note on multi-source and interoperability
AtScale connects to warehouses over JDBC. The C360 walkthrough targets Amazon Redshift Serverless. The same SML model works over Snowflake, Databricks, and Google BigQuery, and AtScale documents the connection pattern for each. What changes when you swap the connection is the SQL dialect AtScale emits, not the SML in Git.
One architectural property is worth stating explicitly because it differs from the first two posts in this series. A single AtScale query resolves in one warehouse engine. If the C360 model spans two warehouses (dimensions on Snowflake, facts on Amazon Redshift, say), a query that touches both must be reconciled in one of two ways. The first is upstream, by consolidating an analytical copy in one warehouse through a replication path. The second is by the warehouse itself, using engine-level federation such as Amazon Redshift Spectrum for querying Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), or Apache Iceberg tables that both engines can read. AtScale plans a dimensional query and pushes it to one engine. The cross-engine story lives one layer down.
That choice cuts both ways. It rules out the live cross-engine federation Stardog and Denodo perform at query time, but it lets AtScale’s planner and aggregate manager work against a single-engine execution model, which is what makes the aggregate story load-bearing at scale. Enterprises that already run a warehouse-centric analytical architecture with change data capture (CDC) pipelines from operational systems reuse that architecture. Enterprises whose answers require live federation across engines are better served by the semantic layers in the first two posts.
Governed access: Identity propagation and runtime enforcement
Customer 360 data is regulated. Some users (HR, fraud) need to see personally identifiable information such as Social Security numbers and card numbers. Most users (marketing, analytics) must not. Row-level filters restrict analysts by geography, and a per-user audit trail must survive from the human’s browser through to the warehouse.
AtScale enforces these requirements at the semantic layer, before any query reaches the warehouse. Enforcement happens identically whether the caller is the Strands agent over MCP, an analyst in Excel over XMLA, or a notebook over JDBC. One row-security object in SML, one perspective, one set of role bindings, applied to each consumer of the model.
Identity propagation from the user to AtScale
The chain follows the same shape as the one in the Denodo post, with the terminal hop landing at the AtScale engine rather than continuing to the warehouse.
- The human authenticates to the application against the enterprise IdP and receives a JWT.
- The application forwards the JWT as a bearer token to the Strands agent through AgentCore Gateway, which validates it (issuer, audience, signature) and routes the request to AgentCore runtime.
- When the agent invokes a tool call to the AtScale MCP server, AgentCore Identity supplies the OAuth 2.0 access token issued by AtScale’s bundled Keycloak, mapped to the human user’s identity. The AtScale credential does not enter agent code.
- The AtScale MCP server accepts the OAuth token. The AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, resolves the caller to an AtScale role, and plans the query with the caller’s row-security constraints and perspective bindings applied. The warehouse is reached with the AtScale connection identity from AWS Secrets Manager.
RBAC, row security, and perspectives
AtScale expresses access control as three composable primitives. RBAC assigns roles to callers based on Keycloak claims. Row security is a model object that filters rows returned to the caller based on the caller’s identity or attributes. A perspective is a publishable subset of the model exposed to a specific role or group.
For the C360 walkthrough, we define two roles.
- hr_user: sees the full C360 model, including ssn and card_num.
- marketing_user: sees the Marketing perspective, which hides ssn and card_num at the model layer.
When marketing_user asks a question that references ssn, the agent’s describe_model call returns the Marketing perspective, one that does not include ssn. The agent has no attribute to project. Row-level filters compose the same way: an SML row-security object that scopes customers by state restricts a caller to a specific set of rows without any change to the agent’s prompt.
Audit fidelity
Queries through the AtScale engine are logged with the caller’s identity, the model, the LLM-generated dimensional SQL, the AtScale-translated pushdown SQL that Amazon Redshift saw, the security policies applied, whether an aggregate served the query, and the row count returned. Because the record captures both the query the model wrote and the query the warehouse executed, an auditor can trace an answer from the human question to the SQL that produced the number. Neither the first nor the second post in this series captures both forms of the query in one record.
An audit record for a governed query looks like this:
The generated_sql and translated_pushdown_sql fields are the ones that make the trail complete: an auditor sees both the query the LLM composed against the semantic model and the query the warehouse actually ran.
Expose the layer through the AtScale MCP server
The AtScale MCP server is a component of the AtScale distribution, exposed at <atscale-host>/mcp. It’s generally available in the AtScale C2026.7 release and speaks the standard Model Context Protocol. Any MCP-compatible client (the Strands agent in AgentCore runtime, Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code) can connect to the same endpoint against the same deployed model.
The server exposes a set of tools scoped to querying the semantic model. The AtScale documentation publishes a tools reference per release. The tools that matter for an agent-driven workload are:
- list_models: Enumerate the models the caller can see, along with the column groups that describe how dimensions map to facts.
- describe_model: Return the dimensions, hierarchies, measures, calculations, and business descriptions for a chosen model. This is the payload the agent’s system prompt is loaded with before it starts composing queries.
- search_columns: Keyword search over the model’s columns. Useful when a full describe_model payload would use too much of the LLM’s context window.
- validate_query: Check that a dimensional SQL statement is compatible with the model without executing it against the warehouse. This lets the agent iterate on its query cheaply before firing anything Amazon Redshift will bill for.
- run_query: Execute a dimensional SQL statement against the model and return the rows.
- run_queries: Run multiple statements in a batch, useful for open-ended prompts where the agent fires several exploratory queries in parallel.
- get_version: Report the MCP server version, so a client can decide whether to cache the model schema.
The AtScale MCP endpoint accepts two authentication modes. The bearer-token path uses an API token minted from Design Center. Every request runs as the token owner, and this path suits a proof-of-concept or a single-identity service. The OAuth 2.0 path uses AtScale’s bundled Keycloak with a pre-provisioned client whose ID is exactly atscale-mcp, documented on the AtScale Connecting with Claude page. AgentCore Gateway presents the access token on the agent’s behalf, the AtScale engine validates it against Keycloak, and downstream policy evaluation uses the human user’s identity.
Registering the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target follows the standard Gateway MCP target flow. The tools listed earlier appear to the agent as ordinary tools, with AgentCore Identity handling the credential at the Gateway hop.
Sidebar: Extending the model with AI-assisted modeling
The AtScale MCP server exposes tools scoped to querying, and AtScale has been extending the MCP surface with author-side tools that let an agent introspect a warehouse schema, generate a candidate SML model from source metadata, validate the SML against the specification, and commit the result to Git. This pattern, in which an agent shapes the semantic model rather than only reading from it, is a natural fit for Claude Code and Cursor workflows. In those workflows, a data engineer collaborates with the LLM to bootstrap a model over a new dataset.
AtScale groups this direction into three capabilities. A Semantic Discovery Engine scans warehouse schemas, query history, and lineage to infer candidate joins, hierarchies, and metric definitions. A Model Recommendation System suggests dimensions, measures, and relationships based on observed query patterns. A Governed Feedback Loop keeps human review of AI suggestions in the SML-and-Git workflow, so changes are versioned and auditable.
The specific tools available at the time of publication are documented in the AtScale MCP tools reference. Check the current release notes for what is generally available and what is still in preview. The rest of this post covers the consumer path, an agent querying a deployed model, which is what a production C360 workflow relies on today.
Deploy and run the agent
Strands Agents is a small framework for building agents. A short Python entry point wires Claude Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock to the AtScale MCP server as a tool source. AgentCore runtime hosts the process. AgentCore Gateway terminates inbound requests and holds the outbound AtScale credential through AgentCore Identity. Foundation model availability on Amazon Bedrock varies by AWS Region. For the current list, see Regional availability by models.
The system prompt matters. The AtScale documentation and the reference demos in the AtScale corpus consistently recommend a three-step call pattern for the agent: list_models to see what is available, then describe_model on the target model to load the dimensions and measures into context, and only then run_query (or validate_query first, if the query is expensive to iterate on). The reasoning is that the LLM should not fabricate column names or metric names. It should reference only what describe_model returned. The system prompt should say so explicitly, and it should include a short section on the business terminology in the target model (total_revenue means sales dollars, not units) so the agent maps user questions to the right measure.
Turn on Amazon Bedrock prompt caching for the reused portion of the system prompt. The describe_model payload runs to a few thousand tokens and does not change within a model version, so caching it drops the input-token cost per query on repeated calls. The cache-point configuration is a request parameter on the BedrockModel object. See the Strands documentation for the current parameter name.
Verification
To confirm the semantic layer, the agent, and the identity flow work as intended, we ran three queries through the agent and then a governance rerun of one of them under a different role. The following behavior is what should reproduce in a working deployment.
Query 1, single dimension
List our customers in Wisconsin, with their city.
The agent generates a dimensional SQL query against the C360 model that selects first_name, last_name, and city from dim_customer and dim_address where state = 'WI'. AtScale’s planner resolves the dimensional path to the customer and address tables in Amazon Redshift, pushes a single SQL statement down, and returns the rows.
Query 2, aggregation with aggregate hit
What are our top 10 products by units sold?
The agent aggregates units_sold by product and orders descending. AtScale’s aggregate manager finds a matching demand-defined aggregate and rewrites the query to hit the summary table in Amazon Redshift rather than scanning fact_purchase. The Queries page shows both the LLM-generated dimensional SQL and the aggregate-routed warehouse SQL side by side.
Query 3, cross-domain
Which of our top 20 customers by lifetime spend haven’t enrolled in the rewards program yet?
The agent generates a query that joins dim_customer, dim_address, dim_rewards, and fact_purchase, and aggregates customer_lifetime_value by customer. The query restricts to customers where dim_rewards.account_id is null. The left join to dim_customer on cid keeps never-enrolled customers, who surface with a null enrollment record. The agent returns the top 20 by lifetime spend. AtScale’s planner resolves the joins to native SQL against Amazon Redshift and returns the ranked list. The customer_lifetime_value formula is not something the LLM had to invent. It’s a calculated measure defined once in customer_lifetime_value.yml and referenced by name in the query.
Governance rerun
We run a variant of Query 1 that adds ssn to the projection (Show me our customers in Wisconsin, with their SSN) as two different callers. As hr_user, describe_model returns the full C360 model, the agent composes the query, and the result set includes the SSN values. As marketing_user, describe_model returns the Marketing perspective, which does not expose ssn. The agent has no attribute to project, so it returns an answer without SSN. Nothing changes between the two runs except the caller’s identity. The query text, the agent code, the MCP server, the AtScale engine, and Amazon Redshift are all untouched.
Cross-consumer confirmation
We opened the same C360 model in Excel through the AtScale XMLA endpoint and dragged Customer.State and Total Revenue onto a PivotTable. The state-level totals match the ones the agent returned for equivalent questions, to the exact number.
Extending across data sources
Adding a new data source to the C360 model is a modeling exercise, not an integration one. Suppose the customer support team asks that the model include ticket volumes so an agent can answer Which of our top spenders opened a support ticket in the last 30 days? The steps are:
- Land the support-ticket data in Amazon Redshift alongside the other C360 tables, using the same replication pattern used for the operational tables.
- Add an SML dataset that maps the new table to a logical object.
- Add or extend a dimension (dim_ticket) and add the join to dim_customer on cid.
- Add any new measures the model needs (open_ticket_count, avg_resolution_time).
- Commit the SML changes, review them as a pull request, and deploy through the AtScale CI hook.
Nothing changes in the agent code or the AgentCore configuration. The next time the agent calls describe_model, it sees the new dimension and measures, and it can compose questions against them. The same pattern applies to a different warehouse. If a source lands in Snowflake or Databricks rather than Amazon Redshift, the connection is a new SML dataset with a Snowflake or Databricks connection, and queries resolve in that engine per the earlier multi-source note.
Deployment: AtScale on Amazon EKS
AtScale runs on Kubernetes, and the reference deployment on AWS is Amazon EKS. AtScale ships an official Helm chart at oci://docker.io/atscaleinc/atscale, and the AtScale K8S Blueprints repository provides infrastructure as code (IaC) scaffolding for standing up an EKS cluster with the components AtScale expects: an ingress controller, a persistent store for the AtScale metadata database, a Redis instance for query caching, and an AtScale-configured Keycloak instance for identity federation.
The AtScale deployment on EKS runs across a small set of Kubernetes pods. atscale-engine is the core query planner and executor. atscale-mcp-server is the MCP endpoint the agent talks to. atscale-keycloak is the bundled identity provider that federates to Amazon Cognito, Okta, Azure Active Directory, and other OpenID Connect (OIDC)-compliant IdPs. Supporting pods handle the SML API and the Design Center UI (atscale-sml-api, atscale-sml-web), PostgreSQL metadata storage (atscale-db), the query cache (atscale-redis), and ingress (atscale-ingress, typically fronted by an AWS Network Load Balancer).
The C360 application (a chat UI or a client library that calls the agent) can run in the same EKS cluster in its own namespace. It uses an IAM role for service account (IRSA) to reach Bedrock and AWS Secrets Manager without embedding credentials.
Networking is standard: AtScale reaches Amazon Redshift through the virtual private cloud (VPC) endpoint or a security-group rule that permits the AtScale namespace’s egress to Amazon Redshift, and the human user reaches the application through the ingress load balancer.
AtScale offers cloud deployment options beyond self-managed EKS. Check the AtScale website for current offerings and AWS availability. The rest of this post assumes the self-managed pattern described earlier.
Conclusion
Agentic access to enterprise data needs three things working together: a foundation model that can plan and generate queries, a semantic layer that computes governed, business-meaningful answers over the live warehouse, and a runtime that hosts the agent and manages the identity flow. Amazon Bedrock, AtScale, and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore each play one of those roles.
The agent talks to the semantic layer, not directly to the warehouse. Dimensions, hierarchies, measures, perspectives, and row security live in SML in Git. When a schema drifts or a governance rule changes, the update happens in one file, and each consumer (the agent, Excel, Tableau, Power BI) picks it up on the next query.
Where to start
Most teams that get this working start narrow and expand.
- Pick one workflow that spans two or three data sources and takes longer than it should to answer today.
- Write 3–5 questions the workflow needs to answer. These are the queries the semantic layer has to support on day one.
- Consolidate the analytical data into Amazon Redshift (or the warehouse of your choice), using AWS Database Migration Service or Amazon Aurora zero-ETL for operational data.
- Bootstrap the SML from the warehouse schema in Design Center, then refine it against the competency questions.
- Deploy AtScale on Amazon EKS with the AtScale Helm chart and the AtScale K8S Blueprints, register the AtScale MCP server as an AgentCore Gateway target, and wire a Strands agent through it.
Further reading
- AtScale MCP server documentation: Connect to AtScale with AI
- AtScale C2026.7 release notes: documentation.atscale.com
- AtScale MCP tools reference (published per release with the AtScale documentation)
- AtScale K8S Blueprints: github.com/AtScaleInc/atscale-k8s-blueprints
- Semantic Modeling Language specification: github.com/semanticdatalayer/SML
- Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide
- Amazon Bedrock prompt caching
- Strands Agents on AWS Prescriptive Guidance
- Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Stardog and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (first post in this series)
- Build a semantic layer for agentic AI on AWS with Denodo and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (second post in this series)

articles.title: Ukraine rescues wounded soldier using drone in daring 'world's first' UAV evacuation of a human — heavy-lift hexacopter carried injured 176-pound soldier 11 miles back to safety from minefield
articles.text:
Ukraine rescues wounded soldier using drone in daring 'world's first' UAV evacuation of a human — heavy-lift hexacopter carried injured 176-pound soldier 11 miles back to safety from minefield
In heavily mined terrain and surrounded by Russian kamikaze drones, 'Kostya' was hoisted by a Gurzuf Defence heavy UAV and guarded to safety by a fleet of smaller drones.
The Ukrainian military is claiming a world’s first after using an unmanned drone to rescue an injured soldier on the eastern Kharkiv front. Ukraine’s United24 news shared a video of the historic first. It also explained that the wounded infantryman was stuck in a heavily mined area, guarded by Russian kamikaze drones.
The above video starts with the Ukrainian drone locating the soldier, callsign ‘Kostya,’ in enemy territory. Various media reports suggest he was 11 miles (18km) behind enemy lines, at the mercy of Russian kamikaze drones, and perilously located in a minefield. Traditional land-based rescue was therefore not possible, but Kostya bravely agreed to be part of the first-ever human drone-lift rescue plan.
After being located, the injured infantryman clipped himself into a harness. He said, “That’s it, we can take off,” when he was fully buckled into the rudimentary-looking harness. UAV operator, callsign ‘Black’ from the 20th Mechanized Battalion, 30th Infantry Brigade, then appeared in the video and explained: “We were constantly in touch with him."
Ukrainian drone rescue key facts:
- Drone used: Gurzuf Defense hexacopter
- Drone capable of carrying 130kg (~287 pounds)
- Drone’s known range: it has previously transported 90kg (~198 pounds) loads up to 25km (16 miles)
- Infantryman weight: 80kg (~176 pounds)
- Rescue distance: 8km (11 miles)
- Hazards: enemy kamikaze drones, mines, gravity, many more
Being in constant touch with the operations HQ would have been reassuring. However, the surrounding presence of a fleet of Ukrainian support drones, both kamikaze devices and UAVs with anti-drone nets, was probably most comforting.
Eventually dropping back into safe(r) territory, after what must have been an arduous, nerve-wracking journey, control said, “Congratulations, you’re on the ground,” to Kostya, as he touched down in a field. Then the control room erupted into applause. They got their man back safely, and he is now being treated and is in recovery.
UAV operator ‘Black’ was delighted with the concerted efforts that brought back this wounded soldier. “A lot of people were involved, and everything worked out for us,” he said. Importantly, this may be the start of a whole new system of personnel evacuations for wounded and/or stranded soldiers using drone technology, indicated brigade leader ‘Napalm’ toward the end of the video.

articles.title: UniUni go-public deal falls through as SPAC terminates agreement | BetaKit
articles.text:
Richmond, BC-based last-mile delivery company UniUni will need to find a new path to the public markets after its deal with a special purpose acquisition company (SPAC) was terminated.
The news: MAK Acquisition, a Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX)-listed SPAC led by ex-Dye & Durham CEO Matthew Proud, announced on Tuesday morning that it terminated its merger agreement with UniUni. Earlier this year, UniUni signed the deal to merge with MAK and trade on the TSX; a deal that would’ve valued the combined entity at more than $1 billion USD ($1.4 billion CAD).
The termination followed MAK warning UniUni nearly one month ago that it was in breach of its interim covenant, meaning UniUni wasn’t meeting a certain standard in the lead-up to the deal closing, as its business and financial performance had deteriorated. BetaKit has reached out to UniUni for comment.
From the source: “Under the Purchase Agreement, UniUni had 15 business days following receipt of the notice of breach to cure the breach, however the breach was incurable as UniUni exceeded its maximum cumulative pre-tax loss,” MAK said in its release. “As a result, MAK has exercised its right to terminate the Purchase Agreement, and the Proposed Transaction will not proceed.”
The context: The day after MAK warned UniUni of the breach, UniUni announced it was entering into a term sheet for a private funding round led by an undisclosed existing investor. It’s unclear if this funding was intended to improve its fiscal position for the SPAC deal, or as an alternative source of liquidity in preparation for the deal to fall through. UniUni said at the time that the funding was meant to support its continued growth across North America and strengthen its financial position heading into peak delivery season.
Final thought: Based out of Richmond, BC, UniUni uses gig workers and passenger vehicles to deliver goods to consumers. It has partnered with outlets like Temu, Shein, and AliExpress, and in 2025 claimed a network of more than 100,000 registered drivers across Canada and the US. While the company has raised multiple large funding rounds, recent reporting has suggested the company is “deeply unprofitable” as it faces several lawsuits, including class action allegations of unfair labour practices.
Feature image courtesy UniUni.

articles.title: Wii Sports is back on the Switch 2, and it rules
articles.text:
Wii Sports holds an important place in Nintendo’s history. It’s the best-selling piece of software the company has ever made, one that permeated culture in surprising ways, and its success helped rejuvenate Nintendo after a period of steady decline. It also kicked off one of the company’s most important and unassuming franchises. While subsequent sports titles from Nintendo never sold quite as well as the original Wii Sports, they’ve become a fixture for each new console, much like a new Mario Kart or Pokémon. And now the Switch 2 has its own version, Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, and it’s the best so far.
Wii Sports is back on the Switch 2, and it rules
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is quietly one of the console’s most important games.
You’d be forgiven for not realizing that Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is launching this week. The game is coming out during a particularly hectic time for new video game releases, and it’s sandwiched between two flashier Switch 2 titles in Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave and the upcoming remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time. Amid all of that, it’s easy to forget a game about thumb wrestling and bowling. But Sports Resort is also a refined and expansive version of the concept, and one that will likely become a constant over the Switch 2’s life.
The core of the game is the same as always: giving you a bunch of athletic activities — they’re not exactly all “sports” — that require some form of motion controls to play. That means swinging a Joy-Con controller to simulate using a tennis racket or tossing a bowling ball. There are 12 sports in all, and they vary quite a bit. The aforementioned returning favorites tennis and bowling are joined by things like skateboarding, thumb wrestling, and flying a plane.
What makes the game work is its simplicity. Almost each activity is incredibly easy to pick up; I don’t know much about golf, but it only took me a minute or so to get down the fundamentals of swinging a club using a Joy-Con. This means that Sports Resort excels as an arcade-style experience, the kind of game you pull out when friends are over and you want to have some fun. Thumb wrestling is ideal for this. It’s so simple — you move your hand back and forth and use a single button to try and “pin” your opponent — yet gets extremely intense and fun in the competitive two-player mode. And unlike IRL thumb wrestling, no one can actually cheat.
There are some exceptions to the general simplicity. I still find basketball to be a little too complex, and I just can’t seem to figure out a successful strategy in table tennis. But there are enough games in Sports Resort that you’re almost certain to find a handful of favorites you’ll stick with, so having a few duds isn’t the end of the world. There’s also a decent amount of depth, both in terms of the skill ceiling for games — I have spent hours trying to perfect the spin on my bowling release — but also the various modes for each sport. Bowling, for instance, includes the returning option to play with 100 pins at once, which is chaotic as it sounds.
But the biggest addition to Sports Resort is that it now takes place in an open world. That may sound strange for a collection of arcade games, but it also allows it to introduce three new activities that are centered on exploring the beautiful island setting. There’s prop plane (where you hold the Joy-Con like a paper airplane to fly), power cruising (where you hold two Joy-Con horizontally, like the handlebars of a Jet Ski), and skateboarding (where you use the Joy-Con’s mouse controls to simulate controlling a tiny skateboard). There are competitive ways to play these games, like a skateboard race, but I’ve spent most of my time with a sightseeing mode where the goal is to find as many landmarks and secrets across the resort as you can within a five-minute time limit. It’s sort of like a more fleshed-out version of the free roam mode in Mario Kart World. The island is surprisingly detailed and interesting to explore, with lots of caves and hidden paths, and the three modes of transportation let you check it out via land, water, and air.
These exploration-focused modes add a nice new dimension to the experience, fitting snugly within the more traditional sports while offering a very different vibe. I’ve become particularly drawn to skateboarding — there’s something very satisfying about pulling back on the Joy-Con to simulate pushing a board — especially since you can collect items that let you purchase new clothes and other accessories to customize your character.
One of the biggest keys to Nintendo’s success during the Switch era has been consistency. Even in the midst of a tumultuous period for the broader games industry, the company has managed to put out a steady stream of games, many of which have had a surprisingly long life. Nintendo’s biggest hits aren’t always what you expect. The first Nintendo Switch Sports has sold more than 18 million copies, topping beloved games like Super Mario Bros. Wonder and Splatoon 3.
A little over a year into its existence, that style of perennial seller is exactly what the Switch 2 needs, the kind of game that people pick up alongside Mario Kart when they buy a new console. Wii Sports showed just how transformative a game like that can be, and Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is quietly keeping that spirit alive.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort launches on the Switch 2 on October 22nd.

articles.title: Hacker übernehmen CDU-Mailkonto und verschicken 6.500 Phishing-Nachrichten – auch an Kanzler Merz
articles.text:
Hacker übernehmen CDU-Mailkonto und verschicken 6.500 Phishing-Nachrichten – auch an Kanzler Merz
In den vergangenen Tagen haben zahlreiche Politiker:innen der CDU eine oder sogar mehrere E-Mails erhalten, auf die sie lieber nicht klicken sollten. Denn statt echter interner Kommunikation handelte es sich dabei um getarnte Phishing-Mails von Hacker:innen. Sie hatten es geschafft, sich Zugang zu echten E-Mail-Adressen von CDU-Politiker:innen zu verschaffen und darüber betrügerische Nachrichten zu verschicken.
Phishing-Mail an Merz: Was in den Nachrichten stand
Wie Heise berichtet, hatten sich die Hacker:innen Zugriff auf das Konto des Geschäftsführers des CDU-Kreisverbands in Heilbronn verschafft. Wie es dazu kam, ist bislang nicht final geklärt. Möglich wäre, dass auch der Geschäftsführer zunächst Opfer einer Phishing-Mail geworden ist. Sicher ist, dass sie Angreifer:innen das Konto im Anschluss genutzt haben, um mehr als 6.500 Mails an CDU-Politiker:innen in ganz Deutschland zu verschicken, darunter auch Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz.
Nachdem der Vorfall entdeckt wurde, hat der CDU-Kreisverband das Landeskriminalamt eingeschaltet. Noch ermittelt die Polizei, ob es unter den Empfänger:innen jemanden gab, der betrügerische Mails geöffnet hat. Die Mails lockten unter anderem mit vermeintlichen echten Betreffzeilen wie „Einladung zur 19. Böckinger Prominentenpredigt“ oder „Ummeldung / … / CDU SBK zu CDU Neckarsulm“.
In den Phishing-Mails wurden die Empfänger:innen dazu aufgefordert, auf einen Link zu klicken. Dieser sollte angeblich zu einem Dokument führen, das sie ausfüllen müssten, um an den Veranstaltungen teilzunehmen. Was stattdessen passiert, wenn der Link angeklickt wird, ist nicht bekannt. Die zuständige IT‑Sicherheitsfirma empfiehlt allerdings Betroffenen, die auf den Link geklickt haben, umgehend die eigene IT-Administration zu kontaktieren und Passwörter zu ändern. Zudem sollten Anmeldesitzungen terminiert werden, um schon im System befindliche Hacker:innen wieder auszusperren.

articles.title: 6 800 conversations avec Meta Muse se retrouvent en public : une seule requête DNS a suffi — Frandroid
articles.text:
Muse, l’agent IA lancé par Meta le 8 septembre 2026, permet de partager une conversation avec un simple lien. Sauf que ce lien ne reste pas vraiment confidentiel. Le nom Muse désigne aussi la famille de modèles d’IA de Meta, qui enchaîne les annonces, de Muse Wonder, censé rattraper les meilleurs modèles du marché, à Muse Spark Open, un modèle ouvert qui tourne en local.
Claroc est une société de sécurité qui aide les entreprises à surveiller les applications SaaS et IA de leurs salariés. Dans un billet publié le 18 octobre, elle explique avoir retrouvé plus de 6 800 pages de partage Muse avec une seule requête. Ses chercheurs ont pu les ouvrir sans compte et sans connexion, et ils sont tombés sur des documents personnels et professionnels que personne n’avait l’intention de rendre publics.
Mark Zuckerberg, le patron de Meta, présentait pourtant Muse en septembre comme un assistant « conçu de A à Z pour la confidentialité et la sécurité ». D’autant que Muse demande un accès très large aux comptes de ses utilisateurs : leur messagerie, leur e-mails, leur agenda et leur fichiers.
L’agent avait déjà connu un problème de sécurité. Le 21 septembre, moins de deux semaines après le lancement, le chercheur Patrick Wardle, fondateur de l’association Objective-See, a publié une faille zero-day dans l’application Mac de Muse. Celle-ci permettait à un logiciel malveillant déjà installé sur le Mac de détourner la dictée vocale et de voler le jeton d’authentification de l’assistant.
Le titre de la conversation finit dans un registre public
Toutes les pages de partage Muse sont hébergées sur le domaine cf.metaaiusercontent.com. Pour chaque page, Muse crée une adresse qui commence par le titre de la conversation, suivi d’un identifiant aléatoire. Par exemple : home-sale-budget-9f21c8a3.cf.metaaiusercontent.com, pour un budget de vente de maison.
L’identifiant aléatoire est là pour qu’on ne puisse pas deviner le lien. Le problème vient du DNS, l’annuaire qui traduit le nom d’un site en adresse de serveur. Quand le destinataire ouvre le lien, son navigateur interroge cet annuaire. Des services de DNS passif enregistrent alors l’adresse complète, titre et identifiant compris, dans des bases où l’on peut faire des recherches. Il suffit ensuite de chercher le domaine de Muse pour obtenir toute la liste.
Claroc appelle ces pages des GhostShares, des « partages fantômes » qui s’ouvrent pour des gens qui n’ont jamais reçu le lien. Muse demande bien aux moteurs de recherche de ne pas indexer ces pages. Mais les chercheurs ne sont jamais passés par un moteur de recherche.
La plupart des pages ouvertes étaient banales : sites de petites entreprises, annonces, agendas d’événements. Une minorité contenait des données sensibles, que Claroc décrit sans nommer personne :
- les notes d’un candidat qui préparait un entretien confidentiel avec un laboratoire d’IA, avec le nom de son contact et l’heure du rendez-vous ;
- la revue des revenus internes d’une entreprise de marketing, destinée à son patron ;
- la demande de prêt d’un patron de petite entreprise, avec le montant demandé ;
- une liste de tâches qui mentionnait une alerte de fraude bancaire, avec un numéro de compte partiel ;
- le rapport d’un investisseur immobilier, avec deux adresses et les chiffres exacts de rendement et d’emprunt ;
- le calendrier des congés de toute une équipe sur un an.
Claroc a signalé le problème le 8 octobre au programme de bug bounty de Meta, qui récompense les chercheurs qui signalent des failles. D’après Asaf Aprozper, cofondateur et CTO de Claroc, Meta n’a jamais répondu. Meta n’a pas répondu tout de suite non plus aux questions d’Ars Technica, qui a relayé l’étude.
Pour Claroc, ce fonctionnement est voulu. Muse ne partage que par lien public, et c’est la seule façon pour le destinataire d’ouvrir la page. Les chercheurs précisent aussi que leurs 6 800 liens ne mesurent pas toutes les conversations exposées. Ils n’ont interrogé qu’un seul service de DNS passif, sur une courte période.
Que faire avant de partager une conversation Muse ?
Partez du principe qu’un lien Muse partagé est public, et que son titre peut être lu par n’importe qui dans les bases DNS.
Les chercheurs conseillent de ne pas mettre d’informations personnelles inutiles dans une conversation que vous comptez partager. Ils conseillent aussi de supprimer le lien une fois qu’il a servi. Méfiez-vous également du titre, puisque c’est lui qui dit aux curieux ce que contient la page.
Pour les entreprises, Claroc recommande de repérer les salariés qui utilisent Muse. Si l’entreprise ne peut pas surveiller ces partages, Claroc conseille de bloquer muse.ai et metaaiusercontent.com sur les appareils qu’elle gère.
Les bons plans n’attendent pas : abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp Frandroid Bons Plans ! (zéro spam, promis, juste de super bons plans).
Vous aimez nos contenus ? Dites-le à Google en ajoutant Frandroid à vos sources préférées en un clic.

articles.title: Aspirateur robot UV : comment fonctionne la détection des taches invisibles ? — Frandroid
articles.text:
Un sol qui paraît propre peut encore porter des taches séchées invisibles à l’œil nu : urine d’animal, soda renversé, éclaboussures de sauce. L’aspirateur et la serpillière passent souvent à côté, faute de les voir. Ces taches collent pourtant sous le pied ou ressortent sous un éclairage rasant.
Pour en venir à bout, les fabricants d’aspirateurs robots commencent à intégrer une technologie jusqu’ici peu répandue dans les appareils ménagers : la lumière ultraviolette (UV). Celle-ci permet de révéler certaines taches invisibles à l’œil nu, afin de mieux cibler le nettoyage. Le robot aspirateur est alors capable de concentrer son nettoyage sur la tache qu’il a repérée pour nettoyer efficacement le sol. C’est le cas chez Shark avec sa technologie UV Stain Detect, associée au lavage HyperSonic.
Pourquoi un sol peut-il sembler propre sans l’être ?
Un sol peut sembler propre sans l’être, car l’aspirateur et la serpillière éliminent surtout les saletés visibles : poussière, miettes, cheveux ou traces de pas. Les taches de liquide qui ont séché se fondent dans le revêtement et échappent au regard, donc souvent au nettoyage.
Certaines sont particulièrement difficiles à repérer une fois sèches. C’est notamment le cas :
- Des traces d’urine laissées par les animaux de compagnie, parfois invisibles une fois le liquide (et l’odeur) évaporé ;
- Des éclaboussures de boissons renversées, comme les jus de fruits ou les sodas, qui peuvent laisser des résidus collants sans pour autant former une tache uniforme bien visible ;
- Des résidus alimentaires, notamment les éclaboussures de sauce ou de matières grasses.
Ces saletés tenaces ne gâchent pas seulement l’aspect de vos sols. Certaines de ces salissures peuvent favoriser l’apparition d’odeurs persistantes et, selon les conditions, le développement de micro-organismes, parfois pathogènes. C’est d’autant plus gênant si vous avez des enfants en bas âge qui se déplacent à quatre pattes.
Comment la lumière UV permet-elle de révéler les taches invisibles ?
La lumière ultraviolette (UV) permet de révéler des taches séchées invisibles à l’œil nu, comme l’urine d’animaux, la sueur ou les restes de boissons, grâce à un phénomène physique appelé fluorescence. Les aspirateurs robots à détection UV s’en servent pour savoir où concentrer leur lavage.
Sous un éclairage ultraviolet, certaines substances absorbent la lumière puis en réémettent une partie sous forme de lumière visible. Des traces indiscernables sous un éclairage classique peuvent ainsi apparaître plus nettement.
C’est notamment le cas de certains résidus organiques, comme l’urine, la transpiration ou les restes de liquides alimentaires. Toutes les substances ne réagissent cependant pas de la même manière aux UV, et cette méthode ne permet pas de détecter systématiquement toutes les salissures.
La lumière UV est déjà utilisée dans différents domaines professionnels, notamment pour rechercher des traces biologiques ou contrôler la propreté de certaines surfaces. Elle fait maintenant son entrée dans les appareils d’entretien de la maison.
Les aspirateurs robots comme le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal peuvent désormais se servir de la lumière UV pour repérer les zones qui demandent un nettoyage plus poussé. Une fois la tache repérée, le lavage HyperSonic de Shark prend le relais avec un frottement intensif concentré sur la zone.
Il faut toutefois distinguer la détection UV de la désinfection UV. Dans un aspirateur robot équipé de cette fonction, la lumière sert à repérer les taches, et non à éliminer directement les bactéries. Pour l’hygiène, le PowerDetect UV Reveal compte sur sa base, qui lave le tampon à l’eau chaude puis le sèche à l’air chaud.
Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal : un aspirateur robot qui repère les taches invisibles
Le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal est un aspirateur robot laveur de la collection Luxe de Shark. C’est le premier modèle de la marque à utiliser la lumière ultraviolette pour rechercher des taches invisibles à l’œil nu, comme l’urine d’animaux, la sueur ou les éclaboussures de boissons séchées, puis à concentrer son lavage dessus.
Pour cela, Shark a développé la technologie UV Stain Detect, qui associe un éclairage UV à des capteurs RGB, capables d’analyser les couleurs et les informations visuelles du sol.
Lorsque le PowerDetect UV Reveal parcourt une pièce, ses capteurs examinent la surface en temps réel pour identifier les salissures visibles, mais également certaines traces qui échappent à l’œil humain.
Une éclaboussure de jus de fruits séchée dans la cuisine ou une ancienne trace d’urine accidentelle laissée par votre animal peuvent ainsi être repérées par l’appareil, même lorsqu’elles ne sont plus clairement visibles.
Grâce à la détection UV, le PowerDetect UV Reveal ne dépend plus uniquement d’un parcours de lavage prédéfini. Le robot peut identifier les zones qui nécessitent une attention particulière, puis adapter son nettoyage en conséquence.
La détection UV complète les cinq autres technologies PowerDetect du robot : Dirt Detect repère la saleté peu visible et augmente l’aspiration, Floor Detect reconnaît le type de sol, Object Detect évite les obstacles, Edge Detect aspire le long des plinthes et dans les coins, et Wet Edge Detect étend le tampon de lavage jusqu’aux bords.
Voici ce que la détection UV change au nettoyage des sols :
| Sans détection UV | Avec détection UV | 
| Certaines taches séchées passent inaperçues | Les UV révèlent certaines traces invisibles à l’œil nu | 
| Le nettoyage peut manquer des zones souillées | Le robot identifie des zones qui nécessitent un nettoyage ciblé | 
| Des résidus peuvent persister après un passage | Le lavage peut être renforcé sur les taches détectées | 
| Le nettoyage repose sur les capteurs classiques | La détection UV complète les capteurs pour une analyse plus précise du sol | 
Détecter les taches, puis renforcer le lavage pour les éliminer
Une fois une tache repérée, le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal passe au lavage HyperSonic, un frottement intensif concentré sur la zone détectée par UV Stain Detect pour venir à bout des salissures incrustées.
Selon Shark, cette technologie offre une puissance de frottement jusqu’à sept fois supérieure à celle du PowerDetect NeverTouch Pro (RV2820ZE), un précédent robot laveur de la marque.
Le PowerDetect UV Reveal dispose également d’autres fonctionnalités conçues pour automatiser l’entretien des sols :
- Automatic Mop-Up : cette technologie permet au robot de gérer automatiquement son tampon de lavage. Il relève automatiquement son tampon dès qu’il détecte un tapis ou une moquette, pour ne pas les mouiller ni y transférer de saleté.
- Floor Detect : le robot identifie les différents types de sols afin d’adapter automatiquement sa puissance d’aspiration.
- La base sans sac ThermaCharged NeverTouch Pro : elle vide le collecteur de poussière, remplit le réservoir d’eau, lave le tampon à l’eau chaude et le sèche à l’air chaud. Shark annonce jusqu’à 60 jours sans y toucher. Après chaque utilisation, le constructeur conseille cependant de vider le bac d’eau sale pour éviter la prolifération des germes.
Le PowerDetect UV Reveal associe ainsi la détection des taches, leur nettoyage ciblé et l’entretien automatisé du robot. Shark promet des sols mieux lavés et moins de temps passé au ménage.
En septembre 2026, le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal de la collection Luxe est vendu 999,99 euros, en exclusivité sur la boutique en ligne de Shark.
FAQ : tout savoir sur la détection UV et les aspirateurs robots
La lumière UV permet-elle de détecter l’urine de chat ou de chien sur le sol ?
Oui, certaines traces d’urine de chat ou de chien deviennent visibles sous une lumière UV, même après avoir séché. La technologie UV Stain Detect du Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal exploite ce phénomène pour repérer ces salissures et cibler leur nettoyage.
Comment le robot Shark élimine-t-il les taches une fois détectées par les UV ?
Lorsqu’une tache est repérée, le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal active son lavage HyperSonic pour effectuer un frottement intensif sur la zone concernée. Selon le fabricant, cette technologie offre jusqu’à sept fois plus de puissance de frottement que le PowerDetect NeverTouch Pro (RV2820ZE), un précédent robot laveur de la marque.
La technologie UV est-elle sans danger pour les sols fragiles ?
La lumière UV du Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal sert à détecter les taches et non à traiter directement les surfaces. Le robot utilise également Floor Detect pour adapter son aspiration au type de sol, mais il reste nécessaire de respecter les recommandations d’entretien propres à chaque revêtement.
Le robot risque-t-il de mouiller mes tapis en cherchant des taches ?
Non, le Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal est conçu pour éviter de mouiller les tapis et les moquettes lors du lavage. Sa technologie Automatic Mop-Up lui permet de gérer automatiquement son tampon de lavage et de le relever lorsqu’il rencontre ces surfaces.

articles.title: This program is pushing startups to plan for security sooner | BetaKit
articles.text:
Startup founders spend plenty of time thinking about their product, customers, and capital. Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst wants security added to the top of that list.
The Catalyst’s upcoming Cyber for Startups program aims to show that cybersecurity can play an outsized role in the most critical stages of company-building. The no-cost program will offer online and in-person cohorts this fall. Participating early- and mid-stage Canadian technology startups will have access to assessments, workshops, tools, templates, and coaching, all aimed at building security into products, operations, and growth plans, from the beginning.
“Cybersecurity doesn’t have to be overwhelming or prohibitively expensive.”
Charles Finlay,
Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst
“For startups, cybersecurity isn’t just about protecting against threats but about creating opportunities,” said Charles Finlay, founding executive director at Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst. “Strong security practices can help founders win customers’ confidence, attract investment, and compete for larger contracts. When security is treated as an afterthought, startups risk closing doors to opportunities they’ve worked hard to create.”
According to Finlay, strong security practices should be considered part of best practices, as those practices help startups with customer trust, enterprise procurement, investment readiness, and access to regulated markets. It also helps companies avoid technical debt, which becomes more costly to address as they grow. Cyber for Startups is geared toward companies that are building or scaling technology products, preparing to sell into enterprise or regulated markets, or looking to strengthen their cybersecurity posture as they grow. These companies face security expectations across several important parts of the business.
Enterprise buyers and regulators, for example, usually want to understand how a startup protects sensitive information, and often ask about controls, policies, or even SOC 2 attestation. Investors may also scrutinize security practices as part of due diligence. Security can also reach back into product development itself, influencing decisions around architecture and how data is handled within a product.
Cyber for Startups is designed to help companies work through each of those challenges in a structured way. During the program, participants will assess their current security posture, identify gaps, and turn those findings into a tailored, long-term roadmap that details which issues need attention now and which should become a milestone later. Crucially, the program focuses on how to communicate security posture to potential clients, helping founders gain trust even when the work is in progress.
“One of the biggest challenges comes when a startup moves from building a product to selling it,” Finlay added. “Suddenly, prospective customers are asking detailed questions about how their data will be protected, what security controls are in place, and how risks are managed. Founders can find themselves scrambling to meet expectations they hadn’t anticipated. We want to help companies prepare for those conversations well before they’re sitting across the table from a potential customer.”
Cyber for Startups is designed to help founders build security into their product development and go-to-market strategies from the outset because cybersecurity requirements need to inform how a product is built, who it will be sold to, and which markets the company plans to enter. Startups that put off these critical decisions risk accumulating technical debt, leaving them with costly and complex security problems to untangle as the business grows.
“Decisions about how data is collected and stored, who has access to systems, and how security is built into a product can seem relatively minor when a company is small,” Finlay said. “But those decisions become much harder and more expensive to reverse as the business grows. Getting the fundamentals right early on can save founders from having to rebuild critical parts of their technology down the road.”
The program is targeted toward the people making these decisions, including technical founders, product leaders, and executives responsible for compliance, risk, or growth. No prior formal cybersecurity training is required.
Cyber for Startups will be delivered across several cohorts across Canada this fall, both virtually and in person. The first in-person cohort will take place in Brampton, Ont., on Nov. 12, in partnership with the City of Brampton, Brampton Innovation District, and the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange, with funding provided in part by the Government of Ontario. Applications for the Brampton cohort are open until Oct. 30.
“When security is treated as an afterthought, startups risk closing doors to opportunities they’ve worked hard to create.”
Charles Finlay,
Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst
RBC will support two other offerings: an online cohort running through November and December, and an in-person Vancouver cohort scheduled for February. Rolling registration will be available for both.
Offering both formats is intended to make the program more accessible to startups in different regions and stages of growth in Canada. In-person cohorts will run over a single day and prioritize networking and coaching, while the online version spreads the program across four weeks, focusing on roadmapping work.
As startups grow, the financial stakes of cybersecurity can grow with them. Data from the Canadian Internet Registration Authority found that 39 percent of Canadian organizations surveyed this year had experienced a cyber attack in the last 12 months.
The costs of these incidents can also be significant. Statistics Canada’s most recent survey on the topic found that Canadian businesses spent roughly $1.2 billion recovering from cybersecurity incidents in 2023, nearly double the amount reported in 2021.
Cyber for Startups is designed to make security an early decision for founders, before growth turns it into a more expensive one.
“I want founders to leave understanding that they don’t need to have everything figured out on day one, but they do need a plan,” Finlay said. “Cybersecurity doesn’t have to be overwhelming or prohibitively expensive. It’s about understanding your risks, making informed decisions, and taking practical steps as your business grows. That’s exactly what we’re trying to help startups do through this program.”
PRESENTED BY
Build security into your startup from the start. Apply for the next cohort of Cyber for Startups.

articles.title: Subaru veut prouver qu'il sait faire de vraies voitures électriques sans Toyota
articles.text:
Subaru veut concevoir lui-même ses prochaines voitures électriques. Le 18 octobre 2026, sur sa piste d’essai de Sano, au nord de Tokyo, le constructeur japonais a montré un prototype étrennant sa future plateforme électrique. Jusqu’ici, toutes les Subaru électriques ont été développées avec Toyota. Une dépendance industrielle que Subaru aimerait bien voir disparaitre.
D’après Automotive News, présent sur place, la marque déploiera ses premières technologies maison à partir de 2029 environ, sans préciser sur quel modèle. « En développant nos véhicules en interne et en disposant de nos propres technologies en matière de véhicules électriques, nous pouvons rapidement offrir à nos clients la tranquillité d’esprit et le plaisir de conduite qui caractérisent Subaru, même en cette période de changement », explique Takatomo Watamori, directeur exécutif en charge de l’ingénierie.
Une Subaru électrique faite maison, avec Aisin, Panasonic et AMD
Pour l’instant, la nouvelle plateforme roule sous une carrosserie d’Outback. Subaru a dû élargir les passages de roue de cette carrosserie, parce que la plateforme est plus longue entre les deux essieux. Le prototype a deux moteurs, un de 150 kW à l’avant et un de 230 kW à l’arrière, pour un cumul de 380 kW, soit environ 517 ch.
Subaru ne travaille évidemment pas totalement seul. Il a conçu les moteurs avec Aisin, un fournisseur… du groupe Toyota. Quant à la batterie, elle est développée avec Panasonic Energy depuis 2024. D’après les ingénieurs de Subaru, les moteurs sont 30 % plus efficaces que la moyenne du secteur, tandis que la batterie pèserait 25 % de moins que la précédente. De quoi faire gagner 100 kg à la plateforme.
Cependant, Subaru ne précise pas de quelle « moyenne du secteur » il parle. L’autonomie, la capacité de la batterie ainsi que la vitesse de recharge sont également inconnues pour le moment. La raison étant que le modèle de série n’aura pas forcément les caractéristiques du prototype.
Le logiciel non plus ne viendra pas de Toyota
Subaru a aussi conçu une puce sur mesure avec l’américain AMD. Elle fera tourner un calculateur central unique, qui gérera l’aide à la conduite EyeSight de nouvelle génération, le châssis, la motorisation et l’info-divertissement. Avec ce boîtier, les modèles conçus par Subaru pourront pour la première fois être mis à jour à distance, qu’ils soient électriques, hybrides ou à essence.
Selon Nikkei Asia, Subaru veut lancer d’ici la fin de la décennie ses premiers véhicules « définis par logiciel », c’est-à-dire des voitures construites autour de leur logiciel et dont les fonctions évoluent avec les mises à jour. Par ailleurs, le constructeur veut aussi réduire de 40 % le temps de développement de ses modèles grâce à la simulation numérique.
Subaru a d’ailleurs dit n’avoir « aucun projet à ce stade » d’adopter Arene, la plateforme logicielle de Toyota, qui détient pourtant 21 % de son capital, a rapporté Reuters. Deux jours plus tôt, Toyota avait annoncé viser 10 millions de véhicules par an sous cette plateforme d’ici 2030.
Pour amortir ces développements maison, Subaru veut vendre davantage de voitures. En novembre 2025, Atsushi Osaki, CEO du constructeur, a fixé un objectif de 1,2 million de livraisons par an d’ici la première moitié des années 2030, avec dix nouveaux modèles. Le record actuel de Subaru, 1,1 million de voitures, date de 2018.
