articles.title: Copenhagen’s Plinto raises €2.9 million to help finance teams catch and fix errors with AI agents | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Plinto, a Copenhagen-based startup building AI for real-time controlling, has secured €2.9 million in pre-Seed funding.
The round was led by People Ventures and Emblem, with participation from a group of business angels.
“Companies have systems that record every single transaction, but checking whether those transactions actually match agreements and rules is still largely manual. We’re building AI agents that find deviations, investigate them and take action, so errors get fixed,” said Jakob Nielsen, co-founder and CDO of Plinto.
Plinto was founded in early 2025 by Nermina Suljevic, Nielsen, and Sebastian Rehnby, who previously worked for Peakon, the employee engagement platform acquired by US-based Workday in 2021. The company’s CTO Andreas Garnæs is also an alumnus of Peakon. Together, they bring experience across product development, engineering, commercial scaling, and working with large international organisations.
In large organisations, the volume of financial transactions exceeds what finance teams can review manually. This work is handled by controllers, who typically resort to spot checks or end-of-month reconciliations, leaving enough room for errors such as incorrect prices, duplicate invoices, or mismatched deliveries.
Plinto wants to solve this problem with AI agents that sit on top of the systems companies already use, such as ERP, documents, bank, and collaboration tools like Slack or Microsoft Teams.
When a transaction is flagged, Plinto’s agents are designed not only to alert someone but also to investigate, gather evidence, and follow up with relevant people within the organisation and external contacts. Plinto says the agents are capable of contacting a supplier about a wrongful invoice, requesting a credit note or preparing a correction for approval.
It says one of its customers uncovered around 430 deviations per month in a single part of the business. At another customer, the agents identified a duplicate invoice submitted with a different supplier name in the same minute it arrived.
“Many of our customers work with low margins, so even small errors can quickly add up. The problem is that they’re often only discovered after the money has been paid. We want companies to catch and fix errors before they hit the bottom line,” said Suljevic, co-founder and CEO of Plinto.
Plinto platform integrates with major ERP platforms, including Microsoft Business Central, Xero, and Visma, and connects to major Scandinavian banks as well as over 2,700 other banks. It counts paying customers and pilots in logistics, real estate, facility services, and food production. The platform covers both order-to-cash and procure-to-pay workflows, and all data is processed and stored within the EU. Plinto also says it never uses customer data to train AI models.
The company plans to use the pre-Seed funding for product development, bringing on more enterprise customers and making Plinto’s first move outside Denmark. It wants to bring its agents to enterprises beyond its home market and aims to help them find financial errors in real time.

articles.title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground.
In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity.
Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast:
Transcript
[MUSIC]
CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity. You know, I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so I think that that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts.
[THEME MUSIC]
STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast, where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI.
[MUSIC ENDS]
WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. I’m Weishung Liu, a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research, and today I’m talking to Dr. Christopher White, who leads Microsoft Research’s Catalyst Lab.
Chris has one of those careers that sounds almost made up: a Harvard postdoc, on-the-ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan, a DARPA program manager, a dark web search pioneer, and a public-good technologist. And his work has been featured in Popular Science (opens in new tab) as well as recognized with honors, including the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons (opens in new tab).
But what I’m most interested in today is the person behind that résumé. How someone who has seen some of the worst as part of his work still comes to the office with a smile and a commitment to building tools that make the world better.
Chris, thanks for joining me.
WHITE: Thanks for having me, Wei. Nice to see you.
LIU: Yeah, good to see you, too. And so let’s get started. So I’ve known you for, I think, maybe around five or maybe six years, and now I work with you in Catalyst Lab. I love your story, and when I tell people about you, I say that you lead the newly formed Cat Lab, or Catalyst Lab, in Microsoft Research, you were a senior executive at DARPA, and you are married to an incredibly accomplished woman and scholar. And I personally think that your life story would make a very watchable Hollywood film. So when you tell your own story, though, where do you start?
WHITE: Well, you start from where you are. And where I am today is leading research at Microsoft during a period of great fear and hope about changing technology and society.
LIU: But, like, that’s now. There’s clearly lots of time from now into before, you know, the before times. So, like, tell me a little bit about the before times. Like, where were you at—I think you grew up in Oklahoma maybe. Tell me about that. Tell me about Chris White, the child.
WHITE: Well, I was nerdy. I was a nerdy Eagle Scout. [LAUGHTER] I liked to build my own computers and have local area network [LAN] parties with my friends. But I also really liked being outside. I liked being in nature and camping and rock climbing. Those were all important to me.
LIU: OK, you mentioned LAN parties. Tell me about … what did we play with our friends?
WHITE: Well, you know, we played everything. I preferred playing sports games, but I lost a lot of the other ones.
LIU: [LAUGHS] Wait, so you played like LAN party sports games, like, in basements? Like, with your … were we all in the same … ?
WHITE: Yeah. Attics. It was attics. Yeah, not basements. [LAUGHTER] Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everybody had to bring their own computer or bring their own Ethernet cable. And the more that you had your own machine that was higher powered, the better you were going to play.
LIU: So did you have the best machine?
WHITE: I had the best machine. I built the best machine. Until someone built a better machine. But it was the best for a while.
And I had a budget for it. And my family didn’t understand that the budget also included two giant speakers, like the size of a computer tower, like subwoofer speakers. They didn’t know that was part of the computer building process. But it turns out that excellent audio-visual is a critical part of a well-functioning machine.
LIU: I love it. But, OK, we’re going to focus a little bit … continue focusing on childhood. So you mentioned nerdy kid, which means—I’m going to generalize here—debate team or math competition team or chess team?
WHITE: Oh, it was the debate team. Yeah. Debate was a really wonderful activity. It taught me how to understand many sides of an issue and taught me how to think about evidence and research in that way.
LIU: So, Chris, take me back again. Like, we’re talking a little bit about Oklahoma, and, you know, at some point, you chose researcher. Like, I—for example—when I was a kid, I was convinced I would be an architect. I am not an architect as you can see. But did you always think you were going to be a researcher? Was there an epiphany there? Like … or was it always kind of like a slow hunch that you were going to pursue research as a career?
WHITE: Yeah, I kind of always felt like it. You know, as I was applying for school, those were the kinds of jobs I was interested in. You know, the kinds of things that you do, you know, once you finish degrees that have research in them. Those were the people, when I visited their work, I was inspired by. The people that were discovering, you know, that were inventing, that were innovating, that were … they’re pushing the boundaries that were kind of in that unknown, you know, space and making sense of it.
And so I’ve always had that curiosity, you know, and that approach to discovery. And so as I increased my education, it just changed the nature of what research meant and the ways in which I imagined that process evolving.
LIU: Was a doctorate always on the cards then? Or did that come, like, as you were in college and then gradually learned and thought, you know, I could keep going?
WHITE: Yeah, you know, I didn’t know about doctorates really when I went to college. I wasn’t as familiar with higher education. And so I knew that I wanted, you know, advanced degrees. And I knew that I wanted more than was being taught in the undergraduate level. But I didn’t know, you know, for example, that when you apply to PhD programs, that often you get paid to go. You know, you get admitted and you get a stipend.
You know, I was familiar with law and medicine and that you take out loans and you have to do it this way. And so for me, it was a surprise to know that I could apply to PhD programs directly from college. And from then, I just really was excited, you know, that I could explore different universities and different areas of focus and build on, you know, strong technical foundations of math and science and physics.
And it was really amazing mentors that helped me and opened doors and inspired me. You know, mentors at Oklahoma State University, Johns Hopkins, and Harvard, really people that took their time and helped me. I’m really grateful for my teachers.
LIU: So let’s talk about your first mentor of your life, and I’m going to assume … Dad?
WHITE: Yeah, Dad’s a big influence.
LIU: OK, Dad’s a big influence. And so we’re going to, I’m going to go down this path. So Catalyst Lab landed a huge commitment from our executive, kind of, leadership team on a project that has been, I think, like a decade in the making. And then … so we all, I know we all came together on a call. We’re like, “Wow, let’s debrief. Let’s talk about it.” Like, oh, energy’s up. And then at the very end of the meeting, you said, “OK, now I’m going to go clean some toilets.”
WHITE: [LAUGHS] Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
LIU: And I think all of us kind of thought, like, wha-what does that mean? So before we get kind of more into the specifics of mentorship and the, like, follow-on in your career, what— please tell me—does cleaning toilets have to do with success?
WHITE: Well, you know, like I said, Dad’s a big influence, and he taught me so many things, and he taught me about respecting people. And most importantly, he taught me about humility and service. And so his way of making sure I understood that was every time something really good happened to me, he’d remind me to go clean some toilets and, sort of, embody that. And so I did. I did it last weekend actually. I went to a community event and volunteered to do bathroom clean.
LIU: Is this like … are you … so in, like, the household chores, are you, like, the bathroom cleaner? Like, is this just always your job when we’re dividing up chores in the house?
WHITE: No, no, no. We trade off, and also we have a complicated household, and so we have a lot of help that also helps with cleaning. And so this is something that I choose to do, especially if I can do it in a community context, because it again reminds me, you know, about humility and about service and of respect for other people and other jobs.
LIU: So I think this … there’s some Eagle Scout vibes that I’m getting from here, as well, based on sort of humility and service. What is the Boy Scout badge you are most proud of?
WHITE: Oh, that’s really hard. Each badge is something that you earn, including the Eagle Scout badge. And the Eagle Scout badge for me was maybe the most difficult to earn because it requires an Eagle project. And I was really close to my Eagle project. I was, I was … had it set up and it was ready to go. And it was in this church in downtown Oklahoma City in 1995. And right as I was about to do this project, the Murrah Building blew up in a terrorist incident (opens in new tab), …
LIU: Whoa.
WHITE: … and it blew up part of the church. And, therefore, my Eagle project was not realistic, and it was not a priority, and it got shelved. And it took me several years after that to then come back to plan and execute an ambitious Eagle project right before I turned 18. And so that badge, …
LIU: Wow.
WHITE: … you know, completing the project, overcoming significant setbacks, including being a teenager and having other interests, to come through and finish it, I’m really proud of finishing it.
LIU: That’s awesome. So you … so that was, so there were a few years then in between when you ideated, had the idea for the project, and then … I appreciate the story around resilience because of when you completed the project. Like, what is the biggest takeaway that you took from there? Like what is that big lesson? You turned 18, you finished it, you celebrate. Actually, you know, maybe I’ll ask you, how did you celebrate?
WHITE: Oh, with my family. You know, the Boy Scouts is a long process. It’s many years, many kinds of roles, many kinds of learning, and to finish it—I finished it with another of my fellow scouts that had been together for a long time. And so our families, we had a ceremony, and it was something we could celebrate. And every time I think about it, I think about the things that you keep repeating when you attend the scout things, like the motto, “being prepared,” and the, kind of, laws about being respectful and courteous. And those are things that continue to be, you know, principles that influence my priorities and also inspire me and help me in my job.
LIU: Before we get to your job then, we’re going to talk about this interim period where I’ll just say you chose to go to war and a few other things in between. Let’s jump to 2010, when you joined DARPA, which is the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, within the Department of War. And then, I think, very quickly afterwards you were sent to Afghanistan to help implement a new approach to wartime analysis. And then … but before that, I think you were a Harvard postdoc, and you had actually mentioned it was a mentor who encouraged you to attend a meeting with DARPA that resulted in this course change.
And so now I’m super curious, how did this conversation happen where you were, you know, promising Harvard postdoc, which became a mentor going, “Hey, there’s something happening. You should go attend.” Like, what happened there?
WHITE: Yeah. DARPA invests taxpayer money, and they have a record of really creating innovations, massive innovations (opens in new tab). You know, the internet, GPS, stealth, UAVs. And at the time, there was different ways of building programs, and one of the kind of tested ways was to bring together different fields of expertise.
And so we were in wartime in Afghanistan. DARPA was not involved very much. And there was a question: you know, could we bring together social scientists with math people, computer science and defense experts, and together could they help us make sense of what’s happening in the data? Could that be useful to prevent violence and to protect our soldiers? And it was an experiment because it required all these different areas of expertise coming together—from sensors through analysis through social behavior—and a culture change. And so the summer was a Skunk Works to understand, was there something to contribute?
And at the end of it, they asked me, they said, “Well, you know, do you believe in your work?” And I was like, “Yeah.” You know, like, “Well, do you … can you prove it? You know, can you go see if it can help protect our soldiers and help prevent violence?” And so they asked me to be of service, and I said yeah.
And it was something that I was really unprepared for. I was supposed to go for nine days the first time, and on the third day, I got a battlefield promotion and was put in charge and then ended up staying for 90 days and then went back a few times after that even. And so, you know, our work was towards … oriented towards protecting, you know, soldiers and toward preventing violence and using AI and advanced technology to do that. And it was a, really, a big opportunity.
LIU: So you attended a meeting, you contributed some work, and then, you know, “Do you believe in your work? Prove it.” What was the time frame between, you know, like, showing up at meeting, participating in some of the research before, like, “prove it”? Was it years, or was it months?
WHITE: The … no, no, the … so the Skunk Works was a summer. It was like, you know, 40 days of, kind of, like focused effort. But at the end of it, I was expecting to go back to Harvard and continue my postdoc. But instead, you know, they sat us down; they said, “Look, you know, we think this can make a difference. You know, do you think so?” And when I said yeah, from then to getting over there was like a week. It was an extremely fast …
LIU: What?
WHITE: … turnaround. It was extremely urgent and, you know, unexpected.
LIU: OK, so, like, how … so you said, yes, like I believe in my work. They gave you … they essentially said, OK, then go next week. And how, how does somebody prepare for an experience like that? If you can even prepare.
WHITE: Yeah, I don’t know. You know, this was an experiment. You know, sending researchers—even having a presence from DARPA—in the war zone, (opens in new tab) it was new. And the idea was there could be a difference made because technology was advancing quickly. And that meant that many of the mechanisms in place for other ways of getting prepared were not available. And there was a bunch of training, like crash courses in training on what to do in certain situations, how things work, you know, how to handle yourself in different ways. But it was … it was very brief.
And so there wasn’t a lot of preparation because also we were planning to be there for nine days. But because there was an opportunity to do something good, that extended, and there was a lot of learning on the job and a lot of support in theater, a lot of people really willing to help us because we were helping them.
LIU: So, OK, so you talked about lots of people there, lots of people supporting. I’m not going to focus too much on your time in Afghanistan because that was covered really well in a Popular Science article. But I do have to ask, can you tell me the origin story of the nickname Dr. Spaghetti Man?
WHITE: [LAUGHS] Sure. Sure. You know, I’m a long-time yoga practitioner. You know, 20-plus years. It’s how I keep myself calibrated. And in Kabul, I was practicing yoga in the gym, and all these people were staring at me. You know, they were staring at me before their … they had a class; they had, like, a combatives class, a kind of different judo-mixed-martial-arts class.
And, you know, I had a little bit of training, and so after a couple of times, I decided I’d just join in. And I joined in, and I won a lot. I won a lot of the matches. And one of the matches I won, turns out, it was against the Marine who was guarding the entrance to the building I was working in across the headquarters. And he told everyone. He told everyone, you know, that this, like, lanky spaghetti guy, you know, like, got out of things and beat him, and he did it in such a way that everyone in the building knew. And so I got all this respect, and I got that cool nickname.
LIU: Did other folks challenge you as a result of this Marine telling your story?
WHITE: I mean, everyone that came to that class was game, you know. And I didn’t, you know, I couldn’t beat everybody, but I held my own, and that was really surprising to a lot of people. And again, once you establish yourself in different ways, you know, there is a lot of respect and, um, camaraderie.
LIU: So, you know, tell me, what did that whole experience teach you about, like, a life lived, and how do those lessons show up in your work today, including the, you know, Spaghetti Man experience?
WHITE: You know, the whole thing, it taught me about, you know, service and what it means to serve, and it taught me about the reality of both peace and violence in the world. And that continued to motivate me to make a difference.
LIU: After your time in Afghanistan, you continued on with DARPA as a program manager, and in that role, you developed Memex (opens in new tab), which I believe is a set of tools that could be mixed and matched to help uncover some really shady and dark parts of the web, which from what I understand was really hard to do up until that point.
I think this work also is what helped you … what you received your 2016 presidential award on. And, you know, like, can you … how do you explain the Memex project and this dark web work to someone outside tech? And what about this project inspired or appealed to you to even pursue it?
WHITE: Yeah, well, the inspiration started when I was overseas because I saw the benefit of evidence when it came to stopping bad things from happening and prosecuting them. And coming back to the US, I saw more and more opportunities where collecting evidence at large scale was a really useful mechanism. And so, you know, people think of search engines a lot, and search engines are a great tool for finding something, but when you need to connect the dots, there wasn’t a great tool that could work at the scale of the web and connect the dots, especially some of the dots being in difficult places that were not very visible.
And so by creating a technology that would connect the dots across parts of the internet (opens in new tab), it allowed the prosecution of these kinds of really awful [trafficking] crimes, and so for example, in New York City, it allowed them to increase their prosecutions by 10 times because it gave them new evidence and different kinds of evidence than they had before, and they could use that in a way to really deal with the issue differently.
LIU: OK, from what I understand, the dark web is a pretty—ha-ha—dark place, [LAUGHS] and so, like, you’ve worked in some very dark spaces and close to some very dark uses of the technology. So, like, how again, like, you and I interact a lot, and so it’s always curious to me, how has that not made you cynical and how do you stay hopeful?
WHITE: You know, I think what it’s done is it’s really increased my motivation. You know, my motivation to make a contribution. You know, my motivation to stay aware and be realistic. And by being realistic and motivated to address some of these very challenging issues, you know, around violence, around harm, and instead to focus on empowerment and to focus on justice, it gave me something to do.
And so I have seen a lot of really bad humanity, you know. I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so it’s really been inspiring to, you know, for example, come to Microsoft, where there is a mission of empowerment and there is that perspective that technology can make a difference. And so I think that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts.
LIU: I mean, that’s a very powerful message, right? Because even with the darkest parts of humanity, there is light, or, you know, you cannot have darkness without light, as well.
I think there may have been a 60 Minutes interview (opens in new tab) that included a short snippet of you talking about your work, and you had shared with me that—which, by the way, I cannot find the 60 Minutes episode, and I desperately want to. But, you know, I heard perhaps through you, Chris, that that 60 Minutes episode actually contributed to you coming to Microsoft maybe or, you know, getting a job at Microsoft, and that made me curious. Like, after some really incredible experiences, after all of that, why did you choose Microsoft?
WHITE: Oh, it was a … it was a really good choice. And at the time, I had a lot of options, and I was looking around, and this mix of the mission of the company—this mission of empowering everyone—and the scope of the company, you know, being, you know, IT for the world, you know, platforms and infrastructure for the world, and my confidence in its leader. You know, the CEO was part of my interview process. And, you know, that together gave me, you know, this perspective that I could do something here. You know, that there … I could start to envision moving from, you know, for example, very high-powered, expensive lasers to table knives. They both cut, and the world needs both of them.
LIU: One of the things that you talk a lot about is problem selection. And I think sometimes that also gets referred to as taste these days. So how do you think about problem selection in Microsoft Research, in Catalyst Lab, given the breadth of what Microsoft does?
WHITE: Oh, I think it’s just the most important part of research. You know, it’s the place where the angle of the whole thing changes, and it allows you to start to imagine a different future, you know, or to work backward from that future that you want to see and see what you can do to contribute to it now. And the amazing thing about Microsoft Research is there’s tremendous freedom, and so there’s tremendous creativity in problem selection.
And it’s the kind of thing where you have that latitude to go from idea to evidence to this potential for growth and thriving and along the way get feedback about value and usability and benefit or policy or adaptability, integration. And so its scope provides so many vehicles for growth and utility of advanced research ideas.
And its mission, you know, allows the focus of those to address absolutely critical problems. You know, problems of, you know, impending security challenges due to AI, problems of advanced, you know, memory and storage; it allows for, you know, personalization automation, just, you know, for example. And I think that this mix of freedom combined with responsibility and mechanisms, you know, to prove out and demonstrate value, that that combination is just really remarkable and it really motivates me to take the opportunity seriously.
LIU: So it’s almost going to be like asking you about your favorite kids now. What are some, what are some accomplishments in Microsoft Research or Catalyst Lab that you are particularly proud of?
WHITE: Oh, you know, I think that, you know, right now, for example—again, focusing on kind of where we are—I think that we have a real opportunity to contribute something in the cyber defense space. I think our work on security and AI and hacking, it’s really in, you know, based on such a deep expertise and also based on, you know, people with a lot of experience, and I think it’s growing in need, you know, the need to protect our digital infrastructure, the need to deter and interdict people that would like to break systems or cause harm, that’s really growing right now. And so being able to show up in a way that creates breakthrough that can scale with relevance to address that growing need, it’s really something that’s, you know, awesome to me.
And also I think that again kind of extending from the, sort of, Memex conversation, where we’re trying to connect the dots, you know, these days, trying to analyze lots of content as part of being more efficient, as part of being more creative, as part of being more capable, you know, using tools to augment that human taste and creativity and ingenuity, that’s really never been as powerful as it is before and continues to grow. And so I think making contributions in these areas, you know, where we have state-of-the-art technology and we’re creating changes in the way systems are getting built and used, to me, it shows that, you know, despite the fast pace of change and despite the extreme competitiveness in the technology sector, that specialized expertise with good problem selection and an environment to grow and get feedback can create the kind of breakthroughs that matter. And so I really like that.
Maybe to give one more example from the past––just maybe something emblematic of the group and some of my predecessors––was this underwater datacenter called Project Natick (opens in new tab), [LAUGHTER] where this experiment, you know, put a datacenter in a submersible on the bottom of the ocean connected to a wind farm, and it tested this design about, could you build something that didn’t require human intervention? Could it be more efficient with power? Could it be more efficient with heat?
And the program manager that created that is one of the best I’ve ever worked with. And it just performed incredibly well as this huge surprise, and it led to us being, you know, named the most innovative company [World Changing Company of the Year] in 2021 (opens in new tab) and other awards (opens in new tab). And it’s just an example of really out-there thinking, imagining a world that had challenges with water access and power access and land but where we need, you know, computation and data storage and technical capability available.
So a little bit out there, but I really … I feel like we have to be imagining these different futures. We have to be radical in that way so that we can start to work back and make contributions now.
LIU: I love the Natick example because I feel like Natick is the gift that keeps on giving. And, you know, if I can digress for a minute, I remember that I think one of the first TikTok videos that the Microsoft account posted was of Natick (opens in new tab)[1], but it was using, like, a meme at the time which had, like, human eyes and a mouth being lowered into, uh, and it was of Natick being lowered into the ocean, including like a Clippy, like a real-life Clippy swimming across the … it was … I still love that video for reasons why I don’t understand. [LAUGHTER] But if you haven’t seen it, highly recommend. Maybe we can link it [LAUGHS] if the video still exists.
WHITE: Definitely. Look, look, one of the highlights was the fish cam.
LIU: Yes!
WHITE: You know, people were concerned that it might disrupt the marine ecosystem. And we did a lot of preparation and study for that. And just to be sure, we put cameras and watched it happen.
LIU: Yep.
WHITE: And all these fish kept coming around and making it home. And there was, like, computer vision that was analyzing which fishes and their movement, and it became like an always-on thing that people would just tune in to online to watch the fish.
LIU: There was a seal. There was a seal. There were a couple seals that came by, …
WHITE: Yeah.
LIU: … too, which, yeah, I remember that. That’s really cool. Thanks for sharing.
WHITE: Yeah, so you have to go not just out of the box but out of the datacenter.
LIU: [LAUGHS] Oh no. All right. All right.
So, Chris, before letting you go, it would be a missed opportunity if I did not ask you to share some practical advice and reflections given the breadth of your experience and lessons that you learned. So I’m going to do … maybe it doesn’t have to be a super-fast lightning round, but it’s going to be a lightning round of a couple of questions.
WHITE: Sure.
LIU: All right. One, what is the advice that you have received in your life that blew your mind or changed your perspective?
WHITE: You’ve got to look out for the right place and the right time with the right people because it takes all those things to come together for magic to happen and to make a difference.
LIU: OK, I’m going to have to ask. This is not … I’m breaking my own lightning round. How do you know? Like, how do you know if it’s the right place or the right time or the right people?
WHITE: The universe gives a lot of feedback. You know, it’s something that with good listening, you can hear.
LIU: What did … what did the universe tell you?
WHITE: Told me to marry my wife.
LIU: [LAUGHS] Ohhhh. Good choice. Good universe. Good universe. OK, next.
WHITE: Yeah. Told me to have my kids. Absolutely.
LIU: All right, next. Lesson you learned the hard way or the misstep that humbled you?
WHITE: I’ve got to slow down. My tendency is to push too fast and too hard, and that can really lead to problems. And slowing down, it doesn’t in the end slow everything down. It just actually makes it just right and just enough.
LIU: What’s an example of slow down?
WHITE: Well, you know, I think there’s slowing down in making decisions, especially about people, compared to other kinds of decisions. Or even in my yoga practice. Slowing down the way that I use my body so that it can be healthy and strong for a long time.
LIU: I do believe that one of your … the advice that you often give us in Cat Lab is take a vacation.
WHITE: Absolutely.
LIU: So slow down definitely fits that.
WHITE: Get some perspective.
LIU: So next question: talent or accomplishment you’re most proud of if given the chance to brag. And you have stated humility many times, and I’m going to ask you to just turn that bit off for a little bit and brag a little bit instead.
WHITE: Mm-hmm. Well, I think it would be putting my leg behind my head and saying [LAUGHTER] the alphabet backwards while playing a percussion instrument.
LIU: Hold on. Like, this is for realsies, and this is, like, this is not an AI-generated statement …
WHITE: No.
LIU: … or prompt? This is … And you’ve done this before?
WHITE: I have. I’ve done it in a leadership offsite.
LIU: [LAUGHS] You did not.
WHITE: I did.
LIU: I am going to need to ask some of our colleagues about that particular experience, but there was a percussion instrument?
WHITE: Yeah. There was. But, you know, all kidding aside, you know, the 2016 presidential medal, you know, being able to make such a difference in a way for so many people that were affected and to also change the way technology was used from the data collection evidence, you know, through judicial proceedings, that process and arc, you know, is definitely something I’m extremely proud of, was extremely difficult, and I would definitely go for it again.
LIU: I love it. OK, I love asking this one. You know I’ve asked people this a lot. Career path you would have chosen if you did not become a researcher—and you’re not allowed to say yoga teacher.
WHITE: [LAUGHS] No, I would just be a different kind of researcher.
LIU: No!
WHITE: Yeah, definitely. Yeah.
LIU: Really? OK, so if not an AI or computer science researcher, what else would we be researching?
WHITE: Oh, the brain. You know, the …
LIU: OK, how about a non-STEM research topic? [LAUGHS]
WHITE: Anthropology.
LIU: OK, OK, fine. So, like, no, there’s no scenario where research is not in the picture.
WHITE: No, it just seems to be part of me, you know, part of my drive, you know, part of what gives me energy, keeps me motivated and curious. And this, you know, frontier, it allows that evolution to keep unfolding.
LIU: OK. All right. Good to know. So not yoga teacher. Always some form of research.
WHITE: Well, I mean, yoga teacher is a kind of researcher into the universe.
LIU: What?! [LAUGHS]
WHITE: You know, it’s a researcher into the states of consciousness and being. Into the alignment between the mind and the body. It’s full of research. Full of personal research.
LIU: This is why I believe when once upon a time at a leadership offsite you were asked to prompt AI to demonstrate, to build, like, a mascot for you, and I think that mascot was also doing yoga.
WHITE: It was. I asked my … I asked one of my copilots to generate a picture of me based on everything it knows, and it created a cat doing yoga.
LIU: [LAUGHS] I love it. OK, so lastly, and this is less “lightning round” and more like “take your time.” What would you like listeners of this podcast to take away from this conversation? You know, about you, about professional life, about research, about making … or maybe even just making choices.
WHITE: You know, I think it’s about the power of adaptability and the diversity of experience. You know, it’s about being open to what wants to happen, what needs to happen. You know, being open, called to serve, willingness to change.
LIU: I like that.
So thank you, Chris—Dr. White—for joining me, and to our audience, thank you for listening.
WHITE: Thanks, Wei.
[MUSIC]
STANDARD OUTRO: You’ve been listening to the Microsoft Research Podcast. Check out more episodes of the podcast at aka.ms/researchpodcast (opens in new tab) or on YouTube and major podcast platforms.
[MUSIC ENDS]
[1] The Project Natick video (opens in new tab) was one of the Microsoft account’s early TikTok videos, posted on May 12, 2022, about four months after the account’s launch.

articles.title: Votre smartphone connecté à un satellite sans passer par Starlink ? Orange et trois géants européens préparent la riposte
articles.text:
Ce n’était encore qu’une rumeur en septembre, comme nous l’expliquions alors. C’est désormais officiel. Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica et Vodafone ont annoncé ce lundi 19 octobre avoir signé une lettre d’intention pour étudier « une éventuelle candidature conjointe » à l’attribution, en Europe, des fréquences réservées aux services mobiles par satellite. Ce sont elles qui permettent à un smartphone classique de se connecter directement à un satellite, sans antenne particulière, là où le réseau terrestre ne passe pas.
Les quatre opérateurs ne construiront pas leurs propres satellites. Ils prévoient de déployer en Europe les infrastructures au sol ainsi que les fonctions de coordination et de supervision du réseau, la constellation étant fournie par « un partenaire satellitaire qui reste à sélectionner ». Ils promettent aussi un accès « ouvert et non discriminatoire » à tous les opérateurs mobiles. Bouygues Telecom, Free ou SFR pourraient donc, en théorie, en profiter eux aussi.
Des fréquences convoitées par SpaceX
Tout se joue sur la bande des 2 GHz, dont les licences actuelles, détenues par Viasat et EchoStar, expirent en mai 2027. Or SpaceX a racheté en 2025 une partie du spectre d’EchoStar, et les licences européennes de ce dernier doivent lui être transférées en 2027, selon le site spécialisé Light Reading. Pour garder la main sur ces fréquences, la Commission européenne a proposé en mai, la Commission européenne a proposé en mai de découper la bande en trois parts égales : une pour les communications gouvernementales, intégrée à la constellation IRIS², une réservée aux nouveaux entrants européens et une ouverte à tous, Starlink compris. C’est la part européenne que vise le quatuor. Le texte doit encore être adopté, et l’attribution des nouveaux droits n’est pas attendue avant 2029.
L’alliance n’est pas dénuée de paradoxes. La lettre d’intention des quatre opérateurs « ne remplace pas les partenariats satellitaires existants », et ils sont nombreux. Deutsche Telekom a signé avec Starlink pour un lancement en 2028, Vodafone partage une coentreprise avec l’américain AST SpaceMobile, et Orange, qui vend déjà son option Message Satellite, travaille aussi avec AST. Seulement, aucun d’eux n’a seul la puissance de feu de SpaceX, qui vient encore de racheter pour près de 8 milliards de dollars de fréquences aux États-Unis. En s’alliant, les opérateurs évitent surtout que Starlink ne vende un jour ses propres forfaits mobiles en se passant d’eux.
Washington brandit la menace
Le projet européen irrite déjà les États-Unis. L’ambassadeur américain auprès de l’Union européenne, Andrew Puzder, a averti dans le Financial Times que les entreprises européennes présentes aux États-Unis pourraient subir des représailles « dévastatrices » si Bruxelles restreignait l’accès de Starlink à ces fréquences. La Commission assure de son côté que son projet reste ouvert aux acteurs non européens.
Pour les abonnés, l’enjeu concerne surtout les zones blanches, la montagne, la mer et les situations où les antennes terrestres tombent en panne. Il faudra toutefois s’armer de patience : trouver un partenaire satellitaire, de préférence européen, ne sera pas simple, alors qu’IRIS² n’est pas attendu avant 2030.

articles.title: “Un moment majeur de l’histoire scientifique” : un ancien d’OpenAI pense avoir ouvert la “boîte noire” de l’IA
articles.text:
“Un moment majeur de l’histoire scientifique” : un ancien d’OpenAI pense avoir ouvert la “boîte noire” de l’IA
Un neurone qui s'allumait devant une tête de chat comme devant une calandre de voiture a longtemps servi de preuve que l'IA serait indéchiffrable. L'un des chercheurs qui avaient forgé cette lecture la démolit aujourd'hui dans un essai fleuve, chiffres à l'appui, et la communauté se divise déjà.
Depuis des années, la recherche répète que les grands modèles d'IA échappent à leurs propres concepteurs. Le 15 octobre, Nick Cammarata, chercheur chez Goodfire, laboratoire spécialisé dans l'interprétabilité, a publié Neural Networks Are Already Clean, un essai d'une heure de lecture qui prend ce dogme à rebours. Coauteur en 2020 de Zoom In avec Chris Olah, il a contribué à installer la théorie qu'il conteste désormais. En 2023, le projet d'interprétabilité automatisée qu'il avait lancé chez OpenAI ne jugeait lisibles qu'environ 1,7 % des neurones.
	
Je crois avoir une bonne nouvelle sur la nature des réseaux de neurones.
Le fameux neurone "chat-voiture" détectait en réalité des formes en V
Tout part d'un cas d'école. Dans InceptionV1, modèle de vision conçu par Google en 2014, un neurone réagissait aux têtes de chat comme aux faces avant d'automobiles. L'explication admise, la superposition, voulait qu'un réseau à court de neurones entasse des notions sans rapport. Cammarata y voit un détecteur de formes pointues : museaux de renard, flammes, jets d'eau. Les formes rondes, comme la lettre O, l'inhibent.
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came…
— Nick (@nickcammarata) October 15, 2026
Le reste du désordre apparent relèverait d'une "généralisation récursive" : un neurone bourgeonne comme une branche. L'un d'eux réagissait à "iy", puis à "diy", et enfin à "do it yourself". Passé au crible par des agents IA, le modèle ouvert Qwen3-32B d'Alibaba compterait environ 90 % de pôles de neurones voués à une tâche principale. Seuls 2 à 4 % résistent encore à l'analyse.
Interprétabilité de l'IA : la sécurité en ligne de mire, des experts divisés
Des circuits lisibles permettraient de traquer la tromperie ou les dérives d'un modèle à la source. Roon, salarié d'OpenAI très suivi sur X, parle d'un travail qui "pourrait rester comme un moment majeur de l'histoire scientifique".
when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a 'normal science' https://t.co/7k4jzO2XIR
— roon (@tszzl) October 15, 2026
Neel Nanda, qui dirige l'interprétabilité mécaniste chez Google DeepMind, tempère l'enthousiasme. Selon lui, les modèles de langage stockent bien plus de faits qu'ils ne comptent de neurones, et des résultats tirés de petits modèles de vision ne valent pas forcément pour eux.
	
C'est un travail intéressant, mais je ne pense pas qu'il modifie significativement le tableau d'ensemble de l'interprétabilité. Je pense toujours que la superposition est réelle.
This is interesting work, but I don't think it's a significant update to the big picture of interpretability.
I'm on board with the broad idea of doing exploratory interpretability with neurons, e.g. neuron-based attribution graphs, for pragmatic problems like why did a model do… https://t.co/r9IpQuF1FY
— Neel Nanda (@NeelNanda5) October 15, 2026
L'essai se présente lui-même comme une "hypothèse de travail". L'article technique censé l'étayer n'a pas encore paru, et aucune équipe extérieure n'a, pour l'heure, reproduit ses résultats. Goodfire, qui commercialise des outils d'interprétabilité, a tout intérêt à voir cette thèse l'emporter.

articles.title: NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
articles.text:
At OCP 2026, we saw the new NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for Context Memory (CMX). Partners had been asking for this, and NVIDIA delivered. Onboard, we have a lower-cost design than the dual-Vera setup we saw previously. Let us take a look at the new board.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 STX Server for CMX at OCP 2026
For context, this is the previously shown BlueField-4 DPU. That one, pictured below, is a dual Vera CPU setup, each with SOCAMM memory, plus four ConnectX-9 SuperNICs. NVIDIA calls this a DPU, but it is clearly more costly than a BlueField-1 or BlueField-3, which are much smaller and lower-power devices. For partners looking at building storage platforms, the below is more akin to a dual CPU server than a traditional DPU.
At OCP 2026, multiple partners showed off the BlueField-4 STX server for context memory (CMX). Here is the much smaller card, which still uses high-density connectors for PCIe and system connectivity.
NVIDIA BlueField-4 DPUs encompass both NVIDIA Grace and Vera CPU cores, but this one looks like a Vera package. That is a very substantial CPU. To be clear, this is not like the embedded-class CPUs that we typically have seen in DPUs previously. This is more like having a high-end single-socket server platform.
Another interesting feature is that the boards at OCP 2026 are using SOCAMM memory, so these should be relatively easy to put either a heatsink or a liquid cooling block on top of it.
Onboard, there is an M.2 slot. Usually these are for OS drives, but if you saw our recent Inside the Secretive AWS Networking Lab, the M.2 SSDs there are being used for log devices.
This may seem like a small feature, but it means NVIDIA designed this less like a traditional motherboard replacement and more like something that is easy to assemble automatically.
Something that may not immediately hit you if you are looking at photos is just the size of this board. A soldered CPU and LPDDR5X here, over traditional DDR5 DIMM slots, give NVIDIA a platform where the “motherboard” is roughly the size of an Intel DMR 16-channel socket or a 16-channel AMD EPYC Venice platform.
Final Words
This is just a neat platform. It almost feels like NVIDIA needs some brand between the Vera server line and the traditional BlueField DPU line. Something notable that we did not see on the boards shown at OCP 2026, or at least in our photos of them from various booths, is an NVIDIA ConnectX-9 SuperNIC. We expected that, but did not see it on this board. For context memory platforms, a single Vera versus a dual Vera makes this a lower-cost platform, and that will likely help the STX/ CMX systems come to market as the price of NAND has been rising meaningfully over the past year.

articles.title: Au Japon, l’eSIM Ubigi aide à éviter les frais d’itinérance
articles.text:
Partir au Japon coûte cher et les frais de téléphonie peuvent empirer les choses. Une facture salée attend de nombreux voyageurs à leur retour. Il existe heureusement une solution pour éviter ça : l’eSIM.
Le pays du soleil levant est bien loin de l’Europe et la connexion n’est pas donnée. En quittant le mode avion à l’aéroport, les données mobiles s’activent et le compteur se met à tourner sans que vous le sachiez. L’eSIM Ubigi vous aidera à sauver votre budget.
Rester connecté au Japon peut coûter plus cher que prévu
Impossible de se passer de smartphone au Japon, mais encore faut-il ne pas tomber dans certains pièges.
Les usages qui font flamber la facture dès votre arrivée
À peine arrivé à Tokyo, votre téléphone est déjà sollicité : il faut présenter votre QR Code Visit Japan Web aux contrôles, lancer Google Maps pour vous guider, ouvrir votre application de traduction pour déchiffrer les menus, mais aussi installer la carte Suica pour prendre les transports ou réserver vos billets de Shinkansen… Sur le chemin, vous souhaiterez probablement aussi partager des photos avec vos proches ou envoyer des messages via la messagerie Line. Le problème ? Ces usages vont rapidement engendrer des frais d’itinérance considérables.
SIM locale, Wi-Fi public, itinérance : des solutions qui aggravent les choses
Le Japon est hors de la zone d’itinérance UE et votre forfait va en pâtir. En misant sur votre opérateur habituel, vous aurez, au mieux, accès à une enveloppe plafonnée ou devrez, au pire, payer une option journalière au prix fort. En cas de hors-forfait, vous ne découvrirez le montant qu’en rentrant chez vous.
En optant pour une SIM locale, les choses ne seront pas plus simples : les lignes voix sont réservées aux résidents et vous devrez vous contenter d’un routeur Wi-Fi de poche, à récupérer à l’aéroport, ou d’une SIM data limitée. En misant sur le Wi-Fi public, votre porte-monnaie sera sauf, mais pas vos données : ces réseaux n’offrent, en effet, aucune garantie de sécurité.
L’eSIM, une solution incontournable pour maîtriser votre budget communication au Japon
Véritable alliée des voyageurs, l’eSIM Ubigi est indispensable au Japon.
Une carte virtuelle aux multiples avantages
Créée en 2016, l’eSIM est intégrée aux appareils compatibles et désimlockés : iPhone, iPad, smartphones Android, mais aussi PC Windows 10 et 11. Ce dispositif virtuel vous permet de garder votre numéro habituel sur votre SIM physique et de communiquer via une application de messagerie de type WhatsApp. Vous direz, de plus, adieu aux frais d’itinérance tout en faisant du bien à la planète : l’eSIM évite, en effet, la surproduction de plastique.
L’eSIM Ubigi, un dispositif primé parfait pour visiter Tokyo et bien plus encore
Pionnier de l’eSIM, Ubigi est présent dans plus de 200 destinations dont le Japon. Cet opérateur lancé en 2017 par Transatel, filiale du groupe NTT, s’appuie sur les réseaux NTT Docomo, KDDI, et maintenant aussi Softbank pour la couverture la plus étendue possible en 4G et 5G.
Élue « eSIM la plus rapide 2025 » par Travel eSIM Expert et « Meilleure connexion 2025 » par Alertify, cette eSIM vous permettra de voyager en toute tranquillité : votre connexion est chiffrée, le partage de connexion est autorisé et vous pourrez communiquer sans craindre la facture à votre retour grâce à ses formules bloquées.
Visitez le Japon sans laisser de côté votre smartphone
Proposée à des tarifs compétitifs, l’eSIM Ubigi est simple à installer et à recharger.

articles.title: El Pentágono deja de utilizar las herramientas de IA de Anthropic tras incluir a la empresa en una lista negra, según pudo saber la BBC
articles.text:
El Departamento de Defensa de Estados Unidos ya no utiliza la herramienta de inteligencia artificial Claude, según declaró el pasado 5 de octubre un funcionario del Pentágono, que indicó que el departamento “ha dejado de utilizar los productos de Anthropic”.
El secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth, había fijado como límite finales de agosto, y nadie ha explicado por qué se tardó más de un mes en completar la retirada.
Hasta finales de septiembre, Claude se utilizaba para investigación, análisis y recopilación de inteligencia, así como para operaciones militares contra Irán, según exfuncionarios del Departamento de Defensa y contratistas que han trabajado con el Pentágono en proyectos de inteligencia artificial, la mayoría de ellos bajo anonimato porque no estaban autorizados a hablar con la prensa. Para estas fuentes, Claude era una herramienta fundamental para procesar grandes cantidades de información, y Anthropic no ha querido hacer declaraciones al respecto.
Las relaciones comerciales comenzaron en 2024, cuando en noviembre Anthropic, Palantir y Amazon Web Services anunciaron una alianza para llevar Claude a agencias de inteligencia y defensa en un entorno certificado para información clasificada, denominado nivel IL6. Palantir presumió entonces de ser el primer socio que llevaba los modelos de Claude a entornos clasificados. A principios de 2026, el Pentágono pidió que Anthropic eliminara las salvaguardas de Claude y diera a las fuerzas armadas acceso sin restricciones.
Sin embargo, la empresa se negó en dos puntos concretos y, en su comunicado del 27 de febrero, pidió excepciones tanto para la vigilancia masiva de ciudadanos estadounidenses como para las armas totalmente autónomas. Ese mismo día, Pete Hegseth anunció que la empresa sería designada “riesgo para la cadena de suministro” de la seguridad nacional (una etiqueta que suele reservarse para proveedores de países considerados hostiles), y Donald Trump ordenó a las agencias federales que dejaran de utilizar sus productos.
El plazo de seis meses empezó un día antes de que Estados Unidos e Israel atacaran Irán, y Anthropic, que ya había calificado la medida de “sin precedentes”, demandó al Gobierno el 9 de marzo.
El papel que desempeñaba Claude en Maven
Claude formaba parte de Maven Smart System, la plataforma que opera Palantir (fundada por Peter Thiel, multimillonario aliado de Trump) y que el Pentágono emplea como sistema principal para organizar inteligencia y otros datos.
Se dice que los analistas reunían en Maven imágenes de satélite y grabaciones de drones y luego las pasaban a Claude (y también por otros grandes modelos de lenguaje) para tareas como identificar posibles objetivos militares. Una persona a la que Palantir hizo una demostración a principios de año llegó a contar que se utilizaba con frecuencia para elaborar informes de una página que ascendían por la cadena de mando.
Algunos de los aliados de Estados Unidos también utilizan Maven para compartir inteligencia con Washington. Además, el papel del modelo tiene matices: un análisis sobre Claude en el CENTCOM (el Mando Central, que dirige las operaciones en Oriente Medio), publicado el 30 de marzo, lo describe más como una pieza que coordinaba los módulos y modelos del sistema que como el componente que propone objetivos.
Dicho análisis también enumera que la política del Departamento de Defensa exige que sean personas quienes seleccionen los objetivos, y que el 9 de marzo el subsecretario de Defensa Steve Feinberg ordenó que Maven pasara a la oficina central de datos e IA del Pentágono.
Esa integración explica exactamente la razón de no retirarse de inmediato. “El hecho de que el Pentágono haya tardado hasta ahora en eliminar todo uso de Claude en el sistema indica que estas cosas no son simplemente de ‘conectar y usar’”, afirmó Lauren Kahn, analista del Centro de Seguridad y Tecnología Emergente de la Universidad de Georgetown y antigua funcionaria de Defensa. Y añadió: “Una vez que se integran, puede ser complicado eliminarlas”.
Los empleados del Pentágono siguieron utilizando Claude, incluidos los modelos Mythos, “durante todo el período de la controversia”, según una de las fuentes. Y, cuando llegó la orden, “existía preocupación por pasar de Anthropic a OpenAI” y a otras herramientas, recuerda un exfuncionario de alto rango.
El detalle de Mythos tiene interés porque no era un modelo accesible para cualquiera. Anthropic presentó Claude Mythos Preview el 7 de abril dentro del proyecto Glasswing, reservado a un grupo cerrado de socios (Microsoft, Apple, Google, Cisco o CrowdStrike, entre otros) y a más de 40 organizaciones que mantienen software crítico, debido a la capacidad del modelo para encontrar y explotar vulnerabilidades. La propia empresa avisó de que no pensaba abrir esa versión al público general.
La relación con la Casa Blanca parece ser distinta, ya que entre finales de septiembre y principios de octubre el presidente Trump se reunió dos veces con Dario Amodei, consejero delegado de Anthropic. Amodei declaró a la prensa que le seguían preocupando los riesgos de la inteligencia artificial: “Aún se está discutiendo cómo abordar esos riesgos”. Sin embargo, “si trabajamos con el presidente, podemos ganar de manera segura”, añadió, y el propio Trump lo describió como “genial” y “fantástico”.
OpenAI estableció límites muy parecidos
El Pentágono ha cerrado contratos también con Google, xAI y OpenAI, y dos personas que conocen el uso de la inteligencia artificial en el Departamento de Defensa afirman que las herramientas de OpenAI se han extendido a algunos departamentos durante los últimos meses.
Esa misma noche del 27 de febrero, Sam Altman anunció el acuerdo con el Pentágono y aseguró que el Departamento aceptaba dos principios de la empresa: la prohibición de la vigilancia masiva doméstica y la responsabilidad humana en el uso de la fuerza, armas autónomas incluidas.
Sobre el papel, estos límites son muy parecidos a los que llevaron a Anthropic a la lista negra. Sin embargo, Altman afirmó que la diferencia estaba en que ya figuraban en la ley y la política del Departamento de Defensa, y en que OpenAI los había incorporado al acuerdo con salvaguardas técnicas. El propio Altman reconoció que la vigilancia masiva doméstica ya es ilegal.
Dos tribunales, dos respuestas
Las dos designaciones se basan en normas diferentes. La primera se apoya en el artículo 3252 del título 10 del código federal estadounidense, y la jueza federal Rita Lin, en California, la declaró ilegal el 27 de agosto: la consideró una represalia que vulneraba la libertad de expresión, una decisión arbitraria y sin el debido proceso, y escribió que invocar la seguridad nacional no es “un cheque en blanco” para castigar a los críticos del Gobierno. Ese fallo sigue vigente.
Un mes después, el 25 de septiembre, el Tribunal de Apelaciones del Distrito de Columbia avaló la otra designación por dos votos a uno, la que se apoya en la ley de seguridad de la cadena de suministro en las compras federales (FASCSA). La mayoría consideró que las restricciones de Claude y el hecho de que el contrato siguiera sin cerrarse podían hacerlo poco fiable para operaciones militares, mientras que la jueza Karen LeCraft Henderson votó en contra. Anthropic ha recordado que otro tribunal ya había anulado la designación paralela y está estudiando pedir una nueva revisión.
¿Y si usas Claude?
Si alguien utiliza Claude en casa o en su oficina, nada cambia: Anthropic dejó clara su postura el 27 de febrero y explicó que el acceso de particulares y empresas no se ve afectado por el conflicto.
Para las empresas que trabajan con el Pentágono, en cambio, la situación es más confusa. Según un análisis del fallo de septiembre, el Departamento ha pedido a algunos contratistas que retiren los productos de Anthropic de ciertos sistemas y entregables, e incluso ha sugerido vetarlos en sistemas que no forman parte del contrato, lo cual podría ir más allá de lo que permite la FASCSA. Tampoco ha publicado aún la orden formal de exclusión en el registro federal de contratación (SAM).
Dado que la designación de la FASCSA continúa en vigor, Claude sigue fuera de Maven y Anthropic no ha concretado qué revisión pedirá.

articles.title: 970,000 Medi-Cal Members Affected by Paradigm Healthcare Data Breach
articles.text:
Paradigm Healthcare Services has told the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) that a data breach discovered last year affected more than 970,000 people.
San Francisco-based Paradigm processes billing for Medi-Cal, California’s Medicaid program, under a data use agreement with the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS). It also maintains Medi-Cal member identification numbers on the department’s behalf.
The company says it became aware of unauthorized access to its local network on October 13, 2025. “On August 18, 2026, we determined that certain files containing select individuals’ protected health information may have been accessed by an unauthorized party between October 8, 2025, and October 15, 2025,” Paradigm said.
The compromised files contained names, dates of birth, gender, and Medi-Cal member identification numbers. Paradigm says its online service documentation and billing platform, Student Health Network (SHN), was not impacted.
Paradigm’s notification letters are dated September 14, 2026, roughly 11 months after the intrusion was detected. “We have no evidence that any of your information has been used to commit fraud or identity theft as a result of this incident,” the company said.
The notice doesn’t name the threat actor, explain how the attackers gained access, or say whether data was exfiltrated. Paradigm says it took certain systems offline, notified law enforcement, and brought in outside incident response experts.
No known cybercrime group appears to have taken credit for an attack on Paradigm.
Tarter Krinsky & Drogin and Ridgeway Pharmacy data breaches
The HHS healthcare data breach tracker has been updated to show that a significant number of individuals were affected by separate incidents disclosed recently by the law firm Tarter Krinsky & Drogin (TKD) and Ridgeway Pharmacy Ltd.
TKD, which serves healthcare providers, started notifying individuals in early September that it had detected suspicious activity on its network in September 2025.
The company completed its investigation one year later and determined that attackers accessed certain servers between July 9 and September 9, 2025.
TKD told the HHS that the incident affected more than 196,000 individuals.
Ridgeway Pharmacy, which started sending out data breach notices on September 21, discovered unauthorized access to personal information on August 21, 2026.
The company discovered that its website was hacked and the attacker may have gained access to information such as name, address, date of birth, health and insurance information, prescription information, and payment card information.
Ridgeway Pharmacy informed the HHS that more than 258,000 individuals are affected.

articles.title: AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
articles.text:
AI can act exactly like a human, but we still don't think it's conscious
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München
- Summary:
- A new study reveals that people draw a surprisingly sharp line between human consciousness and artificial intelligence, even when both behave identically. Researchers found that participants considered even the most responsive AI less conscious than the least responsive human. Yet when asked about "awareness" instead, people judged humans and AI much more similarly.
- Share:
Even when artificial intelligence behaves exactly like a human, people are reluctant to consider it conscious, according to a new study from Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU).
As artificial intelligence becomes more advanced, reports of AI systems misleading users, working together, or appearing to pursue independent goals are becoming increasingly common. These behaviors often lead people to describe AI as though it can think, feel, or make decisions for itself. But does behaving like a human actually convince people that a machine has consciousness?
New research from LMU suggests that people make a clear distinction between displaying intelligent behavior and possessing a conscious mind, even when humans and AI act in precisely the same way.
How Scientists Tested Perceptions of AI Consciousness
Published in the journal Cognition, the study was led by Dr. Louis Longin of LMU's Chair of Philosophy of Mind, working alongside Dr. Bahador Bahrami, Professor Ophelia Deroy, and other researchers.
"Whereas previous studies have typically asked general questions about whether AI actually has mental states, our study is the first to directly compare how people attribute the same mental states to AI and humans behaving in exactly the same way, under identical circumstances," says Longin.
"We may be using mental terms to refer to AI, but this may only be because we lack better words," says Ophelia Deroy, philosopher and a senior author of the study. "After all, AI is trained to act and speak like a human, so these descriptions seem natural."
To investigate how people judge consciousness, the researchers conducted experiments involving nearly 1,100 participants. One group read brief descriptions of artificial agents that showed different levels of responsiveness to their environments. For example, some agents reacted to sounds or recognized the emotional states of others.
Another group encountered the same situations, except the characters were described as humans rather than AI systems. Participants then evaluated how conscious or aware each character seemed to be of its surroundings.
A Surprising Gap Between Human and AI Consciousness
The experiments revealed that responsiveness influenced how participants judged both humans and artificial intelligence. Characters that reacted more actively to their surroundings were generally considered more conscious and more aware.
However, a striking difference emerged when participants evaluated consciousness specifically. Even the most responsive AI was rated as less conscious than the least responsive human. In other words, identical behavior did not lead people to assign the same level of consciousness to humans and machines.
The results changed considerably when participants were asked about awareness instead. For this characteristic, judgments of humans and AI followed largely similar patterns, suggesting that people interpret awareness and consciousness in fundamentally different ways.
"There is a growing worry in public discussion that people will see AI behaving in a human-like way and start treating these systems as if they had human-like mental states," says Longin, lead author of the study. "We found something much more nuanced: People are quite willing to say that an AI notices things and is aware of its surroundings. But they clearly draw a line when it comes to the term 'consciousness'. People consistently attribute less consciousness to AI than humans -- even when their behavior is identical."
Although people sometimes describe AI as conscious when discussing its actions, the findings indicate that they still distinguish between artificial systems and human minds.
Why One Word Changes How We Perceive AI
The researchers believe the difference between consciousness and awareness offers an important insight into how people understand artificial intelligence.
Awareness is a relatively neutral term that can describe an agent's ability to detect and respond to information in its environment. Consciousness, however, carries deeper implications about subjective experience and what it means to have an inner mental life.
Because awareness focuses more directly on observable behavior, people appear comfortable applying it to both humans and AI. Consciousness carries a different meaning, leading people to judge the two much less similarly.
The findings also highlight why the language used to discuss artificial intelligence matters, particularly as AI systems become increasingly capable of producing convincing human behavior.
"Our study teaches us lessons for how we communicate about AI," says Bahador Bahrami, who is also a senior author of the study and an expert in social neuroscience. "Companies and journalists often reach for hyped descriptions of AI models, and credit them with intentions, plans, or even moral conscience and hesitation. What our study shows is that everyday judgments are much more discriminating: People do not simply put AI and humans on the same mental scale. But the boundary also depends on which terms we use. For more neutral descriptors such as 'awareness', the distinction can largely disappear. That makes our choice of language important."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Louis Longin, Jurgis Karpus, Nadine Meertens, Bahador Bahrami, Ophelia Deroy. AI is not as conscious as humans: Essentialism in mental state attributions to artificial systems. Cognition, 2027; 278: 106733 DOI: 10.1016/j.cognition.2026.106733
