articles.title: Reaction Dynamics plans rapid expansion to launch new medium-lift rocket by 2031
articles.text:
Reaction Dynamics is looking to raise hundreds of millions in funding and add nearly 300 employees over the next five years to send a new, more powerful rocket toward the stars.
At the SpaceBound Conference in Ottawa on Tuesday morning, the Longueuil, Que.-based rocket maker revealed its plans to develop and send a new medium-lift rocket to space by 2031. Dubbed Borealis, the medium-lift rocket is the larger sibling of Reaction Dynamics’ light-lift Aurora rocket. While Aurora is meant for payloads below half a tonne, Borealis is designed to haul a six-tonne payload to low Earth orbit for larger spacecraft deployments, satellite constellation launches, and other large space missions, similar to SpaceX’s Falcon 9 rocket.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms.”
SpaceX’s rocket is so popular for shipping satellites to space that it’s started turning away customers past 2028. This has opened the door for Canada’s burgeoning space industry, including Reaction Dynamics. The company said it’s already signed 10 agreements and letters of intent with undisclosed prospective launch customers across Canada, the United States, and Europe.
“We see an opportunity to serve Canadian demand while providing additional dedicated launch capacity for customers in the United States, Europe, and allied countries,” Jesse Mikelberg, Reaction Dynamics’ director of business development and strategy, said in an email to BetaKit. “As a result, customers would have greater control over their launch schedule and destination orbit.”
To give those prospective customers a ride to space, Reaction Dynamics has set some big-time goals. First, the company wants to launch Aurora into orbit from Canadian soil by 2028. The company will then build on that base of manufacturing investments, equipment, processes, and expertise to get Borealis into space by 2031, Mikelberg explained.
“Aurora will give us flight experience and practical knowledge of manufacturing, transporting, integrating, and launching an orbital vehicle,” Mikelberg said. “It will also help us establish customer relationships, spaceport operations, and credibility through execution.”
While Mikelberg makes it sound simple, it is literally rocket science. This requires a lot of manpower and capital. Reaction Dynamics is planning for a large influx of both.
Over the next five years, the company aims to increase its headcount from 68 employees to 350. To accommodate all the new staff, Reaction Dynamics is also looking to increase its manufacturing and testing footprint from 60,000 square feet to 375,000 square feet. The company sees a “strong foundation” for this expansion in Québec, Mikelberg said, but it’s also eyeing land in Ontario or Nova Scotia.
RELATED: First Canada, then the world: nation’s rocket builders see a bigger opening in space
Expanding a business like this, let alone one that builds rockets, isn’t cheap. Reaction Dynamics is planning to raise around $350 million CAD in new private investment across two rounds over the next five years: a Series B targeting between $70 million and 100 million CAD to support Aurora’s first orbital launch in 2028, and then a Series C, or a similar funding instrument, targeting between $200 million and 250 million CAD to aid development for Borealis’ first launch in 2031.
This funding would come in addition to the $50 million Reaction Dynamics has already raised to date from private investors and non-dilutive government funding sources.
“Our approach is to broaden the investor base as we demonstrate propulsion performance, establish manufacturing capacity, secure customers, and gain flight experience,” Mikelberg said.
Founded in 2017, Reaction Dynamics has been building rocket propulsion systems since long before space became one of the “key sovereign capabilities” in the federal government’s Defence Industrial Strategy. Under the DIS, the 2025 federal budget committed $182.6 million over three years to the Department of National Defence (DND) to establish a sovereign space launch capability.
Reaction Dynamics benefitted from Canada’s renewed focus on space earlier this year when the company was awarded an $8.3 million grant under the first round of the DND’s Innovation for Defence Excellence and Security (IDEaS) Launch the North contest to build out its rocket launch capabilities. Reaction’s younger Canadian rocket-building peers, Canada Rocket Company and NordSpace, also received that funding.
The IDEaS funding was announced alongside the federal government signing a $200 million lease with Maritime Launch Services to establish a government spaceport in Nova Scotia. Reaction Dynamics has also invested in MLS, and its spaceport just outside Canso, NS, is the planned location for Aurora’s first orbital launch.
“We founded Reaction Dynamics because we believe Canada should be able to reach orbit on its own terms,” Reaction Dynamics founder and CEO Bachar Elzein said in a statement. “Aurora is how we get there in 2028. Borealis is how we build on that foundation to deliver medium lift by 2031. Nearly a decade of propulsion development and engineering, right here in Quebec, has brought us to this point.”
CLARIFICATION (10/20/2026): This story has been updated to note Jesse Mikelberg’s current title.
Feature image courtesy Reaction Dynamics.

articles.title: Final Fantasy dips back into the SNES golden era with Resonance
articles.text:
Final Fantasy is a lot different than it used to be. While many of the early Final Fantasy titles look and play similarly to each other, the series has since grown to encompass blockbuster games like Final Fantasy XVI and the gargantuan Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, which don’t play much like the classics. But there’s still an audience for retro RPGs and old-school Final Fantasy games, especially thanks to the HD-2D style that mixes gorgeous pixel art with detailed 3D graphics to great effect. Square Enix has made a bunch of HD-2D games already, like the remakes of early Dragon Quest titles, but this week, it’s launching the first HD-2D Final Fantasy game: Final Fantasy Resonance.
Final Fantasy dips back into the SNES golden era with Resonance
Square Enix’s latest HD-2D game carries the Final Fantasy name — and a lot of what makes the franchise great.
Resonance, thanks to the HD-2D art, kind of looks like what the classic Final Fantasy games feel like in my memory, but I was surprised at how old-school Resonance feels to actually play, too — which, for the most part, is a good thing. In Resonance, I’ve spent a lot of time wandering around a big world map to get from place to place, tackling random battles along the way and investigating little sparkles to pick up items. The towns have a familiar feel, with the classic inn, item shop, and weapons shop setup. Similarly, battles are traditional turn-based fights, so I’ve found myself spending a lot of time in various battle menus to plan out my attacks. Enemies even flash right before they attack, just like in older RPGs.
At times, Resonance can almost feel rudimentary; I’ve recently been working my way through Final Fantasy VII Remake again ahead of Revelation, and Remake’s action-heavy fights feel much more contemporary. But there’s something soothing about Resonance’s familiar patterns. I really like just grinding through some random baddies to level up.
The story is pretty standard fare, at least during the 10 hours I’ve played. You play as Rain, a plucky blonde hero who is morally pure and fights for those less fortunate than him. After a great magical crystal is destroyed, you and your best bud Lasswell head out on an adventure to stop the destruction of other crystals. So far, Resonance’s story hasn’t done a lot to innovate on a familiar formula — I’ve already come across two people who have amnesia, a JRPG staple — but it all moves along breezily enough that it’s not a huge deal.
Resonance isn’t all old-school, though, as there are a lot of modern touches. In fights, enemies have health bars and stagger bars, forcing you to be strategic instead of just mashing basic attacks; it’s usually smarter to whittle down a stagger bar by exploiting weaknesses through magic and skills. You can speed up fights and even skip long attack animations (of which there are many). On the world map, you can fast travel to any location you’ve already visited, which is especially useful during the multipart side quests. In dungeons, you can teleport from a save near a boss fight back to the entrance if you need to resupply before a big battle.
Resonance also lets you bring in characters from other Final Fantasy games to aid you in battle. (It’s a holdover from Resonance’s roots as a mobile title; the game is an “adaptation” of the first story arc of Final Fantasy Brave Exvius, which was shut down in 2024.) As you move through Resonance, you’ll recruit “Visions” of characters like Final Fantasy VI’s Terra Branford or Final Fantasy VII’s Cloud Strife, and each of the game’s characters can “equip” one Vision to give them new moves in battle. Over time, while using a Vision with a Resonance character, you unlock more moves and abilities that you can use even when you don’t have that Vision equipped. It’s a clever system that offers a lot of possibilities for interesting builds, making the hunt for more Visions feel like more than just a way to get a hit of nostalgia.
But I’m already getting sucked into Resonance like I used to with classic Final Fantasy titles. At one point, as I was nodding my head to heart-pumping music during an intense boss fight on a moving train, I realized I was completely absorbed by the game in a way that only a Final Fantasy can pull off. The game’s old-school structure with modern improvements lets Square Enix have it both ways, as the old-school approach sits comfortably alongside a big-budget game like Final Fantasy XVI. The series has come a long way since the games that Resonance uses as inspiration, but it pulls in enough from newer titles that playing it feels like enjoying the best of both worlds.
Final Fantasy Resonance launches on October 22nd on Nintendo Switch, Nintendo Switch 2, PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X / S.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Oxford. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal References:

- Anton T. Than, Saurabh V. Kadam, Vinay Vikramaditya, Nhung H. Nguyen, Xingxin Liu, Zohreh Davoudi, Alaina M. Green, Norbert M. Linke. Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer. Nature Physics, 2026; DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03402-4

articles.title: How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
articles.text:
How 3 Java Champions are using GitHub Copilot for increased productivity
Three Java Champions share how they use GitHub Copilot to solve problems, accelerate development, and keep humans responsible for the results.
AI coding tools can generate code quickly, but speed alone does not solve the hardest software engineering problems. Developers still need to provide context, validate results, protect maintainability, and remain accountable for what ships.
To learn how experienced developers strike that balance, we spoke with three Java Champions, all with over a decade of experience in using Java. They shared concrete examples of using GitHub Copilot in production and open source, along with the practices they use to turn AI-generated output into reliable software.
Here are the tips they shared with us.
Vlad Mihalcea
GitHub profile: @vladmihalcea
How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?
I’ve been using it to analyze, design, and implement various features in both Hypersistence Utils and Hypersistence Optimizer.
For example, I’ve been wanting for a long time to develop a web application that provides Optimizer event history so we can see how performance improvement efforts are materializing in application performance. Before AI, I kept postponing this task because it would have taken me weeks to develop. But using Copilot is like having a new team member, so I used it to create an app that will ship in the next version of Hypersistence Optimizer. Instead of weeks, this task took just two days to implement.
What’s your typical usage? Are you using GitHub Copilot as an IDE plugin or the GitHub Copilot app?
I use GitHub Copilot in IntelliJ IDEA because it’s convenient to run while reviewing source code or during a debug session.
It’s very useful as a code assistant, and it helps me speed up both investigations and building prototypes for features that need validation.
I still review the plans and the code that is generated by AI since their goal is to improve my productivity, not replace me entirely. While AI provides the right answer in many situations, there are still times when the response is not satisfactory and requires my intervention.
Can you share some tips and best practices? For example, which skills are you using?
I created my own skills so that whatever text Copilot generates looks like something I wrote by hand.
This skill captures my voice from 65 of my published articles, so a draft comes back sounding like my blog instead of like a language model. This is really useful when generating documentation for this project, since it lets the LLM learn from 12 years of blogging and provide examples that follow the same principles, such as expressiveness, testability, and simplicity.
Throughout my career as a software engineer, I’ve learned that we spend far more time on code maintenance than on creating it. Therefore, because maintenance and stability are critical for existing products, I developed skills that help AI mimic existing code practices in accordance with the principle of least astonishment.
One tip is to change the model type based on the type of operation. For thorough thinking, I use Opus with the 1 million context window and Extra High or Max reasoning. However, for simpler tasks, such as generating reports, release notes, or verifying documentation, I use lighter models that consume fewer tokens.
Patrick Baumgartner
GitHub profile: @patbaumgartner
Your work involves coaching teams. What is your approach?
A lot of my work happens while the normal business still has to keep running. You cannot stop everything for six months to “transform.” We usually start by solving immediate problems together, understand where the team currently stands, define where we want to go and how we will know that we are improving, and then move there step by step.
Depending on the situation, that can mean Software Craft practices such as TDD, refactoring, continuous delivery and XP; architecture and modularisation with Spring Boot, Spring Modulith; Spring Security; optimising Java and Spring Boot applications for containers; or increasingly, agentic engineering.
The important part for me is that I work with the team. We make decisions together. I don’t want a team to become dependent on me. Ideally, after some time they no longer need me except perhaps as a sparring partner.
And maybe that explains why I find this new generation of AI tools so interesting: I like working with people, learning, experimenting, and solving problems. AI gives us another very powerful tool for doing exactly that.
Can you share a good story about how GitHub Copilot has helped you recently?
There are actually three very different examples that changed how I think about working with GitHub Copilot.
Let’s start with the first one.
One was a migration of around 900 teaching slides across 15 presentations from Reveal.js to Marp. These were not simple slides. Many contain code, animations, and even interactive examples where I can change JavaScript live while teaching. More importantly, the presentations had already been battle-tested with students. The flow worked. Losing one small piece could break the story I use in the classroom.
Doing that migration manually would probably have taken me a week or more—and realistically, I might simply have avoided doing it because it was such tedious work.
With Copilot, I approached it differently. We first analysed the existing material, defined the target, created a migration plan, established constraints, provided examples, and defined what had to remain intact. Then we worked from the big structural changes down into the details.
The really important part was verification.
We generated screenshots of the Reveal.js and Marp versions and compared them visually and algorithmically. We built a small application where I could run both slide decks next to each other to verify animations manually. We even compared the generated PDFs.
That meant the agent did not just say, “Migration complete.” We had evidence.
The entire migration took me roughly eight to ten hours. I still owned the content, the teaching intent, and every meaningful change. Copilot could fix a typo automatically, but if content, versions, dates or meaning changed, that was something we discussed.
For me, that experience reinforced an important principle: delegate execution, not responsibility. I own the result.
Can you share the second example?
A second example came from building a terminal UI application with Tamboui. It initially worked perfectly in Linux under WSL, and I had completely forgotten that somebody might run it directly in Windows CMD or PowerShell.
And then a real user did.
They discovered that the Enter key was simply ignored in some forms. That is another principle I strongly believe in: ship software early, because you learn from how people actually use it.
We used Copilot to turn that feedback into reproducible UI tests. On Linux, Copilot was navigating the application with tmux. Through working with it, I learned about psmux and could execute similar flows in PowerShell. We reproduced the problem, created a local fix, traced the real problem into Tamboui, and I submitted the upstream fix, which was merged.
During this work, the test descriptions themselves became too large for the available context. So I asked Copilot to help me redesign the way the tests were represented. Instead of verbose tables containing identifiers, names and repeated descriptions, it proposed a much more compact arrow notation: step → step → input, with additional information only where it was critical.
That surprised me. We were not just using AI to execute information; we were working together on how information should be represented for execution. It did not have to be maximally human-friendly. It had to preserve the semantics while being efficient for the agent.
How about the third example?
The third example is completely different again.
Someone close to me needed to practise mathematics, and I thought: why don’t we build a small learning app?
It covers addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and division with remainder for grades one through four. But I did not want to build another simple quiz application. Together with Copilot, I researched learning approaches such as spaced repetition, immediate feedback, adaptive difficulty, motivation, cooperative learning and gamification without dark patterns.
Interestingly, during that research Copilot challenged one of my original assumptions. I initially wanted the application to be generic for children everywhere. The research led us toward looking at the actual school curriculum instead. I realised that the order in which topics are introduced, the operations and number ranges differ enough that making it “universal” immediately was unnecessary.
So we focused on Switzerland first and aligned the progression accordingly. Because Switzerland is multilingual, the application is available in German, French, Italian and English.
It also has cooperative and competitive two-player modes, and when someone gets an answer wrong, the application explains one way to solve it and brings similar questions back through spaced repetition.
I deliberately chose an architecture without a backend. There is no reason for me to collect children’s personal data on a server, so the data stays on the device and the application can simply be hosted on GitHub Pages.
What started as a small experiment is now being used and shared among friends. It accidentally became a little product.
That experience showed me another side of Copilot: don’t only use it to implement your solution. Use it as a sparring partner to expand and challenge the solution space before you start building.
How do you typically use Copilot?
I actually don’t use the classic Copilot autocomplete experience anymore.
My work has moved almost completely toward agentic workflows.
I use VS Code when I need a tight visual feedback loop—when I want to look closely at documents, code, presentations or intermediate results and adapt the process as I go.
For larger execution-oriented tasks, I often work with the coding agent from the terminal. There I am more comfortable delegating a piece of work, letting it execute, and then inspecting the complete result. The interface I choose depends mostly on the feedback loop I need.
I also had a fascinating experience using the coding-agent workflow through GitHub while travelling to JavaLand. I had started exploring an idea for a Maven plugin that optimises which Spring Boot auto-configurations are loaded. During roughly a four-hour journey, I was steering the agent from my phone: giving it a task, reviewing what it had done, thinking about the next step, and sending the next instruction.
By the time I arrived, I had a working Maven plugin, a CI pipeline, performance tests against a sample application, and reports that could demonstrate whether the optimisation actually worked.
That was the first time I had worked that way, and I was amazed that it actually worked. I wasn’t trying to write Java on my phone. I was reviewing, deciding and steering while the agent executed.
I also use MCP servers when they give me useful capabilities or context. For example, I have used Context7 for documentation, integrations with my Logseq knowledge base, and I have experimented with an MCP integration for Adobe Premiere Pro.
But I don’t use MCP just because I can. If a good CLI exists, I often prefer the CLI because it feels more direct and faster to me.
The agent is also not a “junior developer” in my mental model. I think of it much more as a sparring partner. But just like anyone joining a project, it first needs to be brought up to speed.
Context is king.
Can you share some tips and best practices?
The biggest thing I would recommend is: stop one-shot prompting.
For anything non-trivial, I want to understand the problem before execution starts. Quite often I explicitly ask the agent to interview me first. The purpose of that interview is to uncover assumptions and expectations that are still implicit.
A good agent can execute the wrong idea incredibly quickly. That does not make the detour cheaper.
I experienced this myself while working on my Spring Boot auto-configuration optimiser. Initially I wanted to support both Spring Boot 3.5 and 4.x. There were architectural differences, so we implemented both approaches. Later I realised I no longer needed the 3.5 path and removing it was painful.
The lesson was simple: detours are expensive. Get the requirements right before you accelerate.
Once the intent is clear, I want a plan. When I review that plan, four things matter especially to me: are assumptions visible, are verification gates defined, does the approach fit the architecture, and does it avoid unnecessary work?
The second principle is to define task-specific verification gates.
“Done” should not mean that the model says it is done.
For a refactoring, the gates might include passing tests, proving that all intended files were handled, updating documentation and leaving no TODOs behind. For the slide migration, the gates included screenshots, visual diffs, animations, PDF output and content completeness.
The gates depend on the task. The principle does not: the agent should be able to provide evidence that the work satisfies the definition of done.
I recently came across a skill called unlazy that follows a similar idea: create explicit gates, work through them deliberately, and prove that they have been completed rather than taking shortcuts.
The third principle is to turn your lessons into reusable skills.
I have started writing and maintaining my own Agent Skills. When I learn something from an execution—perhaps the agent misunderstood a convention, a useful check was missing, or I found a better way to approach a task—I update the skill.
The next time I perform that task, the lesson is already there.
One example is a skill I call maintainer-audit, inspired by work in the open agent skills community. I use it across my own repositories. It checks and, where appropriate, fixes the things I expect a maintained project to have: repository documentation, CI pipelines, Dependabot configuration, CodeQL, consistent cleanup and other project standards.
The goal is not to generate another audit report for me to read. It brings the repository back toward the baseline I want automatically. That makes my projects more consistent and easier to maintain.
I think of these skills as living engineering knowledge rather than static prompts.
The fourth principle is to put deterministic engineering tools around the probabilistic model.
I have my own quality harness that wraps tools such as Checkstyle, PMD and Spring Modulith architecture checks and produces a consolidated report that the agent can consume. I can run that from hooks and let the agent iterate:
change → execute checks → read findings → fix → execute again.
It continues until there are no findings left.
That does not mean I stop looking at the software. I still run the application, interact with it and decide whether it behaves and looks the way I expect. Sometimes I deliberately implement feature by feature because the feedback loop is much tighter.
I learned that asking for everything at once because “the AI can do it” is usually a bad idea. Large, generic specifications create large, generic implementations—and cleaning them up afterwards can be harder than building smaller increments correctly.
More broadly, I think we developers need to talk much more about how we use these tools. Share the experiments that worked. Share the ones that didn’t. Borrow ideas from each other and adapt them to your own context instead of looking for one universal AI development process.
That is also why I like the idea of AI as a sparring partner. On a Friday night, when I want to experiment with something and no human pair is available, I suddenly have somebody—or something—I can challenge an idea with, review an approach with, or use as a very sophisticated rubber duck.
But I still take those ideas back to real people. Human feedback, product understanding and real-world context remain essential.
How do you think AI is changing our profession?
I don’t think software engineering students should primarily aspire to become code-producing machines. They need to become strong problem solvers. They need to understand users and stakeholders, discover the real problem behind a requirement, challenge assumptions, understand products and markets, make architectural trade-offs, think critically, work in a structured way and transfer useful solutions from one context into another.
The model is extraordinarily good at generating possibilities and executing things. But as a human, I usually know much more of the actual context—including the things nobody ever documented.
So I want to remain in charge of shaping the solution and let the agent take over more of the execution.
In that sense, I think AI is putting the engineering back into software engineering.
And I like that.
Frank Delporte
GitHub profile: @FDelporte
How did you get started in tech?
I’ve been fascinated by computers since I got a Commodore 64 when I was 11. Took some side steps into video production and television work after school but turned back into coding as that video needed to be put on DVD and the very first websites… Yes, I’m that old ;-).
How has GitHub Copilot helped you recently?
It’s a perfect companion to evaluate pull requests and investigate bug reports.
One remarkable story is about the Pi4J library that lets you build Java applications to interact with electronic components on the Raspberry Pi. In February 2026, we released V4 which has a new plugin using the Foreign Function & Memory API. We tested it thoroughly before releasing, but still, shortly after the release someone reported that using 5 input buttons doesn’t work as expected. Pushing one of the first four configured buttons triggers a code execution as expected, while nothing happens with the fifth button.
This is the kind of report you don’t want to get. Nothing was visibly broken. No exception, no warning in the logs, the fifth button was simply silent. And it got worse: with the older gpiod plugin, the exact same hardware and the exact same application, worked fine. So the problem was in our new FFM code, which sits on top of the Linux kernel’s GPIO character device and talks to it through native calls. That is not the part of the codebase where you expect to find a quick answer.
So I assigned the issue to the Copilot coding agent and gave it two file paths as a starting point, the provider class and FFMDigitalInput. About half an hour later there was a pull request, with an explanation I really did not expect.
Each input runs an event watcher that blocks in a native poll() call, waiting for the kernel to report a change on its GPIO line. Those watchers ran in virtual threads. And a virtual thread that blocks inside a native call cannot be unmounted from its carrier thread. It stays pinned there for the whole duration of the call. A Raspberry Pi 4 has four cores, so the virtual thread scheduler has four carrier threads. Register four inputs, and all four carriers are parked in poll() forever. The fifth watcher is created, but is never scheduled. That is exactly the bug that was reported. Not “events are flaky”, but “the fifth one does nothing.”
What I liked most was not the diff, it was the conversation that followed in the review. I left a comment asking Copilot to explain this in more detail:
I thought the goal of virtual threads was exactly to step away from the platform thread limit? So how is this a problem that four virtual threads block the four threads on a four-core processor like the Raspberry Pi?
Check the pull request for the full conversation. Copilot was able to link the use of the Raspberry Pi which has four CPU cores with the reported problem. It was able to propose a simple fix for the problem, plus some extra improvements it found during its investigation.
Can you share some tips and best practices?
- Tell it where to look: For the Pi4J issue #622, I added two file paths. That is a tiny bit of effort that removes a huge amount of searching in a large codebase. You usually have a hunch about the neighbourhood even when you have no idea about the bug. Give it to the tool so it doesn’t need to investigate the complete code.
- Ask for proof and tests: “Add a unit test to validate the change” is something I ask a lot these days. Well, asked, because it has now become a rule in my instructions file. It also prevents cases where the diagnosis was wrong, because the test won’t fail on the old code.
- Ask why: If you don’t understand a fix, say so and ask. The explanation is a deliverable too and should be added into your project documentation or inside the ticket or pull request. It teaches everyone who reads the info later. For example, this also triggered more questions within the Pi4J team about virtual thread pinning on native calls.
- Stay in control: All of these pull requests in Pi4J were reviewed and approved by maintainers before they went in. That’s the model that works best in this project: the agent does the investigation, the humans stay responsible for what ships. But also for my other projects I always do a review of the code that was generated by the tool. I always want to keep code readable and maintainable. Too often, a tool creates duplicate methods or recreates something which is already available in another place and should be combined. That’s your responsibility. You can go very fast these days with AI-assisted coding, which also means you can very fast create a mess. Don’t do that, keep your code manageable, your colleagues and future-self will thank you if they have to investigate bugs or make improvements later.

articles.title: « Une crise » : le nouveau patron d’Apple accorde sa première grande interview et évoque la pénurie de mémoire
articles.text:
John Ternus a accordé sa première grande interview au magazine américain TIME, qui le place en couverture de son numéro consacré aux inventions de l’année, en kiosque le 26 octobre. Le successeur de Tim Cook, en poste depuis le 1er septembre, y revient sur ses débuts éclairs, lui qui a dévoilé l’iPhone Duo huit jours seulement après sa prise de fonction. Interrogé sur la flambée des prix de la mémoire, il répond sans détour : « les contraintes qui pèsent sur la mémoire sont absolument une crise ».
Une crise assumée jusque devant Washington
La phrase répond à la lettre d’un groupe bipartisan de sénateurs, opposés au test de puces mémoire issues d’un fournisseur chinois, une piste explorée pour élargir un approvisionnement devenu critique. Ternus ne cède rien : « notre conviction profonde est que toutes les options doivent être sur la table ».
Le fournisseur en question serait CXMT, le champion chinois de la DRAM, dont des échantillons seraient déjà en cours d’évaluation à Cupertino. Le secrétaire américain au Commerce s’était pourtant opposé publiquement, dès le mois d’août, à l’idée de voir de la mémoire chinoise équiper les produits des grands groupes du pays. La mémoire pèse environ 10 % du coût des composants d’un iPhone, et les calculs de la banque JPMorgan la voient grimper jusqu’à 45 % d’ici 2027. Les prix de la RAM avaient déjà quadruplé au printemps, avant même les records battus cet été.
L’iPhone ne fait plus exception
Fin juin, Apple relevait de plusieurs dizaines à plusieurs centaines d’euros les tarifs des Mac, des iPad et de nombreux accessoires, en épargnant soigneusement l’iPhone. La digue a tenu trois mois. Les iPhone 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max présentés en septembre coûtent chacun 150 euros de plus que leurs prédécesseurs, à 1 479 et 1 629 euros. Les iPhone 17 restés au catalogue ont subi la même hausse, et l’iPhone Duo s’affiche à 2 339 euros.
Le keynote de rentrée a surtout confirmé une absence : aucun iPhone 18 classique n’accompagnait les modèles Pro et le pliable, une première pour la gamme. Le modèle qui porte traditionnellement les volumes de la marque n’arriverait qu’au printemps 2027, accompagné d’un iPhone 18e et d’un nouvel iPhone Air. La pénurie de mémoire est citée parmi les causes de ce décalage, Apple préférant réserver ses stocks de composants aux appareils les plus rentables.
Repousser le modèle le plus vendu, c’est aussi retarder le moment de fixer son prix en pleine tempête. Une hausse de 150 euros passe sur un téléphone à plus de 1 400 euros, beaucoup moins sur celui qui sert de porte d’entrée à l’écosystème.Tim Cook, devenu président exécutif du conseil d’administration, assure de son côté qu’il ne « se mêle pas » de la gestion quotidienne. Cette crise sera donc le premier vrai test de son successeur. Réponse au printemps, lorsque l’on saura si les iPhone grand public échappent encore à l’inflation qui a rattrapé tout le reste du catalogue.

articles.title: Vous n’arrivez pas à payer avec Revolut ? C’est normal, il y a une panne
articles.text:
Mise à jour de 12h27 : Revolut a confirmé la panne à Numerama.
La banque a commenté l’incident en ces termes : « Nous rencontrons actuellement une perturbation de nos services qui en affecte plusieurs. Nous pouvons confirmer que l’argent et les données de tous nos clients sont en sécurité. Nous travaillons à résoudre ce problème depuis qu’il a été identifié ce matin et nous présentons nos excuses aux personnes concernées, ainsi que pour tout désagrément occasionné. »
L’origine viendrait d’une panne d’un prestataire tiers, en l’occurrence Google Cloud. D’autres banques, moins connues en France, sont aussi affectées.
Article original :
Vous n’arrivez pas à payer avec votre carte Revolut, à ouvrir l’application ou à faire un virement ? Vous n’êtes pas seuls : Revolut subit ce mardi 20 octobre 2026 une panne qui touche ses clients dans plusieurs pays, dont la France. Un incident inhabituel pour la banque mobile, peu coutumière des pannes de cette ampleur.
Sur sa page « état du système », Revolut indique que ses 31 services monitorés sont en panne.
Revolut en panne : qu’est-ce qui ne fonctionne plus ?
Les premiers signalements remontent à 8 heures environ (heure de Paris). Sur Downdetector et les sites de suivi de pannes, plusieurs centaines d’utilisateurs se plaignent : paiements par carte refusés en magasin, connexion impossible à l’application, virements bloqués, Apple Pay inutilisable.
Revolut a confirmé la panne sur X : « Nous rencontrons actuellement une interruption de service qui touche plusieurs services. Nous pouvons confirmer que l’argent et les données de tous nos clients sont en sécurité. Nous travaillons à résoudre le problème depuis son identification ce matin et présentons nos excuses à toutes les personnes concernées pour la gêne occasionnée. » L’entreprise ne précise pour l’instant pas l’origine de la panne.
Selon les propres constats de Numerama, les problèmes varient d’un compte à un autre. Certains de nos journalistes arrivent à se connecter, d’autres pas. Les perturbations semblent néanmoins importantes : on vous souhaite de ne pas avoir de paiement important à effectuer.
Le service client également en panne
À 11h50, soit quatre heures après le début de la panne, Revolut était toujours inaccessible. Des utilisateurs indiquent que le service client est également en panne et pointent l’absence de préparation de Revolut : le SAV ne devrait pas être sur les mêmes serveurs que l’application en cas de panne. D’autres banques seraient également touchées, au moins partiellement, ce qui suggère une panne indépendante de Revolut.
Dans certains cas, des paiements sous un certain seuil passeraient sans actualisation de l’application. Le risque pour Revolut serait de créer un découvert non-autorisé, si ses serveurs n’ont pas accès aux paiements.

articles.title: Bloquer les réseaux sociaux pour enrayer les émeutes, Gabriel Attal n'en démord pas
articles.text:
Après les manifestations du 17 octobre, l'ancien Premier ministre et candidat à la présidentielle Gabriel Attal a proposé sur RTL de "bloquer temporairement et de manière ciblée" certaines plateformes. Mais c'est oublier la jurisprudence du Conseil d'État et le règlement européen sur les services numériques.
Le candidat de Renaissance à la présidentielle reproche aux réseaux sociaux de rassembler les casseurs et d'entretenir un effet de meute. Rappelons qu'il avait déjà fait couper TikTok en Nouvelle-Calédonie quand il était Premier ministre.
Le Conseil d'État a fait jurisprudence
Sur RTL, Gabriel Attal parle d’un blocage limité aux territoires sur lesquels se déroulent des émeutes. Selon lui, des lycéens qui ne participaient pas aux saccages se laissent entraîner par ceux qui donnent l’impression d’agir en toute impunité.
Et ce n'est pas la première fois que l'idée lui traverses la tête. Souvenez-vous, en mai 2024, nous rapportions que TikTok restait bloqué en Nouvelle-Calédonie malgré les référés-libertés déposés par plusieurs associations, dont La Quadrature du Net. Le gouvernement s’appuyait sur un cadre de circonstances exceptionnelles, laquelle permet à l’exécutif de s’écarter du droit commun en cas de crise, plutôt que sur l’état d’urgence.
Mais le 1er avril 2025, le Conseil d’État a annulé la décision du 14 mai 2024. Le réseau avait été coupé du 15 au 29 mai. Le juge a pourtant reconnu que les émeutes justifiaient une interruption, et que TikTok avait servi à diffuser des appels à la violence, amplifiés par ses algorithmes. Le Conseil a cependant sanctionné la mise en oeuvre du gouvernement avant de poser trois conditions, et elles doivent toutes être réunies.
D’abord, la situation doit être grave. Une coupure n’est possible que face à des événements d’une gravité particulière, comme les émeutes meurtrières de Nouvelle-Calédonie, et seulement si elle est indispensable. Ensuite, elle doit rester un dernier recours. Si une solution technique permet d’agir tout de suite avec moins de conséquences pour les libertés, par exemple en bloquant une fonctionnalité précise du réseau plutôt que le réseau entier, c’est cette solution qu’il faut choisir. Enfin, la coupure doit être temporaire. Elle ne doit durer que le temps de trouver et de mettre en place ces solutions moins radicales.
Mais rappelons aussi que l'Etat francais n'avait pas uniquement envisagé un blocage des réseaux socaux mais bien de prendre des mesures plus fermes que l'on retrouve appliquées en Iran, en Afghanistan, en Russie, en Inde ou au Pakistan. Au cours d’une audition à l’Assemblée nationale, le ministre de l’Intérieur de l'époque Gérald Darmanin avait avoué avoir envisagé « de baisser de 5G à 2G l’intégralité des réseaux sociaux ». Autrement dit de couper tout l’internet mobile sur l’archipel afin de limiter les communications et donc les rassemblements potentiellement perturbateurs.
Une décision de la Commission européenne, uniquement
Comme le souligne aussi BFM, la plupart des réseaux sociaux présents en France sont positionnés dans la catégorie des très grandes plateformes et doivent donc respecter le règlement européen sur les services numériques (DSA). Dans ce cadre, la France ne dispose d’aucun pouvoir de blocage préventif, même discrétionnaire.
Le DSA prévoit bien une réponse aux crises, à son article 36. La Commission européenne peut l’activer, sur recommandation du Comité européen des services numériques, lorsque des circonstances extraordinaires entraînent une menace grave pour la sécurité publique ou la santé publique dans l’Union.
Elle impose alors aux très grandes plateformes concernées d’évaluer si leur service contribue à cette menace, puis d’appliquer des mesures spécifiques, efficaces et proportionnées, pour trois mois au maximum, avec une prolongation possible de trois mois. Il peut s’agir de désactiver temporairement les fonctions de recommandation ou de modérer de façon ciblée certaines tendance (hashtags). C’est la plateforme qui choisit ses mesures, et l’article ne prévoit aucune coupure d’accès.
Rappelons d'ailleurs que le DSA est aussi au centre d’un désaccord sur les pouvoirs de l’Arcom. En juillet, nous rapportions que Bruxelles rejettait proposition de loi sur l’interdiction des réseaux sociaux aux moins de 15 ans.

articles.title: Trotz Milliardenschulden und Aktienabsturz: Warum Coreweave noch nicht vor dem Aus steht
articles.text:
Coreweave hat Milliardenschulden: Wie sich das auf die KI-Branche auswirken könnte
Coreweave stellt eine KI-Cloud-Plattform sowie Computing-Leistung in Rechenzentren für seine Kund:innen bereit. Dazu zählen unter anderem Microsoft und OpenAI. Seit März 2025 ist das Unternehmen auch am Aktienmarkt gelistet und konnte dort innerhalb von wenigen Monaten den Einstiegspreis von 40 US-Dollar pro Aktie auf mehr als 180 Dollar hochtreiben. Doch seither geht es für Coreweave stetig bergab.
Coreweave: Warum Investor:innen Bedenken haben
Zuletzt hatte die Coreweave-Aktie am 2. Oktober 2026 einen Stand von knapp 91 Dollar. Innerhalb von wenigen Wochen ist der Preis pro Aktie auf 65 Dollar abgestürzt. In den vergangenen sechs Monaten ist die Aktie um knapp 50 Prozent ihres Wertes gefallen. Und das hat einen einfachen Grund. Die Investor:innen von Coreweave haben Bedenken, ob sie ihr Geld überhaupt noch wiedersehen werden.
Das liegt an den enormen Schulden, die Coreweave in den vergangenen Monaten und Jahren auf sich genommen hat, um Rechenzentren weiter auszubauen und KI-Cloud-Computing voranzutreiben. Mittlerweile soll das Unternehmen auf einem Schuldenberg von mehr als 46 Milliarden US-Dollar sitzen, wie Wallstreet Online berichtet. In den vergangenen zwölf Monaten konnte Coreweave zudem keinen Gewinn einfahren. Der Verlust des Unternehmens beläuft sich auf knapp zwei Milliarden Dollar.
Sollte sich dieser Trend fortsetzen und Coreweave eines Tages vor dem Aus stehen, würden auch zahlreiche Kunden, darunter große KI-Riesen der Branche, die Auswirkungen fehlender Computing-Power zu spüren bekommen. Dennoch gibt es selbst unter denjenigen, die das Platzen der KI-Blase genau so vorausgesagt haben, Zweifel, ob das Ende schon vor der Tür steht.
Denn wie The Verge berichtet, kann sich Coreweave noch an einer Hoffnung festhalten. Es gibt immer noch ausstehende, vertragliche Verpflichtungen von diversen Partnerunternehmen, darunter wie erwähnt Microsoft und OpenAI. Insgesamt beläuft sich dieser Betrag auf 103 Milliarden Dollar, wobei 40 Prozent des Betrags bis 2028 an Coreweave gezahlt werden müssen. Das Computing-Unternehmen kann sich also noch zeitweise über Wasser halten und wäre sogar in der Lage, die Schulden mittelfristig zurückzuzahlen. Das ist allerdings auch nur möglich, wenn in der Zwischenzeit nicht noch beträchtlich mehr Schulden dazukommen.

articles.title: Spain-Based Startups Advance Regional Innovation With Barcelona Supercomputing Center
articles.text:
The Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC)’s AI Factory Accelerator Programme, now in full operation following a pilot initiative, gives startups access to sovereign compute, technical support and training to support innovation across industries.
Many of these companies are also members of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups — and as of today, access to some of the BSC AI Factory services are available through the NVIDIA Inception portal.
NVIDIA Inception complements the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme by providing members with training through NVIDIA Deep Learning Institute open courses, business mentoring, venture capital connections and other resources.
An upcoming extension of MareNostrum 5 — BSC’s public infrastructure serving scientific and technological innovation, powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing — will deliver supercomputing access through the BSC AI Factory and other AI Factories across Europe. BSC AI Factory is among Europe’s first AI factories and the first in Spain, and has delivered more than 800 services to private and public-sector clients since its April 2025 launch.
Three Inception members were recently named the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme’s AI Champions at the pilot initiative’s demo day:
Qatium’s water-network platform — already used by more than 250 utilities in 16 countries — is now in early production with its Neural Water Intelligence technology, powered by proprietary AI models trained on MareNostrum 5. Built on NVIDIA accelerated computing, the NVIDIA cuGraph library, the NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework and NVIDIA Nemotron open models, the technology helps water utilities make better operational decisions every day.
OneCareAI, a research spin-off from BSC, used NVIDIA NIM microservices to develop technology designed to identify signs of hidden atrial fibrillation — an irregular heart rhythm — in seemingly normal ECGs, helping clinicians identify patients who may be at risk of stroke before one occurs.
Avatia built a voice-first, multi-agent system that provides pharmaceutical companies with agentic coworkers that support sales representatives and give doctors transparent, curated information about medicines, ultimately helping the right treatment reach the right patient sooner. The system taps into NVIDIA NIM microservices, the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 open model family and the open source NVIDIA NeMo Curator library.
Other BSC AI Factory startups — Agrikola AI, Elna Health, Lokutor, Montevive AI, Oppy, Pack2Earth and Up2Smart — span precision agriculture, medical imaging and knowledge access, speech services, enterprise security, sales intelligence and sustainable packaging.
The cohort reflects the breadth of what advanced intelligence can now unlock: preventing strokes, detecting breast cancer subtypes before biopsy, putting medical knowledge at doctors’ fingertips faster, replacing petroleum-based plastic with biobased compostable materials, protecting crops with robots instead of chemicals and more.
Learn more about NVIDIA Inception and the BSC AI Factory Accelerator Programme.

articles.title: Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (256 GB) alcança menor preço em meses com cupom • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (256 GB) alcança menor preço em meses com cupom
Galaxy Tab S10 Lite com tela LCD, S Pen e chip intermediário fica mais barato ao combinar cupom e pagamento via Pix no Mercado Livre
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (256 GB) está disponível por R$ 2.199,12 no Pix com o cupom OFFSOHJ no Mercado Livre. O tablet intermediário da Samsung com tela de 10,9 polegadas e bateria de até 16 horas, lançado por R$ 3.199, recebe um desconto de 31% e atinge o menor preço desde agosto.
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite traz uma tela LCD de 10,9 polegadas com resolução Full HD+ e taxa de atualização de 90 Hz. O painel com ampla área de trabalho é recomendado para estudos e consumo de mídia, oferecendo mais conforto visual para os usuários.
Apesar da configuração inferior ao S10 e S10 FE, o dispositivo com o chip Samsung Exynos 1380 e 8 GB GB de RAM entrega um desempenho equilibrado para tarefas leves e o uso dos recursos do Galaxy AI. Os 256 GB de armazenamento interno trazem um espaço satisfatório, mas a memória pode chegar até 2 TB utilizando cartões microSD.
Seguindo os padrões dos tablets Samsung, o Galaxy Tab S10 Lite traz a caneta S Pen como parte do kit inicial. Além de facilitar a digitalização de anotações e desenhos à mão, ele permite usar recursos de IA (Apagador de Objetos) e de pesquisa (Circule para pesquisar) para agilizar o dia a dia.
O Galaxy Tab S10 Lite oferece suporte ao Samsung Dex, função que transforma o tablet em um desktop ao ser conectado a um monitor. Ele ainda traz uma câmera frontal de 5 MP para videochamadas em Full HD e uma câmera traseira de 8 MP para fotografar documentos e outros cliques mais simples.
A bateria de 8.000 mAh garante uma autonomia de até 16 horas de reprodução de vídeo, variando conforme o uso das conexões sem fio Wi-Fi 6 e Bluetooth 5.3. Em relação ao software, ele vem de fábrica com o Android 15 e receberá atualizações do sistema operacional até 2032.
Pensando para o transporte em bolsas e mochilas, o Galaxy Tab S10 Lite (R$ 2.199,12 no Pix com cupom OFFSOHJ) é fabricado com corpo em Armor Alumínio com 6,6 mm de espessura e pesa 524 gramas. Por fim, o certificado IP42 de resistência à poeira e à água protege o aparelho de respingos de água.

articles.title: Une prime de 500 € arrive pour installer une borne à domicile, mais presque personne n'y aura droit — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est le genre d’annonce qui fait du bien aux automobilistes, surtout à leur portefeuille. Dans la deuxième phase de son plan d’électrification, présentée le jeudi 15 octobre au Mondial de l’Auto par Maud Bregeon, ministre déléguée chargée de l’Énergie, le gouvernement fait encore un pas vers les acheteurs de voitures électriques : à compter du 1er janvier 2027, une nouvelle aide de 500 euros doit alléger la facture pour l’installation d’une borne de recharge à la maison.
Comme pour les primes CEE, la facture reviendra aux fournisseurs d’énergie : l’aide sera intégrée au dispositif des certificats d’économies d’énergie pour les véhicules électriques. Le montant est un forfait de 500 euros : aucun taux de prise en charge du devis n’a été annoncé.
Des conditions très strictes
Ce montant reprend le plafond de l’ancien crédit d’impôt pour l’installation d’une borne, qui remboursait 75 % de l’achat et de la pose dans la limite de 500 euros, en maison comme en copropriété. Ce crédit d’impôt a disparu le 1er janvier 2026.
Pour ceux qui n’avaient pas équipé leur garage à temps, c’est une seconde chance. Le gouvernement l’assortit toutefois de trois conditions cumulatives, qui écartent une bonne partie des automobilistes. Leur détail (définition technique de la borne, date de signature du devis prise en compte) sera fixé par la fiche CEE, le texte qui encadre chaque prime, pas encore publiée.
La première condition porte sur la voiture. Pour toucher la prime, il faudra impérativement acheter un véhicule électrique d’occasion. Si vous achetez du neuf, la prime vous passera sous le nez. De même, les automobilistes déjà propriétaires d’une voiture électrique qui souhaitent enfin équiper leur garage sont purement et simplement écartés du système.
Pour les acheteurs d’occasion, cette aide s’ajoute à un dispositif qui existe déjà. Depuis quelques semaines et jusqu’au 31 décembre 2026, l’achat d’une voiture électrique d’occasion ouvre droit à une petite prime CEE d’environ 330 euros. Selon le Journal de l’Automobile, la prime borne de 500 euros prendrait la suite de ce dispositif, dont la fin est programmée au 31 décembre.
Le gouvernement mise peut-être sur le fait que les acheteurs d’un véhicule neuf peuvent négocier la borne avec le vendeur. Surtout, ils touchent déjà le coup de pouce CEE à l’achat : jusqu’à 5 700 euros pour les ménages les plus modestes, auxquels s’ajoutent 1 200 à 2 000 euros si la batterie est fabriquée en Europe, soit jusqu’à 7 700 euros selon les montants indicatifs du ministère de l’Économie.
L’obligation d’une borne « intelligente »
La deuxième condition concerne le matériel : une prise renforcée ou une borne classique ne suffira pas. Le gouvernement exige une borne pilotable, capable de recevoir un signal du compteur Linky, du fournisseur ou d’une application pour lancer automatiquement la charge pendant les heures creuses, quand l’électricité coûte le moins.
Ces bornes pilotables coûtent plus cher qu’un modèle basique, et ce surcoût grignote une partie de l’aide. En contrepartie, le gouvernement estime dans son dossier de presse qu’un conducteur type verra son budget annuel de recharge passer de 420 à 270 euros, soit environ 150 euros d’économie par an, sans préciser son kilométrage ni son contrat d’électricité. L’économie grimperait jusqu’à 300 euros par an avec la technologie bidirectionnelle (V2G), encore réservée à quelques modèles et contrats.
Ces économies supposent toutefois un contrat d’électricité dont le prix change selon l’heure, avec des heures creuses par exemple. Avec un tarif identique toute la journée, la borne n’a aucun créneau moins cher à viser. Une borne capable de piloter la recharge ne le fait pas non plus toujours d’office : il faut souvent activer la fonction.
Pour ceux qui comptent équiper leur maison dans les prochaines semaines, le calendrier est serré. Aucune aide nationale ne couvre aujourd’hui une borne posée en maison : le crédit d’impôt a pris fin au 31 décembre 2025, et Advenir exclut les pavillons. La fiche CEE, qui dira notamment si c’est la date de signature du devis qui compte, n’est pas encore parue. D’ici là, mieux vaut faire inscrire sur le devis la référence exacte de la borne et vérifier avec l’installateur qu’elle est bien pilotable.
Enfin, la troisième condition écarte les conducteurs qui vivent en appartement : l’aide est réservée aux maisons individuelles, ce qui exclut d’emblée l’habitat collectif et les copropriétés. Pour eux, le programme Advenir finance toujours 50 % du coût hors taxes d’un point de recharge individuel en immeuble collectif, dans la limite de 1 000 euros HT depuis le 1er avril 2026.
Bref, avec ces trois conditions cumulées (voiture d’occasion, maison individuelle, borne pilotable), la prime de 500 euros ne concernera qu’une poignée de foyers. Rappelons enfin qu’au delà de 3,7 kW, la pose d’une borne doit être confiée à un installateur qualifié IRVE, ce qui conditionne aussi la garantie. Pour une wallbox de 7,4 kW en maison, comptez en général entre 1 200 et 2 000 euros TTC, borne et pose comprises.

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
